starterCases.title: Childhood Absence Epilepsy - Typical Presentation
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief staring spells and unresponsiveness multiple times per day

history.eventDescription: Patient experiences brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, lasting 5-10 seconds, occurring multiple times daily. Events are abrupt in onset and offset.
history.lastEventTiming: Most recent event occurred earlier today

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges, frontally predominant

objectives: Run hyperventilation for at least 3 minutes with age-appropriate coaching
Describe generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave and its frontal maximum
Test and document responsiveness during an absence discharge

taskFlow.title: Planning hyperventilation
taskFlow.description: A 6-year-old is referred for staring spells of 5-10 seconds several times a day. A routine 10-20 recording with photic stimulation and hyperventilation (HV) is planned. The child is cooperative, and there is no history of sickle cell disease, asthma, moyamoya, or recent stroke.
taskFlow.question: Which approach to hyperventilation is most appropriate for this child?
options: Perform HV for 1 minute only, to limit the risk of provoking a seizure
Skip HV because a child under 10 usually cannot cooperate with it
Perform HV but stop it as soon as any rhythmic slowing builds up
Perform HV for at least 3 minutes, coaching with a pinwheel
taskFlow.explanation: HV for at least 3 minutes (with at least 1 minute of post-HV recording) is the standard, and HV is the most effective activator of typical absence discharges; a pinwheel or tissue makes it achievable for a 6-year-old. Skipping HV removes the best activator for this history. One minute is too short to give a fair activation. High-amplitude delta buildup is a normal HV response in children and is not, by itself, a reason to stop; stop for a clinical seizure or patient distress.

taskFlow.title: A discharge during HV
taskFlow.description: At 90 seconds of HV an abrupt, bilaterally synchronous burst of spike-and-wave at 3 per second appears, maximal at Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4 and Fz, and lasts 8 seconds. The child stops blowing and stares, then resumes blowing as soon as the burst ends. The background before and after is normal with a 9 Hz PDR.
taskFlow.question: How should you describe this discharge in your technical notes?
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave, frontally maximal, with HV arrest
Eye-blink artifact at 3 per second from the frontopolar electrodes
HV-induced buildup of high-amplitude rhythmic delta, normal at this age
Bifrontal rhythmic delta (FIRDA) from drowsiness during the HV period
taskFlow.explanation: A regular 3 per second spike-and-wave complex that starts and stops abruptly, is generalized with a frontal maximum, and stops behavior is the classic typical absence discharge. Normal HV buildup is rhythmic slowing without spikes and does not interrupt behavior. FIRDA has no spike component and is not linked to behavioral arrest. Blink artifact is confined to Fp1/Fp2 and lacks a spike-and-wave field over F3, F4 and Fz.

taskFlow.title: Testing responsiveness
taskFlow.description: Two more discharges occur. The ordering neurologist has asked whether awareness is impaired during the bursts. You are watching the live record and can speak to the child through the room microphone.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to test responsiveness during the next discharge?
options: Ask the child after the discharge whether anything felt unusual
Clap loudly near the child's ear once the discharge has ended
Say a test word during the burst and ask for recall afterward
Ask the parent to rate how alert the child appeared afterward
taskFlow.explanation: Responsiveness must be tested while the discharge is running: give a word, number, or simple command during the burst, then ask for recall or check the response, and annotate both. Asking about feelings afterward relies on subjective awareness, which the child usually lacks. A stimulus after the burst tests the interictal state, not the discharge. A parent's impression is not a structured test.

taskFlow.title: Technologist documentation
taskFlow.description: The study is complete: four discharges of 6-10 seconds, all during HV. The test word was given during two of them and was not recalled either time. Photic stimulation produced no photoparoxysmal response.
taskFlow.question: Which technologist note is most appropriate?
options: 4 SW bursts 6-10 s in HV; test word given in 2, not recalled
Findings consistent with childhood absence epilepsy; start ethosuximide
Several absence seizures seen; please call the family with results
Abnormal EEG showing generalized epilepsy; no more testing required
taskFlow.explanation: Technologist notes record observable facts: timing, duration, distribution, and the result of the responsiveness test. Naming a syndrome and recommending a drug is interpretation and treatment outside technologist scope. Calling the family with results is the physician's role. Declaring the EEG abnormal and closing further testing is an interpretive conclusion for the reader.

starterCases.title: Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome (IESS / West) with Hypsarrhythmia
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Clusters of flexor spasms on awakening and developmental regression

history.eventDescription: 5-month-old infant presents with clusters of flexor spasms occurring on awakening. Parents report developmental regression over the past month.

eegSummary.background: Chaotic, high-amplitude slow waves with multifocal spikes
eegSummary.epileptiform: Multifocal spikes and sharp waves in chaotic background

objectives: Plan video-EEG with EMG to capture spasms across sleep and arousal
Recognize hypsarrhythmia in NREM sleep
Identify the electrodecremental correlate of an epileptic spasm

taskFlow.title: Planning the infant study
taskFlow.description: A 5-month-old inpatient has clusters of flexor spasms shortly after waking, and the parents describe loss of skills over the last month. The order reads 'video-EEG to characterize spells.' The infant is currently awake and was fed 30 minutes ago.
taskFlow.question: Which recording plan gives the best yield for this infant?
options: Recording with hyperventilation using a pinwheel to trigger spasms
Awake-only 20-minute recording, avoiding sleep to reduce artifact
Video-EEG through sleep and into arousal, with deltoid EMG leads
Photic stimulation at 1-30 Hz while the infant is fully awake only
taskFlow.explanation: Hypsarrhythmia is often most evident in NREM sleep, and spasms cluster on arousal, so the plan must cover sleep and the waking transition; video plus bilateral deltoid EMG lets each spasm be timed and characterized. A short awake study can miss both the background abnormality and the clusters. HV is not possible at 5 months. Photic stimulation is not the key activation for spasms.

taskFlow.title: Background in NREM sleep
taskFlow.description: In NREM sleep the background consists of very high-amplitude (often above 200 uV), disorganized delta with frequent spikes that shift location from channel to channel. There is no consistent symmetry, and normal sleep features such as spindles are hard to identify.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits this background?
options: Burst-suppression with periods of flat background between bursts
Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic, high-voltage slowing with multifocal spikes
Normal infant sleep with high-voltage slow waves and symmetric vertex waves
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave recurring in long, regular runs
taskFlow.explanation: Chaotic, very high-amplitude slowing with multifocal spikes and loss of organization is hypsarrhythmia. Burst-suppression needs near-flat interburst periods, which are not described. Normal infant sleep is organized, with spindles and symmetric features. 3 Hz spike-and-wave is regular and synchronous, the opposite of this disorganized pattern.

taskFlow.title: A cluster on arousal
taskFlow.description: The infant wakes and a cluster begins: on video, brief flexion of the neck and arms every 10-20 seconds. Each spasm coincides with a high-amplitude generalized slow wave followed by abrupt flattening of the background for 1-3 seconds, and a deltoid EMG burst of about 1 second.
taskFlow.question: What is the EEG correlate of each spasm?
options: Movement artifact only; spasms in infants have no EEG correlate
Hypsarrhythmia becoming more chaotic and higher in voltage each time
Electrodecremental response: a slow transient, then attenuation
Focal rhythmic theta evolving in frequency for at least 10 seconds
taskFlow.explanation: The ictal signature of an epileptic spasm is a generalized high-amplitude slow transient followed by electrodecrement (attenuation), sometimes with superimposed fast activity. Movement artifact can coexist but does not explain time-locked cerebral attenuation. An evolving focal rhythm lasting 10 seconds or more describes a focal electrographic seizure, not a spasm. During spasms the background attenuates rather than becoming more chaotic.

taskFlow.title: Documenting the clusters
taskFlow.description: Three clusters were captured over 2 hours, each of 8-15 spasms. New-onset spasms with this background are treated as time-sensitive by the neurology team, and the unit protocol asks technologists to notify the ordering provider once spasms are captured.
taskFlow.question: What must the technologist document for the clusters?
options: The diagnosis of West syndrome so treatment can begin promptly
Time of each cluster, spasm count, state at onset, and EMG findings
Only the total recording time, since the spasms are on video
That the EEG is uninterpretable because of excessive infant movement
taskFlow.explanation: Clear annotation of each cluster (clock time, number of spasms, sleep/wake state at onset, EMG and EEG correlate) lets the reader confirm and quantify the events, and the provider is notified per protocol. Naming the syndrome is a diagnosis outside technologist scope. Video alone without annotation leaves the reader searching hours of data. The EEG correlate was clear, so labeling the study uninterpretable is inaccurate.

starterCases.title: Normal EEG with Benign Variants
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Normal clinical exam referred for evaluation of possible epilepsy; no spells reported

history.eventDescription: Patient referred for routine EEG evaluation. No clinical events or spells reported. Normal neurological examination.

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.focalFindings: Benign variants: mu rhythm (central), wicket spikes (temporal)

objectives: Meet minimum routine-EEG standards: 20+ minutes with activation
Confirm mu rhythm with contralateral hand movement
Recognize wicket rhythm and refer result questions to the reader

taskFlow.title: Planning a routine study
taskFlow.description: A 28-year-old with a normal neurological exam is referred for a routine EEG to evaluate possible epilepsy. No spells are reported, and there are no contraindications to activation procedures.
taskFlow.question: Which recording plan meets standard routine-EEG practice for this patient?
options: 20+ minutes including HV, photic, and drowsiness when possible
Ten minutes of eyes-closed wakefulness with no activation procedures
A sleep-deprived study is required before any routine EEG is read
At least 20 minutes awake only, skipping HV and photic in adults
taskFlow.explanation: A routine adult EEG should include at least 20 minutes of technically adequate recording, with hyperventilation and photic stimulation unless contraindicated, and drowsiness or sleep when it can be obtained. Ten minutes is below the minimum. Activation procedures are not skipped simply because the patient is an adult. Sleep deprivation is an option for a repeat study, not a prerequisite.

taskFlow.title: Central arciform rhythm
taskFlow.description: With the eyes open, 9-10 Hz arch-shaped waves are present over C3 and C4. Eye opening blocked the posterior dominant rhythm, but this central activity persists.
taskFlow.question: Which maneuver best confirms the identity of this rhythm?
options: Increase sensitivity and look for a phase reversal at C3 and C4
Ask the patient to clench the fist opposite the side of interest
Have the patient close the eyes and watch for attenuation at C3/C4
Begin HV and watch for buildup of the central arciform activity
taskFlow.explanation: Mu rhythm is a 7-11 Hz arciform central rhythm that attenuates with movement, or the intention to move, of the contralateral limb; it does not react to eye opening the way the PDR does. Eye closure tests the PDR, not mu. HV does not identify mu. A phase reversal shows location but does not separate mu from central spikes.

taskFlow.title: Temporal sharp activity in drowsiness
taskFlow.description: During drowsiness there are intermittent runs of arciform, sharply contoured 7-9 Hz waves at T3 and, independently, at T4. Individual waves have no aftergoing slow wave, and the background around them is undisturbed.
taskFlow.question: How should this activity be noted?
options: Electrode pop artifact at T3 and T4 requiring reapplication
Temporal slowing indicating bilateral focal cerebral dysfunction
Sharply contoured arciform runs, consistent with wicket rhythm
Left and right temporal spikes; the patient likely has epilepsy
taskFlow.explanation: Wicket rhythm (wicket spikes) appears in drowsiness in adults as arciform temporal waves occurring in runs, without an aftergoing slow wave or background disruption; it is a benign variant. Calling them epileptic spikes is a common over-reading. 7-9 Hz activity is not slowing. Electrode pops are single, abrupt deflections confined to one electrode, not rhythmic runs at both temporal regions.

taskFlow.title: A call about the result
taskFlow.description: The recording is otherwise normal with a 10 Hz PDR. Before the report is signed, the referring physician calls the lab and asks you directly whether the EEG 'showed spikes.'
taskFlow.question: What is the most appropriate response?
options: Explain the reader will issue the report, and offer to page them
Say the temporal waves were spikes, to make sure they are cautious
Read your notes aloud and give your own impression of the result
Tell the physician the study is normal, as the variants are benign
taskFlow.explanation: Interpretation belongs to the reading physician; the technologist directs the caller to the official report or to the reader. Labeling the waves as spikes is both interpretation and an over-call. Declaring the study normal is also interpretation, even when it is probably correct. Offering a personal impression is outside technologist scope.

starterCases.title: School-age child with GTC seizures and occipital sharp waves
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Recent onset generalized tonic-clonic convulsions associated with headaches. EEG requested to assess for epileptiform activity.

history.eventDescription: School-age child with recent onset generalized tonic-clonic convulsions associated with headaches. EEG ordered to assess for epileptiform activity.

eegSummary.background: Well-organized background, medium amplitude
eegSummary.epileptiform: Focal sharp waves in brief bursts, occipital, bilateral with left predominance, present in wake and sleep
eegSummary.focalFindings: Focal interictal epileptiform discharges in occipital regions bilaterally with left predominance

objectives: Record history details that guide localization of new seizures
Predict how raising the LFF hides slow activity
Solve the end-of-chain problem for occipital discharges

taskFlow.title: Pre-recording history
taskFlow.description: An 8-year-old girl has had recent-onset generalized tonic-clonic convulsions associated with headaches. Before hookup the technologist completes the history section of the requisition.
taskFlow.question: Which history detail is most important to record?
options: The parent's opinion of whether the convulsions were epileptic
Family history of migraine as the confirmed cause of her headaches
Timing of recent convulsions and any visual symptoms before them
The child's most recent school grades and her reading level
taskFlow.explanation: The time of the last event and any aura (for example, visual symptoms suggesting occipital onset) help the reader correlate findings and localize. School grades are not relevant to this request. A family history of migraine is worth noting but cannot 'confirm' a cause. A parent's opinion about whether events were epileptic is not a clinical description.

taskFlow.title: Filter change mid-study
taskFlow.description: During the recording a colleague raises the low-frequency filter from 1 Hz to 5 Hz to remove slow baseline drift in several channels.
taskFlow.question: What is the main effect of this change on the record?
options: The 60 Hz notch filter is disabled and line noise will increase
Sharp-wave amplitude rises, so spikes become easier to identify
Fast activity above 15 Hz is attenuated, flattening muscle artifact
Slow activity is attenuated, so focal or diffuse slowing is masked
taskFlow.explanation: Raising the LFF shortens the time constant (TC = 1 / (2 pi x 5 Hz) = 0.032 s, versus 0.16 s at 1 Hz), so delta and theta lose amplitude and slowing can disappear from view. It does not boost spike amplitude. The LFF is independent of the notch filter. Attenuating fast activity is the job of the high-frequency filter, not the LFF. The fix is to address the electrodes causing drift and return the LFF to 1 Hz.

taskFlow.title: End-of-chain problem
taskFlow.description: In the longitudinal bipolar montage, brief bursts of sharp waves are largest in the P3-O1 channel, with no phase reversal anywhere in the left parasagittal chain. O1 is the last electrode in that chain.
taskFlow.question: How do you best confirm the location of the maximum?
options: Review in a referential or transverse montage including O1 and O2
Conclude the focus is at P3, where the deflection appears largest
Raise sensitivity to 3 uV/mm until a phase reversal appears in P3-O1
Repeat photic stimulation, as occipital sharp waves are photic driven
taskFlow.explanation: When the maximum is at the end of a bipolar chain there is no electrode beyond it to produce a phase reversal (end-of-chain problem). In P3-O1 (input 1 = P3, input 2 = O1), a negative O1 gives P3 minus O1 = positive, a downward deflection. A referential montage shows the highest amplitude at O1, and a transverse chain (T5-O1-O2-T6) shows a reversal at O1. P3 is not the maximum. Changing sensitivity scales amplitude but cannot create a phase reversal. Photic stimulation does not localize.

taskFlow.title: Parent questions
taskFlow.description: Sharp waves are confirmed with a maximum at O1 and also independently at O2, left more than right, in wakefulness and sleep. As you remove electrodes, the mother asks what the test showed and whether her daughter needs an MRI.
taskFlow.question: What is the best response?
options: Say the physician will review the EEG and discuss the next steps
Explain that sharp waves in children are usually benign findings
Tell her the EEG shows occipital epilepsy and an MRI is needed
Tell her the test was normal so that she does not worry needlessly
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist documents the findings (location, laterality, state, montage used to confirm) and leaves interpretation and imaging decisions to the physician. Diagnosing epilepsy and recommending MRI exceeds technologist scope. Saying the test was normal is false. Offering reassurance about benignity is interpretation.

starterCases.title: Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy - Myoclonus on Awakening
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Morning myoclonic jerks and occasional generalized tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening

history.eventDescription: 16-year-old patient reports bilateral myoclonic jerks in the morning, especially after sleep deprivation. Has had 3 generalized tonic-clonic seizures, all occurring within 30 minutes of awakening. Events are worse with sleep deprivation and alcohol consumption.
history.lastEventTiming: Most recent GTC seizure occurred 2 weeks ago after a late night

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges, frontally predominant, activated by sleep deprivation and awakening

activations.photic: Photoparoxysmal response at 18 Hz (generalized PSW with bilateral arm jerks); stimulation stopped
activations.sleep: Sleep deprivation performed, recording upon awakening

objectives: Use sleep deprivation and awakening to activate JME discharges
Describe generalized 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave
Stop photic stimulation at a photoparoxysmal response with jerks

taskFlow.title: Choosing the study
taskFlow.description: A 16-year-old has morning arm jerks and three generalized tonic-clonic seizures, all within 30 minutes of waking and worse after late nights. A routine awake EEG last month was normal.
taskFlow.question: Which study plan offers the best yield?
options: Awake study with photic at 1-3 Hz only, avoiding faster flash rates
Prolonged 10-minute HV as the main activation procedure
Sleep-deprived EEG capturing sleep and the transition to waking
Repeat a 20-minute awake study in the late-afternoon clinic slot
taskFlow.explanation: JME discharges are activated by sleep deprivation and especially by awakening, so a sleep-deprived study that records sleep and the arousal is the best choice. Another routine afternoon study repeats the low-yield approach. HV is useful but is not the main activator here. Photic stimulation should use the full standard range because a substantial minority of JME patients are photosensitive.

taskFlow.title: Discharges on arousal
taskFlow.description: On arousal from sleep there are 1-3 second bursts of generalized discharges made of several spikes followed by a slow wave, repeating at 4-6 per second, with a frontal maximum. The background is otherwise normal.
taskFlow.question: How should these discharges be described?
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave in regular, rhythmic 10-second runs
Bifrontal muscle artifact from jaw clenching on waking
Generalized polyspike-and-wave at 4-6 Hz, frontally maximal
Slow spike-and-wave below 2.5 Hz on a slow background
taskFlow.explanation: Multiple spikes before each slow wave at 4-6 Hz with a frontal maximum is generalized polyspike-and-wave, typical of JME. The bursts are brief and faster than regular 3 Hz absence runs. Slow spike-and-wave below 2.5 Hz with a slow background suggests Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Muscle artifact is very fast, lacks an aftergoing slow wave, and is maximal over temporalis muscles.

taskFlow.title: Photic response with jerks
taskFlow.description: During photic stimulation at 18 Hz, generalized polyspike-and-wave appears and the patient has bilateral arm jerks. The discharge is still present as the flash train continues.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Lower sensitivity and keep flashing to see whether jerks persist
Continue all flash rates so the full photic range is documented
Stop the flashes, observe the patient, and annotate the event
Ask the patient to hyperventilate to confirm the photic response
taskFlow.explanation: A photoparoxysmal response with clinical myoclonus means stimulation should stop at once to avoid provoking a generalized tonic-clonic seizure; then observe, protect, and annotate the frequency and clinical signs. Completing the protocol prioritizes the routine over safety. Lowering sensitivity only shrinks the display and keeps the trigger running. Adding HV is a second provocation at the worst moment.

taskFlow.title: Annotating the event
taskFlow.description: The discharge stops within 2 seconds of stopping the strobe. The patient is alert and has no further jerks. You now write the event annotation.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation best documents the event?
options: 18 Hz IPS: generalized PSW with bilateral arm jerks; IPS stopped
Myoclonic seizure; recommend valproate before discharge from clinic
Photic-induced seizure; JME confirmed, so the parents should be told
Photic stimulation produced artifact; remainder of study is normal
taskFlow.explanation: A good annotation states the stimulus and frequency, the EEG change, the clinical sign, and the action taken, without interpretation. Declaring the syndrome and telling the family are physician tasks. Calling a real cerebral discharge artifact is inaccurate and could hide the finding. Medication recommendations are outside technologist scope.

starterCases.title: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome - Multiple Seizure Types
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Multiple seizure types including drop attacks, atypical absence, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures with developmental delay

history.eventDescription: 5-year-old child with history of multiple seizure types: atonic seizures (drop attacks), atypical absence seizures, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Significant developmental delay and cognitive impairment. Seizures are frequent and difficult to control.

eegSummary.background: Abnormal background with slow spike-and-wave
eegSummary.epileptiform: Slow spike-and-wave (1.5-2.5 Hz), generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) during sleep
eegSummary.focalFindings: Generalized slow spike-and-wave, GPFA during sleep

activations.sleep: Recorded - GPFA most prominent during sleep

objectives: Plan a safe video-EEG that captures NREM sleep in a child with drops
Distinguish slow spike-and-wave from typical 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Recognize GPFA with tonic seizures and notify for a seizure cluster

taskFlow.title: Planning the recording
taskFlow.description: A 5-year-old inpatient has drop attacks, atypical absences, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with significant developmental delay. Medications are valproate and lamotrigine. The child cannot follow multi-step instructions and falls several times a day.
taskFlow.question: Which recording plan is most important for this patient?
options: Awake-only recording with HV, since HV is the best activator here
Video-EEG including NREM sleep, with a helmet and fall precautions
Brief 10-minute awake study to limit agitation, with no sleep or video
Photic stimulation at all flash rates as the primary activation
taskFlow.explanation: Slow spike-and-wave increases in NREM sleep, and generalized paroxysmal fast activity with tonic seizures is typically seen in sleep, so sleep must be captured; video documents semiology, and frequent drops require injury precautions. HV is usually not feasible with this degree of delay and is not the key activator. A short awake study misses the sleep findings. Photic stimulation is not the main activation for this syndrome.

taskFlow.title: Awake interictal pattern
taskFlow.description: Awake, there are frequent runs of generalized spike-and-wave at about 2 Hz with a frontal predominance. The PDR is poorly formed at about 6 Hz, slow for age.
taskFlow.question: What distinguishes this from typical 3 Hz absence spike-and-wave?
options: An occipital maximum with independent phase reversals at O1 and O2
Faster repetition rate (above 3.5 Hz) with a normal background
Slower repetition rate (below 2.5 Hz) on an abnormal background
Strict activation by photic stimulation rather than by sleep
taskFlow.explanation: Slow spike-and-wave repeats below 2.5 Hz and occurs on a slowed, disorganized background, whereas typical absence spike-and-wave is about 3 Hz on a normal background. Faster rates with a normal background describe the generalized epilepsies such as JME. Slow spike-and-wave is not photic-dependent. The described field is frontal, not occipital.

taskFlow.title: Event in NREM sleep
taskFlow.description: In NREM sleep a 10-second run of generalized 10-20 Hz low-to-moderate amplitude rhythmic fast activity appears. On video the child's eyes open and both arms rise and stiffen for the same 10 seconds.
taskFlow.question: How should this be annotated?
options: GPFA with a tonic seizure: eyes opening and both arms raised
Sleep spindles in a prolonged run, a normal finding in NREM sleep
Alpha arousal pattern during a brief awakening from NREM sleep
Muscle artifact from arm stiffening; no cerebral activity is present
taskFlow.explanation: Generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) at about 10-20 Hz in sleep, time-locked to eye opening and bilateral arm elevation, is the EEG correlate of a tonic seizure. Muscle artifact is faster, irregular, and maximal over temporalis and frontalis, not a generalized rhythmic run. Spindles are 11-16 Hz, last 0.5-2 seconds, and are centrally maximal. An alpha arousal does not produce tonic posturing.

taskFlow.title: A seizure cluster
taskFlow.description: Over the next 20 minutes four more tonic seizures occur, each 10-20 seconds, with return toward baseline between them. SpO2 dips to 92% during each event and recovers.
taskFlow.question: What is the most appropriate immediate action by the technologist?
options: Keep recording quietly and summarize the cluster in the report
Notify the nurse and ordering provider now, per unit protocol
Give the rescue benzodiazepine from the bedside kit per the chart
Stop the study to let the child rest and reschedule it for later
taskFlow.explanation: A cluster of seizures with desaturation is clinically significant, and the technologist's role is immediate notification while continuing to record, keeping the child safe, and annotating each event. Giving medication is outside technologist scope. Waiting for the report delays care. Stopping the recording loses the data the team needs to manage the cluster.

starterCases.title: Self-Limited Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (SeLECTS, formerly BECTS/Rolandic)
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Nocturnal facial twitching and speech arrest, normal development

history.eventDescription: 8-year-old child with episodes of facial twitching and speech arrest occurring during sleep. Events are brief and do not cause significant disruption. Normal neurological examination and development. No daytime events reported.

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Centrotemporal spikes (C3, C4, T3, T4), markedly activated by drowsiness and sleep
eegSummary.focalFindings: Centrotemporal spikes, high amplitude, diphasic, activated by sleep

activations.sleep: Recorded - spikes markedly more frequent in sleep

objectives: Plan sleep recording to activate centrotemporal spikes
Work out spike polarity from a negative phase reversal at C3
Describe the horizontal dipole of centrotemporal spikes

taskFlow.title: Recording plan
taskFlow.description: An 8-year-old with normal development has brief episodes of one-sided facial twitching and speech arrest that occur during sleep. No daytime events have been reported.
taskFlow.question: Which plan best increases the yield of the study?
options: Prolonged HV as the main activation for centrotemporal spikes
Record drowsiness and sleep, after sleep deprivation if needed
Photic stimulation at all flash rates as the primary activation
Awake recording only, as spikes are usually maximal when alert
taskFlow.explanation: Centrotemporal spikes increase markedly in drowsiness and NREM sleep and may be rare or absent awake, so capturing sleep (with sleep deprivation if needed) is the priority. They are not maximal in wakefulness. HV and photic stimulation are routine but are not the activators for this pattern.

taskFlow.title: Phase reversal polarity
taskFlow.description: In the left parasagittal chain, at the moment of each spike the F3-C3 channel deflects downward and the C3-P3 channel deflects upward. The amplifier convention is negative-up.
taskFlow.question: What is the polarity and location of the spike maximum?
options: Negative maximum at C3: F3 minus C3 is positive, so F3-C3 goes down
Positive maximum at C3, since the two pens are pointing toward each other
Negative maximum at F3, which is the first electrode in the chain
Positive maximum at P3, since the lower channel deflects upward
taskFlow.explanation: Each channel shows input 1 minus input 2. If C3 is negative: F3-C3 = F3 - (negative) = positive, so the pen goes down; C3-P3 = (negative) - P3 = negative, so the pen goes up. Pens pointing toward each other at a shared electrode is a negative phase reversal at C3. A positive maximum would make the pens point away from each other. F3 and P3 are the neighbors, not the shared electrode.

taskFlow.title: Sleep activation and field
taskFlow.description: In N2 sleep the spikes become frequent, high in amplitude, and diphasic. Referenced to the average, there is maximal negativity at C3 and T3 with simultaneous positivity at Fp1 and F3.
taskFlow.question: How is this field best described?
options: Eye movement artifact, because the frontal leads are involved
Two independent foci, one frontal and one centrotemporal in location
Horizontal dipole: centrotemporal negative, frontal positive
A generalized discharge, because it also involves the frontal leads
taskFlow.explanation: Simultaneous centrotemporal negativity and frontal positivity from one generator is a horizontal (tangential) dipole, a typical feature of centrotemporal spikes. The two poles are simultaneous and opposite in polarity, so they are not independent foci. Involvement of one hemisphere's frontal and central leads is not generalization. Eye movement artifact is maximal at Fp1/Fp2 and does not produce a centrotemporal spike.

taskFlow.title: Notes and a parent's question
taskFlow.description: The recording ends. The parents ask whether this is 'the bad kind of epilepsy' and whether the child will outgrow it.
taskFlow.question: Which documentation and response is best?
options: Note sleep activation and the dipole; the doctor explains results
Leave the dipole out of the notes, as the reader only needs counts
Treat the spikes as an emergency and page the on-call neurologist
Reassure the parents it is a benign epilepsy the child will outgrow
taskFlow.explanation: The notes should capture the sleep activation and the field (dipole) so the reader has full context, and questions about diagnosis and prognosis go to the physician. Reassuring the parents about prognosis is interpretation. Interictal centrotemporal spikes in a stable child are not an emergency. Omitting the field description removes information the reader uses.

starterCases.title: Dravet Syndrome - Febrile Seizures and Photosensitivity
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Recurrent febrile seizures in first year of life, now with myoclonic seizures and developmental delay

history.eventDescription: 18-month-old with febrile seizures beginning at 6 months, often prolonged and one-sided. Now developing myoclonic seizures and developmental slowing in the second year. Seizures triggered by fever, hot baths, and photic stimulation. Status epilepticus occurred once.

eegSummary.background: Early: may be normal. Later: generalized spike-and-wave, polyspike-and-wave, multifocal spikes
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized spike-and-wave and polyspike-and-wave, multifocal spikes; photoparoxysmal response on photic stimulation

activations.photic: Performed - photoparoxysmal response with myoclonic jerk; stimulation stopped

objectives: Record the fever-sensitive, prolonged seizure history of Dravet syndrome
Prevent overheating in a temperature-sensitive patient
Stop photic stimulation at a photoparoxysmal response and annotate it

taskFlow.title: Seizure history
taskFlow.description: The parents report that the first seizure occurred at 6 months during a fever, lasted over 15 minutes, and involved one side of the body. Later seizures followed hot baths, and there was one episode of status epilepticus. Myoclonic jerks began recently.
taskFlow.question: Which history element is most important to record before the study?
options: The parents' preferred diagnosis based on their own online reading
Only the date of the last seizure, since all else is already charted
Whether the child sleeps well, as that is the main seizure trigger
Fever and bath triggers, prolonged one-sided seizures, and status
taskFlow.explanation: Fever- and heat-triggered, prolonged, hemiclonic seizures in the first year, with status epilepticus, are the key features the reader needs and also tell the technologist which precautions to take. The last-seizure date alone omits the pattern. Parents' online conclusions are not a clinical description. Sleep is not the main trigger in this history; temperature is.

taskFlow.title: Preparing a heat-sensitive patient
taskFlow.description: The toddler arrives flushed and bundled in heavy blankets after a warm bath this morning. The recording room is warm.
taskFlow.question: Which preparation step is most important for this patient?
options: Avoid overheating: remove extra blankets and keep the room cool
Begin with photic stimulation before the child becomes drowsy
Delay the study until the child is asleep in a warm, quiet room
Keep the child bundled so the recording is not disrupted by crying
taskFlow.explanation: Seizures in Dravet syndrome are characteristically triggered by rises in body temperature, so preventing overheating is the key precaution, along with knowing where rescue equipment and the rescue plan are. Bundling and a warm room increase risk. Starting with photic stimulation adds a provocation before the child is settled. Waiting in a warm room keeps the trigger in place.

taskFlow.title: Photic stimulation plan
taskFlow.description: The background is mildly slow for age. Photic stimulation is part of the ordered protocol, and the ordering physician has asked for it to be done.
taskFlow.question: How should photic stimulation be handled?
options: Perform IPS under close observation and stop at the first PPR
Omit photic entirely, since young children are never photosensitive
Use only 20-30 Hz flashes, which are least likely to cause seizures
Run the full sequence even if a response appears, for completeness
taskFlow.explanation: Photosensitivity can occur in Dravet syndrome, so photic stimulation is done with close clinical observation and stopped as soon as a photoparoxysmal response appears. Young children can be photosensitive. Frequencies around 15-20 Hz are among the most provocative, so 20-30 Hz is not a safe-only range. Continuing after a response risks a generalized seizure.

taskFlow.title: Annotating the response
taskFlow.description: At 15 Hz, generalized spike- and polyspike-and-wave appear with a jerk of both arms. You stop the strobe and the discharge and jerks end. The child is back to baseline within a minute.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation is best?
options: 15 Hz IPS: generalized PSW, arm jerks; IPS stopped, jerks ended
Photosensitive Dravet syndrome confirmed; recommend SCN1A testing
Myoclonic seizure from fever; give an antipyretic before continuing
Photic response within normal limits; jerks were startle to flashes
taskFlow.explanation: The annotation records the stimulus frequency, the EEG change, the clinical sign, and the action taken. Naming the syndrome and recommending genetic testing is interpretation. Calling a generalized polyspike-and-wave with myoclonus 'normal' misreports a cerebral discharge. The child was not febrile during the event, and medication decisions are not the technologist's.

starterCases.title: DEE-SWAS / EE-SWAS (ESES/CSWS) - Cognitive Regression
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Cognitive regression and behavioral problems, infrequent seizures

history.eventDescription: 6-year-old child with recent cognitive regression and behavioral problems (hyperactivity, attention deficits). Seizures are infrequent. Parents report decline in school performance and language skills over past 6 months.

eegSummary.background: Awake: focal or multifocal spikes. Sleep: marked spike-wave activation in NREM sleep (classically >=85% SWI; many centers use >=50%)
eegSummary.epileptiform: Near-continuous spike-and-wave in NREM sleep; fragmented and much less frequent in REM sleep and wakefulness
eegSummary.focalFindings: Generalized or bilateral, maximal in centrotemporal or frontocentral regions during sleep

activations.sleep: Recorded - spike-wave activated in NREM, fragmented in REM and wake

objectives: Plan a recording that includes a full NREM-REM sleep cycle
Calculate a spike-wave index from NREM discharge time
Document the state dependence of continuous spike-and-wave

taskFlow.title: Planning the study
taskFlow.description: A 6-year-old has had declining school performance and language over 6 months with infrequent seizures, and is on clobazam. The order reads 'EEG to evaluate for ESES.'
taskFlow.question: Which recording plan is required?
options: Sleep recording limited to REM, where discharges are most frequent
Routine 20-minute awake study with HV and photic stimulation
Wake and a full sleep cycle, ideally an overnight video-EEG
Awake recording plus a brief 5-minute nap if the child happens to sleep
taskFlow.explanation: ESES (CSWS) is defined by the burden of spike-and-wave in NREM sleep, so the recording must include sustained NREM and ideally a full sleep cycle; overnight video-EEG is the usual approach. An awake study cannot evaluate it. A 5-minute nap gives too little NREM to measure the burden. Discharges are least frequent in REM, not most.

taskFlow.title: Spike-wave index
taskFlow.description: The reader asks for a spike-wave index. In a 60-minute block of NREM sleep, you measure that spike-and-wave activity is present for a total of 52 minutes.
taskFlow.question: What is the spike-wave index for this block?
options: About 115%, the ratio of total NREM time to discharge time
About 52%, since 52 minutes of discharges were measured
About 87%, which meets the classic 85% ESES threshold
About 13%, the fraction of NREM sleep free of discharges
taskFlow.explanation: SWI = discharge time / NREM time x 100 = 52 / 60 x 100 = 86.7%, about 87%, above the classic 85% threshold (some centers use lower cutoffs; the reader applies the criterion). 13% is the discharge-free fraction (8 / 60). 52% treats minutes as a percentage without dividing by the 60-minute denominator. 115% inverts the ratio (60 / 52).

taskFlow.title: Change with sleep stage
taskFlow.description: The child enters REM sleep: rapid eye movements, a low-voltage mixed-frequency background, and reduced chin EMG. The spike-and-wave becomes sparse and fragmented, and it stays sparse after the child wakes.
taskFlow.question: How should this change be recorded in your notes?
options: Expected state change: discharges peak in NREM, lessen in REM
Clobazam is working, since the discharges were suppressed by it
The ESES has resolved, so the recording can end before more NREM
An electrode failure, since discharges cannot vanish in minutes
taskFlow.explanation: Continuous spike-and-wave in ESES is strongly state dependent: it is activated in NREM sleep and becomes fragmented in REM and wakefulness, so the change should be annotated with the sleep stage and time. It does not mean the condition resolved, and ending early loses later NREM cycles. Attributing the change to medication is interpretation and ignores the state change. Electrode function is confirmed by the intact REM background.

taskFlow.title: Technologist summary
taskFlow.description: The overnight study is complete and you are writing the technologist summary for the reader.
taskFlow.question: Which summary best supports the reader?
options: Continuous spike-wave seen; child appeared to be asleep the whole time
NREM block 60 min: SW 52 min; sparse in REM and wake; states marked
ESES confirmed; recommend steroids and a repeat EEG in three months
Frequent discharges during the night; normal awake background noted
taskFlow.explanation: A useful summary gives measured quantities (the measured NREM block and its discharge time) and the state-related behavior, with sleep stages marked on the record. Confirming the diagnosis and recommending treatment is outside technologist scope. 'Appeared asleep the whole time' gives no staging. 'Frequent discharges' with no measurement or staging cannot support a spike-wave index.

starterCases.title: Epilepsy with Eyelid Myoclonia (Jeavons) - Eye-Closure Sensitivity
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Rhythmic eyelid jerking with eye closure and brief staring spells

history.eventDescription: 7-year-old child with rhythmic eyelid jerking (eyelid myoclonus) that occurs with eye closure. Brief staring spells (3-6 seconds) also occur. Events are triggered by eye closure, photic stimulation, and bright lights. Normal development.

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized 3-4 Hz spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave, triggered by eye closure and photic stimulation

activations.photic: Photosensitive - eye closure during IPS may trigger events

objectives: Include eye closure and photic testing with eye-state markers
Recognize eye-closure-induced polyspike-and-wave with eyelid myoclonia
Separate eyelid artifact from cerebral discharge using eye leads

taskFlow.title: Activation plan
taskFlow.description: A 7-year-old has rhythmic eyelid jerking when closing the eyes and brief staring spells of 3-6 seconds. The parents say bright light and eye closure seem to bring them on.
taskFlow.question: Which procedure must be included and carefully documented?
options: Sleep deprivation only, as the events occur mostly in deep sleep
Recording in a darkened room only, to avoid triggering any seizures
HV only, as it is the best activator for all absence-type seizures
Repeated eye closure in normal light and IPS, with eye-state marks
taskFlow.explanation: Eye closure (in a lit room) and photic stimulation are the main triggers in eyelid myoclonia with absences, so both must be tested and each eye opening and closure marked. HV is useful for absences but misses the key trigger. The events are awake, not sleep-related. Avoiding triggers defeats the purpose of the requested study.

taskFlow.title: Response to eye closure
taskFlow.description: Within 1-2 seconds of each eye closure there are 3-6 second bursts of generalized 3-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave, and the video shows rapid eyelid flutter with upward eye deviation. With the eyes open there are no discharges.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits these findings?
options: Posterior alpha squeak after eye closure, a normal variant
Eye-closure-induced generalized PSW with eyelid myoclonia
Lambda waves triggered by visual scanning after eye closure
Eye-blink artifact at Fp1 and Fp2 from rapid, repeated blinking
taskFlow.explanation: Generalized polyspike-and-wave triggered by eye closure, with eyelid myoclonia on video, is the hallmark of this syndrome. Blink artifact is confined to the frontopolar leads and has no generalized spike field. Alpha squeak is a brief, faster PDR after eye closure without spikes. Lambda waves occur with the eyes open during visual scanning.

taskFlow.title: Artifact or cerebral?
taskFlow.description: During the bursts, eyelid flutter produces large deflections at Fp1 and Fp2 that partly obscure the frontal spikes, and a colleague suggests the whole burst may be artifact.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to separate eye artifact from cerebral discharge?
options: Add infraorbital eye leads and check the field beyond Fp1/Fp2
Turn the HFF down to 15 Hz so that the fast components disappear
Ask the patient to keep the eyes open for the rest of the study
Remove Fp1 and Fp2 from the montage to eliminate the eye signal
taskFlow.explanation: Eye leads (for example infraorbital electrodes) show whether the frontal deflections follow eye movement, and a cerebral discharge has a field that extends to F, C and posterior electrodes. Lowering the HFF to 15 Hz attenuates the spikes themselves and can make a real discharge look like slowing. Keeping the eyes open removes the trigger being studied. Deleting channels discards data instead of characterizing it.

taskFlow.title: Documentation
taskFlow.description: Later, IPS with the eyes closed produced a generalized photoparoxysmal response at 16 Hz, and stimulation was stopped. The rest of the background is normal.
taskFlow.question: Which note is most useful to the reader?
options: Photosensitive epilepsy diagnosed; the child should wear tinted glasses
Several events; parents were told the child has absence epilepsy
PSW 1-2 s after eye closure with eyelid flutter; IPS PPR at 16 Hz
Normal study; eyelid movements were blink artifact throughout
taskFlow.explanation: The note states the trigger, latency, EEG pattern, clinical sign, and the photic frequency at which a response occurred. Calling the bursts blink artifact ignores the generalized field. Diagnosing and prescribing treatment is outside technologist scope. Telling parents a diagnosis is the physician's role.

starterCases.title: Frontal Lobe Epilepsy - Brief Nocturnal Seizures
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief nocturnal seizures with hypermotor behavior and vocalizations

history.eventDescription: 25-year-old adult with brief nocturnal seizures characterized by hypermotor behavior, vocalizations, and bilateral movements. Seizures are very brief (seconds to <1 minute) and occur during sleep. Normal daytime function.
history.lastEventTiming: Events occur during sleep, multiple times per month

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Frontal spikes/sharp waves, activated by sleep. Ictal: Focal onset in frontal region, may show fast activity (beta/gamma) or rhythmic patterns
eegSummary.focalFindings: Frontal spikes/sharp waves (F3, F4, Fz, F7, F8), activated by sleep

activations.sleep: Recorded - frontal spikes activated by sleep

objectives: Choose prolonged video-EEG to capture brief nocturnal events
Separate frontal sharp waves from vertex waves
Manage and document a hypermotor seizure obscured by artifact

taskFlow.title: Capturing nocturnal events
taskFlow.description: A 25-year-old has brief nocturnal episodes of thrashing and vocalization several times a month. A routine awake EEG was normal. Current medication is carbamazepine.
taskFlow.question: Which study is most likely to answer the clinical question?
options: Awake study in the afternoon, after a normal night of sleep
Ambulatory EEG without video, relying on the patient's diary
Repeat a 20-minute awake routine EEG with both HV and photic stimulation
Prolonged video-EEG through the night to capture typical events
taskFlow.explanation: Brief nocturnal hypermotor events need prolonged recording through sleep with video, because semiology is essential and scalp EEG during the event is often obscured. A repeat routine study is likely to be normal again. Ambulatory EEG without video cannot show what the patient did. An afternoon awake study misses the sleep period when events occur.

taskFlow.title: Sharp waves in N2
taskFlow.description: In N2 sleep, sharp waves appear in the anterior channels and a resident suggests they are just vertex waves. On review, they reverse phase at F4 in the right parasagittal chain, are followed by a slow wave, and are absent on the left.
taskFlow.question: Which feature best distinguishes these from vertex waves?
options: They have negative polarity, whereas vertex waves are positive
They occur in sleep, as vertex waves are seen only in wakefulness
A consistent right frontal maximum at F4 with an aftergoing slow wave
They are sharply contoured, while vertex waves are always smooth and rounded
taskFlow.explanation: Vertex waves are maximal at Cz, roughly symmetric, and occur in drowsiness and light sleep; a consistently lateralized maximum (F4) with an aftergoing slow wave points to an epileptiform discharge. Vertex waves are a sleep phenomenon, not a waking one. Both vertex waves and spikes are usually surface negative. Vertex waves are often sharply contoured, especially in children, so sharpness alone does not separate them.

taskFlow.title: An event under artifact
taskFlow.description: In the early morning hours the patient arouses from N2 with thrashing and vocalization lasting about 30 seconds. The EEG is obscured by high-amplitude muscle and movement artifact throughout the event.
taskFlow.question: What is the best immediate action?
options: Turn the HFF down to 15 Hz during the event so the cerebral EEG shows
Keep the patient on camera, protect from injury, test responsiveness
Enter the room and restrain the limbs to reduce movement artifact
Mark the event as nonepileptic, since no clear EEG change could be seen
taskFlow.explanation: During a hypermotor event the priorities are safety, keeping the patient in view, and testing responsiveness during and after the event. Heavy HFF filtering can make muscle artifact resemble rhythmic cerebral activity and hides the true signal. Restraining limbs risks injury. Frontal seizures often have obscured or minimal scalp change, so absence of a visible EEG change does not make the event nonepileptic, and that judgment is the reader's.

taskFlow.title: Event annotation
taskFlow.description: The event ends. Thirty seconds later the patient answers questions and follows commands. You now write the annotation.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation documents the event best?
options: Nocturnal frontal lobe seizure confirmed; carbamazepine should increase
Movement artifact at the event time; study otherwise normal throughout
Patient had a bad dream and moved around; no seizure was observed
Arousal from N2, hypermotor 30 s, EEG obscured; responsive 30 s later
taskFlow.explanation: A good annotation gives the sleep stage at onset, the semiology and duration, the EEG quality, and the recovery of responsiveness. Confirming a diagnosis and suggesting a dose change is outside technologist scope. 'Bad dream' is a guess about cause. Calling the event 'movement artifact' describes only the signal and omits the clinical event entirely.

starterCases.title: Epilepsy with Myoclonic-Atonic Seizures (Doose / MAE)
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Myoclonic jerks followed by drop attacks and atypical absence seizures

history.eventDescription: 3-year-old with myoclonic-atonic seizures (myoclonic jerk immediately followed by atonic drop) and atypical absences. Previously normal development. Variable course: many remit; some have persistent seizures and cognitive impairment.

eegSummary.background: Normal or mildly abnormal background
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave (2-4 Hz) during myoclonic-atonic seizures

objectives: Document medication changes that preceded seizure worsening
Use EMG polygraphy to classify myoclonic-atonic seizures
Recognize and report possible nonconvulsive status during the study

taskFlow.title: Medication history
taskFlow.description: A 3-year-old with previously normal development has jerks followed by falls and atypical absences, and is on valproate. The parents mention a second drug was started elsewhere last month, after which the drops became more frequent.
taskFlow.question: Which history detail is most important to document?
options: The parents' guess about the cause of the drops, as the diagnosis
Whether the child naps daily, which determines the montage choice
Recent drug changes, including any started before the worsening
Only the current valproate dose, as older drugs no longer matter
taskFlow.explanation: Some drugs (for example carbamazepine, phenytoin, or vigabatrin) can aggravate seizures in myoclonic-atonic epilepsy, so a drug change before worsening is important for the reader and treating team; the technologist documents it but does not advise on medication. Recording only the current drug misses the timeline. A parent's guess is not a diagnosis. Nap habits matter for scheduling, not montage choice.

taskFlow.title: Setting up polygraphy
taskFlow.description: The child has several drops per hour. The reader wants to know whether the falls are myoclonic, atonic, tonic, or a combination.
taskFlow.question: Which setup best documents the drops?
options: Recording seated on a parent's lap with the camera turned off
EEG only; an event button press is enough to classify each of the falls
HV with a pinwheel, the main activator of drops in toddlers
Video with EMG from both deltoids and neck, plus fall precautions
taskFlow.explanation: Surface EMG shows whether a fall begins with a brief myoclonic burst, a period of EMG silence (atonia), or a sustained increase (tonic), and video shows the fall itself; frequent drops require injury precautions. An event button gives timing but not mechanism. Turning off video removes semiology. HV is not feasible as a main activator at age 3 and does not classify falls.

taskFlow.title: Reading the polygraphy
taskFlow.description: A drop is captured. The EEG shows a generalized polyspike-and-wave at about 3 Hz. The deltoid EMG shows a brief burst of about 100 ms followed by about 300 ms of EMG silence as the head drops.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the polygraphy is correct for the notes?
options: Pure atonic seizure: EMG silence with no preceding muscle burst
Tonic seizure: a sustained EMG increase lasting several seconds
Epileptic spasm: a high-voltage slow wave followed by electrodecrement
Myoclonic burst then atonic silence: a myoclonic-atonic seizure
taskFlow.explanation: A brief EMG burst followed by EMG silence, time-locked to generalized polyspike-and-wave, is the myoclonic-atonic sequence. A tonic seizure would show a sustained EMG increase of seconds, which is not present. A pure atonic seizure lacks the preceding burst. A spasm has a slow-wave and decrement correlate with an EMG burst of about 1 second, not this pattern.

taskFlow.title: A change in the child
taskFlow.description: Later the child becomes quiet and less interactive. For 15 minutes the EEG shows near-continuous irregular generalized spike-and-wave, and the child responds only minimally, with subtle facial twitching.
taskFlow.question: What is the best technologist action?
options: Lower the sensitivity until the discharges appear less frequent
Wake the child vigorously to end the activity and resume recording
Test responsiveness, document it, and notify the provider now
Continue recording and describe the run in the final notes only
taskFlow.explanation: Near-continuous generalized discharges with reduced responsiveness may represent nonconvulsive status, which can occur in this syndrome; the technologist tests and documents responsiveness and notifies the provider immediately. Waiting for the final report delays treatment. Vigorous stimulation does not address the problem and alters the record. Changing sensitivity changes only the display, not the activity.

learningLinks.label: Syndrome: Epilepsy with Myoclonic-Atonic Seizures (Doose / MAE)

starterCases.title: Early-Infantile DEE (Ohtahara) - Burst-Suppression with Tonic Seizures
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Burst-suppression pattern with frequent tonic seizures in first weeks of life

history.eventDescription: 2-week-old neonate with burst-suppression pattern on EEG and frequent tonic seizures. Onset in first few days of life. Severe developmental delay. Pattern is continuous (present in both wake and sleep).

eegSummary.background: Burst-suppression pattern - alternating bursts of high-amplitude activity and suppression
eegSummary.epileptiform: Burst-suppression pattern, continuous (wake and sleep). Tonic seizures show bursts or electrodecremental pattern.

objectives: Set up a neonatal recording with polygraphy and video
Distinguish invariant burst-suppression from trace alternant
Measure interburst amplitude from deflection and sensitivity

taskFlow.title: Neonatal setup
taskFlow.description: A 2-week-old in the NICU has frequent tonic seizures that began in the first days of life. An EEG has been ordered to characterize the background and the events.
taskFlow.question: Which setup meets neonatal recording recommendations?
options: Eight scalp electrodes for 20 minutes, without any extra channels
Neonatal array with ECG, respiration, EOG, EMG, video, 60+ min
Single-channel aEEG only, since a full EEG cannot be done in NICU
Full adult 10-20 array for 20 minutes, with photic stimulation
taskFlow.explanation: Neonatal EEG uses a neonatal electrode array with polygraphic channels (ECG, respiration, eye movement, chin EMG) and video, recorded long enough (at least about 60 minutes) to include a sleep-wake cycle. Twenty minutes without polygraphy cannot stage state or identify artifacts. The adult array and photic stimulation are not the neonatal standard. aEEG is a trend tool and does not replace conventional EEG.

taskFlow.title: Background characterization
taskFlow.description: The record shows bursts of high-voltage (150-350 uV) mixed slow waves and spikes lasting 2-6 seconds, alternating with near-flat periods of 3-5 seconds. The pattern is the same with the eyes open and awake as in sleep.
taskFlow.question: Which feature most distinguishes this from normal trace alternant?
options: The bursts contain delta waves rather than any theta or faster activity
Near-flat interburst periods present in both wake and sleep
The interburst intervals are shorter than the bursts themselves
The pattern is seen only in quiet sleep, like trace alternant
taskFlow.explanation: Trace alternant is a quiet-sleep pattern of term newborns with attenuated (not flat) interburst activity; a burst-suppression pattern with near-flat interburst periods that does not change across wake and sleep is abnormal and is the pattern described in this syndrome. Normal bursts also contain delta, so that is not distinguishing. Burst and interburst durations overlap and are not the key feature. The pattern here is not limited to quiet sleep.

taskFlow.title: Measuring the interburst
taskFlow.description: At 7 uV/mm the interburst periods look completely flat. To document whether any activity is present, you increase sensitivity to 2 uV/mm, and the interburst activity now measures 3 mm peak-to-peak.
taskFlow.question: What is the interburst amplitude?
options: About 1.5 uV, from 3 mm divided by 2 uV/mm
About 21 uV, from 3 mm multiplied by 7 uV/mm
About 0.7 uV, from 2 uV/mm divided by 3 mm
About 6 uV, from 3 mm multiplied by 2 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: Amplitude = deflection x sensitivity = 3 mm x 2 uV/mm = 6 uV, below the 10 uV level that ACNS 2021 terminology uses for 'suppressed.' Dividing (3 / 2 = 1.5) or inverting (2 / 3 = 0.7) misapplies the formula. Using 7 uV/mm (21 uV) applies the old sensitivity to a measurement taken at the new one.

taskFlow.title: A tonic seizure
taskFlow.description: During a burst the infant stiffens with extension of all limbs for 8 seconds; the EEG shows diffuse attenuation during the event and the heart rate rises on the ECG channel.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation and action is best?
options: Ask the nurse to give phenobarbital, then document the response
Mark onset, tonic semiology, and EEG change; notify the NICU team
Report the trace as Ohtahara syndrome to the parents at bedside
Mark it as movement artifact from limb stiffening and keep recording
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist marks the clock time, the clinical semiology, and the EEG and ECG changes, and notifies the clinical team per protocol. Labeling a seizure with an EEG correlate as artifact loses the event. Directing medication is outside technologist scope. Sharing a diagnosis with parents is the physician's role.

starterCases.title: Myoclonic Epilepsy in Infancy (MEI, formerly BMEI)
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief myoclonic jerks, normal development

history.eventDescription: 18-month-old with brief myoclonic jerks (each under 1 second, sometimes in short series) occurring during wakefulness. No GTC seizures, no absence seizures. Normal neurological examination and normal development. Some jerks follow sudden noise or touch.

eegSummary.background: Normal background for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave time-locked to myoclonic jerks; background normal for age

activations.photic: May be photosensitive in some patients
activations.sleep: Drowsiness and brief sleep recorded; normal sleep features

objectives: Record triggers and clustering of infant myoclonic jerks
Use video and EMG to capture brief myoclonic events
Describe a normal background without interpreting prognosis

taskFlow.title: Event history
taskFlow.description: An 18-month-old with normal development has brief jerks of the head and arms while awake. The parents say some jerks follow a sudden noise or being touched, and they sometimes come several in a row.
taskFlow.question: Which detail is most useful to record?
options: The developmental diagnosis the parents suspect from online sources
Triggers like noise or touch, and whether jerks come in clusters
Whether the child has had a febrile seizure, which rules out BMEI
Only the number of jerks per day, since triggers do not change the EEG
taskFlow.explanation: Triggers such as sound or touch tell the technologist what to try during the recording, and clustering helps the reader classify events. Counting jerks without triggers loses the information that could provoke one during the study. Parent online diagnoses are not clinical data. A febrile seizure history does not rule out this syndrome.

taskFlow.title: Capturing events
taskFlow.description: The toddler is calm and becoming drowsy. Jerks occur several times per hour at home.
taskFlow.question: Which plan best captures the events?
options: Awake-only study with HV, as toddlers cooperate well with pinwheels
A short 10-minute recording to avoid tiring the toddler, then discharge
EEG without video, since the parents can describe the jerks later
Video with deltoid EMG, recording drowsiness and testing triggers
taskFlow.explanation: Myoclonic jerks are very brief, so video plus EMG is needed to time-lock the movement to the EEG; drowsiness and safe testing of reported triggers increase the chance of capturing one. HV is not reliable at 18 months. Without video the jerks cannot be correlated. Ten minutes is unlikely to capture events occurring a few times per hour.

taskFlow.title: The captured jerk
taskFlow.description: A jerk of both arms is captured: a deltoid EMG burst of under 200 ms, time-locked to a generalized polyspike-and-wave lasting about 1 second. The background before and after is well organized for age.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation describes the correlate?
options: Brief generalized polyspike-and-wave with a time-locked EMG burst
Generalized slow wave, then electrodecrement, typical of a spasm
Movement artifact only, since myoclonic jerks lack EEG correlates
Focal rhythmic spikes evolving over 20 seconds in the left temporal
taskFlow.explanation: A brief generalized polyspike-and-wave time-locked to a short EMG burst is the correlate of an epileptic myoclonic jerk. A spasm shows a slow wave and decrement with a longer EMG burst. Epileptic myoclonus often has a clear EEG correlate, so dismissing it as artifact is wrong. An evolving focal rhythm over 20 seconds describes a focal seizure.

taskFlow.title: Background and a parent question
taskFlow.description: The interictal background is normal and well organized for age, with normal sleep features. The parents ask, 'Is this like Dravet syndrome?'
taskFlow.question: Which note and response is best?
options: Tell the parents it is likely Dravet, as myoclonic jerks are present
Tell the parents it is benign and will be outgrown within a year
Note normal background for age; refer the question to the physician
Note an abnormal background, since any myoclonus means encephalopathy
taskFlow.explanation: The background description (normal for age) is an important finding for the reader, and diagnostic questions go to the physician. Promising a benign outcome is prognosis, which is interpretation. Suggesting Dravet syndrome is a diagnosis, which is outside technologist scope. Describing a normal background as abnormal misreports the record.

learningLinks.label: Syndrome: Myoclonic Epilepsy in Infancy (MEI, formerly BMEI)

starterCases.title: Landau-Kleffner Syndrome - Acquired Aphasia
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acquired language loss (aphasia) and infrequent seizures

history.eventDescription: 5-year-old child with acquired aphasia (language loss) - previously normal language development. Verbal auditory agnosia (inability to understand spoken language) and expressive language loss. Seizures are infrequent or absent (paradoxical - seizures rare but EEG shows ESES). Behavioral problems also present.

eegSummary.background: Awake: focal or multifocal spikes (often temporal or perisylvian). Sleep: marked NREM activation of spike-and-wave
eegSummary.epileptiform: Marked NREM activation of spike-and-wave, often near-continuous, maximal temporal/perisylvian; less frequent in REM and wakefulness

activations.sleep: Recorded - spike-wave strongly activated in NREM, reduced in REM and wake

objectives: Document the timeline of acquired language loss
Arrange sleep recording through a full NREM-REM cycle
Describe sleep-activated temporal-perisylvian spike-and-wave

taskFlow.title: Language history
taskFlow.description: A 5-year-old who previously spoke normally no longer responds to spoken words, and the parents wonder whether the child has become deaf. Seizures are infrequent.
taskFlow.question: Which history detail is most important to document?
options: The parents' belief that the child is deaf, recorded as the diagnosis
Whether the child watches television, as screen time causes aphasia
Timeline of language loss, prior normal speech, and any hearing test
Only the seizure frequency, as language is outside the EEG scope
taskFlow.explanation: Acquired loss of language after normal development, with a timeline and the result of any hearing evaluation, is the central history for the reader. Screen time does not cause acquired aphasia. Language regression is directly relevant to this EEG request. Recording a parent's belief as the diagnosis is inaccurate; verbal auditory agnosia can mimic deafness.

taskFlow.title: Getting sleep
taskFlow.description: The child is frightened and resists hookup. The order specifies that sleep must be recorded.
taskFlow.question: Which plan is best?
options: Give a sedative from the unit supply to induce sleep quickly
Arrange natural or ordered sleep and record a full NREM-REM cycle
Record only wakefulness, since sleep findings are not relevant here
Record a 5-minute nap only, as ESES is seen within the first minutes
taskFlow.explanation: The key abnormality in this syndrome is spike-and-wave activated in NREM sleep, so sustained sleep including a full cycle must be recorded, using natural sleep or sedation only if a provider orders it. Skipping sleep misses the finding. Taking a sedative from unit supply without an order is outside technologist scope. A brief nap cannot quantify the NREM burden.

taskFlow.title: Sleep activation
taskFlow.description: Awake, there are intermittent spikes at T3 and C3. In NREM sleep the spike-and-wave becomes near-continuous and bilateral, with a left temporal and perisylvian maximum.
taskFlow.question: Which description best documents the sleep finding?
options: Benign centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole, seen only in wake
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave in absence-like runs while awake
Near-continuous NREM spike-wave, left temporal-perisylvian maximum
Normal sleep spindles that are sharply contoured during N2 sleep
taskFlow.explanation: The description should capture the state (NREM), the near-continuous burden, and the maximum (left temporal-perisylvian). 3 Hz absence runs are a waking generalized pattern, not this sleep-activated one. Spindles are 11-16 Hz central bursts, not spike-and-wave. The activity here is sleep activated, not limited to wakefulness.

taskFlow.title: Technologist summary
taskFlow.description: The overnight study is complete with sleep stages marked. You are writing the summary for the reader.
taskFlow.question: Which summary is best?
options: Seizures are infrequent, so the EEG is likely to be of little use
Landau-Kleffner syndrome in the notes so the reader can confirm it
Night summarized as abnormal, without specifying any sleep stages
State changes with times, and the spike-wave burden in NREM sleep
taskFlow.explanation: The reader needs the timing of state changes and the measured spike-wave burden in NREM sleep. Writing the syndrome name is diagnosis, outside technologist scope. Infrequent seizures do not reduce the value of the EEG in this condition, where the sleep EEG is central. A summary without staging cannot support any measurement of the burden.

starterCases.title: HIPAA Violation: Unauthorized Hallway Discussion
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for evaluation of possible seizures

history.eventDescription: Patient reports episodes of staring and confusion

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior dominant rhythm at 10 Hz, reactive
eegSummary.activation: Hyperventilation and photic stimulation performed, no activation

objectives: Recognize a confidentiality breach in a public area of the lab
Stop and contain a privacy breach before reporting it
Redirect family requests for results to the ordering physician

taskFlow.title: Spot the problem
taskFlow.description: Between recordings, a technologist stands in the hallway outside the waiting room and tells a colleague the patient's full name, her staring spells, and that 'the tracing looked pretty normal so far.' Two visitors are seated within earshot.
taskFlow.question: Which principle is the technologist breaking?
options: Scope of practice for EEG interpretation by technologists
Informed consent for activation procedures
Confidentiality of protected health information
Patient autonomy over consent to testing
taskFlow.explanation: Name, symptoms and findings are protected health information (PHI); sharing them where unauthorized people can hear is a confidentiality (HIPAA privacy) breach. Autonomy and informed consent concern the patient's right to agree to testing, which is not at issue. The 'looked normal' remark also brushes against scope of practice, but the core violation here is disclosure of PHI in a public space.

taskFlow.title: Contain it now
taskFlow.description: The colleague notices the visitors and gives the technologist a look. The patient is still in the recording room waiting for photic stimulation to begin.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do first?
options: Finish the sentence quickly, then go back into the room
Approach the visitors and ask them to forget what they heard
Tell the patient right away that her details were overheard
End the conversation and continue only in a private area
taskFlow.explanation: The first step is to stop the disclosure and continue any necessary discussion only in a private space with people who need to know. Asking visitors to 'forget' it draws more attention and does not undo anything. Finishing the conversation continues the breach. Disclosure to the patient is handled through the organization's privacy process, not improvised mid-study by the technologist.

taskFlow.title: Report the breach
taskFlow.description: The study finishes without further problems. The technologist feels uneasy and asks the lead technologist what happens next.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct follow-up?
options: Write a note about the incident in the patient's EEG report
Apologize to the colleague and agree to be more careful later
Say nothing, since no one complained and nothing was written
Report it to the supervisor or privacy officer per policy
taskFlow.explanation: Privacy incidents are reported through the facility's process (supervisor and/or privacy officer), who decide on any required notification; retraining is a common corrective step. Incident details do not belong in the clinical EEG report. 'No complaint' does not mean no breach, and an informal apology to a colleague does not meet reporting obligations.

taskFlow.title: Family asks for results
taskFlow.description: A week later the patient's adult sister calls the lab. She says she drove the patient to the appointment and asks the technologist whether the EEG 'showed seizures.' There is no authorization on file naming the sister.
taskFlow.question: How should the technologist respond?
options: Read her the technical description but leave out the impression
Share results if she can confirm the patient's date of birth
Confirm only that the study 'looked normal' since she is family
Decline, and refer her to the patient and ordering physician
taskFlow.explanation: Without the patient's authorization, the technologist cannot confirm any results to a relative, and technologists do not give results to anyone; the ordering physician communicates the interpreted report. Saying it 'looked normal' is both a disclosure and an interpretation. Reading the technical description is still disclosure. Knowing a date of birth verifies identity of the patient, not the caller's right to the information.

starterCases.title: Patient Safety: Sparking Electrode Cable
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for evaluation of staring episodes

history.eventDescription: Episodes of staring and unresponsiveness

eegSummary.background: Normal age-appropriate background

objectives: Remove an electrical hazard from the patient before anything else
Assess the patient and notify after an electrical incident
Tag out equipment and document the event for biomedical review

taskFlow.title: Spark at the jack box
taskFlow.description: During electrode hookup on an 8-year-old, the technologist sees a small spark as an electrode lead is pushed into the jack box. The cable insulation looks intact. Eight electrodes are already connected to the child.
taskFlow.question: What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Finish the hookup and watch the child closely for any symptoms
Stop and disconnect the child from that system
Lower the sensitivity so any electrical noise is less visible
Swap in another lead, then continue with the same amplifier
taskFlow.explanation: Any spark means possible current leakage or a fault; the hazard is removed first by stopping and disconnecting the patient from the equipment. Continuing while 'watching' leaves the child connected to a suspect device. Sensitivity changes only alter the display, not the electrical risk. Swapping a lead assumes the fault is in the lead; the spark could come from the jack box or amplifier.

taskFlow.title: Check the child
taskFlow.description: The child is now disconnected. He is calm and says he 'felt a tiny pinch' near the left ear when the spark happened.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do next?
options: Wait for the end of the visit before telling anyone
Check the skin and the child, then notify the supervisor
Move the electrode to a new spot and restart the hookup
Reassure the parent that a small pinch is normal during hookup
taskFlow.explanation: Once the hazard is removed, assess the patient: look at the skin under the electrode for redness or burn, ask about symptoms, and notify the supervisor (and the physician per policy). A pinch at the moment of a spark is not a normal hookup sensation. Moving the electrode ignores a possible injury, and delaying notification prevents timely evaluation.

taskFlow.title: Handle the equipment
taskFlow.description: The skin looks normal and the supervisor is on the way. The child's parent asks whether the study can still be done today. A second EEG system is available in the next room.
taskFlow.question: What should happen to the first system?
