options: Open the jack box and tighten the loose input pin yourself
Keep using it but plug the amplifier into a different wall outlet
Tag it out of service for biomedical engineering testing
Run a calibration and return it to use if every channel is normal
taskFlow.explanation: Equipment suspected of an electrical fault is removed from use, labeled out of service, and inspected by biomedical/clinical engineering (including electrical safety and leakage-current testing) before it returns. A normal calibration says nothing about leakage current. Technologists do not open or repair equipment, and changing outlets does not fix an internal fault. The study can continue on the backup system.

taskFlow.title: Document the incident
taskFlow.description: The study is completed on the backup system without problems. The supervisor asks the technologist to complete the facility incident report before leaving.
taskFlow.question: Which content belongs in the incident report?
options: Objective facts, the child's report, actions and notifications
Your theory of which component failed and who last serviced it
A note that no report is needed because there was no visible injury
Only the equipment serial number, since the child was not harmed
taskFlow.explanation: Incident reports record objective facts: what happened and when, the patient's report and assessment findings, actions taken (disconnect, tag-out, backup system), and who was notified. A visible injury is not required for reporting a safety event. The serial number alone omits the patient-safety details. Speculation and blame are left out; biomedical engineering determines the cause.

starterCases.title: Scope of Practice: Diagnosing in the Technical Report
starterCases.chiefComplaint: EEG for evaluation of absence seizures

history.eventDescription: Episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, triggered by hyperventilation

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior dominant rhythm at 10 Hz
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges, activated by hyperventilation
eegSummary.activation: Hyperventilation activated generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges

objectives: Separate objective description from clinical diagnosis
Test and document responsiveness during a generalized discharge
Answer a parent's diagnostic question within technologist scope

taskFlow.title: Review a draft note
taskFlow.description: A newer technologist's draft technical note reads: 'This EEG is consistent with childhood absence epilepsy. The patient has absence seizures and the ethosuximide dose is too low.'
taskFlow.question: What is wrong with this note?
options: It should name the syndrome as juvenile absence epilepsy instead
It gives a diagnosis and a treatment opinion
It should be signed by the parent before it is filed
It is fine, because the pattern is typical for this age
taskFlow.explanation: Technologists describe what was recorded in standard terms; diagnosing a syndrome or commenting on medication dose is the interpreting physician's role. Swapping one syndrome name for another is still a diagnosis. A 'typical' pattern does not move diagnosis into technologist scope, and parents do not sign technical notes.

taskFlow.title: Rewrite it correctly
taskFlow.description: The supervising technologist asks for a rewrite using objective terminology.
taskFlow.question: Which wording is appropriate for the technical note?
options: Abnormal EEG, consistent with a generalized epilepsy syndrome of childhood
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave, activated by hyperventilation
Patient has absence epilepsy with frequent daily seizures
Seizure disorder present; recommend adjusting medication
taskFlow.explanation: The objective description names the waveform, frequency, distribution and activating factor without concluding a diagnosis. 'Consistent with a generalized epilepsy syndrome' is an interpretation. The other two state a diagnosis and a treatment recommendation, both outside technologist scope.

taskFlow.title: Discharge during hyperventilation
taskFlow.description: At 90 s of hyperventilation, a burst of generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave begins. The child stops breathing deeply and stares. The technologist estimates the burst will last several seconds.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do while the burst is in progress?
options: Stop the recording so the child can rest until she has fully recovered
Shake her shoulder firmly to break the discharge right away
Only annotate 'seizure' at the end once the burst has stopped
Say a test word and later ask her to recall it; mark onset and offset
taskFlow.explanation: Clinical correlation is the technologist's job: give a test word or simple command during the discharge, ask for recall afterward, and annotate onset, offset and the response. Stopping the recording loses the event. Shaking the child is unnecessary and adds artifact. A single 'seizure' label is a diagnosis and lacks the responsiveness data the reader needs.

taskFlow.title: Parent's question
taskFlow.description: After electrode removal, the parent asks: 'You saw it on the screen, so does she still have epilepsy? Should we raise her medicine?'
taskFlow.question: What is the best response?
options: Show the parent the spike-and-wave bursts and explain them
Tell the parent the medicine is probably not working well enough
Explain that the physician will review it and discuss results
Reassure the parent that the EEG was normal to avoid worry
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist acknowledges the question and explains that the interpreting/ordering physician will review the recording and discuss results and treatment. Commenting on medication effectiveness, giving false reassurance, or walking the parent through the discharges are all interpretation and outside technologist scope.

starterCases.title: Emergency Response: Suspected Nonconvulsive Status
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG monitoring in ICU

history.eventDescription: Patient admitted with altered mental status, continuous EEG ordered

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing, 4-6 Hz theta range
eegSummary.epileptiform: Evolving rhythmic discharges lasting several minutes (suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus), resolving after IV lorazepam; later generalized tonic-clonic seizure

objectives: Prioritize patient check and notification for suspected NCSE
Keep recording and annotate treatment during an emergency
Give correct first aid when a convulsion follows NCSE

taskFlow.title: Pattern on the screen
taskFlow.description: On ICU continuous EEG after traumatic brain injury, the technologist sees rhythmic discharges that have been evolving for several minutes. At the bedside the patient does not open his eyes to voice and is not convulsing.
taskFlow.question: What is the FIRST priority?
options: Ask the family whether this has happened before tonight
Watch another 30 minutes to confirm before calling anyone
Write it in the shift log for the morning physician review
Check the patient, then notify the physician per protocol
taskFlow.explanation: Suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus is an emergency: confirm the patient's condition (airway, breathing, responsiveness), then notify the physician/team immediately per protocol. Waiting 30 minutes or leaving it for morning review delays treatment. History from family is useful later but is not the first action.

taskFlow.title: Keep the data
taskFlow.description: The neurologist is on the way and the nurse is preparing medication at the bedside. Electrodes are intact and nothing is blocking care.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do with the EEG recording?
options: Pause the recording so the team has room to work
Keep recording and make sure video captures the patient
Switch the display to a 60 s page to save storage
Remove the frontal electrodes in case of an airway procedure
taskFlow.explanation: When it can be done safely, recording continues: EEG and video during the event are essential for treatment decisions. Pausing loses data, and electrodes are removed only if they physically interfere with care. Display page width is a review setting; it does not change what is stored and is not a priority now.

taskFlow.title: Medication given
taskFlow.description: The nurse gives IV lorazepam at the bedside. Over the next minute the rhythmic discharges slow and then stop.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Annotate drug, dose and time, then note the EEG change
Stop recording, since the pattern has now resolved
Record the dose in the chart and skip the EEG annotation
Annotate only that the seizure was 'successfully treated'
taskFlow.explanation: Accurate time-stamped annotation of medication (drug, dose, time) lets the reader correlate treatment with the EEG change. 'Successfully treated' is an interpretation. Recording continues because seizures often recur after benzodiazepines. The nursing chart does not replace an annotation on the EEG itself.

taskFlow.title: Convulsion begins
taskFlow.description: Twenty minutes later the patient has a generalized tonic-clonic convulsion. He is lying flat; the nurse has stepped out to get the physician.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct first aid while help arrives?
options: Hold his arms and legs still so the electrodes stay in place
Put a padded bite block between his teeth to protect his tongue
Protect his head, time it, and turn him onto his side
Lift his head to give sips of water so he does not choke
taskFlow.explanation: First aid during a convulsion: protect from injury, keep rails up/padded, time the event, and place the patient on his side to keep the airway clear (calling for help per protocol). Do not restrain the limbs. Never put anything in the mouth. Nothing is given by mouth to a patient who is seizing or not fully awake.

starterCases.title: Quality Assurance: Unequal Calibration Deflections
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for evaluation of headaches

history.eventDescription: Recurrent headaches, EEG ordered to rule out seizures

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior dominant rhythm at 9 Hz

objectives: Rule out setting errors before blaming the amplifier
Remove a failing amplifier from service instead of compensating
Calculate pen deflection from calibration voltage and sensitivity

taskFlow.title: Uneven calibration
taskFlow.description: At the start of the study, a 50 uV square-wave calibration should give equal deflections on every channel. Most channels match, but channels 5 and 9 are visibly larger than the rest.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist check first?
options: Order a new amplifier from the vendor before the patient arrives
Lower the sensitivity on channels 5 and 9 until they look equal
Start recording and mention the difference in the technical note
Confirm identical sensitivity and filters, then recalibrate
taskFlow.explanation: Unequal calibration often comes from a channel left at a different sensitivity or filter setting, so verify settings are identical and repeat the calibration. Recording with known unequal gain risks false asymmetries. Adjusting individual channels to 'look equal' hides a fault. Ordering parts is premature before the cause is known.

taskFlow.title: The fault persists
taskFlow.description: All channels are confirmed at the same settings. The repeat calibration shows channels 5 and 9 still about 10% larger than the others, the same as before.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do now?
options: Proceed, since a 10% error is small enough to ignore in routine EEG
Proceed but avoid reading any asymmetry in channels 5 and 9
Reset the software and proceed if the error drops below 10%
Tag the system out of service and use the backup
taskFlow.explanation: A reproducible gain error with correct settings indicates an amplifier problem; the equipment is tagged out, the supervisor notified, and backup equipment used. 'Small' gain errors can create or mask an asymmetry. Working around channels 5 and 9 still produces an inaccurate record, and a software reset does not repair hardware.

taskFlow.title: Check the backup system
taskFlow.description: On the backup system, the technologist applies a 50 uV calibration signal with the sensitivity set to 7 uV/mm.
taskFlow.question: What deflection should each channel show?
options: About 350 mm
About 14 mm
About 7.1 mm
About 0.14 mm
taskFlow.explanation: Deflection (mm) = signal (uV) / sensitivity (uV/mm) = 50 / 7 = 7.1 mm. Multiplying (50 x 7 = 350) is the classic error. 7/50 = 0.14 mm inverts the formula. 14 mm would be the deflection at 3.5 uV/mm, not 7 uV/mm.

taskFlow.title: Document the change
taskFlow.description: The study is completed on the backup system. The technologist writes the technical note and the equipment log.
taskFlow.question: What should be recorded?
options: The faulty channels' gain error in the clinical impression
Nothing, since the study was completed without problems
The failed calibration, tag-out, backup used, and notification
Only that backup equipment was used, with no further detail needed
taskFlow.explanation: The equipment log and technical note should show the failed calibration, that the system was tagged out, the backup system used (with its normal calibration), and supervisor notification. Noting only the backup omits the fault history needed for QA. 'Completed fine' is not a reason to skip equipment documentation. The clinical impression is the physician's, and equipment faults are not interpreted findings.

learningLinks.label: Domain IV: Quality Assurance & Equipment Maintenance

starterCases.title: High Impedance Troubleshooting - Eight Electrodes
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for evaluation of headaches

history.eventDescription: Patient reports frequent headaches over past 3 months

eegSummary.background: Unable to assess due to artifacts
eegSummary.artifacts: High impedance artifacts in multiple electrodes

objectives: Fix high impedance at the electrode, not with settings
Recognize a salt bridge from smeared paste between electrodes
Identify an electrode pop by its single-electrode field

taskFlow.title: Impedance check
taskFlow.description: After hookup, impedances at Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, C3, C4, P3 and P4 read above 10 kOhm; all other electrodes are below 3 kOhm.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Clean, lightly abrade, and reapply paste at each high electrode
Increase amplifier gain on the affected channels to compensate
Record anyway and note high impedance on the requisition
Use a montage that leaves out the eight high-impedance electrodes
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS standards call for impedances below 5 kOhm and reasonably balanced. The fix is at the source: clean the skin, abrade gently, reapply paste/gel and reseat. Gain changes amplify the noise along with the signal. Recording with eight poor contacts gives a noisy, unreliable study, and leaving out those electrodes drops most of the parasagittal coverage.

taskFlow.title: A flat channel
taskFlow.description: After a quick re-prep, all impedances are under 5 kOhm. But the F3-C3 channel is now very low in amplitude compared to F4-C4, and both F3 and C3 read unusually low impedance.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: A broken lead wire at the F3 electrode cup
A salt bridge from paste smeared between F3 and C3
A real decrease in left frontal brain activity
The low frequency filter set too high on that channel
taskFlow.explanation: A salt bridge (paste or gel connecting two electrodes) short-circuits them so they record nearly the same potential; the channel between them becomes low and flat, often with very low impedances. Fix it by cleaning between the sites and reapplying separately. Calling it reduced brain activity misreads an artifact. A broken lead would give high impedance and noise, and a filter error would not explain the low impedance readings.

taskFlow.title: Sudden sharp transients
taskFlow.description: Twenty minutes into recording, abrupt steep transients appear only in channels that contain P4 (C4-P4 and P4-O2), opposite in direction, with nothing in neighboring channels.
taskFlow.question: What is this?
options: Electrode pop at P4
Muscle artifact from the jaw
Eye movement artifact
A right parietal spike
taskFlow.explanation: An electrode pop is a sudden change in electrode-skin potential at one electrode; it appears only in derivations that include that electrode, with opposite deflections in the two bipolar channels and no field spreading to neighbors. A cerebral spike would have a field involving adjacent electrodes. Muscle artifact is fast, frontotemporal, and not limited to one electrode. Eye movement artifact is frontal, not parietal.

taskFlow.title: Document the hookup
taskFlow.description: P4 is re-prepped and the pops stop. The technologist is finishing the technical note.
taskFlow.question: What should the note include about electrodes?
options: Nothing about electrodes, because the problems were corrected
A statement that F3-C3 showed reduced left frontal activity
Only that impedances were acceptable at the start of the study
Final impedances, the bridge and pop, and when each was fixed
taskFlow.explanation: Good documentation lists final impedance values and any artifacts that affected the record (salt bridge F3-C3, pop at P4) with the time each was corrected, so the reader can judge those segments. 'Acceptable at the start' is inaccurate here. Omitting fixed problems hides affected segments. The low F3-C3 amplitude was a salt bridge, so describing it as reduced brain activity would misreport an artifact as a cerebral finding.

starterCases.title: Montage Selection - Phase Reversal at T3
starterCases.chiefComplaint: EEG for evaluation of possible seizures

history.eventDescription: Patient reports episodes of staring and unresponsiveness

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior dominant rhythm at 10 Hz
eegSummary.epileptiform: Focal spikes in left temporal region
eegSummary.focalFindings: Left temporal spikes with phase reversal at T3

objectives: Localize by amplitude in referential and by phase reversal in bipolar
Work out polarity using input 1 minus input 2, negative up
Recognize ear-reference contamination and choose a better reference

taskFlow.title: Referential view
taskFlow.description: In a linked-ears referential montage (each electrode minus A1+A2), a sharp transient is largest in the T3 channel, smaller in F7 and T5, and smallest in Fp1 and O1. All channels deflect upward.
taskFlow.question: In this referential montage, how is the maximum located?
options: By the channel with the earliest onset of the wave
By the channel with the highest amplitude
By looking for a phase reversal between channels
By the channel whose deflection points downward
taskFlow.explanation: In a referential montage every channel shares the same input 2, so the electrode closest to the source shows the largest deflection; here T3. Phase reversals are the localizing sign in bipolar chains, not in referential montages (an apparent reversal there suggests an active reference). Onset timing and direction alone do not define the maximum.

taskFlow.title: Bipolar confirmation
taskFlow.description: In the left temporal chain (Fp1-F7, F7-T3, T3-T5, T5-O1), with the convention input 1 minus input 2 and negative = up: F7-T3 deflects DOWN and T3-T5 deflects UP at the same instant.
taskFlow.question: What does this show?
options: A negative phase reversal at T3, the most negative point
No localization is possible, because the two channels disagree
A negative phase reversal at T5, the end of the chain
A positive phase reversal at T3, the most positive point
taskFlow.explanation: F7-T3 down means F7 minus T3 is positive, so T3 is more negative than F7. T3-T5 up means T3 minus T5 is negative, so T3 is more negative than T5. T3 is the shared electrode and the most negative point: a negative phase reversal at T3 (T7 in modern nomenclature). Calling it positive flips the convention. T5 is not the shared electrode. Opposite deflections in adjacent channels are the localizing sign, not a contradiction.

taskFlow.title: Reference contamination
taskFlow.description: Reviewing the linked-ears montage again, the technologist notices the same transient appearing as a small DOWNWARD deflection in right-sided channels (Fp2, F4, O2), where the bipolar chains show nothing.
taskFlow.question: What is the best explanation and action?
options: The spike is bilateral; report independent right-sided spikes
A1 sits in the spike field; re-reference to Cz for review
The right electrodes are high impedance; re-prep them now
Raise the low frequency filter to remove the downward waves
taskFlow.explanation: A1 lies near the left temporal field, so the linked-ears reference becomes negative during the spike. Channels whose input 1 is quiet (right side) then show input 1 minus a negative reference = positive = downward deflection. The fix is a reference away from the field, such as Cz (or a quiet alternative). The bipolar chains show no right-sided activity, so it is not bilateral. Impedance problems do not produce time-locked mirror waves, and filtering does not remove a reference problem.

taskFlow.title: Technical description
taskFlow.description: On a Cz reference the transient is maximal at T3 with spread to F7 and T5, and no right-sided activity. It recurs about 8 times during drowsiness and sleep.
taskFlow.question: Which entry best fits the technical description?
options: Sharp transients at A1, suggesting a left ear electrode artifact
Bilateral temporal spikes, left greater than right, in sleep
Left temporal lobe epilepsy confirmed, seen mostly in sleep
Left mid-temporal sharp transients; T3 reversal; more in sleep
taskFlow.explanation: The description gives location, localizing evidence (phase reversal at T3 in bipolar, maximum at T3 on Cz reference) and state dependence, without diagnosing. 'Temporal lobe epilepsy confirmed' is a diagnosis. 'Bilateral' repeats the reference-contamination error. Calling it an A1 artifact misreads a cerebral field that A1 simply shared.

learningLinks.label: Domain II: Montages & Strategy During Recording

starterCases.title: Activation Procedures - Hyperventilation and Absence
starterCases.chiefComplaint: EEG for evaluation of absence seizures

history.eventDescription: Teacher reports episodes of staring and unresponsiveness lasting 10-15 seconds

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior dominant rhythm at 9 Hz

objectives: Screen for hyperventilation contraindications before starting
Tell normal hyperventilation build-up from spike-and-wave
Test responsiveness and complete the post-HV recording

taskFlow.title: Screen before HV
taskFlow.description: Before hyperventilation (deep breaths at about 20 per minute for 3-5 minutes), the technologist reviews the intake form for the 12-year-old.
taskFlow.question: Which history item means HV should be held until the physician is consulted?
options: Staring spells reported by her teacher
Skipped breakfast this morning
Seasonal allergies treated with nasal spray
Sickle cell disease
taskFlow.explanation: HV causes cerebral vasoconstriction and is generally avoided in sickle cell disease (also recent stroke, moyamoya, significant cardiopulmonary disease, recent intracranial hemorrhage). A skipped meal can increase HV build-up (low blood glucose) and should be documented, but is not a contraindication. Allergies are irrelevant, and suspected absences are the reason HV is especially useful.

taskFlow.title: Build-up at 60 seconds
taskFlow.description: No contraindications are found. At 60 s of good effort, high-amplitude generalized 2-3 Hz rhythmic delta appears, maximal frontally, without spikes. She keeps counting breaths aloud without pause.
taskFlow.question: How should the technologist handle this?
options: Stop HV immediately and notify the physician of a seizure
Recognize it as HV build-up and continue the procedure
Switch to photic stimulation since HV is now positive
Lower the sensitivity and record it as frontal slowing
taskFlow.explanation: Generalized high-amplitude delta during HV is a normal build-up in children, especially without spikes and with preserved responsiveness (continued counting). Stopping and calling a seizure overreacts. HV is not 'positive' just because it slows, and calling it focal frontal slowing misdescribes a normal response.

taskFlow.title: Spike-and-wave with staring
taskFlow.description: At 2 minutes, generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave begins. She stops counting and stares straight ahead.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do during the discharge?
options: Keep coaching her to breathe faster until the burst stops
Stop the study and wait for her to be fully alert again
Give a test word, then check recall and annotate
Increase the sensitivity so the spikes show more clearly
taskFlow.explanation: During a discharge the key technologist task is clinical correlation: present a word or simple command, check recall afterward, and annotate onset, offset and behavior. Pushing her to breathe harder adds nothing and ignores the event. Stopping the study loses the post-event data. The discharge is already high in amplitude; increasing sensitivity would only make it overlap neighboring channels and is not the priority.

taskFlow.title: After the event
taskFlow.description: The burst stops after 9 s; she cannot recall the test word. HV ends at 3 minutes. Her breathing returns to normal.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do next?
options: Repeat HV at once to capture a second event for comparison
Keep recording at least 1 minute after HV; note effort
Remove the electrodes, since the diagnosis is now clear
Start photic stimulation right away while she is still primed
taskFlow.explanation: Recording continues for at least 1 minute after HV to document recovery, and the technologist notes HV duration, effort quality, the discharge time, and the failed recall. Ending the study early skips post-HV data and the remaining protocol, and 'diagnosis is clear' is not a technologist judgment. Photic should follow after recovery, and a second HV run is not standard.

starterCases.title: Artifact Troubleshooting - 60 Hz in All Channels
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for evaluation

history.eventDescription: Routine evaluation

eegSummary.background: Obscured by 60 Hz artifact
eegSummary.artifacts: 60 Hz line noise in all channels

objectives: Link 60 Hz in every channel to the ground or reference
Remove interference sources without creating a ground loop
Use and document a notch filter only as a last resort

taskFlow.title: Every channel is noisy
taskFlow.description: Shortly after starting, regular 60 Hz sinusoidal activity appears in all channels at roughly the same amplitude, obscuring the background.
taskFlow.question: Which problem should be checked first?
options: The ground electrode or a shared reference
A real cerebral rhythm
Muscle artifact from clenching
A single high-impedance electrode on the scalp
taskFlow.explanation: Interference in every channel points to something common to all of them, such as a poor ground or a shared reference contact. A single bad electrode only affects channels containing it. Muscle artifact is irregular and fast, not a fixed 60 Hz sinusoid, and nothing cerebral oscillates at exactly line frequency.

taskFlow.title: Find the bad contact
taskFlow.description: Impedance check: the ground electrode reads 25 kOhm; all others are 2-4 kOhm.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Add a second ground from the patient's bed monitor
Turn on the 60 Hz notch filter and continue recording
Lower the high frequency filter to 15 Hz on all channels
Re-prep and reapply the ground electrode, then recheck
taskFlow.explanation: Fix the source: re-prep the ground so its impedance matches the others, then recheck. A second ground to another device creates a ground loop, a patient safety hazard. The notch filter only hides the problem. A 15 Hz HFF would hide the noise but also blunt spikes and muscle activity, and it leaves the bad ground in place.

taskFlow.title: It comes back
taskFlow.description: With the ground fixed, the 60 Hz is gone, but it returns whenever the family plugs a phone charger into the outlet beside the bed and drapes the cord over the electrode cables.
taskFlow.question: What is the best next step?
options: Unplug the charger and route cords away from the leads
Increase the sensitivity so the EEG overwhelms the noise
Plug the EEG into the same outlet strip as the charger
Bundle the charger cord tightly together with the leads
taskFlow.explanation: Nearby power cords radiate 60 Hz fields that couple into electrode leads; remove the source and route cables away from power cords. Sharing a power strip and bundling cords together worsens coupling. Changing sensitivity scales both EEG and noise, so it does not help.

taskFlow.title: Notch filter decision
taskFlow.description: Later, a small residual 60 Hz appears in two channels despite good impedances and no nearby devices. The reader wants it reduced.
taskFlow.question: If the notch filter is used, what must the technologist do?
options: Annotate when it was turned on in the technical record
Leave it off the record because notch filters do not alter EEG
Use it from the start of every study to save troubleshooting time
Turn off the high frequency filter to balance out the notch
taskFlow.explanation: The notch filter is a last resort after sources are fixed. When used, its use and timing must be documented, because it attenuates activity near 60 Hz and can blunt sharp waveforms and mask poor contacts. Notch filters do alter the signal, routine use hides electrode problems, and turning off the HFF only adds noise.

starterCases.title: Special Protocols - ICU Continuous Monitoring Seizures
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG monitoring for altered mental status

history.eventDescription: Patient with altered mental status, possible nonconvulsive status epilepticus

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing, theta-delta range
eegSummary.epileptiform: Recurrent electrographic seizures (frontal-onset rhythmic delta evolving in frequency, amplitude and spread; 5 x 3 min in 60 min = electrographic status epilepticus); interictal GPDs at 1.5 Hz with triphasic morphology
eegSummary.focalFindings: Seizures begin frontally and spread to a generalized distribution

objectives: Recognize evolution as the hallmark of an electrographic seizure
Apply the ACNS 2021 20%-of-an-hour status threshold
Describe periodic discharges in ACNS 2021 terms

taskFlow.title: Evolving rhythmic activity
taskFlow.description: On ICU cEEG, rhythmic 2 Hz delta begins frontally, evolves to 4 Hz theta with rising amplitude, and spreads to a generalized distribution over 30 s, then stops.
taskFlow.question: What feature makes this a likely seizure rather than background?
options: The 30 s duration, longer than most sleep events
The frontal start, which is typical of artifact
Evolution in frequency, amplitude and location
The high amplitude of the delta compared to before
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 counts a pattern with definite evolution lasting at least 10 s as an electrographic seizure. Evolution (changing frequency, amplitude and spread) is the key feature. High amplitude of the delta alone does not define a seizure. Frontal onset does not make it artifact, and duration alone does not separate seizures from other patterns.

taskFlow.title: Notify
taskFlow.description: The technologist has marked the event. The patient's eyes are deviated slightly to the right but there is no limb movement.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Mark it and wait for the next scheduled review by the reader
Notify only if limb jerking appears on the video
Lower the display sensitivity and continue watching
Notify the physician and nurse now, per the cEEG protocol
taskFlow.explanation: Possible electrographic seizures on cEEG are reported to the team immediately per protocol; subtle signs such as eye deviation are documented too. Waiting for routine review delays treatment. Nonconvulsive seizures need no limb movement to matter. Display changes do not address the clinical situation.

taskFlow.title: How much seizure per hour?
taskFlow.description: Over the next 60 minutes, the patient has 5 separate seizures lasting 3 minutes each, with no single seizure longer than 3 minutes.
taskFlow.question: Does this meet the ACNS 2021 definition of electrographic status epilepticus?
options: No, because no single seizure lasted 10 minutes
Yes, because it totals 15 min, which is 25% of the hour
Yes, because any 5 seizures in an hour are always status
No, because at least 30 minutes of seizure are needed
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021: electrographic status epilepticus is a seizure lasting at least 10 continuous minutes OR seizures totaling at least 20% of any 60-minute period. Here 5 x 3 = 15 min; 15 / 60 = 25%, which is at least 20%, so it qualifies. The 'no single 10-minute seizure' option ignores the cumulative criterion. 30 minutes is an older clinical definition. Seizure count alone is not a criterion.

taskFlow.title: Interictal pattern
taskFlow.description: Between seizures, the record shows generalized discharges recurring at regular intervals of about 1.5 per second, each with a blunted triphasic shape.
taskFlow.question: Which description uses ACNS 2021 terminology?
options: Generalized rhythmic delta activity at 1.5 Hz
Bilateral PLEDs firing about every 0.7 seconds
Triphasic waves at 1.5 Hz, suggesting a metabolic cause
GPDs at 1.5 Hz with triphasic morphology
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 uses main term 1 (Generalized) plus main term 2 (Periodic Discharges), with frequency and morphology modifiers; 'triphasic' is a morphology modifier, not a stand-alone term, and 'suggesting a metabolic cause' is interpretation. PLEDs is the obsolete name for lateralized PDs and is not generalized. Rhythmic delta has no interval between waves, unlike discrete periodic discharges.

learningLinks.label: Domain II: Event Monitoring & Emergency Response

starterCases.title: Left MCA Stroke - Focal Slowing and Deterioration
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acute onset right-sided weakness and speech difficulty

history.eventDescription: Patient presented with sudden onset right-sided weakness (face and arm > leg) and non-fluent speech. History of hypertension and atrial fibrillation.

eegSummary.background: Continuous polymorphic delta slowing over the left frontal, central, temporal and parietal regions (F3, C3, T3, P3); right hemisphere normal
eegSummary.focalFindings: Focal slowing over the left MCA territory (F3, C3, T3, P3); no right-sided slowing

objectives: Describe focal polymorphic delta over the left MCA territory
Adjust hookup and reactivity testing for anticoagulation and aphasia
Recognize and report neurologic deterioration during the study

taskFlow.title: Hookup on warfarin
taskFlow.description: The 68-year-old is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation and was admitted 2 hours ago with right face/arm weakness and non-fluent speech. A bedside EEG is ordered.
taskFlow.question: Which electrode approach fits this patient?
options: Subdermal needle electrodes to save time in an acute stroke
Disc electrodes and gentle prep; no subdermal needles
Collodion only, after shaving each electrode site first
Vigorous abrasion to get every impedance below 1 kOhm
taskFlow.explanation: With anticoagulation, minimize skin trauma: standard disc electrodes, gentle prep, and no needles. Needles risk bleeding. Aggressive abrasion for sub-1 kOhm values is unnecessary (below 5 kOhm and balanced is the standard) and raises bleeding and infection risk. Shaving is not routine and causes small nicks.

taskFlow.title: Describe the asymmetry
taskFlow.description: The record shows continuous irregular 1-3 Hz delta over F3, C3, T3 and P3 that does not change with eye opening. The right hemisphere has a normal 8-9 Hz posterior rhythm. No sharp waves are seen.
taskFlow.question: Which description is accurate?
options: Continuous left hemispheric polymorphic delta
Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta
Left lateralized periodic discharges at 1-3 Hz
Generalized slowing, left more than right
taskFlow.explanation: Irregular, continuous, non-reactive delta confined to one hemisphere is focal (here hemispheric) polymorphic delta activity, the typical finding over an acute cortical/subcortical lesion. LPDs are repetitive discharges with intervals, not continuous irregular delta. FIRDA is intermittent, rhythmic and bifrontal. 'Generalized' contradicts the normal right hemisphere.

taskFlow.title: Testing reactivity
taskFlow.description: To test reactivity, the technologist asks the patient to 'close your eyes, relax, and open them when I say so.' He looks puzzled and does not respond, but he follows when the technologist points to her own eyes and gestures.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to continue?
options: Repeat the same full sentence louder until he responds
Open his eyes yourself each time without telling him
Short one-step commands with gestures; annotate each
Write 'uncooperative' and skip the eye-opening portion
taskFlow.explanation: Aphasic patients may follow simple one-step commands or gestures; demonstrate, keep commands short, and annotate what was done and how he responded. Labeling him 'uncooperative' loses useful data. Louder repetition of a complex instruction does not help a language deficit. Passive eye opening is a fallback, but he should be told what is happening, and he can participate here.

taskFlow.title: He changes
taskFlow.description: Thirty minutes in, he becomes hard to rouse and vomits once. The left-sided delta has become higher in amplitude and now spreads into the right frontal channels.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Note 'patient sleepy' and continue recording without calling
Finish the protocol first, then mention it to the nurse
Remove the electrodes and send him back to his room
Turn him on his side, get the nurse and physician, annotate
taskFlow.explanation: A sudden drop in alertness with vomiting in an anticoagulated stroke patient may mean bleeding or swelling: protect the airway (side position), get the nurse/physician immediately per protocol, and annotate times and observations. Finishing the protocol first delays care. Writing 'sleepy' misses the change. Removing electrodes loses the record and does not get help.

starterCases.title: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) Stroke - Midline Slowing
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acute onset left leg weakness and urinary incontinence

history.eventDescription: Patient presented with sudden onset left leg weakness (leg > arm > face), urinary incontinence, and behavioral changes (apathy, abulia). History of hypertension.

eegSummary.background: Focal polymorphic delta slowing over the right frontal parasagittal and midline regions (F4, Fz, Cz), maximal at F4
eegSummary.focalFindings: Focal slowing maximal at F4 with spread to Fz and Cz; Fp1/Fp2 slow waves partly due to eye movement

objectives: Add midline and transverse chains for parasagittal findings
Separate frontal eye movement artifact from cerebral delta
Locate a negative phase reversal at F4 in a transverse chain

taskFlow.title: Plan the montages
taskFlow.description: The 72-year-old has left leg weakness greater than arm, incontinence and apathy. The lab's default display is a longitudinal bipolar montage of the two parasagittal and two temporal chains.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist add to cover the likely region?
options: Nasopharyngeal electrodes for the medial frontal lobe
A midline chain (Fz-Cz-Pz) and a transverse montage
A Cz reference montage only, without bipolar chains
Extra temporal electrodes such as T1 and T2
taskFlow.explanation: Leg weakness and frontal behavioral change point to medial frontal/parasagittal cortex, near the midline. A midline chain and transverse (coronal) montage show activity at and across the vertex. T1/T2 and nasopharyngeal electrodes target the anterior/mesial temporal region. A Cz reference sits right in the area of interest and would mask activity there.

taskFlow.title: Frontal slow waves
taskFlow.description: Large slow waves appear in Fp1 and Fp2. The patient's eyes are open and drifting slowly. The technologist cannot tell whether the waves are cerebral.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to tell eye movement from cerebral delta?
options: Assume they are cerebral because the lesion is frontal
Add eye leads at the outer canthi and below one eye
Close her eyes with tape for the rest of the recording
Raise the low frequency filter to 5 Hz to remove the waves
taskFlow.explanation: Eye electrodes (outer canthi and infraorbital) show whether slow waves follow eye movement. Eye artifact is largest at the eye leads and Fp sites and falls off steeply, small at F4/Fz and essentially absent at Cz, whereas cerebral delta has a scalp field that persists posteriorly. A 5 Hz LFF would also erase real delta. Taping the eyes is not appropriate. Assuming cerebral origin skips the check.

taskFlow.title: Transverse chain polarity
taskFlow.description: In the transverse chain F8-F4, F4-Fz, Fz-F3, F3-F7, with input 1 minus input 2 and negative = up, each delta wave deflects DOWN in F8-F4 and UP in F4-Fz. Channels Fz-F3 and F3-F7 show little.
taskFlow.question: Where is the negative maximum?
options: F8
F4
Between F4 and Fz
Fz
taskFlow.explanation: F8-F4 down means F8 minus F4 is positive, so F4 is more negative than F8. F4-Fz up means F4 minus Fz is negative, so F4 is more negative than Fz. The shared electrode, F4, is the most negative point: a negative phase reversal at F4. F8 and Fz are each less negative than F4, and a maximum between F4 and Fz would not make F4-Fz deflect up.

taskFlow.title: Write the description
taskFlow.description: Eye leads confirm that most of the Fp1/Fp2 slow waves are eye movement. Polymorphic delta persists at F4 with spread to Fz and Cz.
taskFlow.question: Which technical description is appropriate?
options: Right frontal lobe dysfunction, likely causing her abulia
Delta maximal at F4, spreading to Fz/Cz; Fp waves are eye movement
Right ACA infarct with frontal slowing, consistent with the imaging
Bifrontal slowing over Fp1, Fp2 and Fz due to the stroke
taskFlow.explanation: The description names the activity, its maximum (F4) and field (Fz, Cz), and records that Fp slow waves were shown to be eye artifact. Linking the finding to an infarct or to symptoms is interpretation by the physician. 'Bifrontal slowing over Fp1, Fp2' ignores the eye-lead evidence.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: EEG Artifacts: Recognition & Differentiation

starterCases.title: Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) Stroke - Absent Right PDR
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acute onset visual field defect

history.eventDescription: Patient presented with sudden onset left homonymous hemianopia (visual field defect). History of hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

eegSummary.background: Loss of the posterior dominant rhythm with polymorphic delta over the right occipital region (O2, P4, T6); normal 9 Hz PDR on the left
eegSummary.focalFindings: Focal slowing over the right occipital region (O2, P4, T6) with absent right PDR
eegSummary.activation: Hyperventilation omitted (stroke 6 hours earlier; reason documented); photic stimulation performed

objectives: Identify the abnormal side when one occipital rhythm is lost
Rule out technical causes before reporting an asymmetry
Omit hyperventilation after acute stroke and keep a hemianopic patient safe

taskFlow.title: Which side is abnormal?
taskFlow.description: With eyes closed, a 9 Hz posterior rhythm is clear over O1 and attenuates with eye opening. Over O2 there is no alpha; instead there is irregular 2-3 Hz delta. The patient has a left visual field defect.
taskFlow.question: Which side shows the abnormality?
options: Left, because its alpha has higher amplitude
Right, where the alpha is replaced by delta
Both, since the rhythms do not match
Neither, since a 9 Hz rhythm is present
taskFlow.explanation: Loss of the posterior rhythm with focal delta marks the abnormal side, here the right occipital region (consistent with a left field defect, but that link is the physician's). The higher-amplitude side is not automatically abnormal. A normal rhythm on one side does not make the record symmetric, and the left side is behaving normally.

taskFlow.title: Rule out a technical cause
taskFlow.description: Before annotating a right occipital abnormality, the technologist wants to be sure the asymmetry is real.
taskFlow.question: Which check comes first?
options: Check O2 impedance and position and the channel settings
Ask the patient to keep the eyes open for the rest of the study
Switch to a 30 s page to make the alpha easier to spot
Increase the sensitivity on the right side until alpha appears
taskFlow.explanation: A misplaced or high-impedance O2, or a channel at a different sensitivity or filter, can mimic asymmetry; verify placement (measurement), impedance and identical settings before documenting. Changing sensitivity on one side creates a false comparison. Page width does not create alpha, and eyes open would abolish the PDR on both sides.

taskFlow.title: Protocol request
taskFlow.description: Everything checks out. The requisition lists the lab's routine protocol, which includes 3 minutes of hyperventilation and photic stimulation. The stroke was 6 hours ago.
taskFlow.question: How should the technologist handle activation?
options: Do HV for 1 minute instead of 3 as a compromise
Skip both HV and photic, since any activation is unsafe
Omit HV, do photic, and document why HV was omitted
Do HV fully as ordered, since it is a routine test
taskFlow.explanation: HV causes cerebral vasoconstriction and is withheld after a recent stroke; the technologist omits it, clarifies with the physician per policy, and documents the reason. A shorter HV still carries the risk. Doing it 'as ordered' ignores the contraindication. Photic stimulation is not contraindicated and can still be performed.

taskFlow.title: Getting up after the study
taskFlow.description: After electrode removal, the patient wants to walk to the bathroom alone. He has a left homonymous hemianopia and has bumped into the doorframe on his left once already.
taskFlow.question: What is the safest approach?
options: Ask him to wait while you clean the electrodes first
Walk on his left side so he learns to scan that side
Let him walk alone, since his leg strength is completely normal
Approach from his right, assist, and use fall precautions
taskFlow.explanation: With a left field defect he cannot see objects or people on his left; approach and speak from the intact right side, assist with walking, and follow the unit's fall precautions. Normal strength does not remove fall risk from a visual field loss. Rehabilitation scanning training is not the technologist's job here. Leaving him waiting may prompt him to get up alone.

starterCases.title: Basilar Artery Stroke - Reactivity and Deterioration
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acute onset diplopia, dysarthria, and decreased consciousness

history.eventDescription: Patient presented with sudden onset diplopia (double vision), dysarthria (slurred speech), vertigo, ataxia, and decreased consciousness. History of hypertension and diabetes.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing, theta-delta range, reduced reactivity
eegSummary.focalFindings: No focal findings; diffuse slowing with reduced reactivity

objectives: Test and annotate reactivity in an unresponsive ICU patient
Identify ECG artifact in an ear-referenced montage
Recognize and report a newly suppressed background

taskFlow.title: Testing reactivity
taskFlow.description: The 58-year-old is unresponsive 3 hours after onset of diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia. The background is diffuse 3-5 Hz slowing. The physician wants reactivity tested.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct approach?
options: Call his name once and stop if the EEG does not change
Test by switching the photic lights on and off near his eyes
Start with a sternal rub, since gentler stimuli rarely work
Escalate from voice to touch to noxious, annotating each
taskFlow.explanation: Reactivity is tested in a graded sequence (auditory: name called loudly; then tactile; then noxious per protocol), with each stimulus annotated at the moment it is given and the patient observed. Starting with noxious stimuli skips steps. Photic flashes are not a standard reactivity test in this setting. One weak stimulus is not an adequate test.

taskFlow.title: Regular sharp transients
taskFlow.description: Sharp, regularly recurring transients appear about once per second in many channels of the linked-ears referential montage, larger on the left. They occur at the same time as each QRS complex on the ECG channel.
taskFlow.question: What are they and what helps?
options: Pulse artifact under one electrode; re-prep that site
ECG artifact; review in bipolar or move the ear leads
Generalized periodic discharges; notify the physician
Ventilator artifact; ask the nurse to pause the ventilator
taskFlow.explanation: Transients locked to the QRS complex are ECG artifact, common in ear-referenced montages and in patients with short, wide necks. Bipolar montages (or moving/rereferencing the ear electrodes) reduce it. GPDs are not time-locked to the heartbeat. Pulse artifact is a slow wave following the QRS at one electrode over an artery, not sharp in many channels. Ventilator artifact follows breaths, and the ventilator should never be paused for EEG.

taskFlow.title: The background drops
taskFlow.description: Two hours later, all background activity falls below 10 uV with no response to stimulation. Impedances are unchanged and display sensitivity is 7 uV/mm.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Turn the display to 15 uV/mm to see the waves more clearly
Raise the low frequency filter to clean up the low trace
View at 2 uV/mm to inspect it, and notify per protocol
Wait for the morning reader, since the patient is already in a coma
taskFlow.explanation: A new drop of all activity below 10 uV (ACNS 2021 'suppression') with no reactivity is a significant change that is reported per protocol. Viewing at higher sensitivity (2 uV/mm) shows any low-amplitude activity. Raising filters removes real activity. Waiting delays notification of a change in an already critical patient. 15 uV/mm makes the display less sensitive, the wrong direction.

taskFlow.title: Document the change
taskFlow.description: The physician has been notified and has come to the bedside. The technologist updates the annotations and the technical log.
taskFlow.question: What should be documented?
options: The pattern name only, since the physician saw it live
A statement that the findings now meet brain death criteria
Only the time the physician arrived at the bedside
Time of change, stimuli, responses, sedation, who was told
taskFlow.explanation: Documentation should include when the change occurred, stimuli and responses, display/filter settings, current sedating medications (which affect amplitude and reactivity), and who was notified and when. Brain death determination is clinical and outside technologist scope. Arrival time alone omits the findings, and the physician's presence does not replace the record.

starterCases.title: Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome - Near-Normal EEG
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Acute onset vertigo, dysphagia, and hoarseness

history.eventDescription: Patient presented with sudden onset vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial pain loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and ataxia. History of hypertension.

eegSummary.background: Mild diffuse theta slowing; otherwise well organized
eegSummary.focalFindings: No focal slowing; the lateral medulla is not seen well by scalp EEG

objectives: Identify nystagmus artifact by opposite F7 and F8 deflections
Protect a dysphagic patient from aspiration during the study
Report a near-normal EEG without implying stroke is excluded

taskFlow.title: Rhythmic frontal deflections
taskFlow.description: The patient has nystagmus. In bipolar channels F7-T3 and F8-T4 (input 1 minus input 2, negative = up), rhythmic waves with a slow drift and a quick return appear, deflecting in opposite directions in F7-T3 and F8-T4 at the same moment.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely source?
options: Bilateral independent temporal sharp waves
Glossokinetic artifact from tongue movement
Lateral rectus muscle spikes in the frontal leads
Nystagmus: horizontal eye movement artifact
taskFlow.explanation: The cornea is positive relative to the retina. With a horizontal movement, the cornea approaches one side, making F7 positive and F8 negative (or the reverse), so F7-T3 and F8-T4 deflect in opposite directions; a slow drift with a fast return is the nystagmus signature. Temporal sharp waves would not mirror each other in time with eye beats. Glossokinetic artifact is diffuse slow activity with tongue movement. Lateral rectus spikes are brief fast potentials, not slow rhythmic drift.

taskFlow.title: A drink of water
taskFlow.description: The patient is hoarse, has trouble swallowing, and asks the technologist for a cup of water from the sink. The nursing plan on the door is not visible from the bedside.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Give small sips slowly, sitting upright, to keep her comfortable
Hold off and check with the nurse on swallowing status first
Give the water but keep suction ready at the bedside
Give ice chips instead, since they are safer than water
taskFlow.explanation: Hoarseness and dysphagia mean a high aspiration risk; stroke patients are usually NPO until a swallow screen is done. The technologist checks with the nurse before giving anything by mouth. Small sips, ice chips and 'suction ready' are all oral intake that has not been cleared.

taskFlow.title: Near-normal tracing
taskFlow.description: The posterior rhythm is 8-9 Hz and reactive, with mild diffuse theta and no focal slowing. The resident asks whether the EEG 'rules out a stroke.'
taskFlow.question: How should the technologist describe and respond?
options: Write 'no stroke seen' as the main finding of the study
Describe findings; the physician answers that question
Reply that a normal EEG rules out a brainstem stroke
Reply that EEG cannot show any stroke, wherever it is
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist documents what was recorded (reactive 8-9 Hz PDR, mild diffuse theta, no focal slowing) and leaves clinical conclusions to the interpreting physician. Scalp EEG reflects cortical activity, so a lesion in the lateral medulla may produce little change; a normal EEG does not exclude it. 'No stroke seen' is an interpretive claim. EEG does show many cortical strokes as focal slowing, so 'cannot show any stroke' is false.

taskFlow.title: Harder to wake
taskFlow.description: Near the end of the study the patient becomes difficult to rouse and vomits. The background now shows new diffuse delta, and her breathing is irregular.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Stop the study and wait for her to wake up on her own
Side position, call for help per protocol, annotate
Give her water to rinse after the vomiting episode
Note drowsiness and finish the last 10 minutes
taskFlow.explanation: New decreased consciousness, vomiting and irregular breathing may mean swelling compressing the brainstem (a known risk with cerebellar involvement in PICA strokes). Protect the airway by side positioning, call the nurse/rapid response per protocol, and annotate the time and findings. Treating it as drowsiness delays care, giving water risks aspiration, and waiting is unsafe.

starterCases.title: 10-20 Measurement Error Creating False Parietal Asymmetry
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for two episodes of transient confusion

history.eventDescription: Two brief episodes of staring and confusion lasting under a minute, no convulsive activity.

eegSummary.background: Well-organized posterior dominant rhythm, apparent left parietal amplitude asymmetry that resolves after electrode remeasurement.
eegSummary.focalFindings: Initially apparent C3-P3 > C4-P4 alpha amplitude; artifactual
eegSummary.artifacts: Technical: P3 placed 2.5 cm too far posterior

objectives: Calculate Fz and Cz positions from a nasion-inion distance
Convert head circumference percentages into lateral electrode spacing
Recognize interelectrode-distance error as a cause of false asymmetry

taskFlow.title: Midline Measurements
taskFlow.description: You measure the nasion-inion distance as 36 cm and the head circumference as 56 cm. You mark Fpz at 10% of the nasion-inion distance (3.6 cm above the nasion).
taskFlow.question: Measured from the nasion, where should Fz and Cz be marked?
options: Fz at 7.2 cm and Cz at 14.4 cm
Fz at 11.2 cm and Cz at 28 cm
Fz at 10.8 cm and Cz at 18 cm
Fz at 14.4 cm and Cz at 21.6 cm
taskFlow.explanation: Fz is 10% + 20% = 30% of the nasion-inion distance: 0.30 x 36 = 10.8 cm. Cz is at 50%: 0.50 x 36 = 18 cm. 7.2/14.4 cm uses 20%/40% (forgetting the initial 10% to Fpz). 11.2/28 cm wrongly uses the 56 cm circumference. 14.4/21.6 cm uses 40%/60%, which shifts both points posteriorly by one 10% step.

taskFlow.title: Lateral Spacing from Circumference
taskFlow.description: Next you lay out the circumferential line through Fpz, T3 and Oz using the 56 cm circumference. Fp1 sits 5% of the circumference to the left of Fpz.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct distance from Fp1 to F7 along the circumference line?
options: 5.6 cm, which is 10% of the circumference
2.8 cm, which is 5% of the circumference
7.2 cm, which is 20% of the nasion-inion line
11.2 cm, which is 20% of the circumference
taskFlow.explanation: Along the circumference, Fp1 is 5% from Fpz (0.05 x 56 = 2.8 cm) and each subsequent electrode (F7, T3, T5, O1) is a further 10%: 0.10 x 56 = 5.6 cm. 2.8 cm is the Fpz-Fp1 half-step, not Fp1-F7. 7.2 cm mixes in the nasion-inion line, which does not govern lateral spacing. 11.2 cm uses 20%, which is the spacing on the midline and coronal arcs, not on the circumference.

taskFlow.title: Unexpected Parietal Asymmetry
taskFlow.description: Twenty minutes into the recording, the alpha rhythm in C3-P3 is about 30% higher in amplitude than in C4-P4, while P3-O1 is lower than P4-O2. Impedances are all 2-4 kOhm. You re-measure and find P3 is 2.5 cm posterior to its correct position.
taskFlow.question: What best explains the pattern and what should you do?
options: A left parietal lesion; mark the asymmetry for the reader
High P3 impedance; abrade the skin and re-apply the paste
An amplifier gain error in C3-P3; recalibrate that channel
Unequal interelectrode distances; re-place P3 correctly
taskFlow.explanation: Moving P3 posteriorly lengthens the C3-P3 interelectrode distance (larger potential difference, higher amplitude) and shortens P3-O1 (smaller difference, lower amplitude). The fix is to re-measure and re-place P3 at the midpoint of C3-O1 and T5-Pz. Calling it a lesion is a cerebral attribution of a technical error. A gain error would not raise one channel and lower the adjacent one. Impedances are already low and balanced, so re-prepping alone leaves the position wrong.

taskFlow.title: Documenting the Correction
taskFlow.description: After P3 is moved, the C3-P3 and C4-P4 alpha amplitudes are symmetric. The first 20 minutes were recorded with the misplaced electrode.
taskFlow.question: How should you document this in the technologist notes?
options: Note P3 misplacement, the time it was corrected, and channels affected
Delete the first 20 minutes so the reader sees only correct data
Note a left parietal asymmetry that resolved during recording
Make no note, since the final placement was correct
taskFlow.explanation: The reader must know that the early asymmetry is technical: document the electrode, the error (2.5 cm posterior), the clock time of correction and the channels involved (those containing P3). Describing it as an asymmetry that resolved implies a physiologic change. Deleting raw data is never acceptable and removes the record of what happened. Omitting the note risks the reader interpreting the early segment as a true asymmetry.

starterCases.title: Time Constant and the 5 Hz Low-Filter Trap
starterCases.chiefComplaint: New right hand weakness and word-finding difficulty

history.eventDescription: Subacute right-sided weakness over 3 days; imaging shows a left frontotemporal mass.

eegSummary.background: Mildly slow background with continuous left temporal polymorphic delta at about 1 Hz when recorded with standard filters.
eegSummary.focalFindings: Left temporal polymorphic delta, markedly attenuated in the segment recorded with LFF 5 Hz
eegSummary.artifacts: Filter misconfiguration for part of the study

objectives: Measure the time constant from a square-wave calibration decay
Convert between time constant and low-frequency filter setting
Predict how a high LFF attenuates focal delta activity

taskFlow.title: Reading the Calibration Decay
taskFlow.description: Square-wave calibration at 30 mm/s: a 50 uV pulse produces a 5 mm deflection at 10 uV/mm. The deflection falls to 37% of its peak (1.85 mm) 9 mm after the onset of the pulse.
taskFlow.question: What are the time constant and the corresponding LFF?
options: TC 0.9 s; LFF 0.18 Hz
TC 0.1 s; LFF 1.6 Hz
TC 0.3 s; LFF 3.3 Hz
TC 0.3 s; LFF 0.53 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: The time constant is the time to decay to 37% of peak: 9 mm / 30 mm/s = 0.3 s. LFF = 1 / (2 pi x TC) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 0.3) = 1 / 1.885 = 0.53 Hz. 3.3 Hz is 1/TC without the 2 pi. 0.9 s treats 9 mm as tenths of a second (10 mm/s). TC 0.1 s / 1.6 Hz is a valid pair but not what was measured here.

taskFlow.title: A Mis-set Filter
taskFlow.description: Reviewing an earlier segment, you see the calibration pulse decays almost immediately. The settings log shows the LFF was set to 5 Hz for that segment instead of 1 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What time constant corresponds to an LFF of 5 Hz?
taskFlow.explanation: TC = 1 / (2 pi x LFF) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 5) = 1 / 31.4 = 0.032 s. 0.2 s is 1/LFF without 2 pi. 0.32 s is off by a factor of 10 (it would correspond to about 0.5 Hz). 5 s confuses the cutoff frequency with the time constant. A shorter TC means faster decay and more attenuation of slow activity.

taskFlow.title: What Happened to the Delta?
taskFlow.description: In the 1 Hz LFF segment, the left temporal channels show 100 uV polymorphic delta at about 1 Hz. In the 5 Hz LFF segment the same channels look nearly normal. A first-order 5 Hz LFF passes about 20% of a 1 Hz signal: 1 / sqrt(1 + 5^2) = 0.196.
taskFlow.question: How should the 5 Hz LFF segment be understood?
options: The filter converted the delta into faster theta activity
The filter removed most of the delta; the focus is still present
The delta resolved, suggesting the slowing is intermittent
The filter reduced the delta by only about 30%, so it is minor
taskFlow.explanation: At 1 Hz the 5 Hz LFF passes about 20%: 100 uV x 0.196 = about 20 uV, so the slowing is hidden, not gone. Calling it intermittent is the false-negative trap. Filters change amplitude (and phase), not the frequency of a component, so delta is not converted to theta. The 30% (-3 dB) attenuation applies only at the cutoff frequency itself (5 Hz), not at 1 Hz, which lies far below it.

taskFlow.title: Correcting the Recording
taskFlow.description: The study is still running. The reader will rely on the record to assess the focal slowing.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct next action?
options: Keep LFF 5 Hz and ask the reader to re-filter later
Keep LFF 5 Hz but double the sensitivity to restore amplitude
Set LFF to 0.1 Hz and HFF to 15 Hz to emphasize delta
Set LFF to 1 Hz or lower, recalibrate, and note the affected segment
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS minimum technical standards call for an LFF no higher than 1 Hz (TC at least 0.16 s) and an HFF no lower than 70 Hz for routine recording. Restore the standard settings, repeat calibration so the record shows them, and document the time span recorded at 5 Hz. Raising the gain does not undo frequency-selective attenuation and also amplifies faster activity. An HFF of 15 Hz removes legitimate fast activity and spikes. A digital record can be re-filtered to a higher LFF, but leaving a non-standard setting and relying on later correction is poor practice and fails if the original filter was hardware.

starterCases.title: Sensitivity Conversions and an Out-of-Calibration Channel
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG after a first unprovoked seizure

history.eventDescription: Single generalized convulsion on waking, preceded by a rising epigastric sensation.

eegSummary.background: Normal background
eegSummary.epileptiform: Occasional right temporal sharp transients for the reader to review
eegSummary.artifacts: One amplifier channel reads about 20% low on calibration

objectives: Convert pen deflection in mm to microvolts at any sensitivity
Quantify a calibration error as a percentage
Choose the correct response to a channel failing calibration

taskFlow.title: Measuring Amplitude
taskFlow.description: At a sensitivity of 7 uV/mm, the posterior dominant rhythm in P4-O2 measures 8 mm peak to trough.
taskFlow.question: What is the amplitude of the rhythm?
options: 87 uV
15 uV
56 uV
1.1 uV
taskFlow.explanation: Amplitude = deflection x sensitivity = 8 mm x 7 uV/mm = 56 uV. 15 uV adds the numbers (8 + 7). 1.1 uV divides (8 / 7), treating sensitivity as mm per uV. 87 uV is not derived from either value correctly.

taskFlow.title: Changing Sensitivity
taskFlow.description: A high-amplitude transient over the right temporal region is clipping, so you change the sensitivity to 20 uV/mm. The transient now measures 6 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is its amplitude, and how tall would it be at 7 uV/mm?
options: 26 uV; about 3.7 mm at 7 uV/mm
3.3 uV; about 0.5 mm at 7 uV/mm
120 uV; about 17 mm at 7 uV/mm
120 uV; about 8.4 mm at 7 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: 6 mm x 20 uV/mm = 120 uV. At 7 uV/mm: 120 / 7 = 17.1 mm, which is why it clipped. 8.4 mm multiplies 120 by 7 and divides by 100, mixing units. 3.3 uV divides 20 by 6. 26 uV adds 6 + 20. Raising the uV/mm number makes the display LESS sensitive (smaller deflections).

taskFlow.title: Calibration Check
taskFlow.description: At the end of the study you run a 50 uV calibration at 10 uV/mm. Every channel shows 5 mm except channel 9, which shows 4 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is channel 9's error, and what does a 4 mm wave in it truly represent?
options: 1 mm low; the difference is within tolerance
20% low; a 4 mm wave represents 50 uV
20% high; a 4 mm wave represents 32 uV
25% low; a 4 mm wave represents 40 uV
taskFlow.explanation: Expected 50 uV / 10 uV/mm = 5 mm; observed 4 mm. Error = (5 - 4) / 5 = 20% low. Because 50 uV in that channel draws only 4 mm, a 4 mm wave there is really 50 uV, not 40 uV. 20% high reverses the direction. 25% uses the observed value as the denominator (1/4). A 20% gain error is not within tolerance; channels should reproduce the calibration signal equally.

taskFlow.title: Responding to the Failed Channel
taskFlow.description: Repeating the calibration gives the same 4 mm result for channel 9. Other channels remain at 5 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is the appropriate response?
options: Reassign the reader's temporal channels without telling anyone
Lower channel 9 sensitivity by hand until it draws 5 mm
Document the fault, tag the amplifier out of service, notify biomed
Continue using the system and mention it at the next yearly service
taskFlow.explanation: A reproducible gain error is an equipment fault. Document the channel and the measured error in the record so amplitudes in that channel are not trusted, and remove the unit from service for biomedical engineering repair. Adjusting one channel by eye hides a hardware fault and is not a valid calibration. Deferring to annual maintenance leaves a known faulty amplifier in clinical use. Silently remapping channels leaves no record and does not repair the fault.

learningLinks.label: Domain IV: Quality Assurance & Equipment Maintenance

starterCases.title: Compressed Time Base - Frequency and Spike Duration
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Long-term monitoring for refractory focal seizures

history.eventDescription: Monthly episodes of staring with lip smacking and post-event confusion.

eegSummary.background: Normal background with intermittent right temporal slowing
eegSummary.epileptiform: Right temporal sharp transients reviewed at compressed time bases

objectives: Convert a page duration into an effective display speed
Calculate frequency correctly on a compressed time base
Classify a transient as spike or sharp wave by its duration

taskFlow.title: Frequency on a 20-Second Page
taskFlow.description: The review screen is 300 mm wide. A reviewer has set it to 20 s per page. A run of rhythmic right temporal slowing shows 9 waves spanning 45 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is the frequency of the run?
options: 9 Hz
3 Hz
1.5 Hz
6 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: 300 mm / 20 s = 15 mm/s. 45 mm / 15 mm/s = 3 s. 9 waves / 3 s = 3 Hz. 6 Hz assumes the standard 30 mm/s (45 mm = 1.5 s), the classic trap with compressed pages. 1.5 Hz halves instead of doubles. 9 Hz counts waves as if the run lasted 1 s.

taskFlow.title: Duration on a 15-Second Page
taskFlow.description: The page is changed to 15 s per page (300 mm / 15 s = 20 mm/s). A right temporal transient has a base width of 3 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is its duration and how is it classified?
options: 150 ms; sharp wave
300 ms; slow wave
100 ms; spike
60 ms; spike
taskFlow.explanation: Each mm at 20 mm/s = 1000 / 20 = 50 ms. 3 mm x 50 ms = 150 ms. Spikes last 20 to under 70 ms; sharp waves 70-200 ms, so 150 ms is a sharp wave. 100 ms assumes 30 mm/s (33 ms/mm). 60 ms divides 3 by 50. 300 ms assumes 10 mm/s.

taskFlow.title: Back to the Standard Page
taskFlow.description: To confirm the measurement, you return to a 10-s page (30 mm/s) and measure the same transient with the time cursor.
taskFlow.question: How wide should the 150 ms transient appear at 30 mm/s?
options: 3.0 mm
2.0 mm
4.5 mm
6.0 mm
taskFlow.explanation: Width = duration x speed = 0.150 s x 30 mm/s = 4.5 mm. 3 mm is the width at 20 mm/s (no change of speed applied). 2 mm divides instead of multiplying (3 x 20 / 30). 6 mm assumes 40 mm/s. A transient looks narrower and spikier on compressed pages, so durations should be confirmed at the standard time base or with cursors.

taskFlow.title: Technologist Documentation
taskFlow.description: The transient recurs about 12 times in the hour, each with a duration of about 150 ms and maximal negativity at T4.
taskFlow.question: Which note best fits technologist scope?
options: Right temporal lobe epilepsy confirmed; consider surgery referral
Normal variant sharp transients; no physician review needed
Right temporal sharp transients, about 150 ms, max T4, ~12/hour
Right temporal spikes, under 70 ms, frequent, highly epileptogenic
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist documents location, measured duration, maximum and frequency without diagnosing. Confirming an epilepsy syndrome or recommending surgery is interpretation outside scope. Calling them spikes under 70 ms contradicts the 150 ms measurement. Labelling them benign and bypassing physician review is both interpretation and a safety error.

starterCases.title: Sampling Rate, Nyquist, and an Aliased Artifact
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG for unexplained decreased responsiveness

history.eventDescription: Post-operative day 2 after cardiac surgery, fluctuating responsiveness.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing with a rhythmic 4 Hz component in several channels that proves to be aliased device artifact
eegSummary.artifacts: High-frequency device interference aliased into the theta range on a misconfigured system

objectives: Calculate how many samples define a spike at a given sampling rate
State the Nyquist frequency for a sampling rate
Explain why only a pre-digitization filter prevents aliasing

taskFlow.title: Samples per Spike
taskFlow.description: Your standard system digitizes at 256 Hz. A reader asks how well a 40 ms spike is represented.
taskFlow.question: About how many sample points fall within a 40 ms spike at 256 Hz?
options: 25 samples
10 samples
6 samples
102 samples
taskFlow.explanation: Samples = duration x sampling rate = 0.040 s x 256 samples/s = 10.24, about 10 samples (one every 1000 / 256 = 3.9 ms). 6 is what about 160 Hz would give. 25 divides 1000 by 40. 102 uses 0.4 s instead of 0.040 s.

taskFlow.title: The Portable Unit
taskFlow.description: An older portable unit used for this ICU study is configured to sample at 200 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What is the Nyquist frequency for this unit?
options: 200 Hz
400 Hz
100 Hz
70 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: Nyquist frequency = sampling rate / 2 = 200 / 2 = 100 Hz, the highest frequency that can be represented. 400 Hz is the minimum sampling rate needed for a 200 Hz signal (the inverse relationship). 200 Hz is the sampling rate itself. 70 Hz is a typical HFF setting, not the Nyquist limit; in practice sampling well above twice the HFF is preferred.

taskFlow.title: A Mysterious 4 Hz Rhythm
taskFlow.description: Several channels show a monotonous 4 Hz sinusoidal rhythm that starts exactly when a bedside device is switched on. Biomed reports the device emits interference at 196 Hz, and the unit's anti-alias filter has been found disabled.
taskFlow.question: What explains the 4 Hz activity?
options: Cerebral theta triggered by the device's electrical field
A 4 Hz subharmonic of 60 Hz line noise from the device
Aliasing: 196 Hz sampled at 200 Hz appears as 200 - 196 = 4 Hz
Muscle artifact from the device vibrating the bed
taskFlow.explanation: A signal above Nyquist (196 Hz > 100 Hz) is folded to a false low frequency: |196 - 200| = 4 Hz. The tight timing with the device and monotonous morphology fit artifact. 60 Hz line noise has no 4 Hz subharmonic; 60 / 4 = 15 is coincidence, not a mechanism. Calling it cerebral theta is interpretation driven by appearance. Muscle artifact is broadband and fast, not a pure 4 Hz sinusoid.

taskFlow.title: Removing the Alias
taskFlow.description: The reader asks whether lowering the display HFF to 15 Hz will remove the 4 Hz rhythm from the existing data.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct technical response?
options: No; enable the anti-alias filter or sample above 392 Hz
No; set a 5 Hz LFF to remove the 4 Hz rhythm instead
Yes, but only if a 60 Hz notch filter is also applied
Yes, a 15 Hz HFF removes all activity originating above 15 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: Once sampled, the aliased energy truly is 4 Hz in the data; no digital display filter can tell it from real 4 Hz activity. Aliasing is prevented only by an analog low-pass (anti-alias) filter applied before digitization below the Nyquist frequency, a sampling rate above twice the interference frequency (>392 Hz; at 256 Hz, 196 Hz would still alias to 60 Hz), or removing the source. A 15 Hz HFF passes 4 Hz. A notch at 60 Hz is irrelevant to a 4 Hz alias. A 5 Hz LFF would also strip genuine delta and theta from the ICU record.

starterCases.title: Referential Values to Bipolar Channels - Temporal Spike
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Focal impaired-awareness seizures with deja vu

history.eventDescription: Episodes of deja vu followed by staring and hand automatisms, about twice monthly.

eegSummary.background: Normal

objectives: Compute bipolar channel values from referential voltages
State pen direction from the sign of input 1 minus input 2
Localize a maximum shared by two electrodes (isoelectric channel)

taskFlow.title: Building F7-T3
taskFlow.description: Referenced to a quiet contralateral reference, a spike peak measures: Fp1 -10 uV, F7 -30 uV, T3 -90 uV, T5 -50 uV, O1 -10 uV. Convention: negative difference = upward deflection.
taskFlow.question: What does the F7-T3 channel show at the spike peak?
options: +60 uV, deflecting downward
-120 uV, deflecting upward
+120 uV, deflecting downward
-60 uV, deflecting upward
taskFlow.explanation: F7-T3 = F7 - T3 = (-30) - (-90) = +60 uV. A positive output deflects DOWN. -60 uV/up reverses the subtraction (T3 - F7). +/-120 uV adds the magnitudes instead of subtracting the voltages.

taskFlow.title: Building T3-T5
taskFlow.description: Using the same referential values (T3 -90 uV, T5 -50 uV), you now calculate the next channel in the chain.
taskFlow.question: What does T3-T5 show?
options: +140 uV, deflecting downward
+40 uV, deflecting downward
-40 uV, deflecting upward
-140 uV, deflecting upward
taskFlow.explanation: T3-T5 = T3 - T5 = (-90) - (-50) = -40 uV. A negative output deflects UP. +40/down reverses the order (T5 - T3). +/-140 uV adds 90 and 50 rather than subtracting signed values.

taskFlow.title: Locating the Maximum
taskFlow.description: In the longitudinal chain Fp1-F7, F7-T3, T3-T5, T5-O1: Fp1-F7 = +20 (down), F7-T3 = +60 (down), T3-T5 = -40 (up), T5-O1 = -40 (up).
taskFlow.question: Where is the maximum negativity?
options: F7, the largest downward channel's first input
T3, where the deflections reverse direction
T5, between the two upward channels
O1, at the posterior end of the chain
taskFlow.explanation: The deflections reverse between F7-T3 (down) and T3-T5 (up); the shared electrode, T3, is the maximum negativity, matching the referential value of -90 uV. F7 is only -30 uV; reading the largest channel's first electrode ignores the phase reversal. T5 is not shared by channels of opposite direction. O1 would be the answer only if all channels deflected the same way with amplitude growing toward O1 (end-of-chain).

taskFlow.title: A Second Spike with a Flat Channel
taskFlow.description: Another spike measures Fp1 -10, F7 -90, T3 -90, T5 -50, O1 -10 uV. The bipolar channels show Fp1-F7 down, F7-T3 nearly flat, and T3-T5 up.
taskFlow.question: How should this field be described?
options: No spike, because F7-T3 shows no deflection
Two independent spikes at Fp1 and T5
Equal maximum at F7 and T3 (isoelectric channel)
Maximum at Fp1, because the chain begins there
taskFlow.explanation: Fp1-F7 = -10 - (-90) = +80 (down); F7-T3 = -90 - (-90) = 0 (flat); T3-T5 = -90 - (-50) = -40 (up). The phase reversal straddles a flat channel, meaning F7 and T3 are equally and maximally negative. Fp1 is only -10 uV. Opposite deflections around one field are not two independent spikes. A flat channel between electrodes at equal potential does not mean no discharge.

starterCases.title: End-of-Chain Frontopolar Spike Missed by the Banana
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief nocturnal episodes of arousal with vocalization

history.eventDescription: Clusters of brief nocturnal arousals with grimacing and vocalization, several per night.

eegSummary.background: Normal
eegSummary.artifacts: Eye movement artifact in the frontopolar channels at times

objectives: Recognize an end-of-chain maximum in a longitudinal bipolar chain
Confirm localization with a transverse chain phase reversal
Separate frontopolar spikes from ocular artifact

taskFlow.title: Longitudinal Chain without Reversal
taskFlow.description: In the left temporal chain at the spike peak: Fp1-F7 -70 uV (up), F7-T3 -20 uV (up), T3-T5 -8 uV (up), T5-O1 -2 uV (up). All channels deflect upward, largest at the front.
