taskFlow.question: Where is the maximum negativity most likely?
options: O1, at the posterior end
T3, the middle of the chain
Fp1, at the anterior end of the chain
F7, the second input of the largest channel
taskFlow.explanation: Every channel is negative (input 1 more negative than input 2), so Fp1 < F7 < T3 < T5 < O1 in voltage: Fp1 is the most negative. With no phase reversal and amplitude largest at one end, the maximum is at the end of the chain (Fp1). T3 assumes a reversal that is not present. O1 reads the gradient backwards. F7 is less negative than Fp1 because Fp1-F7 = Fp1 - F7 is negative.

taskFlow.title: Transverse Confirmation
taskFlow.description: You switch to a transverse frontopolar chain F7-Fp1, Fp1-Fp2, Fp2-F8. Referential values at the peak: F7 -30, Fp1 -100, Fp2 -10, F8 0 uV.
taskFlow.question: What do F7-Fp1 and Fp1-Fp2 show?
options: F7-Fp1 +70 down; Fp1-Fp2 -90 up; reversal at Fp1
F7-Fp1 -70 up; Fp1-Fp2 +90 down; reversal at Fp1
F7-Fp1 +70 down; Fp1-Fp2 +90 down; maximum at F7
F7-Fp1 -130 up; Fp1-Fp2 -110 up; no reversal
taskFlow.explanation: F7-Fp1 = -30 - (-100) = +70 uV -> DOWN. Fp1-Fp2 = -100 - (-10) = -90 uV -> UP. Opposite directions in channels sharing Fp1 = negative phase reversal at Fp1. The choice "F7-Fp1 -70 up; Fp1-Fp2 +90 down; reversal at Fp1" reverses both subtractions. -130/-110 adds magnitudes. Both-down misses the sign of Fp1 - Fp2.

taskFlow.title: Why the Banana Missed It
taskFlow.description: The reader asks why the double banana did not show a phase reversal for a discharge clearly maximal at Fp1.
taskFlow.question: What is the technical explanation?
options: The longitudinal montage uses too short a time constant for spikes
The spike field was too wide for bipolar recording
Phase reversals only occur in referential montages
No electrode lies anterior to Fp1 in that chain to reverse against
taskFlow.explanation: A phase reversal needs a channel on each side of the maximum. Fp1 is the first electrode in the longitudinal chain, so only the posterior side is sampled and the result is an end-of-chain pattern. Time constant is a filter setting, unrelated to montage geometry. Phase reversals are a bipolar phenomenon; referential montages localize by amplitude. A wide field reduces bipolar amplitudes but does not explain the absence of a reversal here.

taskFlow.title: Excluding Ocular Artifact
taskFlow.description: Fp1 is near the eye, and the patient has frequent eye movements during drowsiness. The reader wants assurance that the frontopolar transients are not ocular.
taskFlow.question: What is the most useful technologist action?
options: Add infraorbital/EOG electrodes and check Fp1 impedance
Raise the LFF to 5 Hz so eye movements are filtered out
Ask the patient to keep the eyes closed for the whole study
Move Fp1 2 cm higher so it records farther from the eye
taskFlow.explanation: Infraorbital or LOC/ROC electrodes show ocular potentials out of phase with the frontopolar electrode (cornea positivity moves toward one and away from the other), while cerebral fields are in phase. Checking Fp1 impedance excludes a single-electrode artifact. A 5 Hz LFF distorts the spike and suppresses real slowing. Moving Fp1 off its measured position breaks the 10-20 standard. Eye closure does not stop eye movements and limits the recording.

starterCases.title: Average Reference Contaminated by a High-Amplitude Spike
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Confusion and left-sided focal motor seizures

history.eventDescription: Acute confusion with intermittent right hand twitching over 24 hours.

eegSummary.background: Diffusely slow
eegSummary.artifacts: Average reference contamination creating apparent positive transients

objectives: Calculate the average reference voltage during a focal discharge
Predict the sign of contaminated channels in an average reference
Choose a reference strategy that avoids contamination

taskFlow.title: Value of the Average
taskFlow.description: The average reference is built from the 19 scalp electrodes. At the discharge peak, T3 is -380 uV and the other 18 electrodes are at about 0 uV.
taskFlow.question: What is the value of the average reference at that moment?
options: 0 uV
-20 uV
taskFlow.explanation: Average = sum / number of electrodes = (-380 + 18 x 0) / 19 = -20 uV. -380 uV treats the average as equal to the focus. 0 uV assumes one electrode cannot affect the average. -190 uV divides by 2 as if it were a two-electrode linked reference.

taskFlow.title: Sign of the Uninvolved Channels
taskFlow.description: In the average reference montage each channel is electrode minus Avg. T4 (about 0 uV) is far from the discharge.
taskFlow.question: What does T4-Avg show at the peak?
options: +20 uV, deflecting downward
-20 uV, deflecting upward
0 uV, a flat line
-400 uV, deflecting upward
taskFlow.explanation: T4-Avg = 0 - (-20) = +20 uV -> DOWN. Every uninvolved channel shows a small downward (positive-appearing) deflection time-locked to the discharge, while T3-Avg = -380 - (-20) = -360 uV -> UP. 0 uV ignores that the reference itself moved. -20 up reverses the subtraction. -400 adds the focus to the reference value.

taskFlow.title: Apparent Positive Discharges
taskFlow.description: A trainee notes small synchronous downward deflections in every right hemisphere channel, time-locked to the left discharges, and suggests a separate right-sided positive discharge.
taskFlow.question: What best explains the right-sided deflections?
options: Volume-conducted spread of the left focus to the right
A bilateral generalized discharge with left emphasis
Reference contamination: the -20 uV average is subtracted
Independent right temporal positive sharp waves
taskFlow.explanation: Because the average contains the -380 uV focus, every electrode near 0 uV reads 0 - (-20) = +20 uV, a positive-appearing (down) deflection everywhere with identical timing. Independent right discharges would have their own field and timing. True volume conduction would make right electrodes negative (up), not positive. A generalized discharge would be negative across the head in a clean reference.

taskFlow.title: Avoiding the Contamination
taskFlow.description: The reader wants a referential view of the left focus without the artifactual positivity elsewhere.
taskFlow.question: Which option best addresses the problem?
options: Use a linked-ears reference, which is never contaminated
Use the ipsilateral ear reference A1 for the left hemisphere
Halve the sensitivity so the small deflections disappear
Exclude T3 and adjacent high-voltage electrodes from the average
taskFlow.explanation: Removing the high-amplitude electrodes from the averaging pool (or reviewing in bipolar/Laplacian montages) keeps the reference near zero. A1 sits next to T3 and would be strongly contaminated by a temporal discharge. Reducing gain hides the artifact without removing it and also shrinks real activity. Linked ears contain A1 and are also contaminated by temporal discharges.

starterCases.title: Active Ear Reference from a Left Temporal Spike
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Episodes of rising epigastric sensation and confusion

history.eventDescription: Stereotyped events of rising stomach sensation followed by unresponsiveness and lip smacking.

eegSummary.background: Normal
eegSummary.epileptiform: Left temporal spikes maximal at T3 with spread to A1

objectives: Calculate channel output when the reference electrode is active
Recognize the widespread opposite-polarity sign of an active ear
Select montages that avoid a contaminated ear reference

taskFlow.title: A Spike in the Ear Montage
taskFlow.description: In an ipsilateral ear reference montage (left electrodes to A1), a spike peak measures T3 -150 uV, A1 -100 uV, and C3 about 0 uV (true values against a quiet reference).
taskFlow.question: What does the C3-A1 channel show?
options: +100 uV, deflecting downward
-250 uV, deflecting upward
0 uV, a flat channel
-100 uV, deflecting upward
taskFlow.explanation: C3-A1 = C3 - A1 = 0 - (-100) = +100 uV -> DOWN. Even though C3 is uninvolved, the active reference creates a positive-appearing deflection. 0 uV ignores the reference activity. -100/up reverses the subtraction. -250 adds T3 and A1.

taskFlow.title: Reading the Whole Montage
taskFlow.description: Across the left A1-referenced channels, Fp1, F3, C3, P3 and O1 all deflect downward together, while T3-A1 = -150 - (-100) = -50 uV deflects upward and is smaller than expected.
taskFlow.question: What is the best explanation of this pattern?
options: Two discharges of opposite polarity, at T3 and C3
A reversed amplifier polarity setting on the left side
A broad left hemisphere positive discharge with T3 sparing
An active A1 reference shared by all left channels
taskFlow.explanation: When every channel sharing A1 deflects the same way at the same instant, the common electrode (the reference) is active. T3-A1 looks small because the reference subtracts much of T3's negativity. A positive hemispheric discharge would not be precisely mirrored by A1 activity. Two discharges of opposite polarity misread a shared reference. A polarity setting error would invert all activity, including the background, at all times.

taskFlow.title: Choosing a Better Montage
taskFlow.description: The reader asks for a montage that shows the left temporal spike field without the A1 contamination.
taskFlow.question: Which choice best avoids the problem?
options: Contralateral ear reference A2 at reduced sensitivity
Left mastoid reference instead of A1
Longitudinal bipolar plus a Cz reference
Linked-ears reference (A1+A2)
taskFlow.explanation: A longitudinal bipolar chain localizes by phase reversal and does not depend on an inactive reference, and Cz is far from the temporal focus. Linked ears still include A1, so contamination persists (at about half strength). The mastoid is also adjacent to the temporal lobe and picks up the same field. A2 with reduced sensitivity adds long interelectrode distances (ECG pickup) and lower gain obscures small activity; it is not the first choice.

taskFlow.title: Technologist Note
taskFlow.description: In the bipolar montage the spikes phase reverse at T3, and in the Cz reference T3 is the most negative electrode.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist note include?
options: Left hemispheric positive spikes seen in the ear reference montage
Left temporal lobe epilepsy confirmed by the T3 phase reversal
Ear reference montage invalid; those pages deleted from the study
A1 active during left temporal spikes; bipolar shows reversal at T3
taskFlow.explanation: The note should document the technical observation (active A1) and where the discharges phase reverse, so the reader interprets the ear-referenced pages correctly. Calling them positive spikes repeats the artifactual reading. Confirming a diagnosis is outside technologist scope. Deleting recorded pages is never acceptable; the montage is simply reformatted on review.

starterCases.title: Eye Movement Polarity - Blinks, Lateral Gaze, LOC/ROC
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Fluctuating confusion; rule out frontal rhythmic slowing

history.eventDescription: Waxing and waning confusion over 3 days with frequent blinking and roving eye movements.

eegSummary.background: Mildly slow
eegSummary.focalFindings: Frontal slow transients that prove to be ocular
eegSummary.artifacts: Blink and lateral eye movement artifacts

objectives: Predict blink polarity from cornea-positive dipole and Bell's phenomenon
Predict lateral gaze polarity in F7/F8 bipolar channels
Use out-of-phase LOC/ROC to separate eye movements from cerebral slowing

taskFlow.title: Blink in Fp1-F3
taskFlow.description: The patient blinks repeatedly. During a blink the eyes roll upward (Bell's phenomenon), moving the positively charged cornea toward Fp1 and Fp2.
taskFlow.question: How does the blink appear in the Fp1-F3 channel?
options: Upward, because F3 becomes positive
Upward, because Fp1 becomes negative
Flat, because the eyes move together
Downward, because Fp1 becomes positive
taskFlow.explanation: The cornea is positive relative to the retina. Moving up under the frontopolar electrodes makes Fp1 positive: Fp1-F3 = (+) - (about 0) = positive -> DOWN. Fp1 becoming negative reverses the dipole. Conjugate movement does not cancel within one channel. F3 is too far from the eye to become more positive than Fp1.

taskFlow.title: Lateral Gaze to the Left
taskFlow.description: The patient then looks to the left. The left cornea approaches F7 and the right eye's retina (negative pole) lies nearer F8.
taskFlow.question: What do F7-T3 and F8-T4 show?
options: Both channels down
F7-T3 down; F8-T4 up
F7-T3 up; F8-T4 down
Both channels up
taskFlow.explanation: Left gaze makes F7 positive: F7-T3 = (+) - (about 0) = positive -> DOWN. F8 becomes negative: F8-T4 = (-) - (about 0) = negative -> UP. The opposite directions on the two sides are the signature of lateral eye movement. The choice "F7-T3 up; F8-T4 down" reverses the dipole. Both-down or both-up ignores that the two eyes present opposite poles to F7 and F8.

taskFlow.title: Separating Ocular from Cerebral Slowing
taskFlow.description: The reader wants to know whether the frontal slow transients are eye movements or frontal intermittent rhythmic delta. You add LOC (1 cm below and lateral to the left outer canthus) and ROC (1 cm above and lateral to the right outer canthus).
taskFlow.question: What pattern in LOC/ROC indicates eye movement?
options: Out-of-phase LOC and ROC deflections with the frontal transients
In-phase LOC and ROC deflections with the frontal transients
LOC activity only, with ROC remaining flat
No LOC or ROC activity during the frontal transients
taskFlow.explanation: With one electrode above and one below the eyes, both vertical and horizontal eye movements bring the cornea toward one and away from the other, so LOC and ROC deflect in opposite directions. Frontal cerebral activity reaches both electrodes with the same polarity (in phase). No LOC/ROC activity would argue against an ocular source. LOC-only activity suggests a local electrode problem.

taskFlow.title: Lateral Gaze in LOC-A1 and ROC-A1
taskFlow.description: Both eye channels are referenced to A1. The patient looks to the left again: the left cornea nears LOC and the right eye's retina nears ROC.
taskFlow.question: What do LOC-A1 and ROC-A1 show?
options: Both down, in phase
Both up, in phase
LOC-A1 up; ROC-A1 down
LOC-A1 down; ROC-A1 up
taskFlow.explanation: LOC becomes positive: LOC-A1 = (+) - (about 0) = positive -> DOWN. ROC becomes negative: ROC-A1 = (-) - (about 0) = negative -> UP. The out-of-phase result confirms an ocular source. The choice "LOC-A1 up; ROC-A1 down" flips the dipole. In-phase deflections would point to a cerebral or reference source rather than the eyes.

starterCases.title: ECG and Pulse Artifact Mimicking Periodic Discharges
starterCases.chiefComplaint: cEEG for unresponsiveness after cardiac arrest; query periodic discharges

history.eventDescription: In-hospital cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation after 12 minutes; remains comatose.

eegSummary.background: Low-voltage, diffusely slow, continuous
eegSummary.epileptiform: Apparent periodic sharp transients that prove to be cardiac artifact
eegSummary.focalFindings: Rhythmic slow wave at F8 that is pulse artifact
eegSummary.artifacts: ECG artifact in ear-referenced channels; pulse artifact at F8

objectives: Compare transient intervals to the cardiac R-R interval
Separate ECG artifact from pulse artifact by timing after the QRS
Choose technical fixes for each cardiac artifact

taskFlow.title: Interval Check
taskFlow.description: Ear-referenced channels show sharp transients every 20 mm at 30 mm/s. The monitor shows a regular heart rate of 90 beats per minute.
taskFlow.question: What is the transient interval and how does it compare with the R-R interval?
options: 0.67 s; faster than the 1.5 s R-R interval
1.5 s; slower than the 0.67 s R-R interval
0.67 s; identical to the 0.67 s R-R interval
0.6 s; close to but not equal to the R-R interval
taskFlow.explanation: Interval = 20 mm / 30 mm/s = 0.667 s. R-R = 60 s / 90 beats = 0.667 s. They match exactly. 1.5 s inverts the transient frequency (1.5 Hz). 1.5 s mistakes the 1.5 Hz transient rate (90/60 = 1.5 beats per second) for an interval in seconds. 0.6 s results from rounding 30 mm/s to 33 mm/s.

taskFlow.title: Is It Periodic Discharges?
taskFlow.description: Each transient falls exactly on the QRS in the EKG channel, is maximal in the A1- and A2-referenced channels, and its interval tracks the heart rate when the rate changes.
taskFlow.question: What is the best description?
options: Pulse artifact from an ear electrode
Lateralized periodic discharges, right side
Generalized periodic discharges at 1.5 Hz
ECG artifact time-locked to the QRS complex
taskFlow.explanation: Fixed time-locking to the QRS, an interval that follows the heart rate, and maximum in ear-referenced channels (ears pick up the cardiac dipole) identify ECG artifact. GPDs and LPDs (ACNS 2021 terms) do not follow the heart rate beat for beat. Pulse artifact is a slower wave delayed after the QRS, not simultaneous with it.

taskFlow.title: A Delayed Slow Wave at F8
taskFlow.description: Separately, F8 alone shows a smooth 1-1.5 Hz wave beginning about 200-300 ms after each QRS. F8 sits over a palpable superficial temporal artery.
taskFlow.question: What is the cause and the correct fix?
options: Pulse artifact; move F8 slightly off the artery
ECG artifact; switch to a linked-ears reference
Pulse artifact; raise the LFF to 5 Hz on all channels
Focal delta; report as right frontal slowing
taskFlow.explanation: A slow wave confined to one electrode and following each QRS by about 200-300 ms is pulse artifact from electrode movement over an artery. Moving the electrode slightly off the vessel (and documenting the shift) removes it. ECG artifact coincides with the QRS. Calling it focal delta misses the cardiac time-locking. A 5 Hz LFF on all channels would erase genuine slow activity in a comatose patient.

taskFlow.title: Reducing the ECG Artifact
taskFlow.description: The ECG artifact persists in the ear-referenced channels after the F8 fix. The patient is obese with a horizontal heart axis.
taskFlow.question: What is the most appropriate way to reduce it?
options: Decrease the sensitivity to 30 uV/mm until it is invisible
Remove the EKG channel so it does not distract the reader
Apply a 60 Hz notch filter to all channels
Review in bipolar montages or a balanced linked-ears reference
taskFlow.explanation: ECG artifact is largest with long interelectrode distances such as ear references; bipolar montages with short distances, or linking the ears so the cardiac field partially cancels, reduce it. A 60 Hz notch has no effect on cardiac activity. Lowering gain hides everything, not just the artifact. The EKG channel is essential for proving time-locking and must stay.

starterCases.title: Electrode Pop Versus Salt Bridge Signatures
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Sleep-deprived EEG after a syncope-versus-seizure event

history.eventDescription: Collapse at a summer outdoor event with brief jerking; quick recovery.

eegSummary.background: Normal
eegSummary.artifacts: T4 electrode pops; C3-P3 salt bridge from heavy sweating

objectives: Identify an electrode pop by its single-electrode field
Identify a salt bridge by a low-amplitude channel between neighbors
Match each fault to the correct corrective action

taskFlow.title: Sudden Vertical Transients
taskFlow.description: F8-T4 and T4-T6 show abrupt, very steep deflections in opposite directions at the same instant, with no spread to neighboring channels. T4 impedance reads 22 kOhm; others read 2-4 kOhm.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: Electrode pop at T4
Right temporal spikes with phase reversal at T4
Salt bridge between F8 and T4
Muscle artifact from the right temporalis
taskFlow.explanation: A pop involves only the channels containing one electrode, appears as an abrupt vertical deflection with no physiologic field, and is associated with a poor contact (22 kOhm). Mirror-image deflections can mimic a phase reversal, but cerebral spikes have a field and an aftergoing morphology. Muscle is fast and repetitive. A salt bridge reduces, not adds, activity between two electrodes.

taskFlow.title: Fixing T4
taskFlow.description: The patient is in light sleep, and you want to fix T4 with minimal disturbance.
taskFlow.question: What is the best corrective action?
options: Add more gel over T4 without removing the electrode
Re-prep the skin at T4 and re-apply until under 5 kOhm
Turn on a 35 Hz HFF to smooth the pops
Remove T4 from the montage for the rest of the study
taskFlow.explanation: A pop reflects an unstable electrode-skin interface; re-prepping (abrading) and re-applying the electrode to bring impedance below 5 kOhm and balanced with the others fixes the cause. An HFF does not remove a step-like DC shift. Extra gel without re-prep often fails and may spread to neighbors and create a bridge. Dropping T4 loses coverage of the temporal region.

taskFlow.title: A Nearly Flat Channel
taskFlow.description: Later, the patient is sweating heavily. C3-P3 becomes very low amplitude, almost flat, while Fp1-F3, F3-C3 and P3-O1 look normal. Gel is visible between C3 and P3.
taskFlow.question: What explains the C3-P3 channel?
options: A salt bridge between C3 and P3
Focal suppression over the left central region
A broken C3 lead wire
Excessive impedance at P3
taskFlow.explanation: Sweat or gel connecting two electrodes shorts them together: both record the same potential, so C3 - P3 is near zero. Neighboring channels stay normal. A broken lead would produce noise and artifact in every channel containing C3. Focal suppression would affect more than one channel and is an interpretation. High impedance causes noise and 60 Hz, not a clean flat line.

taskFlow.title: Fixing the Bridge
taskFlow.description: The room is warm and the patient continues to sweat.
taskFlow.question: What is the best fix?
options: Switch to a referential montage to hide the flat channel
Clean and dry between C3 and P3, re-apply, cool the room
Add more paste to both C3 and P3
Increase the C3-P3 sensitivity to 3 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: Remove the conductive path: clean and dry the scalp between the electrodes, re-apply each with a small amount of paste, recheck impedances, and cool the patient to reduce sweating; document the time. More paste widens the bridge. Increasing gain only amplifies near-zero difference and noise. A referential montage displays the same shorted electrodes and conceals the fault without fixing it.

starterCases.title: Single-Electrode 60 Hz Versus Ground Fault in the ICU
starterCases.chiefComplaint: cEEG for altered mental status after subarachnoid hemorrhage

history.eventDescription: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, now drowsy and intermittently confused.

eegSummary.background: Mildly slow
eegSummary.artifacts: 60 Hz interference from a high-impedance O2, later from a detached ground

objectives: Distinguish single-electrode 60 Hz from a whole-montage ground problem
Use the notch filter only after troubleshooting, with documentation
Apply the single-ground rule to prevent ground loops

taskFlow.title: 60 Hz in Two Channels
taskFlow.description: 60 Hz interference appears only in P4-O2 and O2-T6. Impedances: O2 18 kOhm, all others 2-4 kOhm.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: A failing amplifier channel for P4-O2
Nearby IV pump radiating 60 Hz into the whole head
High, unbalanced impedance at O2
A broken patient ground
taskFlow.explanation: 60 Hz confined to the channels sharing O2, with O2 at 18 kOhm versus 2-4 kOhm elsewhere, indicates an impedance imbalance that defeats common-mode rejection at that electrode. A ground problem or environmental field affects many channels. An amplifier fault would involve one channel, not both channels containing O2.

taskFlow.title: Now Every Channel
taskFlow.description: After O2 is fixed, 60 Hz suddenly appears in all channels. You find the ground electrode lying on the pillow.
taskFlow.question: What should you do first?
options: Turn on the 60 Hz notch filter for all channels
Re-apply the ground electrode and recheck impedances
Unplug the ventilator to remove the 60 Hz source
Connect the patient to the bed frame to ground them
taskFlow.explanation: A detached ground degrades the amplifiers' common-mode rejection across all channels; re-applying it fixes the cause. The notch filter treats the symptom and is a last resort. Attaching a patient to a bed frame is unsafe and creates an improper ground path. Disconnecting life support is never a technologist's fix.

taskFlow.title: When the Notch Is Acceptable
taskFlow.description: With the ground re-applied, a low-level 60 Hz remains from unavoidable ICU equipment despite good impedances.
taskFlow.question: How should the notch filter be used?
options: Keep it on routinely for every study from the start
Use it instead of fixing high impedance, since it is faster
Avoid it entirely, even if 60 Hz obscures the record
Use it after troubleshooting, and document when it was applied
taskFlow.explanation: The notch filter is a last resort after electrodes, ground and environment are checked; its use is documented because it can alter sharp transients containing 60 Hz components. Routine use hides electrode problems that also cause other artifacts. Refusing it when residual noise obscures the record harms interpretability. Using it in place of fixing impedance leaves a bad electrode that will cause further problems.

taskFlow.title: A Second Ground
taskFlow.description: A colleague suggests adding a second ground electrode from the bedside monitor's lead set to improve noise, since the monitor already grounds the patient.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct response?
options: Decline; the patient should have one ground only
Accept; the monitor ground can replace the EEG ground
Accept only if both grounds are on the same side
Accept; two grounds halve the 60 Hz amplitude
taskFlow.explanation: Multiple grounds on one patient can form a ground loop, allowing current to flow through the patient between devices at different ground potentials. Keep a single ground and use equipment with isolated patient connections. Two grounds do not halve noise. Removing the EEG ground degrades common-mode rejection. Placing both on one side does not prevent a ground loop.

starterCases.title: Neonatal EEG Setup - Montage, Polygraphy, Duration
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Term neonate with episodes of lip smacking and desaturation

history.eventDescription: Born at 39 weeks after a difficult delivery; on day 2 has brief episodes of lip smacking and oxygen desaturation.

eegSummary.background: Continuous; recording continued until a full epoch of quiet sleep was captured

objectives: Select the reduced neonatal electrode array
Name the polygraphic channels required in a neonatal EEG
Apply neonatal time base and duration (quiet-sleep capture) standards

taskFlow.title: Electrode Array
taskFlow.description: The neonate's head circumference is 34 cm. You prepare to apply scalp electrodes.
taskFlow.question: Which electrode array is appropriate?
options: Full adult array placed at the fixed adult centimetre distances
C3-P3 and C4-P4 only, as for a two-channel aEEG
Reduced array with A1 and A2 used in place of T3 and T4
Fp1, Fp2, C3, Cz, C4, T3, T4, O1, O2 + A1/A2 by percentages
taskFlow.explanation: The neonatal reduced array (Fp1, Fp2, C3, Cz, C4, T3, T4, O1, O2, plus A1/A2 or mastoids), placed by head percentages, is the ACNS suggested minimum; the full 10-20 array is also acceptable when time and head size allow. Cz is always included because positive rolandic sharp waves may be seen only there. Adult centimetre distances do not fit a 34 cm head. A two-channel aEEG array is a trend screening tool, not a conventional EEG. Ear electrodes do not replace temporal coverage.

taskFlow.title: Polygraphic Channels
taskFlow.description: The episodes include desaturation, and the reader will need to assess sleep states.
taskFlow.question: Which polygraphic channels should be recorded?
options: EKG and pulse oximetry only
Respiration and limb EMG only
EKG only, since the scalp montage shows everything else
EKG, respiration, EOG, and chin EMG
taskFlow.explanation: Neonatal EEG requires EKG, respiration, eye movement (EOG) and submental (chin) EMG to identify active and quiet sleep and to interpret apnea or cardiac events. EKG alone cannot stage sleep. Oximetry is a useful monitor, but it does not replace respiration, EOG and EMG channels. Respiration and limb EMG alone omit cardiac and ocular channels.

taskFlow.title: Time Base
taskFlow.description: Your lab displays neonatal studies at 15 mm/s on a 300 mm wide screen.
taskFlow.question: How many seconds of EEG appear on each page?
taskFlow.explanation: Seconds per page = width / speed = 300 mm / 15 mm/s = 20 s. The slower (compressed) display helps show slow neonatal activity and discontinuity. 10 s is the 30 mm/s adult page. 4.5 s multiplies 300 by 15 and drops a factor of 1000. 30 s would require 10 mm/s.

taskFlow.title: Recording Duration
taskFlow.description: After 30 minutes the infant has been in active sleep only, with no quiet sleep yet, and the nurse asks if you can finish.
taskFlow.question: What is the appropriate plan?
options: Continue, typically to at least 60 minutes, until quiet sleep is captured
Stop now and sedate the infant so quiet sleep appears on a repeat study
Continue only until the first clinical event, then stop the recording
Stop now, since 30 minutes already exceeds the 20-minute adult routine minimum
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS Guideline 5 says 20- to 30-minute neonatal recordings are usually insufficient; an adequate record must include a full epoch of quiet sleep, and at least 60 minutes may be needed to show that a pattern does not change. The usual first state is active sleep, so stopping at 30 minutes risks having no quiet sleep. The adult 20-minute minimum does not apply. Sedation is never necessary or desirable to obtain a neonatal sleep record. Stopping after a single event risks missing more events and the quiet-sleep epoch.

learningLinks.label: Domain II: Recording Procedures & Patient Preparation

starterCases.title: Post-Stroke LPDs - Frequency, Plus Modifiers, IIC
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Fluctuating responsiveness three days after a left MCA stroke

history.eventDescription: Admitted with a large left MCA infarct. Nursing reports the patient is less responsive than yesterday, with no witnessed convulsive activity. Continuous EEG ordered to look for nonconvulsive seizures.
history.lastEventTiming: Decline noted over the last 6 hours

eegSummary.background: Continuous left hemispheric polymorphic delta with periodic sharply contoured discharges over the left hemisphere; right hemisphere theta-delta with intermittent faster frequencies
eegSummary.epileptiform: Lateralized periodic discharges, left, 1.5 Hz, with superimposed fast activity
eegSummary.artifacts: Intermittent ECG and IV pump artifact

objectives: Count discharges per second to assign the ACNS frequency of periodic discharges
Separate periodic discharges from rhythmic delta and apply the +F modifier
Recognize when LPDs fall in the ictal-interictal continuum and notify

taskFlow.title: Name the main pattern
taskFlow.description: Thirty minutes into the recording you see sharply contoured discharges maximal at F3, C3 and T7, each followed by a flat stretch of background before the next one. They recur at nearly regular intervals. In a 10-second epoch you count 15 discharges. The right hemisphere shows none.
taskFlow.question: Which ACNS 2021 description fits this activity?
options: GPDs, left predominant, 1.5 Hz
LPDs, left hemisphere, 1.5 Hz
LRDA, left hemisphere, 1.5 Hz
LPDs, left hemisphere, 0.67 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: Frequency is discharges per second: 15 / 10 s = 1.5 Hz. A quantifiable interval between discharges makes them periodic discharges (PDs), and confinement to one hemisphere makes them lateralized (LPDs). LRDA is wrong because rhythmic delta has no interval between consecutive waves. GPDs is wrong because the right hemisphere is uninvolved. 0.67 Hz is the inter-discharge interval (10 s / 15 = 0.67 s) reported as if it were a frequency, a classic inversion error.

taskFlow.title: Add the modifier
taskFlow.description: On closer review at 30 mm/s, each discharge carries a brief burst of low-amplitude 15-20 Hz activity riding on it. There is no rhythmic delta between discharges, and the discharges themselves are already sharp.
taskFlow.question: Which plus modifier is correct?
options: LPDs+FR
LPDs+F
LPDs+S
LPDs+R
taskFlow.explanation: +F means superimposed fast activity, which is exactly what rides on each discharge here. +R would require superimposed rhythmic delta, which is absent. +S applies to rhythmic delta that has sharp waves added (for example LRDA+S); it is not used to describe periodic discharges that are themselves sharp. +FR needs both fast activity and rhythmic delta, and only the fast component is present.

taskFlow.title: Seizure, IIC, or neither?
taskFlow.description: Over the next hour the LPDs+F stay at 1.5 Hz with no change in frequency, location or morphology, and no clinical correlate is seen. They are present in about 70% of the record.
taskFlow.question: How does this pattern sit in the ACNS 2021 framework?
options: IIC: averages >1.0 to 2.5 Hz with no evolution
Electrographic status: present for over 10 minutes
Interictal only: IIC requires at least 2.0 Hz
Electrographic seizure: any LPDs+F are ictal
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 places PDs averaging >1.0 and up to 2.5 Hz over 10 s (more than 10 and up to 25 discharges in 10 s) in the ictal-interictal continuum when they do not meet seizure criteria; 1.5 Hz with no evolution fits. An electrographic seizure needs >2.5 Hz for at least 10 s or definite evolution for at least 10 s, so a plus modifier alone does not make it ictal. There is no 2.0 Hz threshold for IIC. Electrographic status requires the pattern to qualify as a seizure first; duration of an IIC pattern does not convert it to status. Prevalence 70% is documented as 'abundant' (50-89%).

taskFlow.title: Technologist action
taskFlow.description: The record now meets your unit's notification criteria for IIC patterns. The bedside nurse asks what you found and whether she should give a benzodiazepine.
taskFlow.question: What is the most appropriate technologist response?
options: Write 'consistent with acute left MCA infarct' in the technologist note
Hold the finding for the daily read because LPDs are very common after a stroke
Advise the nurse to give lorazepam because the pattern is on the IIC
Notify the neurologist per protocol and document terms, prevalence and times
taskFlow.explanation: Technologists describe, document and notify. Calling the reader per the unit's protocol with ACNS terms (LPDs+F, 1.5 Hz, abundant, no evolution) and annotated times is the correct step. Recommending medication is outside technologist scope. Attributing the pattern to an infarct is interpretation. Holding a finding that meets notification criteria for a routine read delays care.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Ictal EEG & Seizure Patterns

starterCases.title: Hepatic Encephalopathy - GPDs with Triphasic Morphology
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Confusion and somnolence with liver cirrhosis

history.eventDescription: Known cirrhosis admitted with worsening confusion, asterixis and an elevated ammonia. EEG requested because of fluctuating alertness; no witnessed seizures.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse theta-delta slowing without a posterior dominant rhythm
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology, frontally predominant, about 1.8 Hz
eegSummary.activation: Reactivity testing: discharges increase with stimulation

objectives: Use ACNS 2021 wording: GPDs with triphasic morphology, not 'triphasic waves'
Calculate discharge frequency and test it against the IIC range
Perform and document reactivity testing, including SIRPIDs

taskFlow.title: Describe the discharges
taskFlow.description: Bilaterally synchronous, frontally predominant blunt discharges appear at regular intervals with background between them. Each is negative-positive-negative, each phase longer than the one before, with the positive (second) phase the highest in voltage, and the discharge appears slightly later at the occipital electrodes than at the frontal ones.
taskFlow.question: Which ACNS 2021 description is correct?
options: Generalized spike-and-wave at about 2 Hz
GPDs with triphasic morphology and A-P lag
GRDA, frontally predominant, with A-P lag
Triphasic waves of metabolic encephalopathy
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 retired 'triphasic waves' as a stand-alone term; triphasic is a morphology modifier attached to GPDs, and the front-to-back delay is the anterior-posterior lag modifier. 'Triphasic waves of metabolic encephalopathy' adds an etiologic label the technologist should not apply. GRDA has no interval between waves. Spike-and-wave requires a spike or sharp wave followed by a slow wave, which is not what these blunt periodic complexes are.

taskFlow.title: Frequency and the IIC
taskFlow.description: You count 18 discharges in a representative 10-second epoch with no evolution and no clinical change.
taskFlow.question: What is the frequency, and where does it fall?
options: 1.8 Hz, so it already meets electrographic seizure
0.56 Hz, which is below the IIC frequency range
1.8 Hz, but triphasic morphology excludes IIC
1.8 Hz, which is in the >1.0 to 2.5 Hz IIC range
taskFlow.explanation: Frequency = 18 discharges / 10 s = 1.8 Hz (ACNS category 2 Hz). PDs averaging >1.0 to 2.5 Hz over 10 s are on the ictal-interictal continuum if they do not meet seizure criteria. Seizure requires >2.5 Hz for at least 10 s or definite evolution. 0.56 Hz is the interval (10 / 18 = 0.56 s) mistaken for frequency. Triphasic morphology does not exempt GPDs from the IIC; ACNS 2021 applies the same frequency rules.

taskFlow.title: Test reactivity
taskFlow.description: The reader asks for reactivity testing. The patient opens his eyes briefly to loud voice.
taskFlow.question: How should you perform the test?
options: Pause the recording during stimulation to avoid artifact
Annotate each stimulus and escalate from voice to noxious
Call his name once and record 'reactive' if his eyes open
Use sternal rub only, since voice rarely changes the EEG
taskFlow.explanation: Reactivity means a change in cerebral EEG activity with stimulation, so each stimulus (auditory, then tactile, then noxious per policy) must be annotated at the moment it is given and the EEG examined afterward. Skipping graded stimulation loses information. Eye opening is a clinical sign, and eye-blink or muscle artifact does not count as EEG reactivity. Pausing the recording removes the very epochs the reader must review.

taskFlow.title: Document the response
taskFlow.description: With each stimulus the GPDs become more frequent (up to 2.5 Hz) and then return to 1.8 Hz within a minute. No other background change is seen.
taskFlow.question: How should this response be documented?
options: Discard stimulation epochs as artifact
Reactive background; no further detail needed
Stimulus-induced GPDs; reactivity: SIRPIDs only
Seizure provoked by stimulation, notify as status
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 uses the prefix SI- for stimulus-induced patterns and lists 'SIRPIDs only' as a reactivity category, distinct from normal reactivity. Calling the background simply reactive hides that the only change was more discharges. A transient increase to 2.5 Hz is still not >2.5 Hz and is not a seizure. The stimulation epochs are clinically important data, not artifact.

starterCases.title: Nonconvulsive Seizures in the ICU - Electrographic Status Burden
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Not waking up after right subdural hematoma evacuation

history.eventDescription: Postoperative day 1 after evacuation of a right subdural hematoma. Sedation was stopped 8 hours ago, but she remains poorly responsive with no clinical seizure activity.

eegSummary.background: Right hemispheric attenuation with breach-type faster activity; left hemisphere diffuse theta
eegSummary.epileptiform: Recurrent right temporal electrographic seizures without clinical signs
eegSummary.artifacts: Breach rhythm over the craniotomy; ventilator artifact

objectives: Apply the >2.5 Hz for 10 s and evolution criteria for electrographic seizure
Calculate seizure burden in a 60-minute window to identify ESE
Notify promptly and document onset and offset times

taskFlow.title: First event
taskFlow.description: At 01:58 rhythmic sharp waves appear at T8 and F8. You count 28 discharges in the first 10 seconds, and the run lasts 3 minutes. The patient shows no movement, eye deviation or vital-sign change.
taskFlow.question: How does this event meet ACNS 2021 criteria?
options: Not a seizure: there is no clinical change
Electrographic seizure: >2.5 Hz for 10 s
IIC pattern: below the 3 Hz seizure cutoff
BIRDs: any run shorter than 5 minutes
taskFlow.explanation: 28 discharges / 10 s = 2.8 Hz, which exceeds 2.5 Hz for at least 10 s and meets the ACNS 2021 electrographic seizure (ESz) definition. The cutoff is >2.5 Hz, not 3 Hz. BIRDs are limited to runs of 0.5 to under 10 s. ESz is defined on EEG alone; most ICU seizures are nonconvulsive.

taskFlow.title: Second event
taskFlow.description: At 02:20 rhythmic delta starts at T8 at 1.5 Hz, becomes sharper, increases to 2 Hz, then 3 Hz, and spreads to C4 and P8 over the first 50 seconds; the seizure lasts 2.5 minutes in total before stopping abruptly. The first 10 seconds average only 1.5 Hz.
taskFlow.question: How should this event be classified?
options: IIC, because the opening 10 s are below 2.5 Hz
LRDA+S, since this is rhythmic delta with sharp waves
ESz: definite evolution for at least 10 s qualifies
Electroclinical seizure, because the pattern evolved
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 accepts either >2.5 Hz for at least 10 s or any pattern with definite evolution (changes in frequency, morphology or location) lasting at least 10 s. This event evolves in frequency and location over its first 50 s, so it is an ESz even though its start is slow. Judging only the first 10 s misses evolution. LRDA+S describes a non-evolving pattern. An electroclinical seizure needs a time-locked clinical correlate or clinical improvement with treatment, which is absent.

taskFlow.title: Seizure burden
taskFlow.description: Between 01:55 and 02:55 you mark four seizures lasting 3 min, 4 min, 2.5 min (the 02:20 evolving seizure) and 3 min. None lasts 10 minutes.
taskFlow.question: Does this hour meet electrographic status epilepticus (ESE)?
options: No: no single seizure reached 10 minutes
No: ESE requires 50% of the hour, or 30 min
Yes: 12.5 of 60 min is 20.8%, at least 20%
Yes: any seizure of 5 min or more is ESE
taskFlow.explanation: Burden = 3 + 4 + 2.5 + 3 = 12.5 min; 12.5 / 60 = 0.208 = 20.8%. ESE is an ESz lasting at least 10 continuous minutes OR a total of at least 20% of any 60-minute period, so this hour qualifies. Requiring a single 10-minute seizure ignores the burden criterion. There is no 50% rule. The 5-minute threshold applies only to electroclinical status with bilateral tonic-clonic activity; other electroclinical status, like ESE, needs 10 continuous minutes or 20% of any 60-minute period.

taskFlow.title: Respond and document
taskFlow.description: It is 03:00 and the patient remains clinically unchanged. The bedside nurse is unaware of the events.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do first?
options: Save the findings for the morning read since she is clinically stable
Notify the neurologist now and annotate onsets and offsets
Tell the family that she is in status epilepticus
Ask the nurse to increase sedation to stop the seizures
taskFlow.explanation: Recurrent seizures meeting ESE criteria are a critical finding: notify the responsible physician immediately per protocol, inform the nurse, and keep precise onset/offset annotations, testing responsiveness during the next event. Waiting for a routine read delays treatment. Giving a diagnosis to the family and directing medication changes are outside technologist scope.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Ictal EEG & Seizure Patterns

starterCases.title: Post-Cardiac Arrest BIRDs - Definite, Possible, or Seizure
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Comatose after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, now rewarmed

history.eventDescription: Ventricular fibrillation arrest with return of spontaneous circulation after 18 minutes. Completed targeted temperature management and is now normothermic and off sedation for 12 hours, remaining comatose.

eegSummary.background: Continuous diffuse slowing, low voltage, with frequent right frontal sharp waves
eegSummary.epileptiform: Right frontal sharp waves; brief runs of rhythmic >4 Hz activity

objectives: Recognize BIRDs: >4 Hz, at least 6 waves, 0.5 to under 10 s
Separate definite from possible BIRDs using evolution or IED match
Measure duration precisely to avoid under-calling an ESz

taskFlow.title: Name the run
taskFlow.description: A 3-second run of sharply contoured rhythmic 6 Hz activity (18 waves) appears at F4-C4. There is no clinical change, and the background is continuous, not burst suppression.
taskFlow.question: Which ACNS 2021 term fits this run?
options: ESz: frequency above 2.5 Hz
BIRDs: >4 Hz, 0.5 to <10 s
Normal wicket-like variant
LRDA at 6 Hz, right frontal
taskFlow.explanation: BIRDs are focal or generalized rhythmic runs faster than 4 Hz, at least 6 waves, lasting 0.5 to under 10 s, without a definite clinical correlate and not part of a burst-suppression pattern or known benign variant. ESz needs at least 10 s. LRDA is delta (4 Hz or less) by definition. Wicket rhythms are temporal, arciform and seen in drowsy adults, not a comatose post-arrest ICU patient.

taskFlow.title: Definite or possible?
taskFlow.description: The run has a steady frequency and location throughout (no evolution). The same right frontal location and sharp morphology match the patient's frequent interictal sharp waves at F4.
taskFlow.question: How should this run be classified?
options: Definite BIRDs: matches the patient's IEDs
Electrographic seizure: it is over 4 Hz
Not BIRDs: a run must last at least 10 seconds
Possible BIRDs: no evolution is present
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 calls BIRDs definite if they evolve OR if they share morphology and location with the patient's interictal epileptiform discharges or seizures. The IED match alone is enough, so the lack of evolution does not downgrade it. Requiring 10 s confuses BIRDs with ESz. Frequency above 4 Hz does not make a sub-10-s run a seizure.

taskFlow.title: A second run
taskFlow.description: Later a 2-second run of sharply contoured 5 Hz activity (10 waves) appears at P3-O1, where no interictal discharges have been seen. It does not change in frequency, morphology or location.
taskFlow.question: How should the second run be classified?
options: Possible BIRDs: sharply contoured only
Electrographic seizure: new location
Definite BIRDs: every >4 Hz run counts
Not BIRDs: must match the first location
taskFlow.explanation: Without evolution and without a match to known IEDs, a sharply contoured run meeting the BIRDs frequency and duration rules is 'possible BIRDs'. Definite BIRDs need evolution or an IED match. BIRDs can occur anywhere; they need not match earlier runs. A new location does not alter the duration rule for ESz.

taskFlow.title: Measure the next run
taskFlow.description: At the next run of right frontal 6 Hz activity you mark onset at 14:22:05.4 and offset at 14:22:15.9. There is still no clinical change.
taskFlow.question: Based on its duration, how should this run be handled?
options: Possible BIRDs until it shows evolution
10.5 s above 2.5 Hz: an ESz; notify
BIRDs, since there is no clinical sign
BIRDs, since it is under 30 seconds
taskFlow.explanation: Duration = 15.9 - 5.4 = 10.5 s. BIRDs stop below 10 s; a run of 6 Hz (>2.5 Hz) lasting at least 10 s meets the electrographic seizure definition and should be reported per protocol. There is no 30-second BIRDs limit. ESz does not require a clinical sign. Evolution is one route to ESz, but frequency above 2.5 Hz for 10 s is sufficient on its own.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Ictal EEG & Seizure Patterns

starterCases.title: Anesthetic Burst Suppression - Measuring Bursts and IBIs
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Refractory status epilepticus on a pentobarbital infusion

history.eventDescription: Refractory status epilepticus failed benzodiazepines and two ASMs. Pentobarbital infusion started with a target of burst suppression; the team wants the pattern quantified every few hours.

eegSummary.background: Burst suppression: 1-3 s mixed-frequency bursts separated by suppression below 10 µV
eegSummary.epileptiform: No electrographic seizures; no highly epileptiform bursts

objectives: Apply ACNS voltage and percentage limits for burst suppression
Calculate percent suppression and mean interburst interval
Document drug, rate and bolus times and report reactivity correctly

taskFlow.title: Name the pattern
taskFlow.description: Bursts of mixed-frequency activity (50-150 µV, 1-3 s) alternate with periods in which all activity is below 10 µV. The flat periods occupy roughly 80% of the record.
taskFlow.question: Which ACNS 2021 continuity term applies?
options: Discontinuous
Suppressed background
Burst suppression
Burst attenuation
taskFlow.explanation: ACNS 2021 defines suppression as all activity below 10 µV and burst suppression as 50-99% of the record suppressed. Burst attenuation means the interburst periods are at least 10 µV but below 50% of background voltage. Discontinuous applies when 10-49% of the record is attenuated or suppressed. A suppressed background (more than 99%) would contain essentially no bursts.

taskFlow.title: Quantify
taskFlow.description: In a 60-second epoch that begins at the onset of a burst, you count 6 bursts, each about 2 seconds long, and each followed by suppression lasting until the next burst (the sixth suppression ends at 60 s).
taskFlow.question: What are the percent suppression and the mean interburst interval?
options: 48% suppression; mean IBI 8 s
20% suppression; mean IBI 2 s
80% suppression; mean IBI 8 s
80% suppression; mean IBI 10 s
taskFlow.explanation: Burst time = 6 x 2 s = 12 s. Suppression = 60 - 12 = 48 s; 48 / 60 = 80%. There are 6 suppression segments totalling 48 s, so mean IBI = 48 s / 6 = 8 s. 20% and 2 s are the burst fraction and burst duration, swapped in. 10 s divides the whole 60 s by 6 and forgets to subtract the bursts. 48% reports the seconds of suppression as if they were a percentage.

taskFlow.title: Medication documentation
taskFlow.description: The pentobarbital rate was increased 40 minutes ago, and a rocuronium dose was given 10 minutes ago for ventilator asynchrony.
taskFlow.question: What must be on the record for the reader?
options: A single 'sedated' note at the start
Each drug, its rate or dose, and the time given
Only the diagnosis of refractory status
Nothing, because pharmacy keeps the dose records
taskFlow.explanation: Burst-suppression depth and reactivity depend on the anesthetic dose, and neuromuscular blockade removes muscle artifact and masks clinical signs, so the reader needs agent, dose or rate, and time annotated on the tracing. A diagnosis alone does not explain changes in the pattern. Pharmacy records are not visible on the EEG. A single 'sedated' note cannot be matched to changes hours later.

taskFlow.title: Reactivity result
taskFlow.description: You give loud auditory stimulation and then nail-bed pressure. No muscle artifact appears (the patient received rocuronium), and the burst rate and IBIs are unchanged.
taskFlow.question: How should the result be documented?
options: Untestable: rocuronium blocks EEG reactivity
Reactive: heart rate rose with pressure
Unreactive: no change in bursts or IBIs
Reactive: bursts are a response to stimuli
taskFlow.explanation: EEG reactivity is a change in cerebral activity with stimulation; with no change in burst rate or IBIs the record is unreactive, documented alongside the drugs on board. A heart-rate change is an autonomic response, not EEG reactivity. Neuromuscular blockade removes muscle artifact but does not block cerebral activity, so the test remains valid. Spontaneous bursts are not a stimulus response unless time-locked to the stimulus.

starterCases.title: Electrocerebral Inactivity Recording - Technical Standards
starterCases.chiefComplaint: EEG requested as an ancillary test for brain death evaluation

history.eventDescription: Severe traumatic brain injury with absent brainstem reflexes. Apnea testing could not be completed because of hemodynamic instability, so an EEG for electrocerebral inactivity is ordered.
medications: Sedation stopped more than 48 hours ago

eegSummary.background: No cerebral activity above 2 µV at 2 µV/mm
eegSummary.activation: Auditory and noxious stimulation without change
eegSummary.artifacts: ECG artifact of about 2 µV, ventilator artifact

objectives: Set sensitivity and filters to the ACNS ECI guideline
Meet electrode, interelectrode distance and impedance standards
Identify ECG artifact by voltage and time-locking, then stimulate

taskFlow.title: Sensitivity and filters
taskFlow.description: You are setting up the study on a 16-channel ICU system. The routine defaults are 7 µV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz.
taskFlow.question: Which settings meet the ACNS ECI guideline?
options: 2 µV/mm; LFF no higher than 1 Hz; HFF 30 Hz or above
7 µV/mm; LFF 1 Hz; HFF 70 Hz, the usual routine defaults
20 µV/mm; LFF 0.1 Hz; HFF 70 Hz for the artifact
2 µV/mm; LFF 5 Hz; HFF 15 Hz to quiet the trace
taskFlow.explanation: The ACNS guideline requires sensitivity of 2 µV/mm for at least 30 minutes, the LFF not above 1 Hz and the HFF not below 30 Hz. Routine 7 µV/mm makes a 2 µV signal about 0.3 mm tall and invisible. Narrowing filters to 5-15 Hz can remove low-voltage cerebral activity. 20 µV/mm is ten times less sensitive than required.

taskFlow.title: Electrodes and impedance
taskFlow.description: You are choosing the electrode array and checking impedances before recording.
taskFlow.question: Which setup meets the guideline?
options: Full set with impedances driven below 100 ohms
Full 10-20 set incl. Fz/Cz/Pz, pairs ≥10 cm, 100-10,000 ohms
A single Cz-to-ear channel with any stable impedance
Nearest-neighbor 10-20 bipolar pairs, each kept under 50,000 ohms
taskFlow.explanation: The ACNS guideline calls for a complete complement of scalp electrodes covering all major areas, including midline Fz, Cz and Pz, interelectrode distances of at least 10 cm (double-distance), and impedances between 100 and 10,000 ohms. Short interelectrode distances reduce the amplitude of any surviving activity. 50,000 ohms is far too high. One channel cannot sample the cortex. Impedances below 100 ohms suggest an electrolyte bridge or short.

taskFlow.title: Small rhythmic deflection
taskFlow.description: At 2 µV/mm you see a 1 mm deflection in several channels, recurring about every 0.8 s. It occurs at the same time as the QRS complex in the ECG channel.
taskFlow.question: What is its voltage, and what is it?
options: 0.5 µV; cerebral activity below threshold
2 µV; cerebral activity, so not ECI
20 µV; a pulse artifact from one electrode
2 µV; ECG artifact time-locked to the QRS
taskFlow.explanation: Voltage = deflection x sensitivity = 1 mm x 2 µV/mm = 2 µV. Time-locking to the QRS in several channels identifies ECG artifact, which the technologist annotates (and can confirm with a monitor or by repositioning). Dividing 1 by 2 gives the wrong voltage. 20 µV moves the decimal point. Calling it cerebral ignores the ECG relationship, and deciding ECI is the reader's role, not the technologist's.

taskFlow.title: Duration and stimulation
taskFlow.description: The record is technically sound, electrodes have been tested by touching each one, and the ECG artifact is annotated.
taskFlow.question: What completes the recording to the guideline?
options: 20 min, as for a routine EEG, without any stimulation
10 min at 2 µV/mm, since the patient is apneic
30 min at 2 µV/mm with photic stimulation only
At least 30 min at 2 µV/mm with annotated stimuli
taskFlow.explanation: The guideline requires at least 30 minutes of recording at 2 µV/mm (or more sensitive), with intense somatosensory, auditory and visual stimulation, each annotated, plus ECG monitoring and any additional monitors needed to identify artifact. 10 or 20 minutes is too short. A routine duration does not meet the ECI standard, and photic stimulation alone omits the required auditory and somatosensory stimuli.

starterCases.title: Alpha Coma Pattern vs Reactive Posterior Alpha
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Appears unresponsive after basilar artery occlusion

history.eventDescription: Sudden quadriplegia and loss of speech from basilar artery thrombosis. He does not move his limbs or speak and is described by the team as comatose.

state: eyes closed, unresponsive to commands for limbs
eegSummary.background: Posterior dominant 9 Hz alpha with anterior-posterior gradient
eegSummary.pdrHz: 9 Hz, attenuates with passive eye opening
eegSummary.activation: Reactivity testing: alpha attenuates with eye opening and stimuli
eegSummary.artifacts: Vertical eye movement artifact to command

objectives: Test reactivity and distribution before describing alpha in coma
Contrast reactive posterior alpha with the unreactive alpha coma pattern
Annotate and report signs of preserved responsiveness

taskFlow.title: Plan reactivity testing
taskFlow.description: Ten minutes in, a steady 9 Hz rhythm is present with eyes closed. The patient makes no limb movements.
taskFlow.question: What should you do to characterize this alpha activity?
options: Run photic stimulation to look for driving near 9 Hz
Ask him to hyperventilate for 3 minutes
Raise the LFF to 5 Hz so the alpha stands out
Passive eye opening, then voice and noxious stimuli
taskFlow.explanation: Distribution and reactivity separate a normal posterior rhythm from an alpha coma pattern, so passive eye opening and graded, annotated stimuli are the key tests. Photic driving does not show whether the rhythm blocks with eye opening or arousal. A patient who cannot move cannot perform hyperventilation. Changing the LFF does not answer the question and distorts the record.

taskFlow.title: Describe the response
taskFlow.description: The 9 Hz activity is maximal at O1 and O2, attenuates when the eyes are held open, and returns when they close. It also attenuates with loud voice.
taskFlow.question: Which description is accurate?
options: Posterior dominant, reactive alpha
Alpha coma: alpha in a coma patient
Alpha coma: alpha above 8 Hz
Diffuse beta from sedation
taskFlow.explanation: A posterior-maximal rhythm that blocks with eye opening and alerting is a reactive posterior dominant rhythm. The alpha coma pattern is diffuse or frontally predominant, monotonous and unreactive; simply recording alpha in an unresponsive patient is not enough. Frequency alone does not define the pattern. 9 Hz is alpha, not beta, and no sedatives are on board.

taskFlow.title: Unexpected response
taskFlow.description: While testing, you say 'look up' and record a vertical eye movement artifact in Fp1 and Fp2 each time, repeated three times on command. The limbs remain still.
taskFlow.question: What is the appropriate action?
options: Remove the frontal electrodes to stop the eye artifact
Tell the family that he can understand everything
Annotate each command and response and inform the neurologist
Ignore it, since reflex eye movements are very common in deep coma
taskFlow.explanation: Reproducible eye movements to command with a reactive posterior rhythm are important observations; annotating each command and response with times and informing the neurologist is within scope. Dismissing them as reflexive loses critical data. Telling the family what it means is interpretation. Removing electrodes discards the evidence and degrades the montage.

taskFlow.title: The contrasting pattern
taskFlow.description: The resident asks how the alpha coma pattern would have looked on this montage.
taskFlow.question: Which description matches the alpha coma pattern?
options: Diffuse, frontally predominant monotonous alpha; unreactive
Alpha that increases in amplitude with eye opening
Posterior alpha that blocks when the eyes are opened
Alpha with spindles and vertex waves in sleep
taskFlow.explanation: The alpha coma pattern, classically after hypoxic injury or brainstem lesions, is widespread, often frontally predominant, monotonous and unreactive to stimulation. Posterior alpha that blocks with eye opening is a normal reactive PDR. Alpha does not normally increase with eye opening. Spindles and vertex waves in a comatose patient describe a spindle coma pattern, which is different.

starterCases.title: ICU Recording During Cooling, Sedation and Paralysis
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG during targeted temperature management

history.eventDescription: Comatose after in-hospital cardiac arrest. Targeted temperature management in progress with a surface cooling device. Continuous EEG ordered to screen for seizures.

eegSummary.background: Continuous diffuse low-voltage theta-delta slowing
eegSummary.artifacts: Shivering muscle artifact before paralysis; cooling device artifact

objectives: Document temperature and sedative, paralytic doses with times
Handle shivering artifact without hiding the cerebral signal
Describe drug-related changes by time, not by cause

taskFlow.title: Start-of-study documentation
taskFlow.description: You hook up the patient while cooling is in progress. The nurse has the medication administration record open.
taskFlow.question: What should be documented at the start of the recording?
options: Her full list of home medications from last year
Core temperature and sedative and paralytic doses with times
The admitting diagnosis and the attending's name
Only the Glasgow Coma Scale score recorded at the time of hookup
taskFlow.explanation: Temperature and sedative and paralytic agents (name, dose or rate, time) change the EEG and how it is interpreted, so they belong on the record from the start and whenever they change. A coma score alone does not explain EEG changes. Old home medications are less relevant than what is infusing now. Diagnosis and staff names do not help the reader interpret the tracing.

taskFlow.title: Shivering
taskFlow.description: Twenty minutes in, diffuse high-frequency muscle artifact appears in bursts, worst in temporal channels, while the patient is visibly shivering.
taskFlow.question: What is the best response?
options: Lower the HFF to 15 Hz for the rest of the record
Describe the activity as beta from sedation
Stop recording until the patient is rewarmed
Annotate the shivering with times and tell the nurse
taskFlow.explanation: Annotating the source and informing the nurse (who may treat shivering) keeps the record interpretable. Permanently lowering the HFF to 15 Hz can hide spikes and distort cerebral activity; filters can be changed for review, not to erase the data. Stopping the study defeats seizure screening during the highest-risk period. Labeling muscle artifact as cerebral beta is a misidentification.

taskFlow.title: Paralytic given
taskFlow.description: Cisatracurium is given at 09:40. Muscle artifact disappears within minutes, and the EEG shows the same diffuse slowing.
taskFlow.question: Which statement is correct for your note?
options: The paralytic suppresses cortical activity, so pause
EEG stays valid; clinical signs of seizure are now masked
No note is needed because it only affects muscle
Paralytics produce burst suppression, so expect it to appear next
taskFlow.explanation: Neuromuscular blockers act at the neuromuscular junction: they remove EMG artifact without changing cerebral activity, but they also eliminate the clinical manifestations of seizures, which makes the EEG the only seizure monitor. The time must be documented. They do not suppress cortex or produce burst suppression.

taskFlow.title: Bolus and attenuation
taskFlow.description: At 10:15 the nurse gives a propofol bolus. Starting at 10:16 the EEG becomes diffusely lower in voltage for about 6 minutes, then returns to its prior appearance.
taskFlow.question: Which technologist note is appropriate?
options: 10:16 equipment failure, amplifiers suppressed
10:16 diffuse attenuation, 1 min after 10:15 propofol bolus
10:16 worsening hypoxic injury suspected
10:16 pattern consistent with brain death
taskFlow.explanation: A good technologist note records what changed, when, and what was given, without assigning a cause. Calling it brain death or hypoxic progression is interpretation, and both are contradicted by the return of the prior pattern. Equipment failure is unlikely when all channels recover together after a documented bolus, and the calibration and impedance checks would say otherwise.

starterCases.title: Adult Sleep Graphoelements - Staging Without Over-Calling
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Sleep-deprived EEG after a first unprovoked convulsion

history.eventDescription: Single generalized convulsion witnessed by a roommate. Neurological examination is normal. Sleep-deprived routine EEG ordered.

eegSummary.background: Normal awake background
eegSummary.artifacts: Slow roving eye movements in drowsiness

objectives: Identify vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes and POSTS
Use input-1 minus input-2 polarity to confirm POSTS are positive
Write a sleep description that avoids epileptiform labels

taskFlow.title: Sharp waves at the vertex
taskFlow.description: As the PDR fragments and slow roving eye movements appear, sharply contoured waves of about 200 ms appear maximal at Cz, with spread to C3 and C4. They are symmetric and occur singly.
taskFlow.question: What are these waves?
options: Midline spikes needing urgent physician notification
Mu rhythm over the central region
Vertex sharp waves of drowsiness and light sleep
K-complexes that occur only in wakefulness
taskFlow.explanation: Vertex waves are symmetric, sharply contoured transients maximal at Cz that appear in drowsiness and N1-N2 sleep; their sharpness is normal. Calling them midline spikes over-reads a sleep graphoelement. K-complexes are sleep (N2) phenomena, not waking ones. Mu is an arciform 7-11 Hz waking rhythm, not single sharp transients.

taskFlow.title: Stage the next segment
taskFlow.description: Next you see 13 Hz waxing-waning bursts lasting about 0.75 s at C3, C4 and Cz, and high-voltage diphasic waves followed by a spindle. The PDR is absent, and less than 20% of the epoch is 0.5-2 Hz slow activity above 75 µV.
taskFlow.question: Which stage is this?
options: N3 slow-wave sleep with spindles
REM sleep with sawtooth waves
N2 sleep with spindles and K-complexes
Wakefulness with frontal beta
taskFlow.explanation: Sleep spindles (11-16 Hz, at least 0.5 s, centrally maximal) and K-complexes define N2. N3 requires 20% or more of the epoch to be slow waves of 0.5-2 Hz with peak-to-peak amplitude greater than 75 µV over the frontal regions. REM shows low-voltage mixed activity, sawtooth waves and rapid eye movements. Waking beta is low-voltage and continuous, without spindles or K-complexes.

taskFlow.title: Occipital transients
taskFlow.description: Trains of triangular sharp transients appear at O1 and O2 during light sleep. On the ear-referential montage (O1-A1), they deflect downward.
taskFlow.question: What polarity and identity fit these transients?
options: Lambda waves of visual scanning
Surface-positive POSTS of normal sleep
Positive occipital epileptiform discharges
Surface-negative occipital spikes
taskFlow.explanation: In O1-A1, a downward pen means input 1 (O1) is positive relative to input 2 (A1) (negative-up convention). Surface-positive triangular occipital transients in light sleep are POSTS, a normal finding. Surface-negative would deflect upward. Lambda waves are similar positive occipital waves, but they occur awake during visual scanning, not in sleep. Positivity and the sleep context argue against epileptiform discharges.

taskFlow.title: Technologist description
taskFlow.description: The recording ends after 20 minutes of drowsiness and N2 sleep with no clinical events.
taskFlow.question: Which technologist note is most appropriate?
options: Drowsiness and N2 sleep: vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes, POSTS
Multifocal sharp waves at Cz, O1 and O2 during sleep
Epileptiform discharges in sleep; physician called
Abnormal sleep: POSTS suggest occipital epilepsy
taskFlow.explanation: The note should name states reached and normal graphoelements seen, without epileptiform terms. Calling them 'multifocal sharp waves' or 'epileptiform' converts normal sleep transients into an abnormal finding. Linking POSTS to occipital epilepsy is both incorrect and outside technologist scope.

starterCases.title: Wicket Spikes and BETS vs True Temporal Spikes
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Episodes of dizziness and brief confusion

history.eventDescription: Several spells of lightheadedness with brief confusion over 3 months, no convulsions. Routine EEG ordered to look for temporal lobe epileptiform activity.

eegSummary.background: Normal for age
eegSummary.focalFindings: Arciform temporal activity in drowsiness; small sharp transients in light sleep
eegSummary.activation: Photic without abnormality; HV deferred for hypertension

objectives: Recognize wicket spikes by morphology, state and lack of after-going slow wave
Separate BETS from interictal temporal spikes
Describe uncertain transients without labeling them epileptiform

taskFlow.title: Arciform trains
taskFlow.description: In drowsiness, trains of arciform 7-9 Hz waves appear over the left temporal region (F7, T7), sometimes alternating sides. Occasionally a single wave of the same shape stands alone.
taskFlow.question: Which feature best supports a benign wicket pattern?
options: High amplitude compared with the background
Appearance only during drowsiness
No after-going slow wave or background disruption
A clear phase reversal at T7 on a longitudinal bipolar montage
taskFlow.explanation: Wicket spikes are arciform, mid-temporal, seen in drowsy adults, and lack the after-going slow wave and background disruption of true spikes; isolated wickets match the morphology of the trains. Phase reversal only localizes a field; benign transients also phase reverse. High amplitude is not a criterion for epileptiform activity. Drowsiness is typical for wickets but also activates true temporal spikes, so state alone does not separate them.

taskFlow.title: Comparison discharge
taskFlow.description: The reader shows you an older EEG from a different patient with left temporal spikes for comparison.
taskFlow.question: Which feature would distinguish a true temporal spike?
options: Under 50 µV, under 50 ms, light sleep only
Symmetric, rhythmic, and without an after-going slow wave
Arciform, occurs in trains during drowsiness
Asymmetric, disrupts background, slow wave follows
taskFlow.explanation: Interictal epileptiform spikes are typically asymmetric (steeper rise than fall), stand out from and disrupt the background, and are often followed by a slow wave. The arciform, train-like, symmetric descriptions fit wicket spikes. Very low amplitude and very short duration in light sleep describe BETS (small sharp spikes).

taskFlow.title: Tiny sharp transients
taskFlow.description: In N1-N2 sleep you see very brief, low-amplitude (about 40 µV, under 50 ms) monophasic spikes, single, with no after-going slow wave. Some appear over the opposite hemisphere with opposite polarity.
taskFlow.question: What are these transients?
options: 14 and 6 Hz positive spike bursts
Interictal left anterior temporal spikes
Lambda waves from occipital cortex
Benign epileptiform transients (BETS)
taskFlow.explanation: BETS (small sharp spikes) are low-amplitude (under 50 µV), very brief (under 50 ms) transients of adult drowsiness and light sleep, often with a transverse dipole that shows opposite polarity in the other hemisphere. 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts are arciform bursts at those frequencies, best seen on ear-referential montage in adolescents. True spikes are larger and usually have an after-going slow wave. Lambda waves are occipital and occur with visual scanning while awake.

taskFlow.title: Documentation
taskFlow.description: The reader asks you to annotate the temporal activity for review.
taskFlow.question: Which annotation is appropriate?
options: None needed; omit them since they are likely benign
Interictal discharges seen; call the physician urgently
Left temporal epileptiform spikes, frequent in drowsiness
Arciform 7-9 Hz temporal trains in drowsiness; for review
taskFlow.explanation: A technologist annotation should give location, frequency, morphology and state and flag the activity for the reader, without deciding whether it is epileptiform. Labeling it 'epileptiform spikes' over-calls a probable benign variant, a common cause of misdiagnosed epilepsy. Omitting the annotation leaves the reader without a marker. Urgent calls are not indicated for transients that are probably benign.

starterCases.title: Photoparoxysmal Response - Stopping and Documenting Photic
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Convulsion while playing a video game

history.eventDescription: One generalized convulsion while playing a fast-paced video game late at night. No prior events reported.

eegSummary.background: Normal awake background
eegSummary.activation: Photoparoxysmal response at 16 Hz with eyes closed, outlasting the stimulus

objectives: Stop photic stimulation as soon as a photoparoxysmal response appears
Separate a PPR from photic driving and photomyoclonic response
Document flash rate, eye state, duration and clinical signs

taskFlow.title: Discharges appear
taskFlow.description: During stepwise photic stimulation, at 16 Hz with eyes closed, generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges appear in all channels.
taskFlow.question: What should you do immediately?
options: Raise the rate to see if it persists
Have her open her eyes and continue
Finish the full frequency sequence first, then stop
Stop the flashes and observe the patient
taskFlow.explanation: A generalized photoparoxysmal response can progress to a clinical seizure, so the stimulus is stopped as soon as it is recognized, the time is annotated, and the patient is observed and protected. Completing the sequence or increasing the rate prolongs the provocation. Changing eye state and continuing still exposes her to the triggering stimulus.

taskFlow.title: After the flashes stop
taskFlow.description: The discharges continue for about 1.5 s after the strobe stops. They are generalized, not just frontal, and they are not time-locked to individual flashes.
taskFlow.question: How is this response best described?
options: Self-limited PPR that ends with the flashes
PPR outlasting the stimulus (self-sustaining)
Photomyoclonic (myogenic) frontal response
Photic driving at the flash frequency
taskFlow.explanation: Discharges that continue after the stimulus stops are a prolonged (self-sustaining) PPR, which carries greater clinical significance than a self-limited one. Photic driving is rhythmic occipital activity time-locked to the flash rate, not polyspike-and-wave. Photomyoclonic responses are frontal muscle potentials that stop when the flashes stop. A self-limited PPR ends with, or before, the end of the stimulus.

taskFlow.title: What to document
taskFlow.description: You annotate the event on the record.
taskFlow.question: Which details must be included?
options: Flash rate, eye state, duration and any clinical sign
Total photic time with no other details
Only that a photic response was present
The likely epilepsy syndrome and the need for medication
taskFlow.explanation: The reader needs the provoking frequency, eye condition (open, closed, eye closure), the discharge duration relative to the stimulus, and any observed clinical signs. 'A photic response' does not distinguish driving from PPR. Naming a syndrome or treatment is interpretation. Total photic time alone omits the key features.

taskFlow.title: Clinical signs
taskFlow.description: During the discharge, you observed brief jerks of both arms, and she says she 'felt a jolt' but remained aware.
taskFlow.question: What is the best next action?
options: Repeat the 16 Hz train to confirm the jerks
Annotate the jerks with time and check on her
Mark the jerks as artifact since EMG is present
Tell her the EEG shows she has epilepsy
taskFlow.explanation: Time-locked clinical signs are documented exactly, and the patient is assessed for safety and recovery. Repeating the provoking frequency risks a convulsion and is not done without physician direction. The EMG reflects a real clinical event, not artifact. Telling the patient a diagnosis is outside technologist scope.

starterCases.title: Neonatal EEG - Trace Alternant, Jitteriness and Seizure
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Episodes of limb jerking in a newborn

history.eventDescription: Born at 38 weeks 3 days gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy, now 10 days old. Nurses report intermittent rhythmic jerking of the right leg, especially when he is handled.

eegSummary.background: Continuous in active sleep and wake; trace alternant in quiet sleep
eegSummary.epileptiform: One brief evolving left central rhythmic discharge

objectives: Calculate conceptional (postmenstrual) age from GA and postnatal age
Separate trace alternant from burst suppression by interburst activity
Distinguish jitteriness from seizure and apply the 10 s seizure rule

taskFlow.title: Conceptional age
taskFlow.description: Gestational age at birth was 38 weeks 3 days. He is now 10 days old.
taskFlow.question: What conceptional (postmenstrual) age should be entered on the study?
options: 39 weeks 6 days
1 week 3 days
38 weeks 3 days
40 weeks 3 days
taskFlow.explanation: Conceptional (postmenstrual) age = gestational age + postnatal age = 38 w 3 d + 10 d (1 w 3 d) = 39 w 6 d. Entering 38 w 3 d ignores postnatal age. 40 w 3 d adds 2 weeks. 1 week 3 days is the chronological age only. The reader judges maturity against this number.

taskFlow.title: Quiet sleep segment
taskFlow.description: With regular respiration and no eye movements, 3-5 s bursts of high-voltage mixed activity alternate with 4-6 s segments of lower-voltage (about 25-50 µV) mixed activity that is never suppressed. The pattern gives way to continuous activity when the baby stirs.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits?
options: Trace discontinu expected at 40 weeks
Trace alternant of normal term quiet sleep
Activité moyenne of active sleep
Burst suppression with unreactive interburst intervals
taskFlow.explanation: Trace alternant is the normal quiet sleep pattern near term: bursts alternate with lower-voltage but not suppressed interburst activity, and it changes with state. Burst suppression has interburst periods of suppression (below 10 µV) and is invariant and unreactive. Trace discontinu is the preterm pattern with very low-voltage interburst intervals. Activité moyenne is continuous activity of active sleep or wake, not alternating.

taskFlow.title: Leg jerking
