taskFlow.description: During handling, the right leg jerks rhythmically. When you gently hold the leg, the movement stops at once. The EEG shows only movement artifact with no change in background.
taskFlow.question: How should you document this event?
options: Neonatal seizure, as the jerks were rhythmic
Movement stopped with gentle restraint; no EEG change
Increase stimulation to provoke a larger event
Disconnect the ECG lead to reduce artifact during events
taskFlow.explanation: Stimulus-provoked rhythmic movements that stop with gentle restraint and lack an EEG correlate are features of jitteriness; the technologist documents the observation and the restraint test. Rhythmicity alone does not define a seizure. Deliberately provoking larger events is inappropriate. The ECG channel is required in neonatal recordings to identify artifact.

taskFlow.title: A subclinical event
taskFlow.description: Later, during quiet sleep, rhythmic sharp waves appear at C3, increasing in amplitude and slowing in frequency over 22 seconds before ending. The baby does not move.
taskFlow.question: Which statement guides your documentation?
options: Neonatal seizures must last 3 minutes before they count
No clinical sign, so no seizure: no note needed
Neonatal seizures must last at least 30 seconds
Evolving pattern of 10 s or more: mark it and notify
taskFlow.explanation: The ACNS neonatal definition of an electrographic seizure is a sudden, repetitive, evolving pattern lasting at least 10 s. This 22-s evolving event qualifies, so onset and offset are annotated and the team notified per NICU protocol. Many neonatal seizures are electrographic only. The 3-minute and 30-second durations are not neonatal seizure criteria.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Ictal EEG & Seizure Patterns

starterCases.title: EMU Event with Preserved Posterior Rhythm - Testing and Notes
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Admission to characterize frequent convulsive-appearing spells

history.eventDescription: Weekly spells of side-to-side head and body shaking with eyes closed lasting 2-5 minutes, despite two ASMs. Admitted to the EMU for video-EEG.

eegSummary.background: Normal awake background
eegSummary.artifacts: Heavy movement and muscle artifact during the event

objectives: Perform safety and responsiveness testing during an EMU event
Describe the EEG during an event, including a reactive posterior rhythm
Document observations objectively without diagnostic labels

taskFlow.title: Event begins
taskFlow.description: The push button is pressed by the patient's partner. On video the patient has her eyes closed and side-to-side head and trunk movements.
taskFlow.question: What should you do first at the bedside?
options: Ensure safety, then test responsiveness and recall
Stay outside so you do not add artifact
Hold her limbs firmly to stop the movements
Ask her directly whether she is faking the whole event
taskFlow.explanation: Bedside testing begins with safety (bed rails, clear area, uncovered face for video), then responsiveness: speak to her, give a word or color to remember, and ask her to follow commands. Restraining limbs risks injury and obscures the semiology. Accusatory questions are unprofessional and unhelpful. Staying outside loses responsiveness data, which is a core purpose of EMU testing.

taskFlow.title: EEG during the event
taskFlow.description: Between movement bursts the EEG shows a 10 Hz posterior rhythm. When you gently open her eyes, the rhythm attenuates and returns when they close.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the EEG is accurate?
options: Generalized seizure hidden beneath the movement artifact
Reactive 10 Hz posterior rhythm during the event
Postictal slowing from the event onset
Alpha coma pattern because she is unresponsive
taskFlow.explanation: A posterior rhythm that attenuates with eye opening during apparent unresponsiveness is an important objective finding to document. Claiming a hidden seizure is not supported by the visible rhythm. Postictal slowing would be slower activity after an event, not a reactive alpha rhythm during it. The alpha coma pattern is diffuse and unreactive, which this is not.

taskFlow.title: Observations
taskFlow.description: She resists passive eye opening. After the event ends she recalls the test word 'blue' and describes hearing you speak.
taskFlow.question: What should be documented?
options: Faked event; patient remembered everything
Resisted eye opening; correctly recalled 'blue'
Pseudoseizure with intact recall of the test word 'blue'
No behavioral notes; the EEG is enough
taskFlow.explanation: Objective, time-stamped behaviors (eye closure, resistance to eye opening, recall of the test item) are exactly what the reader needs. 'Pseudoseizure' is an outdated and diagnostic label, and 'faked' is judgmental and inaccurate. Omitting behavior loses the clinical correlation that video-EEG is designed to capture.

taskFlow.title: Event summary
taskFlow.description: You complete the event log for the epileptologist.
taskFlow.question: Which summary is appropriate?
options: 02:14-02:17 functional event; epilepsy excluded
02:14-02:17 psychogenic nonepileptic seizure, her typical type
02:14-02:17 eyes closed, shaking, recalled word, 10 Hz PDR
02:14-02:17 typical seizure captured successfully
taskFlow.explanation: The summary should record times, behaviors, test results and the EEG description, leaving diagnosis to the physician. 'Psychogenic', 'functional' and 'epilepsy excluded' are diagnostic conclusions. 'Typical seizure' both interprets and contradicts the objective findings.

starterCases.title: Pediatric HV - Normal Buildup vs Absence Seizure
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Teacher reports daydreaming spells in class

history.eventDescription: Several brief staring spells a day reported at school, with no falls or convulsions. Routine EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation ordered.

eegSummary.background: Normal for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: One 8-second burst of generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave during HV
eegSummary.activation: HV: high-voltage rhythmic delta buildup; 3 Hz spike-and-wave at 3 min with staring
eegSummary.artifacts: Glossokinetic and movement artifact during HV

objectives: Screen for HV contraindications such as sickle cell disease and moyamoya
Separate normal HV buildup from 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Test and document responsiveness during a generalized discharge

taskFlow.title: Before hyperventilation
taskFlow.description: You are about to start 3-5 minutes of hyperventilation. The parent is present.
taskFlow.question: Which screening questions are most important before HV?
options: Allergy to collodion or paste, and the time of her last meal and snack
Recent fever, dental work, and current screen time
Sickle cell disease or trait, moyamoya, stroke, heart or lung disease
Family history of migraine and motion sickness
taskFlow.explanation: HV causes cerebral vasoconstriction and hypocapnia, so it is withheld or modified for sickle cell disease or trait, moyamoya, recent stroke or hemorrhage, and significant cardiac or respiratory disease, per lab policy and physician direction. Collodion allergy and meal time matter for hookup and drowsiness, not HV safety. Family history of migraine, fever, or screen time are not standard HV contraindications.

taskFlow.title: At 2 minutes
taskFlow.description: High-voltage 3-4 Hz rhythmic delta appears, frontally predominant, waxing and waning. There are no spikes, and she keeps blowing and answers your questions.
taskFlow.question: How should you characterize this?
options: FIRDA requiring immediate notification
Electrographic seizure by frequency
Normal HV buildup; responsive throughout
3 Hz spike-and-wave absence seizure
taskFlow.explanation: Rhythmic high-voltage delta during HV in a responsive child, without spike components, is the normal buildup, common in children. Absence seizures show generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave with impaired responsiveness. FIRDA outside HV may be significant, but a buildup during HV is expected. The ACNS critical-care seizure criteria are not applied to routine HV buildup.

taskFlow.title: At 3 minutes
taskFlow.description: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave begins abruptly. She stops blowing and stares, with eyelid flutter.
taskFlow.question: What is the best testing step?
options: Say a test word during the burst and ask for it after
Stop the recording to avoid missing the post-HV period
Continue HV silently and annotate it from the video later
Shake her shoulders firmly until she responds again
taskFlow.explanation: Saying a test word or giving a simple command during the discharge and checking recall afterward documents impaired awareness, which the reader needs. Vigorous shaking is unsafe and adds artifact. Stopping the recording loses the post-event data. Annotating later without testing loses responsiveness information that cannot be reconstructed.

taskFlow.title: Documentation
taskFlow.description: The discharge lasts 8 seconds. She does not recall the word 'apple' and resumes blowing when prompted. HV is completed, and the background returns to baseline within 1 minute.
taskFlow.question: Which note best captures the event?
options: HV 3 min good effort; 8 s GSW with staring, no recall of 'apple'
Normal HV buildup at 3 min with brief inattention, fully recovered
Absence epilepsy confirmed by 3 Hz spike-and-wave at 3 min
HV stopped early at 3 min because she became tired and bored
taskFlow.explanation: The note should record HV effort and duration, the time and length of the discharge, the clinical behavior and the result of responsiveness testing. Stating 'absence epilepsy confirmed' is a diagnosis. Calling it a normal buildup with inattention mislabels spike-and-wave with impaired recall. Claiming HV stopped early contradicts what happened.

starterCases.title: Choking Infant in the Waiting Area - Back Blows and Chest Thrusts
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Infant scheduled for routine EEG suddenly cannot cry or cough while eating in the waiting area

history.eventDescription: A 9-month-old waiting for a routine EEG after febrile seizures was given a piece of cracker by a sibling. He abruptly stopped crying, has a silent, ineffective cough, and his lips are turning dusky. He is awake and looking around in distress.

eegSummary.background: Study not yet started; no electrodes applied.

objectives: Recognize severe airway obstruction in a responsive infant
Apply AHA 2025 infant back blows and one-hand chest thrusts
Switch to CPR when the infant becomes unresponsive

taskFlow.title: Recognize and act
taskFlow.description: The infant cannot cry, his cough is silent and weak, and his lips are dusky. He is still awake and moving. The mother is screaming for help.
taskFlow.question: What is your first action?
options: Sweep his mouth with a finger to hook out the piece of cracker
Give quick abdominal thrusts as you would for a school-age child
Lay him flat on the exam table and give two rescue breaths right away
Call for help and give 5 back blows, face-down on your forearm
taskFlow.explanation: A silent, ineffective cough with color change is severe obstruction in a responsive infant, so act immediately: call for help and deliver 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the infant face-down, head lower than chest, supported on your forearm. Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper. Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of liver and abdominal injury. Rescue breaths are not the first step while the infant is responsive; they are part of CPR once he becomes unresponsive.

taskFlow.title: Object still lodged
taskFlow.description: You have delivered 5 back blows. Nothing came out, the infant is still unable to cry, and he remains awake.
taskFlow.question: What do you do next?
options: Turn him face-up and give 5 quick upward abdominal thrusts
Keep giving back blows, without stopping, until the cracker comes out
Turn him face-up and give 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand
Turn him face-up and give 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the sternum
taskFlow.explanation: AHA 2025 infant foreign-body airway obstruction care alternates cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; the 2025 update describes chest thrusts with the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the sternum). Continuous back blows alone skip the chest-thrust half of the cycle. The two-finger technique is older teaching that the 2025 guidelines moved away from. Abdominal thrusts are not used for infants.

taskFlow.title: Infant becomes unresponsive
taskFlow.description: After two more cycles the infant goes limp and stops responding. A colleague has called the emergency team and is bringing the AED and pediatric pads.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct next action?
options: Do blind finger sweeps between each set of thrusts to find the object
Lay him on a firm surface and start CPR, beginning with compressions
Keep holding him and continue cycles of back blows and chest thrusts
Feel for a brachial pulse for a full 30 seconds before doing anything
taskFlow.explanation: Once a choking infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR on a firm, flat surface beginning with chest compressions. Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object only if you can see it. Continuing back blows and thrusts is the responsive-infant sequence. A pulse check takes no more than 10 seconds, never 30. Blind finger sweeps remain contraindicated.

taskFlow.title: After the handoff
taskFlow.description: The object is expelled during compressions; the infant starts crying and the emergency team takes over and transports him for evaluation. The EEG is postponed.
taskFlow.question: What is your responsibility afterwards?
options: Record only that the study was cancelled, leaving out event details
Ask his mother to write down the account of what happened instead
Go ahead with the scheduled EEG once he is calm and feeding again
Document times, actions, and handoff, and file an incident report
taskFlow.explanation: An emergency in the lab requires objective documentation by the staff involved: time of onset, signs observed, interventions (back blows, chest thrusts, CPR), who responded, and the handoff, plus an incident or safety report per policy. An infant who needed CPR must be medically evaluated, so the EEG is not simply resumed. Recording only 'cancelled' omits the event. A parent's account can be noted, but it does not replace staff documentation.

learningLinks.label: Domain IV: Patient Safety & Professional Standards

starterCases.title: Cardiac Arrest During a Routine Outpatient EEG
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for recurrent syncope versus seizure; patient collapses in the chair mid-recording

history.eventDescription: Three episodes of sudden loss of consciousness in two months. Twelve minutes into the recording, sitting at rest with eyes closed, he slumps forward.

eegSummary.background: Well-organized posterior dominant rhythm before the event, then diffuse slowing followed by marked attenuation about 15-20 seconds after the ECG change.
eegSummary.artifacts: ECG channel changes from regular QRS complexes to a chaotic, irregular undulating waveform

objectives: Treat an ECG channel change plus collapse as a patient problem first
Sequence BLS steps: help, AED, pulse/breathing check, compressions
Manage ECG electrodes at AED pad sites and document the arrest

taskFlow.title: The ECG channel changes
taskFlow.description: The ECG channel abruptly loses its regular QRS complexes and shows a chaotic, irregular waveform. Within seconds the patient slumps sideways in the chair and the EEG background slows and then flattens.
taskFlow.question: What is your first action?
options: Mark the event and keep recording so that it is captured in full
Increase the sensitivity to see whether any cerebral activity remains
Go to the patient, tap and shout, and check for normal breathing
Check the ECG electrode impedance for a lead-off or loose-wire problem
taskFlow.explanation: A sudden ECG rhythm change plus collapse and progressive cerebral slowing then attenuation is a clinical emergency until proven otherwise; the technologist assesses the patient first. Troubleshooting impedance or changing sensitivity treats it as a technical problem and wastes seconds. Annotating can wait; the patient cannot.

taskFlow.title: No response, gasping
taskFlow.description: He does not respond to tapping and shouting. He makes occasional gasping sounds but is not breathing normally.
taskFlow.question: What do you do next?
options: Give two rescue breaths first, before calling for any outside help
Lower the sensitivity and phone the reading neurologist right away
Feel for a carotid pulse for a full 30 seconds to be certain
Shout for help, activate the code team, and send for the AED
taskFlow.explanation: Gasping is agonal breathing and is treated as no normal breathing. AHA BLS: once unresponsive with abnormal breathing, call for help, activate the emergency response (code) and get the AED, then check breathing and pulse together for no more than 10 seconds and begin compressions. Rescue breaths first is outdated sequencing for an adult. A 30-second pulse check delays compressions. The neurologist is not the emergency team.

taskFlow.title: AED arrives
taskFlow.description: CPR is under way (30:2, at least 2 inches deep, 100-120/min). The AED arrives. ECG electrodes for the EEG ECG channel sit below the right clavicle and on the left lower chest, exactly where the pads go. Scalp electrodes are still attached to the head box.
taskFlow.question: How do you handle the electrodes?
options: Stop compressions and remove all scalp electrodes before going on
Pause CPR until the EEG instrument has been unplugged from the wall
Place the AED pads directly on top of the ECG electrodes to save time
Pull off the chest ECG electrodes at the pad sites, then apply pads
taskFlow.explanation: Pads need direct skin contact at the correct sites, so quickly remove any ECG electrodes or wires lying where the pads go and apply the pads with minimal interruption to compressions; everyone stands clear for analysis and shock. Placing pads over electrodes impairs contact and can cause burns or arcing. Removing every scalp electrode or unplugging equipment before continuing CPR creates long, unnecessary pauses in compressions.

taskFlow.title: After the code
taskFlow.description: One shock is delivered, the patient regains a pulse, and the code team transports him to the ED. The EEG kept recording throughout.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do with the recording and documentation?
options: Delete the CPR artifact segment so the reader sees only cerebral activity
Document the event tomorrow, once you have had time to reflect on it
Write in your notes that the EEG showed a hypoxic brain injury pattern
Annotate collapse, CPR, shock, and handoff times; keep the full record
taskFlow.explanation: The recording is part of the medical record: preserve it and annotate the times of collapse, start of CPR, AED analysis and shock, return of pulse, and handoff, plus who responded, then complete the incident report promptly while details are accurate. Deleting segments alters the record. Characterizing the EEG as hypoxic injury is interpretation, outside technologist scope. Delayed documentation is less accurate and violates timely-charting expectations.

starterCases.title: Sedated Child Desaturating During a Sleep EEG
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Sedated sleep EEG for staring spells in a child with autism who cannot tolerate electrode application awake

history.eventDescription: Daily brief staring spells. Oral sedation was given by the sedation nurse under a physician order. She is lying supine on the stretcher with continuous pulse oximetry, snoring loudly.

eegSummary.background: Sedated sleep with vertex waves and spindles before the event; arousal and movement artifact during the desaturation.
eegSummary.activation: Sleep obtained; HV and photic not possible
eegSummary.artifacts: Snoring-related movement, then abrupt arousal artifact

objectives: Recognize upper-airway obstruction in a sedated child
Open the airway before troubleshooting the oximeter
Know who monitors a sedated child and what to document

taskFlow.title: Snoring stops
taskFlow.description: The loud snoring suddenly stops. Her chest and abdomen are moving in a see-saw pattern with suprasternal retractions, and SpO2 has fallen from 97% to 89% and is still dropping. The oximeter waveform is clean.
taskFlow.question: What do you do first?
options: Open the airway with a jaw thrust or chin lift and call for help
Keep recording; silence after snoring means she has entered deep sleep
Re-site the oximeter probe, as this is most likely a motion artifact
Start photic stimulation to arouse her and restore her breathing
taskFlow.explanation: Snoring that suddenly stops while the chest keeps working (see-saw movement, retractions) with a falling SpO2 and a good pleth waveform is upper-airway obstruction, not artifact. The first action is to open the airway (jaw thrust or head tilt-chin lift, repositioning) and call the sedation nurse/physician. Re-siting the probe delays treatment of a real hypoxemia. Photic stimulation is not an airway intervention. Assuming deep sleep ignores clear signs of obstruction.

taskFlow.title: Monitoring standards
taskFlow.description: With a jaw thrust the snoring returns, retractions stop, and SpO2 climbs to 96%. The sedation nurse arrives and asks how monitoring was arranged.
taskFlow.question: Which monitoring arrangement meets pediatric sedation standards?
options: The technologist checks vital signs between electrode impedance checks
Monitoring can stop once the child is asleep and lying still
Spot-checks of oxygen saturation every 30 minutes throughout the EEG
Continuous pulse oximetry by trained sedation staff until discharge
taskFlow.explanation: Pediatric sedation guidance (AAP/AAPD) calls for continuous monitoring, including pulse oximetry, by appropriately trained personnel able to rescue the airway, continuing until the child meets discharge criteria. Intermittent spot checks would miss an event like this one. A technologist focused on the recording is not a substitute for dedicated sedation monitoring. Risk does not end when the child falls asleep; it is highest while she is most deeply sedated.

taskFlow.title: Continue or stop?
taskFlow.description: The nurse stays at the bedside supporting the airway and SpO2 is stable at 96%. About 15 minutes of sleep remain in the protocol, and no events have been captured yet.
taskFlow.question: How do you proceed with the study?
options: Ask the nurse for another sedative dose so that she stays asleep longer
Take your break now, since the sedation staff are at the bedside
Begin hyperventilation now to add an activated sample to the study
Keep recording with sedation staff at the bedside; annotate the event
taskFlow.explanation: With the airway supported and qualified staff present, the study can continue, and the desaturation is annotated on the record. Requesting extra sedation after an airway event is inappropriate and outside technologist scope. Hyperventilation cannot be performed by a sedated child. The technologist remains responsible for the recording and for observing the patient; leaving the room is not appropriate.

taskFlow.title: Technologist notes
taskFlow.description: The study ends uneventfully and the child is recovering in the sedation area.
taskFlow.question: What belongs in the technologist documentation?
options: Nothing about the event, as the sedation nurse charts the vital signs
A statement that the event shows the child has obstructive sleep apnea
SpO2 values, times, the airway intervention, and who was notified
Only the sedative name, dose, and time, as given by the nurse
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist notes should let the reader understand the arousal and artifact on the record: the time snoring stopped, SpO2 nadir and recovery, the airway maneuver, who was called, and when. Leaving it out because another discipline also charts it creates gaps. 'Obstructive sleep apnea' is a diagnosis, outside technologist scope. Sedative name and dose are useful, but alone they do not describe the event.

starterCases.title: Generalized Convulsion Mid-Recording - Timing and Aftercare
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Sleep-deprived EEG after a first unprovoked convulsion

history.eventDescription: First generalized convulsion two weeks ago on waking after a night out. Sleep-deprived today. During drowsiness he suddenly stiffens, cries out, and then develops rhythmic jerking of all limbs.

eegSummary.background: Normal wake and drowsy background before the event; ictal record obscured by muscle artifact, then diffuse post-ictal slowing and attenuation.
eegSummary.epileptiform: Ictal pattern partly obscured by muscle and movement artifact
eegSummary.artifacts: Heavy muscle and movement artifact during the convulsion

objectives: Give correct seizure first aid while keeping the EEG running
Apply the 5-minute threshold for convulsive status epilepticus
Perform and document post-ictal responsiveness testing

taskFlow.title: Onset
taskFlow.description: He stiffens with a cry and begins rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. He is on the stretcher with side rails down on one side. The clock reads 10:14:20.
taskFlow.question: What is your first action?
options: Hold his arms and legs down firmly so that he cannot injure himself
Slip a padded bite block between his teeth to protect his tongue now
Stop the recording and disconnect the head box so he can be moved
Note the time, call for staff, and cushion his head; keep recording
taskFlow.explanation: At onset: note the time, summon help, keep him safe (rails up or move hazards, cushion the head) and keep the EEG and video running, since the ictal record is the most valuable part of the study. Nothing goes in the mouth; bite blocks can break teeth and obstruct the airway. Restraining limbs can cause injury. Stopping the recording loses the ictal data.

taskFlow.title: Still convulsing
taskFlow.description: At 10:18:10 he is still having generalized jerking. The nurse who arrived asks when this becomes status epilepticus.
taskFlow.question: At what point should continuous convulsive activity be treated as status epilepticus?
options: After 5 minutes of continuous convulsive activity
After 30 minutes of continuous convulsive activity
Only once the EEG shows a flat post-ictal background
After 10 minutes, and only if he also turns cyanotic
taskFlow.explanation: Current practice (ILAE operational definition) treats a generalized convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more as status epilepticus requiring emergency treatment; 30 minutes is the older definition and the point where long-term harm becomes more likely, not when to start acting. The post-ictal background is irrelevant to when to escalate, and cyanosis is not a required criterion. Here 10:14:20 to 10:18:10 is 3 minutes 50 seconds, so the team must be ready to escalate at 10:19:20.

taskFlow.title: Convulsion stops
taskFlow.description: Jerking stops at 10:18:40 (4 minutes 20 seconds). He has noisy breathing and secretions, is unresponsive, and the EEG shows diffuse attenuation then slowing.
taskFlow.question: What is the immediate next step?
options: Begin hyperventilation now so that the protocol can be completed
Remove the electrodes now so that he can rest more comfortably
Turn him onto his side, check his breathing, and keep recording
Offer him small sips of water to help clear the mouth secretions
taskFlow.explanation: After the convulsion stops, place him in the recovery (lateral) position so secretions drain, check breathing, and stay with him while recording the post-ictal period. Hyperventilation is not done after a convulsion. Nothing by mouth until he is fully alert because of aspiration risk. Removing electrodes ends recording of the post-ictal state, which is clinically useful.

taskFlow.title: Post-ictal testing
taskFlow.description: At 10:26 he opens his eyes to his name but is confused. The neurologist will review the record later today.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do and document now?
options: Write that the EEG confirms a diagnosis of generalized epilepsy
Record only the time the seizure ended and the date of the study
Test commands and code-word recall; note time back to baseline
Document the word 'seizure' without describing his movements
taskFlow.explanation: Technologists test and document: ask him to follow commands, name objects, and remember a code word, then later check recall; record the semiology (tonic cry, generalized clonic jerking), onset 10:14:20, end 10:18:40, duration 4 min 20 s, post-ictal state and time to return to baseline, and who was notified. A bare label of 'seizure' is not useful. 'Confirms generalized epilepsy' is a diagnosis outside technologist scope. The end time alone omits most of the clinically relevant data.

learningLinks.label: Domain II: Event Monitoring & Emergency Response

starterCases.title: Fall Risk and Seizure Precautions in the EMU
starterCases.chiefComplaint: EMU admission for presurgical characterization of focal impaired-awareness seizures

history.eventDescription: Focal impaired-awareness seizures with post-ictal confusion and wandering. Antiseizure medications are being tapered on the physician order to capture events.

eegSummary.background: Normal background with intermittent right temporal slowing.
eegSummary.epileptiform: Occasional right anterior temporal sharp waves
eegSummary.artifacts: Movement and electrode pop on several channels after she gets out of bed

objectives: Set up EMU seizure and fall precautions at admission
Respond to a confused post-ictal patient trying to get up
Handle a fall safely and document it with an incident report

taskFlow.title: Admission set-up
taskFlow.description: She is admitted for a 5-day study with a medication taper. She has post-ictal wandering and osteopenia.
taskFlow.question: Which room set-up best fits EMU seizure and fall precautions?
options: Bed low, padded rails up, call bell in reach, fall-risk alerts on
Bed kept in the high position so staff can reach her more quickly
All bed rails removed so that she cannot strike them in a seizure
Wrist restraints at night so that she cannot get out of bed alone
taskFlow.explanation: Standard EMU precautions: bed in lowest position and locked, padded side rails, call bell and bed or chair alarm, fall-risk identification, clear floor, and supervised bathroom trips. Restraints are not a fall-prevention measure and need a specific order; they increase injury risk during seizures. Removing rails increases the chance of a fall during a seizure. A raised bed makes falls more injurious.

taskFlow.title: Up after a seizure
taskFlow.description: At 02:10 the video shows a typical seizure, then she sits up, looks confused, and starts climbing over the rail with the leads stretched. The bed alarm is sounding.
taskFlow.question: What is the right response?
options: Get to the bedside, or alert bedside staff, to guide her back
Silence the bed alarm so that other patients are not woken up
Use the intercom to tell her firmly to lie back down and wait
Note the time now and review the video once she has settled down
taskFlow.explanation: A confused post-ictal patient cannot reliably follow instructions; someone must reach her immediately (or alert bedside staff) to guide her safely and stay with her, while the event is marked. Intercom instructions are unlikely to work during post-ictal confusion. Reviewing later leaves her at risk now. Silencing the alarm removes a safety alert.

taskFlow.title: She has fallen
taskFlow.description: Before staff reach her she slides to the floor beside the bed. She is awake, holding her left hip, and two electrodes have pulled off.
taskFlow.question: What do you do first?
options: Reattach the two dislodged electrodes first so no data is lost
Have her stand up and walk a few steps so you can check her hip
Lift her back into bed by yourself right away so she feels safe
Keep her still, call the nurse, and assess for injury first
taskFlow.explanation: After a fall, keep the patient still and comfortable, summon nursing and medical help, and assess for injury (head strike, hip pain, deformity) before any move; use enough staff or equipment for a safe transfer. Lifting alone risks injury to both of you. Electrodes come after the patient. Weight-bearing on a possibly fractured hip in someone with osteopenia can worsen the injury.

taskFlow.title: Documentation
taskFlow.description: She is assessed, the hip X-ray is ordered, and she is back in bed with electrodes reapplied.
taskFlow.question: What documentation is required?
options: Note it only on the EEG recording as a period of movement artifact
Leave it to nursing, as technologists do not report falls
Chart the fall and notifications, and file an incident report
Ask the patient to sign a written statement saying that she fell
taskFlow.explanation: Falls are reportable safety events: document the time, what happened (post-ictal confusion, attempt to exit bed), immediate findings, who was notified, and electrode reapplication, and complete an incident report per policy. An artifact annotation alone hides the event. Every staff member who witnesses an event may need to report it. Patients are not asked to sign statements about incidents.

starterCases.title: Contact Precautions for C. difficile and MRSA Patients
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Portable EEG for confusion in a patient with C. difficile colitis

history.eventDescription: Hospitalized with C. difficile diarrhea; became confused overnight. A contact precautions sign (with soap-and-water instruction) is on the door. Tomorrow you have a second portable study on an MRSA-colonized patient.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse theta slowing, reactive to stimulation.

objectives: Choose PPE for contact-precautions rooms
Use soap and water after C. difficile contact
Disinfect equipment and reusable electrodes correctly

taskFlow.title: Before entering
taskFlow.description: The door sign shows contact precautions for C. difficile. You have the portable EEG cart outside the room.
taskFlow.question: What PPE do you put on?
options: An N95 respirator and eye protection, with no gown or gloves
Gown and gloves on entry; remove them before leaving the room
Gloves only, since you are working at the scalp and not the body
No added PPE, because he has not had diarrhea this morning
taskFlow.explanation: C. difficile requires contact precautions: gown and gloves for room entry and patient or environment contact, removed before exiting, followed by hand hygiene. Spores contaminate the bed and surfaces, not just the perineal area, so gloves alone are insufficient. N95 and eye protection address airborne or splash risks, not C. difficile. Precautions continue regardless of symptoms at that moment.

taskFlow.title: Hand hygiene
taskFlow.description: You finish, remove your gown and gloves at the doorway, and step out.
taskFlow.question: How should you clean your hands?
options: Wash with soap and running water
Alcohol-based hand rub for 20 seconds
Put on a fresh pair of gloves instead
An antiseptic hand wipe from the cart
taskFlow.explanation: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; washing with soap and running water physically removes them, which is why the door sign specifies soap and water. Hand wipes are not a substitute. Gloves are not hand hygiene, and the next contact would be made with contaminated hands under them.

taskFlow.title: Cleaning the cart
taskFlow.description: The head box, cables, and cart rails were in the room.
taskFlow.question: How should this equipment be cleaned?
options: Use the same quaternary ammonium wipes used for routine rooms
Wipe all surfaces with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air dry
Dry-wipe the paste off and return the cart to storage right away
Wipe with an EPA-registered sporicidal product, such as bleach
taskFlow.explanation: Spores survive alcohol and many routine quaternary ammonium products, so a sporicidal disinfectant (for example, a bleach-based EPA-registered product with a C. difficile claim, compatible with the equipment per manufacturer) is required, with the label contact time. Dry wiping removes visible paste but does not disinfect.

taskFlow.title: MRSA patient electrodes
taskFlow.description: The next day you record an MRSA-colonized patient under contact precautions, using reusable gold cup electrodes on intact scalp.
taskFlow.question: How do you reprocess the cup electrodes afterwards?
options: Discard all reusable electrodes that were used on an MRSA patient
Rinse them under warm tap water and leave them out to air dry
Clean off the paste, then disinfect with an approved product
Steam-sterilize every cup electrode after each MRSA-colonized patient
taskFlow.explanation: Electrodes on intact skin are noncritical items (Spaulding): clean first to remove paste and debris, then disinfect with an approved disinfectant at the correct contact time, following the manufacturer's instructions. MRSA does not require sterilization or discarding them. A water rinse alone does not disinfect. Electrodes on broken skin are a higher category and need a higher level of processing.

starterCases.title: Suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease - Electrode Handling and Disposal
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus; CJD on the differential

history.eventDescription: Over 3 months: memory loss, ataxia, and now startle-sensitive myoclonic jerks. The neurology team has flagged suspected CJD and asked for EEG.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing with generalized periodic sharp complexes at roughly 1 per second.
eegSummary.epileptiform: Generalized periodic sharp waves, many time-locked to myoclonic jerks

objectives: Choose electrodes for a suspected prion disease patient
Describe periodic complexes and their relation to myoclonus
Dispose of prion-exposed items and apply the right precautions

taskFlow.title: Choosing electrodes
taskFlow.description: The order notes 'suspected CJD - prion precautions'. You have reusable gold cups, single-use disposable cup electrodes, and subdermal needles on the cart.
taskFlow.question: Which electrodes should you use?
options: Single-use disposable electrodes, and no subdermal needles
Reusable cups, followed by routine high-level disinfection
Reusable cups, wiped down with 70% alcohol after the recording
Subdermal needles, to cut down on paste and skin handling
taskFlow.explanation: Prions resist routine disinfection and sterilization, so EEG practice for suspected CJD is single-use disposable electrodes that are discarded afterward, avoiding needles that breach the skin. Routine high-level disinfection and alcohol do not reliably inactivate prions. Needle electrodes add puncture and blood exposure risk.

taskFlow.title: The recording
taskFlow.description: The EEG shows generalized periodic sharp complexes at about 1 per second; many coincide with visible jerks of the arms. The daughter asks if this means CJD.
taskFlow.question: What is the technologist's correct approach?
options: Describe the complexes and annotate the timing of jerks
Label the complexes as movement artifact caused by the jerks
Stop the recording now, because the diagnosis is already clear
Tell the daughter that the EEG confirms the diagnosis of CJD
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist documents what is seen: generalized periodic sharp complexes (ACNS terminology: generalized periodic discharges) at about 1 Hz, noting the time relationship of jerks to discharges, and tells the family that the physician will interpret it. Diagnosing CJD to the family exceeds scope. The complexes are cerebral and persist between jerks, so calling them artifact is wrong (an EMG or video channel helps separate the two). Shortening the study removes data the reader needs.

taskFlow.title: Disposal
taskFlow.description: The study is finished. You have used disposable electrodes, gauze, and cotton tips; paste residue is on the head box clips.
taskFlow.question: How do you dispose of the electrodes and contaminated items?
options: Bag them for incineration per the facility prion protocol
Place them in the regular trash bin on the nursing unit
Autoclave them on a routine cycle and return them to stock
Soak them in alcohol and keep them for this patient only
taskFlow.explanation: Items in contact with a suspected prion patient are discarded and incinerated according to the facility's prion protocol, and infection control is informed so that surfaces and any reusable equipment are handled with the approved method. A routine autoclave cycle does not reliably inactivate prions. Regular trash and alcohol soaks are not acceptable.

taskFlow.title: Level of precautions
taskFlow.description: A colleague asks whether everyone entering the room needs an N95 respirator.
taskFlow.question: Which precautions apply to routine contact with this patient?
options: Droplet precautions with surgical masks at all times
Standard precautions; CJD is not spread by air or casual contact
Airborne isolation, with N95 respirators for everyone entering
Refuse the study until the diagnosis has been confirmed by biopsy
taskFlow.explanation: CJD is not transmitted by airborne, droplet, or casual contact; standard precautions apply to routine care, with the special handling directed at instruments and items that contact the patient. Airborne or droplet isolation is unnecessary. Refusing the study is not appropriate; the right precautions make it safe.

starterCases.title: Skin Breakdown During Long-Term ICU and NICU Monitoring
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG on day 3 after cardiac arrest; intubated and supine

history.eventDescription: Comatose after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, on continuous EEG with collodion-applied cup electrodes. Head kept supine, minimal repositioning. A neonate in the NICU is also due to start long-term monitoring this week.

eegSummary.background: Continuous diffuse slowing with intermittent low-voltage periods.
eegSummary.artifacts: Rising impedance at O1 and O2 on day 3

objectives: Plan skin checks for multi-day monitoring
Respond to breakdown under an electrode
Choose safer application methods for neonatal skin

taskFlow.title: Planning a multi-day study
taskFlow.description: Monitoring is expected to last several more days. He has diabetes and poor peripheral circulation, and lies supine with little repositioning.
taskFlow.question: Which plan best prevents electrode-related skin injury?
options: Change to subdermal needles to avoid any adhesive-related injury
Leave all electrodes undisturbed until the monitoring study ends
Scheduled checks of all sites, especially occipital pressure areas
Add extra collodion over the occiput to stop the electrodes slipping
taskFlow.explanation: Long-term monitoring needs scheduled inspection of every electrode site per lab protocol, paying particular attention to sites under the weight of the head (O1, O2, Oz, P sites) and to high-risk patients (critically ill, poor perfusion, diabetes, neonates). Leaving electrodes undisturbed means breakdown is found late. More collodion does not relieve pressure. Subdermal needles carry their own infection and injury risks and are not a skin-protection strategy.

taskFlow.title: Breakdown found
taskFlow.description: During the check, the skin under O2 is red with a small blister and an area that does not blanch; impedance there has climbed.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Re-glue the electrode on the same spot using fresh collodion and gauze
Remove and relocate the electrode, tell the nurse, and document
Abrade the site again gently to bring the impedance back down
Cover the area with protective tape and continue the recording
taskFlow.explanation: A non-blanching, blistered area is a pressure injury. Remove the electrode, relieve pressure (relocate to a nearby intact site and note the substitution on the montage), notify nursing for wound care, and document. Re-gluing or taping over it keeps the injury under pressure. Abrading injured skin worsens the wound and raises infection risk.

taskFlow.title: The NICU baby
taskFlow.description: Later that week you set up long-term monitoring on a 2-day-old term neonate in the NICU.
taskFlow.question: Which application approach is most appropriate?
options: Paste or neonatal adhesive electrodes; no collodion or acetone
Firm skin abrasion to bring every impedance under 1 kOhm
Subdermal needles, to spare the fragile skin from adhesive
Collodion, because neonatal monitoring studies run for many hours
taskFlow.explanation: Neonatal skin is thin and permeable: use paste or neonatal-specific electrodes with gentle prep, and avoid collodion and acetone, whose solvents and fumes are inappropriate for newborns. Aggressive abrasion damages neonatal skin; impedance targets are reached gently. Needles break the skin and are not used for routine neonatal monitoring.

taskFlow.title: Documentation
taskFlow.description: You return to the adult ICU patient's chart to record what you found and did.
taskFlow.question: What should the documentation include?
options: Nothing at all, unless the skin is actually broken open
A photo from your phone, texted to the neurologist on call
Site, size, appearance, action taken, and who was notified
'Skin intact', so that the family is not alarmed by the note
taskFlow.explanation: Document objectively: which electrode site, size and appearance (redness, blister, non-blanching), electrode removed and relocated, nurse notified, and the time, plus any incident report your facility requires. Falsely charting intact skin is falsification. Pre-break-down redness is exactly what must be recorded. Personal phones and texting images breach privacy policies; use approved systems only.

starterCases.title: Collodion and Acetone Safety - Fumes, Fire, and Eye Splash
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Electrode application and removal for an ambulatory EEG

history.eventDescription: Ambulatory EEG for nocturnal events. Electrodes are applied with collodion and later removed with acetone in a small procedure room.

eegSummary.background: Normal set-up recording before ambulatory unit disconnected.

objectives: Apply collodion with ventilation and no ignition sources
Give first aid for an acetone splash to the eye
Use the SDS and report chemical exposures

taskFlow.title: Applying collodion
taskFlow.description: The procedure room is small. A colleague suggests using a heat gun to dry the collodion faster because the schedule is behind.
taskFlow.question: Which practice is correct?
options: Keep the opened bottle uncapped on the cart for the whole day
Use ventilation or fume extraction; keep heat and flame away
Dry it quickly with the heat gun set on its lowest setting
Close the room door so that the fumes stay inside one room
taskFlow.explanation: Collodion and acetone are highly flammable, and their vapors are irritating, so use them with good ventilation or fume extraction, away from heat and ignition sources, and keep containers capped. Collodion is dried with compressed air, not heat. Closing the door concentrates vapors. An open bottle releases vapor and increases fire risk.

taskFlow.title: Eye splash
taskFlow.description: During removal, acetone drips from the gauze into the patient's right eye. He cries out and the eye is tearing and red.
taskFlow.question: What is the immediate first aid?
options: Instill diluted vinegar drops to neutralize the chemical
Flush with running water or eyewash for at least 15 minutes
Tape a patch over the eye and then finish removing electrodes
Rub the eye gently with dry gauze to soak up the acetone
taskFlow.explanation: Chemical eye exposure is flushed immediately and copiously with water or an eyewash station, eyelids held open, for at least 15 minutes (the usual SDS first-aid instruction), then medical evaluation. Rubbing spreads the chemical and can abrade the cornea. 'Neutralizing' drops are never used. Patching traps the chemical against the eye.

taskFlow.title: Finding the hazard information
taskFlow.description: The patient asks what is in the liquid and whether it can harm his eye. The nurse wants the exact first-aid and hazard information.
taskFlow.question: Where should you look?
options: The operator's manual supplied with the EEG recording instrument
The hospital pharmacy, using the barcode on the bottle
An online discussion forum for EEG technologists
The product's Safety Data Sheet, kept in the work area
taskFlow.explanation: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard requires employers to keep Safety Data Sheets for hazardous chemicals readily accessible to employees; the SDS lists hazards, first aid, fire-fighting, and spill measures. The instrument manual does not cover chemicals. Pharmacy is not the source for workplace chemical SDS information, and forums are not authoritative.

taskFlow.title: Follow-up
taskFlow.description: After 15 minutes of flushing, his eye feels better but is still mildly red.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct follow-up?
options: Ask him to sign a form saying that he declined any further treatment
Record it as an equipment fault in the lab maintenance log
Note it in the chart only if his eye is still red tomorrow
Report the exposure, chart first aid, and arrange an eye exam
taskFlow.explanation: A chemical exposure to a patient is a reportable safety event: arrange evaluation (ED or eye clinic per policy), document the time, chemical, first aid given and duration, and notifications, and file an incident report. Waiting until tomorrow delays care. Patients are not pressured to sign declinations. It was a chemical handling event, not an equipment fault.

starterCases.title: Wrong-Patient Near Miss - Two Identifiers and Order Clarification
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Portable EEG ordered for altered mental status on a busy medical ward

history.eventDescription: Two men with the same surname are on the same ward. The requisition lists a routine EEG; the bedside nurse thinks the team wanted continuous video EEG.

eegSummary.background: Study not yet started.

objectives: Use two patient identifiers matched to band and order
Stop for any identifier mismatch before starting
Clarify an ambiguous order and report a near miss

taskFlow.title: Identification
taskFlow.description: You arrive at bed 12. The patient is awake and able to answer questions. Another patient with the same surname is in bed 14.
taskFlow.question: How do you identify the patient?
options: Confirm that the room and bed number match those on the order
Check the name written on the whiteboard above the head of the bed
Ask him 'Are you Mr. Smith?' and wait for him to answer yes
Ask his full name and date of birth; match to band and order
taskFlow.explanation: Two identifiers (for example full name and date of birth, or medical record number), stated by the patient when able and matched to the ID band and the order. Room or bed numbers are never identifiers. Yes/no questions invite a confused patient to agree. Whiteboards are not verified sources.

taskFlow.title: A mismatch
taskFlow.description: He states his name and date of birth. The band matches what he says, but the date of birth on the EEG requisition is different by one year.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Correct the date of birth on the requisition yourself and go on
Record the study now and sort out the date discrepancy later
Proceed, since the name matches exactly on all three sources
Stop and resolve the mismatch before applying any electrodes
taskFlow.explanation: Any identifier discrepancy halts the procedure until resolved with the nurse or ordering provider; with two same-surname patients on the ward, the order may belong to the other man. Matching only the name defeats the two-identifier rule. Technologists do not alter orders. Recording first risks a study filed under the wrong patient.

taskFlow.title: Which study?
taskFlow.description: The order is confirmed to be for this patient, but it reads 'routine EEG'. The nurse says the team asked for continuous video EEG to look for subtle seizures.
taskFlow.question: How do you proceed?
options: Call the ordering provider to clarify and get a corrected order
Record the longer study to be safe, so that both requests are covered
Do the routine EEG as written and leave a note for the nurse
Start continuous video EEG based on the nurse's verbal account
taskFlow.explanation: When an order and the clinical request disagree, the technologist clarifies with the ordering provider and obtains a correct order before starting. Acting on a verbal secondhand account or choosing a study yourself is outside scope. Proceeding with the written routine study while knowing it may be wrong can miss the clinical question.

taskFlow.title: After it is resolved
taskFlow.description: A corrected order for continuous video EEG is entered, and you complete a pause to confirm patient, order, and study type with the nurse before starting.
taskFlow.question: What should happen to the near miss?
options: No report is needed, since the error was caught in time
Mention it privately to the unit clerk so they are more careful
Report it only if the patient or family later finds out about it
Report it in the safety event system, though no harm occurred
taskFlow.explanation: Near misses are reported through the facility's event reporting system so system causes (same-surname alerts, order-entry errors) can be fixed; that is the purpose of a just-culture reporting system. 'No harm, no report' loses the learning. Reporting does not depend on whether the patient knows. Informal comments do not trigger system fixes.

starterCases.title: Consent for a Minor and a Relative Phoning for Results
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for new-onset staring spells, brought in by her adult sister

history.eventDescription: A 16-year-old with episodes of staring at school arrives with her 22-year-old sister; her parents are at work. She is not emancipated.

eegSummary.background: Normal waking background.

objectives: Identify who can consent for a non-emancipated minor
Refuse to release information to unverified callers
Respond to a social media privacy breach

taskFlow.title: Who consents?
taskFlow.description: The lab requires signed consent before the study. The sister offers to sign, and the patient says she can sign for herself.
taskFlow.question: Who may give consent?
options: The 22-year-old sister who brought her today
The referring physician on the family's behalf
A parent or legal guardian, with the teen's assent
The 16-year-old herself, since she is over 14 years old
taskFlow.explanation: A non-emancipated minor's consent comes from a parent or legal guardian (reached by phone with a witness if policy allows), and the teen's assent is sought. An adult sibling is not a legal guardian without documentation. Minors consent for themselves only in specific legal situations (emancipation or statutory exceptions), which do not apply here. The referring physician cannot consent for the patient.

taskFlow.title: A phone call
taskFlow.description: Two days later a man phones the lab, says he is her uncle, gives her date of birth, and asks whether the EEG showed epilepsy.
taskFlow.question: How do you respond?
options: Share the result once he correctly confirms her date of birth
Decline, and refer him to the ordering physician's office
Read him the technologist notes, but not the final report
Confirm that she had the test, but do not give any results
taskFlow.explanation: Under HIPAA, information goes only to the patient's authorized representatives through proper channels; knowing a date of birth does not verify authority. Results are released by the ordering physician, not the technologist. Confirming that she was a patient is itself a disclosure of protected health information.

taskFlow.title: A social media post
taskFlow.description: A coworker posts an 'amazing tracing from today' on a public social media account. The face is cropped, but the date, study time, and part of the patient label are visible.
taskFlow.question: What is the right action?
options: Share it further, since it is educational for other techs
Ask for it to be removed and report it to the privacy officer
Post a public comment under it warning the coworker
Ignore it, because the patient's face is not shown in the image
taskFlow.explanation: Dates, times, and partial labels can identify a patient, so this is a potential privacy breach; it must be removed and reported through the privacy officer per policy so required steps can be taken. Cropping the face does not de-identify. Public comments spread it further. Educational intent does not authorize disclosure.

taskFlow.title: Record request
taskFlow.description: The patient's mother later calls asking for a copy of the EEG report for a school nurse.
taskFlow.question: Where do you direct her?
options: Tell her parents may not see a teen's record
Print the raw EEG for her at the front desk
To health information management (medical records)
Email her the PDF report from your work email account
taskFlow.explanation: Release of records goes through health information management, which verifies identity and authority and logs the disclosure. Technologists do not email reports or hand out raw EEG data. A parent of a minor is generally the personal representative and can request records (state law exceptions aside), so a blanket refusal is wrong.

starterCases.title: Asked 'Is It Epilepsy?' - Scope and Critical Findings
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Continuous EEG for persistently reduced consciousness after a convulsion

history.eventDescription: Admitted after a witnessed convulsion; not back to baseline after 12 hours. Family and the night resident ask the technologist questions during set-up and recording.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing.
eegSummary.epileptiform: Left hemisphere rhythmic sharp activity that evolves in frequency and location, lasting over a minute

objectives: Answer family questions without interpreting
Refer clinical interpretation to the reading physician
Follow the critical-findings notification chain and document it

taskFlow.title: The family asks
taskFlow.description: During set-up his mother asks, 'Can you see if it is epilepsy? Is his brain damaged?'
taskFlow.question: How do you respond?
options: Explain that the sharp waves you can see suggest epilepsy
Explain that the neurologist reads it and reports to his team
Tell her the tracing looks normal so far, so she can relax
Say that technologists are not allowed to talk with any families
taskFlow.explanation: Technologists can be warm and explain the procedure, but interpretation belongs to the reading physician, who reports to the treating team. Reassuring 'normal' or suggesting epilepsy are both interpretations. Refusing all conversation is unprofessional; you can explain the process and who will discuss results.

taskFlow.title: The resident asks
taskFlow.description: An hour later the night resident calls: 'What did the EEG show? Should we load another drug?'
taskFlow.question: What is the appropriate reply?
options: Refer him to the reading neurologist for the interpretation
Read him your technical notes as the final result of the study
Tell him it looks epileptic and that a second drug is needed
Give him your impression, since he is a physician
taskFlow.explanation: Even with a physician asking, interpretation and treatment advice come from the reading neurologist; the technologist can connect them and share technical observations per lab policy. Recommending medication is clearly outside scope. Technical notes are not a final report. The requester's credentials do not expand technologist scope.

taskFlow.title: A pattern on the screen
taskFlow.description: You see left hemisphere rhythmic sharp activity that evolves in frequency and spreads, lasting more than a minute. The bedside nurse sees no clinical change.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Annotate it and wait for the scheduled morning review session
Ask the nurse to give him a dose of a benzodiazepine right away
Notify the team only if a clinical seizure becomes visible at bedside
Notify the reading physician now per the critical-findings policy
taskFlow.explanation: An evolving rhythmic pattern in an ICU patient may be an electrographic seizure; most labs define it as a critical finding requiring immediate notification of the reading physician (and team per policy), plus responsiveness testing and annotation. Waiting for morning delays treatment. Technologists do not direct medication. Electrographic seizures are frequently nonconvulsive, so lack of clinical signs does not lower urgency.

taskFlow.title: Documenting the call
taskFlow.description: You reach the reading neurologist by phone at 03:42 and describe the finding.
taskFlow.question: What must you document?
options: That the technologist diagnosed seizures on the EEG recording
Time, who was notified, what was reported, and their read-back
That you left a voicemail, recorded as the physician notified
Nothing further, as long as the physician personally answered the phone
taskFlow.explanation: Critical-findings documentation records the time, the person notified, what was communicated, and confirmation by read-back, plus any instructions. The technologist reports observations, not a diagnosis. Undocumented calls leave no record that notification happened. A voicemail is not a completed notification; escalate per policy until a person is reached.

starterCases.title: Latex Allergy and a Vagus Nerve Stimulator During EEG
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for medication adjustment in drug-resistant epilepsy with a VNS

history.eventDescription: Drug-resistant epilepsy since childhood with a vagus nerve stimulator; generator in the left upper chest. Known latex allergy (hives and wheeze). Her mother carries the VNS magnet.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing for age.
eegSummary.artifacts: Recurrent bursts of high-frequency artifact on the ECG and left-sided channels on a fixed on-off cycle, with hoarse voice and throat clearing

objectives: Prepare a latex-safe set-up and ask about adhesive reactions
Recognize VNS stimulation artifact by its fixed cycle
Annotate magnet swipes and document device details

taskFlow.title: Set-up
taskFlow.description: The chart lists a latex allergy (hives, wheeze). Your usual kit includes latex gloves, an elastic head-cap chin strap containing latex, and tape.
taskFlow.question: What do you do before touching the patient?
options: Use latex-free gloves and supplies; ask about adhesive reactions
Proceed as usual, since latex allergy matters only in surgery
Wear latex gloves, but avoid touching her skin directly with them
Ask the nurse to give an antihistamine before you start
taskFlow.explanation: With a latex allergy, every item that touches the patient must be latex-free (gloves, straps, tape, bands), and you also ask about reactions to adhesives or collodion so the application method can be chosen. Latex proteins transfer from gloves to the patient and airborne particles can trigger reactions, so 'not touching skin' is not protection. Premedication is a physician order, not a technologist decision. Reactions can occur outside the OR.

taskFlow.title: Recurring bursts
taskFlow.description: Twenty minutes in, you notice bursts of high-frequency activity on the ECG channel and left-sided electrodes. They last about the same time, recur on a fixed cycle, and coincide with hoarseness and throat clearing.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely source?
options: 60 Hz interference from a nearby wall outlet or bed motor
VNS stimulation artifact; note the on-off cycle and annotate it
Lateralized periodic discharges arising from the left hemisphere
Muscle artifact from intermittent chewing or teeth clenching
taskFlow.explanation: A VNS delivers stimulation trains on a programmed on-off cycle; the artifact is high frequency, strongest near the left neck and chest (ECG and left-sided channels), regularly timed, and may come with hoarseness or cough from vagal (recurrent laryngeal) stimulation. Cerebral periodic discharges are not tied to voice changes or a machine-like cycle. 60 Hz interference is continuous, not on a cycle. Chewing artifact is irregular and bilateral temporal.

taskFlow.title: The magnet
taskFlow.description: Her mother says, 'She is having her warning feeling,' and swipes the magnet over the generator. A burst of stimulation artifact follows.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Turn the VNS off with the programming wand until the study ends
Annotate the magnet swipe time and test her responsiveness
Hold the magnet on the generator for the whole study
Take the magnet away so that the recording stays artifact-free
taskFlow.explanation: A magnet swipe triggers an on-demand stimulation and is part of her seizure plan; annotate the time and the reason, and perform responsiveness testing as for any event. Removing the magnet interferes with treatment. Holding the magnet over the generator stops stimulation, which is not what the family intends. Programming the device is done only by authorized clinicians.

taskFlow.title: Technologist notes
taskFlow.description: The study ends without further events. The reader will review the record tomorrow.
taskFlow.question: Which notes are essential?
options: Device, generator side, artifact cycle, and magnet swipe times
Your opinion that the VNS does not seem to be working well for her
None, since the stimulator artifact is obvious to readers
The generator settings you changed to reduce the artifact
taskFlow.explanation: Documenting the implanted device, its location, the observed stimulation artifact pattern and timing, magnet use, latex precautions, and the patient's report of an aura lets the reader separate artifact from cerebral activity and correlate events. Technologists never change device settings. Efficacy judgments are clinical interpretation. Readers should not have to guess what an artifact is.

starterCases.title: Calibration Gain Fault and Swapped Labels Found After the Study
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for suspected focal epilepsy; QA problems recognized during review

history.eventDescription: Focal impaired-awareness seizures with oral automatisms and right-arm dystonic posturing. During post-study review the technologist rechecks calibration and finds labeling problems.

eegSummary.background: Normal background.
eegSummary.epileptiform: Sharp waves with phase reversal labeled at T4 in the recording
eegSummary.focalFindings: Intermittent temporal slowing on the same labeled side

objectives: Calculate expected calibration deflection and spot a gain error
Use biocalibration polarity to find reversed inputs
Correct and document a labeling error, and quarantine equipment

taskFlow.title: Square-wave calibration
taskFlow.description: Sensitivity is set to 7 uV/mm on all channels. The 50 uV square-wave calibration produces about 7 mm deflections on every channel except channel 6, which deflects only 3.6 mm.
taskFlow.question: What does channel 6 tell you?
options: It is normal, because 3.6 mm is the expected deflection at 7 uV/mm
It has a high-impedance electrode connected at its input
It is twice as sensitive, at an effective 3.5 uV/mm
Its gain is about half; effective sensitivity is near 14 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: Deflection = signal / sensitivity = 50 uV / 7 uV/mm = 7.1 mm expected. Channel 6 gives 3.6 mm, so its effective sensitivity = 50 uV / 3.6 mm = 13.9 uV/mm, about half the gain of the other channels. A higher sensitivity value means less deflection, not more, so 'twice as sensitive' flips the relationship. Square-wave calibration is injected at the amplifier inputs, bypassing the electrodes, so electrode impedance cannot explain it.

taskFlow.title: Biocalibration
taskFlow.description: You run a biocalibration with every channel connected to Fp1-O2 and ask the patient to blink. Blinks make Fp1 positive relative to O2. All channels deflect downward with each blink except channel 4, which deflects upward.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely cause for channel 4?
options: Its inputs are reversed, so it records O2 minus Fp1
Its 60 Hz notch filter is switched on for that channel
Its low-frequency filter is set too high for this study
Its electrode impedance is high on one of the inputs
taskFlow.explanation: Each channel displays Input 1 minus Input 2, with negative up. For Fp1 - O2, a blink makes Fp1 positive, so the output is positive and the pen deflects down, as on the correct channels. Channel 4 deflects up: the output is negative, which happens when the inputs are swapped (O2 - Fp1). A high LFF changes the shape and amplitude of slow waves but not their polarity. Impedance and the notch filter do not invert the signal.

taskFlow.title: Labels swapped
taskFlow.description: During review you find the head box jacks for T3 and T4 were mislabeled: the electrode on the left mid-temporal scalp was plugged into the jack labeled T4. The sharp waves with phase reversal labeled 'T4' actually arose at the left electrode. The report has not been finalized.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct action?
options: Delete the study and rebook him without telling anyone
Notify the reading physician and add a dated note on the swap
Edit the raw file so that the labels are right, without any note
Leave it, since the reader will spot it from the symmetry
taskFlow.explanation: The reader must know before the report is finalized, because the side of the focus has reversed (left, consistent with the right-arm dystonic posturing). Corrections are made transparently: notify the physician, add a dated, signed addendum or annotation describing the error and its effect, and, if the system allows a corrected channel remapping, document it. Silent edits to the raw record are falsification. Deleting data is never appropriate. Symmetry does not reveal a swapped pair.

taskFlow.title: Before the next patient
taskFlow.description: Your next patient arrives in 20 minutes and is due to use the same instrument and head box.
taskFlow.question: What do you do with the equipment?
options: Tag it out of service, have it checked, and use a verified backup
Swap the two cables back and start the next study without testing
Use it, and mentally relabel T3 and T4 when reviewing the study
Bring it up at next month's staff meeting instead
taskFlow.explanation: Equipment with a known gain fault (channel 6) and mislabeled inputs is removed from service and tagged, reported to biomedical engineering or the lab supervisor, and returned only after repair and a passed calibration and biocalibration; the next patient uses verified equipment. Mental relabeling and untested fixes risk repeating the error, and delayed reporting exposes more patients.

starterCases.title: Central Arciform Rhythm That Ignores Eye Opening
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG after a single fainting episode

history.eventDescription: A 41-year-old felt light-headed while standing in a long line and briefly lost consciousness, with no jerking or tongue biting. Routine awake EEG was ordered.

eegSummary.background: Well-organized awake background
eegSummary.pdrHz: About 10 Hz, reactive to eye opening
eegSummary.focalFindings: Arciform 9 Hz activity over C3 and C4

objectives: Confirm normal posterior alpha reactivity on a live page
Localize an arciform central rhythm by phase reversal
Use contralateral hand movement to test mu blocking

taskFlow.title: Eye-opening check
taskFlow.description: The first awake page is displayed in the longitudinal bipolar montage at 7 uV/mm. You asked the patient to open her eyes at 0.9 s and to close them at 6.6 s; both events are marked under the page.
taskFlow.question: Compare T5-O1 and T6-O2 before 0.9 s, between the markers, and after 6.6 s. What does the posterior ~10 Hz rhythm do?
options: It continues unchanged with eyes open, so it does not react
It attenuates only on the left side, leaving the right unchanged
It attenuates after eye opening and returns after eye closure
It increases in amplitude after eye opening, then fades at 6.6 s
taskFlow.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm in T5-O1 and T6-O2 drops to low amplitude after the 'Eyes open' marker and returns after 'Eyes closed': normal, symmetric reactivity. A rhythm that persisted unchanged would be unreactive, which is the opposite of what the page shows. Alpha does not grow with eye opening (paradoxical alpha is a drowsiness phenomenon). The attenuation is bilateral; a one-sided failure to block (Bancaud phenomenon) would be a finding worth noting, but it is not present here.

taskFlow.title: The central rhythm
taskFlow.description: Between the eye markers, an arciform rhythm of about 9 Hz remains in F3-C3, C3-P3, F4-C4 and C4-P4. Its sharp phase alternates with a rounded one. Look at the direction of the sharp peaks in each pair of channels.
taskFlow.question: Where is this rhythm maximal, and what on the page shows it?
options: At C3 and C4, because F3-C3 and C3-P3 deflect in opposite directions
At Fz and Cz, because it is largest in the midline Fz-Cz channel
At T3 and T4, because the temporal channels carry the sharp phase
At O1 and O2, because the occipital electrodes end each chain
taskFlow.explanation: In F3-C3 the subtraction is F3 minus C3; with C3 negative the result is positive and the pen goes down. In C3-P3 the subtraction is C3 minus P3, so the same negativity gives an upward pen deflection. Opposite deflections in the two channels sharing C3 are a phase reversal at C3 (and likewise at C4). O1/O2 is where the posterior alpha lives, and that rhythm blocked. Fz-Cz is small on this page. The temporal chains do not carry the arciform activity.

taskFlow.title: Confirming mu
taskFlow.description: The physician asks whether you can show that the central rhythm is mu. You still have several minutes of awake recording, and the patient is cooperative and seated with her eyes open.
taskFlow.question: Which bedside test best confirms that this is mu rhythm?
options: Run photic stimulation at 9 Hz and watch for driving at C3 and C4
Ask her to open and close her right hand and watch the C3 activity
Ask her to open and close her eyes again and watch C3 and C4
Start hyperventilation and look for the central rhythm to build up
taskFlow.explanation: Mu rhythm attenuates with movement (or even the intention to move) of the contralateral limb, so a right-hand fist should block mu over C3, and left-hand movement should block it over C4. Repeating eye opening adds nothing, because the page already shows the central rhythm persists with eyes open; that is what separates it from alpha but does not prove it is mu. Photic driving and hyperventilation build-up test other things and do not block mu.

taskFlow.title: Technologist note
taskFlow.description: With repeated right-hand fist clenching, the 9 Hz activity over C3 attenuated within a second and returned after she relaxed. Left-hand movement did the same over C4. You now write your technologist comments.
taskFlow.question: Which note is accurate and within your scope?
options: 9 Hz arciform C3/C4 activity, persists with eyes open, blocks with hand use
Impression: rolandic spikes over C3 and C4; abnormal EEG, epileptiform
Central 9 Hz activity, normal variant, so it does not need documenting
Impression: mu rhythm only; normal EEG; no further review is needed
taskFlow.explanation: The technologist documents what was seen and how it reacted: frequency, location, morphology, persistence with eyes open and blocking with contralateral hand movement, with the tests annotated on the record. Writing 'rolandic spikes, abnormal' mislabels a normal rhythm and is an interpretation. Leaving it out loses the observation the reader needs to classify it. A final impression of 'normal EEG' is the physician's call, not the technologist's.

starterCases.title: Arciform Posterior Alpha Mistaken for Mu Rhythm
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for recurrent headaches with visual aura

history.eventDescription: A 37-year-old with migraine with visual aura had an EEG requested to exclude an occipital seizure focus. No loss of awareness has occurred.

eegSummary.background: Awake, eyes closed

objectives: Localize an arciform 10 Hz rhythm to the occipital region
Separate arciform alpha from mu by location and reactivity
Describe a posterior rhythm without mislabeling its shape

taskFlow.title: Where is it?
taskFlow.description: A trainee flags this awake, eyes-closed page as 'mu rhythm'. The page shows an arciform rhythm of about 10 Hz. Switch between the longitudinal and referential montages before you answer.
taskFlow.question: Where is this arciform rhythm maximal?
options: At T3 and T4, largest in the mid-temporal channels
At Fz and Cz, largest in the midline Fz-Cz channel
At O1 and O2, largest in the O1-A1 and O2-A2 channels
At C3 and C4, largest in the F3-C3 and C4-P4 channels
taskFlow.explanation: In referential (ipsilateral ear) the largest channels are O1-A1 and O2-A2. In longitudinal the activity is largest in T5-O1 and T6-O2, the last channel of each chain, where O1/O2 is input 2 and there is no phase reversal (end-of-chain). C3-P3, C4-P4 and Cz-Pz carry some of it only because P3, P4 and Pz lie at the edge of the occipital field. F3-C3, F4-C4 and Fz-Cz are nearly flat, so there is no reversal at C3/C4 and this is not where mu lives. The mid-temporal channels do not carry it.

taskFlow.title: Choose the test
taskFlow.description: The trainee still thinks the shape alone proves mu. You can ask the patient to do one simple maneuver before the next page.
taskFlow.question: Which maneuver best separates this rhythm from mu?
options: Start 3 minutes of hyperventilation and watch the central channels
Run photic stimulation at 10 Hz and look for occipital driving
Lower the HFF to 15 Hz to see whether the sharp phase disappears
Ask him to open his eyes, since alpha blocks and mu does not
taskFlow.explanation: Posterior alpha attenuates with eye opening; mu persists with eyes open and blocks with contralateral movement instead. Lowering the HFF changes the displayed morphology and can hide the harmonic that makes the waves look arciform, but it says nothing about what the rhythm is. Hyperventilation and photic driving test other responses and do not separate alpha from mu.

taskFlow.title: Compare with true mu
taskFlow.description: For teaching, you open a second page from another patient whose central rhythm was confirmed as mu. Its eye-opening and eye-closing markers are shown.
taskFlow.question: Compared with the first page, what is different on this comparison page?
options: Its arciform rhythm is posterior and faster, at about 12 Hz
Its arciform rhythm is only on the left, over C3 and P3
Its arciform rhythm is central and blocks after 'Eyes open'
Its arciform rhythm is central and continues after 'Eyes open'
taskFlow.explanation: On the comparison page the arciform rhythm (about 9 Hz) reverses phase at C3 and C4 and keeps going between 'Eyes open' and 'Eyes closed', while the posterior 10 Hz rhythm blocks. That is mu. It is central, not posterior, and slightly slower, not 12 Hz. It does not block with eye opening, which is the whole point. It is bilateral, seen in both F3-C3/C3-P3 and F4-C4/C4-P4.

taskFlow.title: Describe it correctly
