taskFlow.description: Back on the first patient, you asked him to open his eyes: the arciform 10 Hz rhythm over O1 and O2 attenuated and returned on eye closure. You now write your technologist comments.
taskFlow.question: Which description is accurate?
options: 10 Hz arciform posterior rhythm at O1/O2, blocks with eye opening
No posterior rhythm seen; central mu rhythm present over C3/C4
Posterior rhythm absent; arciform waves at C3 and C4 persisting
Sharply contoured 10 Hz occipital waves, possibly epileptiform
taskFlow.explanation: The arciform waves are the posterior dominant rhythm itself, with a superimposed harmonic giving the arciform look: 10 Hz, maximal O1/O2, symmetric and reactive. Calling it 'no PDR, mu present' mislocalizes it and loses the normal PDR. 'Possibly epileptiform' turns a rhythmic background rhythm into a concern it does not warrant; a continuous rhythm that blocks with eye opening is not a train of discharges. The rhythm is not central and it does not persist with eyes open.

starterCases.title: Frontal Rhythmic Delta in Metabolic Encephalopathy
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Stupor with rising ammonia and creatinine

history.eventDescription: A 61-year-old with cirrhosis and acute kidney injury became progressively drowsy over two days and now opens his eyes only briefly to loud voice. No witnessed convulsions.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse theta-delta slowing, no posterior dominant rhythm

objectives: Measure the frequency of rhythmic delta with the caliper
Describe frontally predominant GRDA in ACNS 2021 terms
Test and annotate reactivity, and recognize muscle artifact

taskFlow.title: Measure the rhythm
taskFlow.description: Bedside EEG at 10 uV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz. The page shows runs of high-amplitude rhythmic slow waves. Use the caliper on one full wave (trough to trough) in Fp1-F7 or F3-C3, or count waves within one second.
taskFlow.question: What is the frequency of this rhythmic activity?
options: About 1.8 Hz, in the delta band
About 5 Hz, in the theta band
About 3.6 Hz, at the top of the delta band
About 0.9 Hz, in the slowest part of the delta band
taskFlow.explanation: One cycle measures about 550 ms, and frequency = 1 / period = 1 / 0.55 s = 1.8 Hz, which is delta (below 4 Hz). Counting gives the same answer: just under 2 waves per 1-s grid box. 3.6 Hz comes from counting each peak and trough as a separate wave. 0.9 Hz comes from measuring two cycles as one. 5 Hz theta is the faster, lower-amplitude background between runs, not the rhythmic runs.

taskFlow.title: Distribution and name
taskFlow.description: Switch to the referential montage and compare the frontal and the posterior channels. The rhythmic runs start near 0.2 s and 5.3 s.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits the page in ACNS 2021 terminology?
options: Generalized periodic discharges at about 2 per second
An electrographic seizure, evolving in frequency and location
Generalized rhythmic delta activity, frontally predominant
Lateralized rhythmic delta activity over the left frontal region
taskFlow.explanation: The delta is bilateral and synchronous, largest at Fp1/Fp2 and F3/F4/Fz and small over O1/O2: GRDA with frontal predominance, the pattern classically called FIRDA. It is not lateralized, because both sides are equal. Periodic discharges are discrete waveforms separated by background; these are continuous sinusoidal waves (rhythmic, not periodic). Nothing evolves in frequency, morphology or location, so the page does not meet seizure criteria.

taskFlow.title: What to do now
taskFlow.description: The nurse asks whether this is a seizure and whether she should call the rapid response team. The patient's vital signs are stable, and the physician is reachable by phone.
taskFlow.question: What is your best next action?
options: Test reactivity with voice, then noxious stimulus, and annotate each
Call a seizure alert now, since rhythmic delta is status epilepticus
Raise the LFF to 5 Hz so that the slow waves stop hiding the background
Give the PRN lorazepam ordered for seizures, then notify the physician
taskFlow.explanation: Frontally predominant GRDA is common in toxic-metabolic encephalopathy and is not epileptiform by itself. The technologist's job is to describe it, test and annotate reactivity (auditory, then tactile or noxious), check responsiveness and notify per protocol. Giving a benzodiazepine is outside technologist scope. Calling it status epilepticus over-reads a non-evolving pattern. Raising the LFF to 5 Hz would erase the very finding the reader needs to see.

taskFlow.title: End of the page
taskFlow.description: Look at the last 1.5 s of the page in the frontopolar and anterior temporal channels before you finalize your annotations.
taskFlow.question: What is the high-frequency activity there, and how do you handle it?
options: Frontal muscle artifact; annotate it and keep the HFF at 70 Hz
60 Hz line noise; turn on the notch filter for the rest of the study
Excess beta from the benzodiazepines; document a drug effect
Low-voltage fast seizure onset; call the physician as a seizure
taskFlow.explanation: Very fast, irregular activity limited to Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8, appearing abruptly with no cerebral field, is muscle (frontalis/temporalis, often with grimacing or stimulation). Annotate it and leave the HFF at 70 Hz so the record is not distorted. Line noise is a monotonous 60 Hz sine wave, typically in channels with poor impedance, not a burst of irregular spikes. A fast seizure onset would evolve and have a field. Benzodiazepine beta is diffuse and ongoing, and none has been given here.

starterCases.title: Left Polymorphic Delta After Ischemic Stroke
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Aphasia and right arm weakness, EEG for a possible seizure

history.eventDescription: A 41-year-old with a left middle cerebral artery infarct three days ago had a 30-second episode of staring. EEG was ordered to look for seizures. He is awake and follows simple commands.

eegSummary.background: Asymmetric

objectives: Lateralize continuous polymorphic delta on a live page
Recognize attenuated faster activity on the lesion side
Separate focal polymorphic delta from FIRDA and artifact

taskFlow.title: First look
taskFlow.description: Awake page at 7 uV/mm in the longitudinal bipolar montage. Compare the left temporal and parasagittal chains (top and third blocks) with the right ones.
taskFlow.question: Which description matches the page?
options: Intermittent occipital delta that blocks with eye opening
Rhythmic 2 Hz delta in brief runs, bilateral and frontal
Continuous irregular 1-2 Hz delta over the right hemisphere
Continuous irregular 1-2 Hz delta over the left hemisphere
taskFlow.explanation: Fp1-F7 through T5-O1 and Fp1-F3 through P3-O1 carry continuous delta of varying shape and duration (polymorphic), while the right chains do not: left hemispheric polymorphic delta, consistent with a structural lesion such as the infarct. The right side is the normal one. Brief bilateral frontal runs of monomorphic delta describe FIRDA, not this page. Posterior slowing that blocks with eye opening describes a different pattern; the delta here is left hemispheric and continuous.

taskFlow.title: Faster activity
taskFlow.description: Now compare the faster frequencies: the alpha in T5-O1 and P3-O1 against T6-O2 and P4-O2, and the low-voltage beta across both sides.
taskFlow.question: How does the faster activity differ between the hemispheres?
options: Alpha and beta are symmetric; only the delta is lateralized
Alpha and beta are lower on the left; right PDR is about 10 Hz
The right PDR is absent and the left alpha is preserved
Alpha and beta are higher on the left, a breach rhythm effect
taskFlow.explanation: A destructive lesion reduces the faster frequencies on its side, so the left alpha and beta are attenuated while the right shows a normal ~10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm. A breach rhythm (higher, sharper faster activity) occurs over a skull defect, and this patient has had no craniotomy. Symmetric faster activity is not what the page shows. The right posterior rhythm is the preserved one.

taskFlow.title: Not FIRDA
taskFlow.description: A colleague suggests the slowing is 'just FIRDA from the stroke'. You open a reference page of FIRDA from another patient to compare.
taskFlow.question: Which feature best separates the stroke page from the FIRDA page?
options: Stroke page: rhythmic frontal runs; FIRDA page: continuous and left-sided
Both pages show the same pattern; only the amplitude differs between them
Stroke page: continuous, irregular, lateralized; FIRDA: rhythmic, frontal
Stroke page: delta that blocks with eyes open; FIRDA page: unreactive
taskFlow.explanation: The FIRDA page shows monomorphic, sinusoidal ~1.8 Hz delta in runs, bilateral and frontally maximal. The stroke page shows continuous, irregular delta confined to one hemisphere, with reduced faster activity on that side. The choice "Stroke page: rhythmic frontal runs; FIRDA page: continuous and left-sided" swaps the two descriptions. They are different patterns, not one pattern at two amplitudes. Eye-opening reactivity does not separate them here.

taskFlow.title: Is the asymmetry real?
taskFlow.description: Before you document a left-sided abnormality, you want to be sure the asymmetry is not technical or ocular.
taskFlow.question: Which check is the most useful?
options: Raise the LFF to 3 Hz so that the delta disappears from both sides
Confirm symmetric measurement and impedances; check beyond Fp1/F7
Swap left and right inputs in the montage to see if the delta moves
Lower the left-channel sensitivity until the two sides look equal
taskFlow.explanation: A true asymmetry survives a check of electrode placement (symmetric 10-20 measurements) and balanced impedances, and polymorphic delta that extends into T3, T5, C3, P3 and O1 is not explained by eye movement, which is maximal at Fp1/Fp2 and F7/F8. Filtering out the delta hides the finding instead of verifying it. Changing sensitivity on one side creates a false picture. Swapping inputs in software just relabels the same electrodes and does not test the recording.

starterCases.title: Right Occipital Spikes in Sleep - End of Chain
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Episodes of flashing lights in the left visual field followed by confusion

history.eventDescription: A 57-year-old with a remote right occipital hemorrhage reports brief episodes of flashing colored lights on the left, sometimes followed by a few minutes of confusion. EEG was recorded including sleep.

eegSummary.background: Stage N2 sleep with vertex waves and spindles

objectives: Apply end-of-chain logic when no phase reversal is seen
Use the transverse montage to find the reversal at O2
Measure discharge duration to classify a spike (<70 ms)

taskFlow.title: Longitudinal: read the polarity
taskFlow.description: Stage N2 page at 10 uV/mm in the longitudinal bipolar montage. Repetitive brief transients appear in the right posterior channels. Look at T6-O2 and P4-O2 for each of them.
taskFlow.question: What do those two channels tell you about the field?
options: No phase reversal is present, so the transients must be artifact
They point down, so negativity is maximal at O2, the chain's end
They reverse phase with T4-T6, so the maximum is at T6
They point down, so O2 is positive; this is a positive transient
taskFlow.explanation: T6-O2 is T6 minus O2. If O2 is the most negative point, the result is positive and the pen goes down (negative up). P4-O2 behaves the same. Both channels end at O2, so the maximum sits at the end of the chain, where no reversal is possible: end-of-chain phenomenon. A downward deflection in a bipolar channel does not mean the input-2 electrode is positive; here it means input 2 is more negative. There is no reversal with T4-T6 here. Lack of a reversal in one montage never proves artifact.

taskFlow.title: Transverse confirms
taskFlow.description: You switch the display to the transverse bipolar montage to place O2 in the middle of a chain. Find the bottom row: T5-O1, O1-O2, O2-T6.
taskFlow.question: Where is the phase reversal now, and what shows it?
options: At Pz: P3-Pz and Pz-P4 deflect in opposite directions
At O2: O1-O2 points down while O2-T6 points up
At O1: T5-O1 and O1-O2 deflect in opposite directions
At T6: P4-T6 and O2-T6 deflect in opposite directions
taskFlow.explanation: O1-O2 = O1 minus O2; with O2 negative the result is positive, so the pen goes down. O2-T6 = O2 minus T6, which is negative, so the pen goes up. Opposite deflections around O2 are a phase reversal at O2, confirming the longitudinal reading. T6, O1 and Pz are only weakly involved; the transients barely appear in their other channels.

taskFlow.title: Spike or sharp wave?
taskFlow.description: Return to the longitudinal page. Turn the caliper on and drag across the base of one transient in T6-O2, from where it leaves the baseline to where it returns.
taskFlow.question: What duration do you measure, and how is the transient classified?
options: About 140 ms, so it is a sharp wave (70 to 200 ms)
About 50 ms, so it is a spike (20 to under 70 ms)
About 50 ms, so it is a sharp wave (70 to 200 ms)
About 250 ms, so it is a slow transient, not epileptiform
taskFlow.explanation: The caliper reads about 50 ms across the base of each transient (1 / 0.05 s = 20 Hz equivalent), only one-twentieth of a 1-s grid box. Spikes last 20 to under 70 ms; sharp waves 70 to 200 ms. So these are spikes. Calling a 50 ms transient a sharp wave misapplies the cutoff. 140 ms is the duration of a sharp wave, not these. 250 ms would be a slow wave and would look much broader on the page.

taskFlow.title: Technologist note
taskFlow.description: You also see two broader, diphasic sharp transients at about 3.4 and 7.9 s that reverse phase at Cz between Fz-Cz and Cz-Pz, and low-amplitude 13 Hz activity near 1.2 and 5.6 s. You now write your technologist note.
taskFlow.question: Which note is accurate?
options: Spikes at O2 and Cz in N2; the Cz spikes are larger and more frequent
Spikes at O2 in N2, reversal at O2 in transverse; vertex waves at Cz
Positive sharp waves at O2 in N2; no reversal, so likely artifactual
Spikes at T6 in N2 with phase reversal at T6; spindles over Cz
taskFlow.explanation: The note should give the location (maximal O2), how it was confirmed (reversal at O2 in the transverse montage, end-of-chain in the longitudinal), the state (N2), and how often (about 9 in 10 s). The broad midline transients at 3.4 and 7.9 s are vertex waves, normal sleep transients, and the 13 Hz bursts are spindles. Calling the vertex waves Cz spikes turns normal sleep architecture into an abnormality. The O2 discharges are surface negative, not positive, and a missing reversal in one montage does not make them artifact. T6 is not the maximum.

starterCases.title: Right Posterior Temporal Sharp Waves - Measure Before Naming
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Episodes of deja vu followed by lip smacking

history.eventDescription: A 20-year-old has episodes of a rising feeling and deja vu, then 1 minute of lip smacking with impaired awareness. Admitted to the EMU for characterization.

eegSummary.background: Stage N2 sleep with vertex waves and spindles

objectives: Localize a discharge by phase reversal at T6
Measure ~140 ms and classify it as a sharp wave (70-200 ms)
Contrast sharp waves with spikes on a comparison page

taskFlow.title: Localize
taskFlow.description: Stage N2 page at 10 uV/mm, longitudinal bipolar montage. Repetitive transients with an after-going slow wave appear in the right temporal chain. Compare T4-T6 and T6-O2 for each discharge.
taskFlow.question: Where is the discharge maximal?
options: At O2, because T6-O2 and P4-O2 point the same way
At T4, because F8-T4 and T4-T6 point in opposite directions
At T6, because T4-T6 points down and T6-O2 points up
At P4, because the parasagittal chain carries the largest wave
taskFlow.explanation: T4-T6 = T4 minus T6: with T6 negative the result is positive, so the pen goes down. T6-O2 = T6 minus O2, which is negative, so the pen goes up. Opposite deflections around a shared electrode mean a phase reversal at T6. O2 is not the shared electrode of the reversing pair. F8-T4 is small here, so there is no reversal at T4. The parasagittal P4 channels are smaller than the temporal ones.

taskFlow.title: Measure it
taskFlow.description: Turn on the caliper and drag across the base of the sharp component of one discharge in T6-O2, excluding the slow wave that follows.
taskFlow.question: What duration do you measure, and how is the transient classified?
options: About 40 ms, so it is a spike (20 to under 70 ms)
About 480 ms, so it is a slow wave and not epileptiform
About 140 ms, so it is a sharp wave (70 to 200 ms)
About 140 ms, so it is a spike (20 to under 70 ms)
taskFlow.explanation: The sharp component spans about 140 ms (about 7 Hz equivalent on the caliper). Spikes last 20 to under 70 ms; sharp waves 70 to 200 ms, so this is a sharp wave. Calling a 140 ms transient a spike ignores the duration cutoff. 40 ms would be far narrower than what the page shows. About 480 ms is the whole sharp-and-slow-wave complex, which includes the after-going slow wave, not the sharp component you are measuring.

taskFlow.title: Compare with spikes
taskFlow.description: To teach a student, you open a page from another patient with O2 spikes in N2 and measure one of those discharges the same way.
taskFlow.question: How do the O2 discharges on the comparison page differ from the T6 discharges?
options: They reverse phase at O2 in the longitudinal montage
They are about 140 ms long and have an after-going slow wave
They are about 50 ms long and lack an after-going slow wave
They are about 200 ms long, at the top of the sharp-wave range
taskFlow.explanation: The comparison discharges are about 50 ms (spikes) with no clear after-going slow wave, while the T6 discharges are about 140 ms (sharp waves) followed by a slow wave. The choice "They are about 140 ms long and have an after-going slow wave" describes the T6 discharges, not the comparison. O2 is the end of the longitudinal chain, so those spikes show no reversal there (T6-O2 and P4-O2 both point down). 200 ms is not what the caliper shows.

taskFlow.title: A borderline discharge
taskFlow.description: Later in the night you measure one discharge at T6 at about 155 ms. Its rising phase is very steep, and a colleague wants to call it a spike because it 'looks spiky'.
taskFlow.question: How should you document this discharge?
options: As a sharp wave at T6 with its measured duration noted
As a spike, because a steep rising phase defines a spike
As a slow wave, because it is longer than 150 ms
As an artifact, because its duration differs from the others
taskFlow.explanation: Spike versus sharp wave is defined by duration: 20 to under 70 ms is a spike and 70 to 200 ms is a sharp wave, so a 155 ms discharge is a sharp wave. Some readers loosely call a very steep sharp wave 'spike-equivalent', but the technologist documents the measured duration and location and leaves clinical weighting to the physician. Steepness alone does not make a spike. A slow wave is longer than 200 ms. Variation in duration between discharges from the same focus is expected and does not mean artifact.

starterCases.title: Staring Spell in an 11-Year-Old - Counting the Discharge
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief staring spells noticed by teachers

history.eventDescription: An 11-year-old has had several daily episodes of blank staring for a few seconds, with eyelid fluttering, that stop abruptly. Her grades have dropped.

eegSummary.background: Normal awake background

objectives: Count spike-and-wave frequency from a live page
Recognize generalized, bilaterally synchronous onset
Test responsiveness during a burst and document its duration

taskFlow.title: Count the complexes
taskFlow.description: Awake resting page at 10 uV/mm, LFF 0.5 Hz. Partway through the page the background is interrupted by a high-amplitude rhythmic discharge. Count complexes in the 1-s boxes between 6 and 9 s, or use the caliper from one spike to the next.
taskFlow.question: What is the frequency of the discharge in that part of the page?
options: About 1.5 Hz, counting one complex every two boxes
About 3 Hz, one spike-and-wave complex per 330 ms
About 10 Hz, matching the background before the burst
About 6 Hz, counting each spike and each wave
taskFlow.explanation: There are about 3 complexes per 1-s box, and spike-to-spike intervals measure about 330 ms: 1 / 0.33 s = 3 Hz. At its onset the discharge is slightly faster (about 3.4 Hz) and then settles to 3 Hz, which is typical. Counting the spike and the slow wave as two events doubles the rate to 6 Hz. 1.5 Hz halves it. 10 Hz is the posterior rhythm before the burst.

taskFlow.title: Field
taskFlow.description: Switch to the referential montage and compare onset timing and amplitude across left and right, front and back.
taskFlow.question: How is this discharge best described?
options: Left frontal onset with later spread to the right side
Generalized and bilaterally synchronous, frontally predominant
Right temporal maximum with phase reversal at T4
Occipital maximum with spread forward to the frontal leads
taskFlow.explanation: The complexes start at the same time on both sides and are largest in F3-A1 and F4-A2, slightly smaller at Fp1/Fp2 and C3/C4, and small posteriorly (P3/P4, O1/O2): generalized, bilaterally synchronous, frontally predominant spike-and-wave. A focal onset with secondary spread would show one side leading. There is no occipital maximum and no temporal phase reversal.

taskFlow.title: During the burst
taskFlow.description: A burst like this starts again while she is sitting quietly. Her mother is in the room. You have a few seconds to act while the discharge is on the screen.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to test responsiveness?
options: Pinch the trapezius to see whether she withdraws from pain
Turn on the photic lamp to see whether the flash stops the burst
Say a code word and ask her to recall it after the burst ends
Wait for the burst to end, then ask her if she felt anything
taskFlow.explanation: Giving a word or simple command during the discharge and asking for recall afterwards tests awareness during the burst itself, and you annotate when it was given and what she recalled. A noxious stimulus is inappropriate for an awake child and tests a different thing. Asking only after the burst misses the testing window. Photic stimulation is an activation procedure, not a responsiveness test.

taskFlow.title: Document the burst
taskFlow.description: She did not recall the code word. The discharge began at 3.2 s on the page and is still running at the right edge of the page. Hyperventilation is still to be done.
taskFlow.question: Which documentation and plan are correct?
options: Duration 6.8 s, ending at 10 s; skip HV since the burst was captured
Duration 10 s, the page length; do HV for 30 s to limit further bursts
Duration about 3 s, one second per Hz; stop the study and notify
Duration at least 6.8 s, check the next page; then do HV for 3-5 min
taskFlow.explanation: On this page the burst runs from 3.2 s to the page end at 10 s, so it lasted at least 10 - 3.2 = 6.8 s, and the offset must be read on the next page. Hyperventilation for 3-5 minutes is the standard activation for suspected absence seizures, with responsiveness testing during any burst. Recording 6.8 s as the exact duration ignores that the burst continues. The page length is not the burst length. Frequency in Hz has nothing to do with duration in seconds.

starterCases.title: Myoclonic Jerk - Polyspike-Wave or Muscle Artifact?
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Sudden arm jerks, sometimes dropping objects

history.eventDescription: A 15-year-old has brief, shock-like jerks of both arms, mostly within an hour of waking and after late nights, and has dropped a cup twice. Consciousness seems preserved. EEG was requested to characterize the jerks.

eegSummary.background: Drowsy background
eegSummary.epileptiform: Brief generalized burst with a clinical jerk

objectives: Recognize polyspike-and-wave time-locked to a jerk
Separate a muscle-only burst from a cerebral discharge
Document the jerk and plan photic stimulation in scope

taskFlow.title: The marked event
taskFlow.description: Drowsy page at 10 uV/mm. You saw both arms jerk and pressed the 'Jerk' marker at 4.3 s. Look at all channels around the marker.
taskFlow.question: Which description matches the cerebral activity at the marker?
options: Muscle artifact only, with no change in the cerebral channels
A vertex wave of drowsiness, maximal at Cz, with no fast part
Rhythmic 3 Hz spike-and-wave complexes lasting several seconds
A generalized burst of several spikes over 0.25 s, then a slow wave
taskFlow.explanation: Around 4.3 s every chain shows a cluster of about 5 spikes within roughly 0.25 s, followed by a slow wave: a generalized, irregular polyspike-and-wave discharge, with high-frequency muscle superimposed in the temporal channels at the moment of the jerk. It is a single burst, not seconds of 3 Hz complexes. A vertex wave is a single midline wave without polyspikes. The large spikes and slow wave in parasagittal and midline channels are cerebral, not just muscle.

taskFlow.title: Compare with absence
taskFlow.description: A student asks whether this is 'the same as absence spike-and-wave'. You open a reference page of a typical absence discharge from another child.
taskFlow.question: Which difference is most important?
options: The reference has a slower PDR, so it cannot be compared
The reference is focal at Fz, while the jerk page is generalized
The reference shows polyspikes; the jerk page shows single spikes
The reference is rhythmic 3 Hz, one spike per wave, for seconds
taskFlow.explanation: The reference page shows rhythmic, regular 3 Hz spike-and-wave with one spike per complex, lasting more than 6 s, frontally predominant and generalized. The jerk page shows one brief, irregular burst with multiple spikes. The choice "The reference shows polyspikes; the jerk page shows single spikes" reverses the two. The reference discharge is generalized, not focal. Both pages show a normal-for-age background before the discharge, so comparison is valid.

taskFlow.title: A second burst
taskFlow.description: Later on the same page there is another burst of fast activity, between about 7 and 8 s. Look at which channels contain it and whether any slow wave follows.
taskFlow.question: What is the second burst?
options: 60 Hz line noise from a loose F7 electrode lead
An electrode pop at T3 from a drying electrode
Muscle artifact confined to F7 and T3, with no cerebral field
A left temporal polyspike discharge, a focal seizure onset
taskFlow.explanation: The burst is very fast and irregular, appears only in channels containing F7 and T3 (Fp1-F7, F7-T3, T3-T5), has no field spreading to neighbors and no after-going slow wave: muscle artifact, for example from jaw clenching. A cerebral polyspike discharge would have a field and a slow wave. An electrode pop is a single steep deflection at one electrode, not a 1-s burst. Line noise is a monotonous 60 Hz sine wave rather than an irregular burst.

taskFlow.title: Document and continue
taskFlow.description: The patient is now awake and well. Photic stimulation is next in the protocol. The parent asks you whether this means 'juvenile myoclonic epilepsy'.
taskFlow.question: What is the best action?
options: Note the jerk at 4.3 s with the discharge; do photic per protocol
Annotate the second burst as a focal seizure for the physician
Skip photic stimulation because a jerk has already been captured
Tell the parent this is JME and that medication will be needed
taskFlow.explanation: Document that the bilateral arm jerk at 4.3 s was time-locked to a generalized polyspike-and-wave burst, then perform photic stimulation per protocol, because photosensitivity is common in myoclonic generalized epilepsies such as JME; stop flashing if a generalized photoparoxysmal response appears, and annotate any jerks. Naming the syndrome to the family is the physician's role. Capturing one jerk does not make the photic test unnecessary. The 7-8 s burst is muscle, not a seizure.

starterCases.title: Serial EEGs in Drug-Induced Encephalopathy: Days 1 to 8
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Progressive confusion and drowsiness after several days of vomiting

history.eventDescription: A 49-year-old woman who takes lithium long term was admitted after several days of vomiting and poor fluid intake. She became tremulous, then confused, then hard to rouse. Daily bedside EEGs are requested while the team corrects her fluids and follows her drug level.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse slowing that changes in frequency, amplitude and form from day 1 to day 8
eegSummary.pdrHz: Absent on days 1, 3 and 5; about 9 Hz on day 8
eegSummary.focalFindings: None; slowing is diffuse and frontally predominant on days 5 and 8
eegSummary.activation: Stimulation trial for reactivity per lab policy
eegSummary.artifacts: Brief right frontocentral muscle artifact on day 1

objectives: Read delta frequency and amplitude on each daily page
Recognize intermittent blunt triphasic-looking waves on day 5
Document state and returning alpha without diagnosing

taskFlow.title: Day 1: the starting page
taskFlow.description: Day 1, bedside, 7 uV/mm. She does not open her eyes to voice and withdraws weakly to a firm squeeze. The requisition lists lithium; a level was drawn on admission but the result is not yet on the form. Use the caliper on a few waves of the background.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits the background on this page?
options: Low-amplitude irregular delta near 1 to 1.5 Hz, little fast activity
Large rhythmic 3 Hz delta in frontal runs on a faster background
Diffuse 20 Hz beta that hides all of the slower activity present
A clear 9 Hz posterior rhythm, with only a few scattered 2 Hz delta waves
taskFlow.explanation: A single delta wave measures roughly 700 to 1000 ms with the caliper (1 / 0.8 s is about 1.25 Hz), so the dominant activity is irregular delta near 1 to 1.5 Hz. It is diffuse and low in amplitude (tens of microvolts at 7 uV/mm) with very little theta or beta, which fits a deeply depressed state. There is no 9 Hz posterior rhythm, so a clear 9 Hz posterior rhythm is wrong. The delta is irregular and not a rhythmic 3 Hz run, so large rhythmic 3 Hz frontal runs describe a different pattern. Beta is scant here, not dominant. The brief fast burst in the right F4 and C4 channels at the start is muscle artifact, not a cerebral finding, and a couple of low-voltage blunt waves near 3 and 7 s are worth noting as seen. Slowing like this does not point to a cause; the requisition and the clinical team supply that.

taskFlow.title: Day 3: what changed
taskFlow.description: Day 3, same 7 uV/mm and the same longitudinal montage. She now opens her eyes to voice but drifts off at once (stupor). Overlay the caliper on several delta waves and compare them with your memory of day 1.
taskFlow.question: Compared with day 1, which change is on this page?
options: Slower delta near 1 Hz with lower amplitude than on day 1
Faster delta near 2 to 3 Hz, larger, with theta added
Bursts of generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave, abrupt onset
A 9 Hz posterior rhythm that blocks when the eyes open
taskFlow.explanation: Single delta waves now last about 330 to 500 ms (2 to 3 Hz), the amplitude is somewhat higher, and a theta component of about 5 to 6 Hz is mixed in. That is a faster, richer background than day 1. Slower, smaller delta describes the earlier page, so slower, smaller delta reverses the trend. No 9 Hz posterior rhythm is present yet, and there are no spike-and-wave bursts or other epileptiform discharges on this page. Better frequency often tracks clinical improvement, but it is nonspecific: many toxic and metabolic conditions give the same picture, so you describe what you see and leave the cause to the physician.

taskFlow.title: Day 5: busier, not simpler
taskFlow.description: Day 5, still stuporous but the nurse says she is a little more alert and the lithium level is falling. The page looks larger and busier than day 3. Frontal channels show repeating blunt waves in two bursts, roughly 2 to 3.7 s and 7 to 8.2 s.
taskFlow.question: What is the best handling of this recording?
options: Describe the bursts and her state, test reactivity, and tell the reader
Write lithium toxicity waves on the report so that the reader can confirm it
Treat the busier page as a poor run and repeat it later that same day
Leave the bursts out of the notes because she is clinically improving
taskFlow.explanation: EEG can lag behind, or even look worse than, the bedside picture during recovery: here the delta is larger (about 1.7 Hz) and intermittent blunt triphasic-looking waves have appeared, while the nurse reports slight improvement. A technologist describes what is on the page (the bursts, their timing and frontal maximum), records the level of alertness, performs a stimulation trial for reactivity per lab policy, notes medications and the drug level from the requisition, and informs the reading physician so the change is not missed. Naming a cause on the report is interpretation outside scope, and the same waves occur in other toxic and metabolic states. Repeating the study because it looks worse treats a real finding as technical failure, since nothing on the page suggests an artifact or a recording problem. Omitting the bursts because she seems better hides a finding the reader needs, and the page is not a measure of the bedside exam.

taskFlow.title: Day 8: documenting the follow-up
taskFlow.description: Day 8, awake and talking, drug level now low. The tracing is on screen. Count one cycle of the posterior rhythm with the caliper and note where slow activity appears (about 1 to 3 s and 6.4 to 7.8 s).
taskFlow.question: Which entry best describes this page in your notes?
options: Awake; about 9 Hz posterior rhythm, two brief runs of frontal delta
Encephalopathy resolved; no residual abnormality remains on the page
Normal awake EEG; nothing further needs to be said to the reader
Stupor pattern persists; slowing unchanged from the day 5 page
taskFlow.explanation: One posterior cycle measures about 110 ms (1 / 0.11 s is about 9 Hz) and the rhythm is roughly 40 to 50 uV peak to peak, so a posterior dominant rhythm has returned, with irregular delta of about 2 Hz still present in two short frontal-predominant runs. Your note should state that factually, with the state (awake) and the drug history. Calling it normal ignores the delta runs and is an interpretation. Saying the stupor pattern persists contradicts the page, which now has an organized posterior rhythm and only brief slow runs. Declaring resolution goes beyond a technologist's role. Recovery can be uneven: the EEG may lag the bedside, so findings are reported as seen at each study.

starterCases.title: Triphasic Waves vs Epileptiform Discharges in Liver Failure
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Worsening confusion and sleepiness with decompensated cirrhosis

history.eventDescription: A 63-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis has had two days of worsening confusion and sleepiness. His family saw no jerking or staring spells. A routine EEG is requested to look for a cause of the altered mental status.

eegSummary.background: Diffuse delta with theta, frontally predominant, no posterior dominant rhythm
eegSummary.epileptiform: Repeating blunt waves in two bursts; no sharp spike-and-wave
eegSummary.activation: Stimulation trial for reactivity per lab policy

objectives: Describe triphasic wave morphology and frontal maximum
Measure the front-to-back lag with the caliper
Separate triphasic waves from 3 Hz spike-and-wave

taskFlow.title: Shape of the repeating waves
taskFlow.description: The patient is stuporous at 7 uV/mm, shown in the referential montage. Between 2 and 3.7 s the frontal channels show repeating waves, and they appear again between 7 and 8.2 s. Look at the shape of a single wave in Fp1-A1 and F3-A1, with negative up.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits one of these repeating waves?
options: Rhythmic 3 Hz spike-and-wave starting abruptly in every channel
Blunt wave with a large down-going phase and smaller up phases
A 14 Hz spindle burst at Cz that waxes and wanes over a second
A sharp spike under 70 ms with a slow wave, maximal at the vertex
taskFlow.explanation: Each wave is blunt (not sharp) and has three phases: a small up-going phase, a larger down-going middle phase (surface positive, since negative is up), and an up-going phase after it of similar or smaller size, with the largest amplitude frontally (roughly 80 to 100 uV in Fp1-A1 and F3-A1). They repeat at about 1.8 per second (0.55 s apart) in two bursts over a slow background, not as rhythmic 3 Hz complexes. A true spike is under 70 ms and sharp, which these waves are not. A spindle is a 12 to 14 Hz burst in sleep, and this patient is stuporous. These features describe triphasic morphology without saying what causes it: the same morphology is seen in several metabolic and toxic states, so describe it and leave the cause to the reader.

taskFlow.title: Measuring the front-to-back lag
taskFlow.description: Still in the referential montage. Pick one burst, for example near 3.1 s. Drag the caliper from the peak of the down-going phase in Fp1-A1 or F3-A1 to the matching peak in O1-A1 or O2-A2, and read the milliseconds.
taskFlow.question: What does the caliper show?
options: Occipital first, with frontal channels peaking about 100 to 150 ms later
Frontal first, with occipital channels peaking about 400 ms later
Frontal first, with occipital channels peaking about 100 to 150 ms later
No measurable delay; all channels peak within a few milliseconds of each other
taskFlow.explanation: The down-going peak is at the frontal electrodes first and reaches O1 and O2 about 100 to 150 ms later (roughly 1/8 of a second); this front-to-back lag is a classic descriptive feature of triphasic waves. Occipital-first is the reverse of what the caliper shows. A discharge with no delay is typical of the generalized spike-and-wave you will compare next. A delay of about 400 ms is nearly the length of a whole wave and would put the posterior peak most of the way to the next frontal wave 550 ms later, so it reflects a mismatched peak. Read the lag in the referential montage so each wave is measured at one electrode rather than across a bipolar pair.

taskFlow.title: Comparing with an absence page
taskFlow.description: A colleague opens a reference recording from an 11-year-old child, in the longitudinal montage. A discharge begins abruptly at 3.2 s and continues to the end of the page. Compare it with the bursts you just measured on the adult page.
taskFlow.question: Which comparison of the two pages is correct?
options: Both begin abruptly out of a normal background and also stop abruptly
The child page runs at about 1.8 per second and has a front-to-back delay
Child page: about 3 per second, no delay; adult: slower, with a delay
They differ only in amplitude; both are synchronous at about 3 per second
taskFlow.explanation: On the child page, complexes start abruptly at 3.2 s, repeat at about 3 to 3.4 per second, each with a sharp component followed by a slow wave, and they are bilaterally synchronous: the caliper shows no meaningful front-to-back delay. The adult bursts are blunt, run at about 1.8 per second, show the 100 to 150 ms lag, and sit on a slow background, so slow, blunt and delayed separates them. Amplitude is not the difference, and only the child page runs near 3 Hz. A child-page rate near 1.8 per second with a front-to-back delay would reverse what the two pages actually show. The adult page has no normal background before the bursts, and the child discharge does not stop before the page ends, so abrupt onset and offset out of a normal background do not describe both pages. Resemblance in rate can still raise a question for the reader, which is why the technologist reports the measurements.

taskFlow.title: What the technologist does
taskFlow.description: Back on the adult page. The physician has not yet seen the recording. The patient moves little, has no visible jerking, and you wonder whether the bursts could mean ongoing seizure activity. Medications and the liver history are on the requisition.
taskFlow.question: What is the best next step for you?
options: Stop recording, since triphasic waves are expected in liver failure patients
Write nonconvulsive status epilepticus on the requisition and phone it in
Ask the nurse to give a benzodiazepine to see whether the waves stop
Test reactivity, note alertness and medications, notify the reading physician
taskFlow.explanation: A technologist tests responsiveness and reactivity to stimulation per lab protocol, documents alertness, any clinical correlate or lack of one, and medications from the requisition, and notifies the reading physician promptly when seizure activity is possible, describing the findings rather than labeling them. Writing a diagnosis is interpretation and out of scope. A benzodiazepine challenge is a physician decision, with monitoring and a clinical plan, and a technologist neither orders nor requests it. Stopping early assumes the waves are benign, which is also interpretation, and how the pattern is classified, including whether it meets ACNS 2021 criteria for periodic discharges and whether triphasic morphology applies, is for the reader to decide. Complete the protocol and report what you saw.

starterCases.title: Occipital Rhythmic Delta and a 3 Hz Burst in a Child
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Several short lapses in attention each day at school

history.eventDescription: A 10-year-old girl is referred after her teacher noticed several brief lapses in attention each day. She develops normally, is alert and cooperative, and takes no medicine. Her pediatrician requested a routine awake EEG that includes hyperventilation.

eegSummary.background: Mildly slow posterior background for age with intermittent runs of rhythmic delta
eegSummary.epileptiform: One generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave burst of about 2 s at 6.2 s
eegSummary.focalFindings: Occipital-predominant rhythmic delta, about 0.5 to 5.4 s
eegSummary.activation: Hyperventilation per lab protocol, still to come

objectives: Measure a rhythmic delta run with the caliper
Tell occipital from frontal rhythmic delta by rate and location
Test responsiveness and document a spike-and-wave burst

taskFlow.title: A run of smooth, regular waves
taskFlow.description: The child is awake, and the page runs at 10 uV/mm in the double banana montage. Between about 0.5 and 5.4 s the background gives way to a repeating run of large smooth waves. Drag the caliper from one peak to the next in T5-O1, then compare the size of the waves in the frontal and occipital chains.
taskFlow.question: Which description matches this run?
options: Rhythmic 6 Hz theta, largest in the temporal chains T3-T5 and T4-T6
Rhythmic 3 Hz delta, largest in Fp1-F7 and Fp2-F8, with small occipital channels
Irregular 1 Hz delta, restricted to the left hemisphere with reduced alpha
Rhythmic 3 Hz delta, largest in T5-O1 and T6-O2, with small frontal channels
taskFlow.explanation: One wave measures about 330 ms from peak to peak (1 / 0.33 s = 3 Hz), which is in the delta range, and the spacing stays regular through the run, so it is rhythmic. The waves are largest in T5-O1 and T6-O2 (roughly 280 to 290 uV peak to peak), next in P3-O1 and P4-O2 (about 205 uV) and Cz-Pz, while the frontal chains stay near 40 to 55 uV. That is occipital intermittent rhythmic delta, here lasting about 5 s. The frontal-maximum answer reverses the location. A 6 Hz theta rhythm would measure about 165 ms per cycle and would not sit in the temporal chains. Irregular 1 Hz delta over one hemisphere describes focal polymorphic slowing, and this run is regular and bilateral. A technologist describes the rate, location and timing; this pattern is seen mainly in children and is sometimes associated with generalized or absence epilepsy, but it is not specific, so the reading physician decides what it means.

taskFlow.title: A second page for comparison
taskFlow.description: A colleague brings a page for comparison: a 61-year-old patient who is stuporous, same montage and 10 uV/mm. Runs of large rhythmic waves appear from 0.2 to 4.4 s and again from 5.3 s. Measure one wave and look at where the waves are largest. Fast muscle activity also appears over the front from about 8.6 s; measure the first run.
taskFlow.question: How does this run differ from the child's run?
options: Same occipital maximum as the child's run, but irregular waves of changing shape
Faster, about 5 to 6 Hz, with the same occipital maximum as the child's run
Same 3 Hz rate, but largest in the left temporal chains rather than occipital
Slower, near 1.8 Hz, and largest in the frontal chains such as Fp1-F7 and Fz-Cz
taskFlow.explanation: One wave here measures about 550 ms (1 / 0.55 s = 1.8 Hz), slower than the child's 330 ms, and the largest deflections are in the frontal chains: Fp1-F7 and Fp2-F8 near 185 to 195 uV in the first run, F3-C3 about 195 uV and Fz-Cz about 215 uV, while T5-O1 is only about 60 uV. Rhythmic delta with a frontal maximum is a separate named pattern from the occipital one, and like it, it is not specific, so rate and location are what you report. The left temporal answer is wrong because both runs are bilateral and symmetric. A 5 to 6 Hz rate would be theta. Irregular changing waves would be polymorphic, but these are monomorphic. The pair shows why you report both rate and location rather than age alone.

taskFlow.title: The pattern changes at 6.2 s
taskFlow.description: Back to the child, now on the referential (ear) tab. The slow rhythm continues at nearly the same rate from about 6.2 to 8.2 s, but the page looks different from the earlier run. Compare one cycle in P3-A1 and O1-A1 at 6.5 s with a cycle at 3 s, and check the frontal channels.
taskFlow.question: What separates the event at 6.2 to 8.2 s from the earlier run?
options: The rate falls to about 1.5 Hz and a spike appears in T3-A1 alone
A sharp spike now leads each slow wave, and it is visible from front to back
The waves stay smooth and sinusoidal, and only their size changes over both parietal areas
The rate rises to about 6 Hz and the waves stay limited to O1-A1 and O2-A2
taskFlow.explanation: The rate barely changes (about 3.1 Hz, one cycle every 320 ms), so frequency does not separate the two. What changes is shape and spread: each cycle now has a steep negative spike followed by a rounded slow wave (the steepest 12 ms slope is about two to four times larger than in the earlier run, depending on the channel), and the activity appears in every region. It is largest posteriorly (P3-A1 and P4-A2 about 260 uV, O1-A1 and O2-A2 about 230 uV, C3-A1 and C4-A2 about 140 uV) but is also present in the frontal channels at lower amplitude (about 35 to 50 uV). That is a generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave burst lasting about 2 s, here with a posterior emphasis, which is less typical than the usual frontocentral maximum. A 6 Hz posterior rhythm, an unchanged smooth wave, or a slow lateralized spike would all describe other pages. The technologist records the time and appearance and reports it; the physician names it.

taskFlow.title: The child stops counting
taskFlow.description: While the child counts aloud for the technologist, she stops mid-count at about 6.2 s and picks it up again near 8.3 s. The protocol still includes hyperventilation, and the technologist has marked the page at 6.2 s.
taskFlow.question: What is the best next step for the technologist?
options: Hold her attention with conversation so the bursts stop, and log only the EEG changes without her behavior
Keep everything else as planned but skip hyperventilation, since a burst has already appeared and more could follow
Note the pause, test responsiveness in later bursts, run hyperventilation per protocol, and report it
Label the event an absence seizure in the log, end the recording, and tell the family the diagnosis is confirmed
taskFlow.explanation: The page shows a 2 s generalized burst that coincides with a pause in counting, so the useful, in-scope step is to record exactly what she did and when, then test responsiveness during later bursts (give a few words to remember and ask for them afterward, or have her repeat a phrase), continue with hyperventilation per the lab protocol unless the physician says otherwise, and report the findings. Calling it a seizure and giving the family a diagnosis is outside the technologist's scope, and ending the test early loses the activation. Skipping hyperventilation because a burst already appeared drops a standard activation that often brings these discharges out. Keeping the child busy so the bursts stop hides the finding, and leaving her behavior out of the log removes the clinical correlate the reader needs.

starterCases.title: Eye, Tongue or Brain: Sorting Frontal Deflections
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Four routine recordings from different patients, reviewed with the lab's eye-check montage

history.eventDescription: The lab has added an ear-referenced eye-check montage: Fp1-A1, IO1-A1, Fp2-A2, IO2-A2, LOC-A1, ROC-A2, then F3 through O2. IO is an infraorbital electrode below the eye, LOC sits above eye level at the left outer canthus and ROC below eye level at the right outer canthus. A technologist works through four recordings from one day to decide which deflections are ocular, which come from another source, and which are cerebral.

eegSummary.background: Posterior alpha in three recordings; drowsy frontal slowing in one
eegSummary.activation: Eyes closed and open on request; looking left and right on request
eegSummary.artifacts: Blinks, vertical eye movement, tongue potentials, lateral gaze

objectives: Use in-phase versus out-of-phase logic at Fp and IO
Separate tongue potentials and frontal delta from eye movement
Read LOC and ROC to tell the direction of gaze

taskFlow.title: Recording 1: the blink at 2.9 s
taskFlow.description: Awake, 30 years old, 7 uV/mm, eye-check tab first. The patient blinked near 1.3, 2.9 and 8.6 s, and was asked to close and then open her eyes at the two markers. Look at the blink at 2.9 s in Fp1-A1, IO1-A1, LOC-A1 and ROC-A2.
taskFlow.question: What do these four channels do during the blink?
options: Fp1-A1 and IO1-A1 both go up together, while LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 stay close to baseline
Fp1-A1 goes down while IO1-A1 goes up, and LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 move in opposite directions
Fp1-A1 goes up while IO1-A1 goes down, and LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 move in the same direction
Fp1-A1 and IO1-A1 both go down together, and LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 also both go down together
taskFlow.explanation: The cornea is positive, and when the eyes roll up in a blink the cornea moves toward Fp and away from the infraorbital electrode below the eye. Fp1-A1 swings positive (down, about +43 uV) while IO1-A1 swings negative (up, about -81 uV): out of phase. LOC and ROC mirror each other (LOC about +77 uV, ROC about -79 uV) because one electrode sits above and the other below eye level, so vertical movement such as a blink is out of phase between them. The same pattern repeats at the Eyes closed and Eyes open markers, and the posterior channels O1 and O2 become much smaller after Eyes open at about 7.2 s. Same-direction movement at Fp and IO would not be explained by the eyes, and a reversed Fp and IO polarity swaps positive and negative.

taskFlow.title: Recording 2: slow waves all across the front
taskFlow.description: Drowsy, 62 years old, 7 uV/mm, eye-check tab. From about 1.2 to 8.8 s repeating slow waves of 100 to 180 uV appear at Fp1-A1 and Fp2-A2 and in F3-A1 and F4-A2. Measure one wave, then compare Fp1-A1 with IO1-A1, and LOC-A1 with ROC-A2.
taskFlow.question: What do the timing and the phase relationship say?
options: About 2 Hz, with Fp and IO moving in opposite directions, so this fits slow vertical eye roving in drowsiness
About 2 Hz, with Fp and IO moving together, so this fits two steady blinks every second
About 5 Hz, with Fp and IO moving together, so this fits tongue movement potentials
About 2 Hz, with Fp and IO moving together, so this is cerebral frontal delta, not eye movement
taskFlow.explanation: One wave measures about 500 ms (1 / 0.5 s = 2 Hz). Fp1-A1 and IO1-A1 swing the same way throughout (IO about 100 to 110 uV, Fp about 170 to 180 uV), and LOC and ROC move together too instead of mirroring each other as they do for eye movement. Same-direction movement over the whole front, with F3 and F4 nearly as large as Fp, points to cerebral activity spreading across the frontal region. Steady blinks at two per second for nearly eight seconds, in a drowsy patient, would look like sharp lid movements in opposite directions at Fp and IO. Opposite-direction movement is the signature of eye movement, and this page does not show it. The rate is 2 Hz, not 5 Hz. The technologist describes it as rhythmic 2 Hz frontal slowing in a drowsy patient, and the reading physician interprets it.

taskFlow.title: Recording 3: three slow potentials
taskFlow.description: Awake, 35 years old, 7 uV/mm, eye-check tab, alpha present at O1 and O2. Single slow waves arrive near 1.8, 4.5 and 7.0 s, each far slower than a blink. Compare their size in Fp1-A1, IO1-A1, F3-A1, LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 and note which way each moves.
taskFlow.question: Which reading and response fit this page?
options: Vertical eye roving, so add more eye-monitor leads and annotate the eye movement
A tongue movement potential, so ask for a still tongue and jaw and annotate the page
Frontal cerebral delta, so describe it as rhythmic slowing and notify the physician
Blinks, so ask the patient to keep the eyes open and annotate the blink rate
taskFlow.explanation: All of these channels move in the same direction (Fp, IO, LOC and ROC together), which rules out eye movement, and the waves are the largest at the infraorbital leads (IO1 and IO2 about 75 to 77 uV, Fp1 and Fp2 about 50 to 57 uV, F3 and F4 about 40 uV). That infraorbital-greater-than-Fp distribution, with slow single waves about 2.5 s apart rather than a rhythmic run, is typical of tongue movement (glossokinetic) potentials. The technologist can ask the patient to hold the tongue still and relax the jaw, then annotate the page. Blinks would give out-of-phase, sharper waves. The page already has eye-monitor leads and shows in-phase behavior, so adding more would not help. A rhythmic delta run would repeat regularly, not as three isolated waves.

taskFlow.title: Recording 4: looking left, then right
taskFlow.description: Awake, 28 years old, 7 uV/mm, eye-check tab. The technologist asked her to look left when ready, return to center, then look to the other side. At the first deflection near 2.0 s, which is the look to the left, LOC-A1 goes down and ROC-A2 goes up. Now find the deflection near 6.0 s.
taskFlow.question: What do LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 do near 6.0 s, and where is she looking?
options: LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 stay flat, so the movement at 6.0 s is cerebral rather than ocular
LOC-A1 goes up and ROC-A2 goes down, so she is looking to the right
LOC-A1 goes down and ROC-A2 goes up again, so she is looking to the left a second time
LOC-A1 and ROC-A2 both go up, so she is looking upward
taskFlow.explanation: A lead the eyes move toward goes positive (pen down), because the cornea is positive. Looking left brings the left cornea toward LOC and takes the right cornea away from ROC, so LOC goes down and ROC goes up, a mirror pair because the two electrodes sit on opposite sides of the face. At 6.0 s the polarities are reversed (LOC about -62 uV up, ROC about +61 uV down), which means gaze has moved the other way, to the right. The 1 Hz low-frequency filter lets a held position fade, so the deflections occur mostly at the start and the end of each gaze shift: the return from the left near 3.3 to 3.6 s also reverses sign and can look like a look to the right, and the return from the right at about 7.3 to 7.6 s reverses the 6.0 s deflection. In the longitudinal tab the Fp1-F7 and Fp2-F8 chains also show opposite polarity at each gaze shift. A repeat of the left-gaze polarity or a pair moving the same way would not fit, and flat LOC and ROC would mean no eye movement. The cerebral channels stay quiet during these deflections, so the technologist annotates left and right gaze and moves on.

starterCases.title: Four Independent Spike Foci in a Young Child
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Delayed development with several kinds of brief spells

history.eventDescription: A 4-year-old boy has delayed language and motor milestones. His parents describe brief staring, head drops and occasional stiffening on one side. A routine awake EEG is requested to look for epileptiform discharges.

eegSummary.background: Posterior rhythm of about 7 to 8 Hz with excess theta for age
eegSummary.epileptiform: Eight sharply contoured events at four separate sites
eegSummary.focalFindings: Left parietal, left temporal, right central and right posterior temporal
eegSummary.artifacts: Fast irregular muscle bursts in the right and left temporal chains

objectives: Localize each focus by its phase reversal
Judge independence from timing and sites
Separate temporal muscle from discharges in the log

taskFlow.title: Counting the foci
taskFlow.description: Awake, 4 years old, 10 uV/mm, double banana. The page shows eight sharply contoured events spread over 10 s, some larger than the background by a wide margin. Find the phase reversal for each one by following where the up-going and down-going pen deflections meet.
taskFlow.question: How many separate sites are discharging?
options: Four: P3, T3, C4 and T6, each with its own phase reversal
Five: P3, T3, C4 and T6, plus the burst in the right temporal chains
Three: P3, T3 and T6, with the C4 event spreading from T6
Two: a left parieto-temporal area and a right centro-temporal area, each with spread
taskFlow.explanation: Each event has its own reversal: C3-P3 down with P3-O1 up at 1.8 and 6.3 s (P3), F7-T3 down with T3-T5 up at 3.3 and 7.0 s (T3), F4-C4 down with C4-P4 up at 4.1 and 8.8 s (C4), and T4-T6 down with T6-O2 up at 5.2 and 9.3 s (T6). That is four sites, two events each. A two-area answer merges sites that reverse at different electrodes and in different lobes. The C4 events do not trace back to T6, because their reversal is at C4 and they do not occur together with the T6 events. The burst at 0.2 to 0.9 s in the right temporal chains is fast, irregular muscle with no after-going slow wave, so it is not a fifth focus.

taskFlow.title: Are they independent?
taskFlow.description: List the time and site of each event: P3 at 1.8 s, T3 at 3.3 s, C4 at 4.1 s, T6 at 5.2 s, then P3 at 6.3 s, T3 at 7.0 s, C4 at 8.8 s and T6 at 9.3 s. The sites repeat in the same order in the second half of the page. Compare the gaps from one site to the next in the first and second rounds.
taskFlow.question: What best shows these sites are independent?
options: Every event is surface-negative, so a single deep source must be producing all of them
The gap between one site and the next changes from the first round to the second
The same four sites repeat in the same order, so the order proves a single spreading source
All eight events have a similar size and shape, which fits one generator seen from four angles
taskFlow.explanation: A single focus spreading to neighbors keeps a roughly fixed delay between sites. Here P3 to T3 takes about 1.5 s the first time and about 0.7 s the second, T3 to C4 about 0.8 s and then about 1.8 s, and C4 to T6 about 1.1 s and then about 0.5 s, so there is no fixed latency, and the events never occur together. Two rounds that happen to visit the same four sites in the same order do not prove one source, because the delays between them are not constant. Similar size and shape is common to discharges from different foci in the same child. A surface-negative polarity is expected for every spike or sharp wave and does not show a shared source. Multifocal independent discharges point to widespread cortical hyperexcitability, and the seizure types seen with them vary, so the technologist describes the sites and times and leaves interpretation to the physician.

taskFlow.title: The T3 event in the referential montage
taskFlow.description: Switch to the referential (ear) tab and look at the T3 event near 3.3 s. Fp1-A1, F3-A1, C3-A1, P3-A1, O1-A1, F7-A1 and T5-A1 all deflect down together by roughly 55 to 90 uV, while T3-A1 goes up by about 60 uV.
taskFlow.question: What explains this pattern?
options: The left-side amplifier has more gain than the right side, which flips the polarity of T3-A1
Those channels see a widespread left discharge, while T3-A1 alone has a loose electrode
The discharge has spread across the whole left hemisphere, and T3 is the least involved electrode
A1, shared by every left channel, picks up the T3 discharge, so those channels move together
taskFlow.explanation: A1 is the second input of every left-sided channel. When the T3 discharge reaches the ear electrode (as can happen with an anterior-to-mid temporal discharge), A1 turns negative, so every left channel that uses it as the reference is pushed positive (down), while T3-A1 itself goes up because T3 is even more negative. The same T3 event at 7.0 s shows the same pattern. This is reference contamination, and the way to locate the focus is the bipolar chain: F7-T3 goes down and T3-T5 goes up, a phase reversal at T3. A loose electrode would give a different, nonepileptiform appearance and would not time-lock to the event. A hemisphere-wide discharge would not make T3 move the opposite way. Gain differences between sides would not flip polarity with an event-locked pattern. The technologist notes the contamination and switches montage to localize.

taskFlow.title: What goes in the record
taskFlow.description: At 0.2 to 0.9 s there is a burst of fast irregular activity in Fp2-F8, F8-T4 and T4-T6 with no after-going slow wave, and a smaller one appears in the left temporal chains just before the T3 event near 7.0 s. The child was awake and active, and the technologist saw no change in behavior during any of the eight events.
taskFlow.question: Which entry is best?
options: Awake, no clinical change seen; four seizure foci found at P3, T3, C4 and T6, and the temporal bursts counted as extra sharply contoured events
Awake, no clinical change seen; eight sharply contoured events at P3, T3, C4 and T6 listed by time; temporal bursts noted as muscle
Awake, no clinical change seen; discharges listed at P3, T3, C4 and T6, but the temporal muscle bursts left out of the notes entirely
Awake, no clinical change seen; generalized discharges noted, with the individual sites left unlisted because each event is brief
taskFlow.explanation: A useful record lists the sites and times of the discharges, states the child's state and that no clinical change was seen, and mentions the temporal muscle bursts so the reader can see they were considered and set aside, especially the left one that comes just before a T3 discharge. Calling the foci seizure foci goes beyond describing the tracing, and counting muscle bursts as sharp events inflates the findings. Leaving the muscle out gives the reader no way to know the fast activity was reviewed. Calling the discharges generalized misdescribes a page where each event is focal, and leaving out the sites drops the information the physician needs. Multifocal independent discharges are associated with widespread cortical hyperexcitability and with several seizure types, which the physician, not the technologist, interprets.

starterCases.title: Irregular Polyspike-Wave Bursts vs Rhythmic 3 Hz Bursts
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief arm jerks, mostly in the first hours after waking

history.eventDescription: A 25-year-old woman describes sudden brief jerks of both arms, mostly soon after waking, and sometimes drops things. She is otherwise healthy and sleeps irregularly. A routine awake EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation is requested. A comparison page from a 12-year-old with staring spells is also on the review table.

eegSummary.background: Normal posterior rhythm continues between bursts
eegSummary.epileptiform: Three irregular generalized polyspike-and-wave bursts; two marked Jerk
eegSummary.activation: Hyperventilation and photic stimulation still to come

objectives: Read the transverse montage for a symmetric discharge
Separate irregular polyspike-wave from rhythmic 3 Hz bursts
Document jerks and test responsiveness without diagnosing

taskFlow.title: Three bursts in the transverse montage
taskFlow.description: Awake, 25 years old, 10 uV/mm, transverse montage first. Text markers read Jerk near 2.2 s and 7.4 s. Count the bursts, then compare left chains (F7-F3, T3-C3) with right chains (F4-F8, C4-T4) at the start of each burst.
taskFlow.question: What does the page show?
options: Two bursts, both marked Jerk; left pairs go down while right pairs go up at the same instant
Three bursts, the one near 4.6 s unmarked; left chains start first and the right chains follow about 100 ms later
Three bursts, the one near 4.6 s unmarked; left pairs go down while right pairs go up at the same instant
Three bursts, the one near 4.6 s unmarked; left pairs and right pairs go the same direction at the same instant
taskFlow.explanation: There are three bursts, at about 2.2, 4.6 and 7.4 s, and only the first and third carry a Jerk marker. In the transverse montage each pair subtracts the medial electrode from the lateral one on the left (F7-F3, T3-C3) and the lateral electrode from the medial one on the right (F4-F8, C4-T4). A negative discharge centered near the midline therefore makes the left pairs go down (about +65 to +90 uV) and the right pairs go up (about -65 to -100 uV) at the same instant, a mirror image with no measurable lag, which is how a symmetric generalized discharge looks. The pairs that cross the midline (Fp1-Fp2, F3-Fz, Fz-F4) stay small, about 30 to 60 uV. Same-direction deflection or a left-to-right delay would point to a different arrangement, and counting only the marked bursts misses the middle one.

taskFlow.title: A comparison page
taskFlow.description: The comparison page is a 12-year-old, awake, 10 uV/mm, LFF 0.5, longitudinal tab. Two bursts appear near 1.4 to 2.8 s and 6.3 to 7.9 s with a normal posterior rhythm between them. Drag the caliper across one full cycle of the burst, then look back at the shape of the polyspike bursts.
taskFlow.question: How do these bursts differ from the first page?
options: They repeat at about 3 Hz with an identical spike-and-wave shape, unlike the uneven spike clusters
They are regular single-spike complexes at about 6 Hz, brief in duration and limited to posterior chains
They are slower, near 1 Hz, with a single spike riding on each slow wave in every cycle
They are clusters of four to five uneven spikes followed by a slow wave, about once every 2.5 seconds
taskFlow.explanation: One cycle measures about 320 ms (1 / 0.32 s = 3.1 Hz), and every cycle has the same single spike and slow wave in the same arrangement for about 1.5 s: a rhythmic, monomorphic discharge, largest in central and parietal chains (Cz-Pz about 170 to 195 uV, C3-P3 and C4-P4 about 140 to 150 uV). The first page is different on both counts: each burst is a cluster of several spikes of varying size and spacing, then a slow wave, with about 1.5 to 2 s of ordinary background between bursts, so it is polymorphic and arrhythmic. A 1 Hz rate or a 6 Hz rate does not match the caliper reading, and the description of four to five uneven spikes about every 2.5 seconds fits the first page, not this one. Rhythmic 3 Hz bursts are what absence epilepsy classically shows, whereas irregular polyspike-wave bursts with jerks are typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and related myoclonic epilepsies, though neither pattern is specific; the technologist describes and documents and leaves the classification to the physician.

taskFlow.title: During a brief rhythmic burst
taskFlow.description: Back on the comparison page, the child is counting aloud and stops partway through the burst that begins at about 6.3 s, then continues after about 7.9 s. The protocol still includes hyperventilation and photic stimulation.
taskFlow.question: What should the technologist do?
options: Mark each burst, test responsiveness with words to repeat and recall, continue activation per protocol, report it
Stop the recording and call a rapid response, since spike-and-wave bursts always mean a convulsive event
Note the bursts only on the page, since bursts of 1.5 s are too short to test and need no behavior notes
Start photic stimulation at once to see whether it lengthens the bursts, and tell the physician afterward
taskFlow.explanation: Bursts of about 1.5 s are long enough for a quick responsiveness check: a few words to remember and recall afterward, or a phrase to repeat, with the response noted against the burst time. The technologist then continues the activation procedures per the lab protocol unless the physician says otherwise, and reports the findings. Writing only on the page leaves out the behavioral correlate the reader needs. A rapid response is for an event the lab's seizure protocol treats as an emergency, such as a convulsion or a prolonged seizure, not a brief burst with a short pause in counting. Starting photic stimulation out of order, outside the protocol and to provoke longer bursts, goes beyond the technologist's role and could put the child at risk.

taskFlow.title: Logging the jerks
taskFlow.description: Back to the 25-year-old on the transverse tab. The technologist saw both arms jerk with the first and third bursts and noted no visible movement with the middle one. The patient was awake and answering questions. Hyperventilation and photic stimulation are still ahead.
taskFlow.question: Which entry is best?
options: Three polyspike-wave bursts logged by time, jerks seen with the first and last, none with the middle; continue activation per protocol and notify the physician
Bursts logged without times because the polyspike shape makes the exact moments hard to pin down; activation continued
Two jerk events at 2.2 and 7.4 s recorded, and the middle burst left out because it did not produce a jerk
Three myoclonic seizures at 2.2, 4.6 and 7.4 s, consistent with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; photic stimulation omitted to avoid provoking more
taskFlow.explanation: The page has three bursts, so the record lists all three with times, notes which were accompanied by visible jerks (those marked at about 2.2 and 7.4 s), states that no movement was seen with the burst at about 4.6 s, records the patient's state and responsiveness, and continues activation per the protocol while notifying the physician. Naming a syndrome and writing seizure types is a diagnosis and outside the technologist's scope, and dropping photic stimulation or the activation without a physician order removes a standard part of the study. Leaving out the middle burst because no jerk was seen erases a finding that the physician needs to see. Omitting the times removes the link between the movements and the EEG, which is the point of the event markers.

starterCases.title: Sensitivity: Making the Wave Readable
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine outpatient EEG; display needs adjusting for readability

history.eventDescription: A routine outpatient EEG session runs through three recordings in a day. The lab default is 7 uV/mm, but the first page is displayed at 10 uV/mm. As the pages change, you must decide whether to raise or lower the sensitivity so waves can be read, and then record what you changed.

eegSummary.background: Waking background whose apparent height depends on the sensitivity chosen for each page
eegSummary.pdrHz: About 10 Hz posteriorly on the first page

objectives: Convert ruler millimeters to microvolts with S = V / H
Decide whether to raise or lower the sensitivity number
Document a sensitivity change so amplitudes stay comparable

taskFlow.title: Ruler reading to microvolts
taskFlow.description: The first page is displayed at 10 uV/mm (see the header). With the amplitude ruler, the 50 uV calibration pulse at the start measures about 4.5 mm. One of the larger posterior waves in T5-O1 around 3 to 4 s measures about 5.5 to 6 mm from trough to peak.
taskFlow.question: What is the peak-to-peak amplitude of that wave?
options: 83 uV
60 uV
30 uV
42 uV
taskFlow.explanation: Amplitude = sensitivity x height = 10 uV/mm x 6 mm = 60 uV. The pulse agrees roughly: 50 uV at about 4.5 to 5 mm is close to 10 uV/mm, so a 6 mm wave is about 60 uV (50 x 6/5). 30 uV multiplies the two heights (6 x 5) and mixes units. 42 uV inverts the ratio (50 x 5/6), and it is also close to what you get by reading the wave at the usual 7 uV/mm (6 x 7), a reminder to use the header or the pulse rather than a remembered default. 83 uV inverts the arithmetic in the other direction (50 x 10/6). Read the setting printed for the page you are measuring.

taskFlow.title: Waves too flat to read
taskFlow.description: The next recording is displayed at 7 uV/mm. The 50 uV pulse stands about 6 mm tall, but most of the background waves are only about 1 mm high and the largest posterior waves reach about 3 mm. A careful read of the page is difficult.
taskFlow.question: Which display change, within lab protocol, makes these waves easier to read?
options: Lower the LFF from 1 Hz to 0.1 Hz to bring up the amplitude
Increase the sensitivity, for example from 7 to 3 uV/mm
Turn on the notch filter to clean up the background
Decrease the sensitivity, for example from 7 to 15 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: A smaller uV/mm number means a more sensitive display, so each microvolt takes more millimeters: a typical 10 uV wave becomes about 3 mm at 3 uV/mm (V/S = 10/3), and the pulse becomes about 15 mm. Going to 15 uV/mm does the opposite and shrinks the waves to under 1 mm. Lowering the LFF changes which slow frequencies pass, not the overall height of a faster background, and it invites drift. A notch filter targets 60 Hz and does nothing for a low-voltage page. Changing sensitivity is a display adjustment the technologist can make within protocol, and the change should be annotated.

taskFlow.title: Waves that overlap their neighbors
taskFlow.description: A new page, displayed at 7 uV/mm, shows a generalized run beginning near 3 s. The waves collide with the channels above and below. A ruler drag on the tallest wave in Cz-Pz measures about 30 mm, which is about 210 uV at 7 uV/mm. You want the largest wave to occupy about 10 mm.
taskFlow.question: Which sensitivity does the arithmetic point to?
options: 10 uV/mm
40 uV/mm
5 uV/mm
20 uV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: S = V / H = 210 uV / 10 mm = 21, so 20 uV/mm is the nearest standard setting; the tallest wave would then be about 10.5 mm. At 5 uV/mm the same wave would be 42 mm tall, so the overlap worsens, because a smaller number is more sensitive. At 10 uV/mm it would still be about 21 mm and would keep colliding with neighbors. At 40 uV/mm it would shrink to about 5 mm, which avoids overlap but wastes readability for the smaller waves. A larger number (less sensitive) is the correct direction when waves are too tall.

taskFlow.title: After the change: what to record
taskFlow.description: You moved the display to 20 uV/mm. On this page the header reads 20 and the pulse measures about 2.3 mm. The largest waves now fill about 10 to 11 mm. Later, a colleague comparing with the 7 uV/mm page says the discharge looks about two thirds smaller on the new page.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct reading, and what belongs in the record?
options: The amplitude fell on this page; report the discharge as lower in voltage than it was before
The 2.5 mm pulse means the gain dropped; run a new calibration and repeat the whole recording
The voltage is unchanged; no entry is needed because sensitivity is only a display choice here
Voltage is unchanged; annotate the 7 to 20 uV/mm change and its time, and quote amplitudes in uV
taskFlow.explanation: The signal did not change; only its drawing did. 50 uV at about 2.3 mm is close to 20 uV/mm, which matches the header, so the pulse is behaving correctly and no recalibration is needed. The pulse height and the printed sensitivity are what let anyone reconvert millimeters to microvolts (2.3 mm pulse, 10.5 mm wave: about 50 x 10.5/2.3, roughly 210 to 230 uV, in line with the 210 uV measured earlier). Calling the discharge smaller confuses height with voltage. Skipping the entry removes the information a reader needs to compare pages, so changes are annotated with the time. Reporting amplitudes in uV avoids the mismatch.

starterCases.title: Time Base: Measure Before You Name It
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Staring spells noticed at school; routine EEG

history.eventDescription: An 8-year-old boy is referred after teachers noticed brief staring spells. You are recording at 30 mm/s (10 s per page, 7 uV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz). You use the caliper to read the duration of sharp-looking events before labeling them in your technologist notes.

eegSummary.background: Awake background with posterior alpha-range activity
eegSummary.epileptiform: Technologist describes events by measured duration; interpretation is left to the physician
eegSummary.focalFindings: Brief sharp events at left temporal and right parietal sites

objectives: Use the caliper to read event duration in ms
Apply spike (20 to under 70 ms) and sharp wave (70 to 200 ms) ranges
Keep frequency and duration independent of page length

taskFlow.title: Sharp-looking wave at left temporal
taskFlow.description: On this 10 s page, a pointed wave with an after-going slow wave appears in the left temporal channels (F7-T3 and T3-T5) at about 2.2 s. Use the caliper across the whole sharp negative wave.
taskFlow.question: What does the caliper show, and how is it classed?
options: It spans about 100 to 140 ms, so it counts as a spike because it looks sharply pointed
It spans about 250 to 300 ms, so it is a slow wave, longer than 200 ms
It spans about 100 to 140 ms, so it is in the sharp-wave range (70 to 200 ms)
It spans about 30 to 40 ms, so it is a spike, shorter than 70 ms
taskFlow.explanation: At 30 mm/s one millimeter is 33 ms, so a wave 3 to 4 mm wide lasts roughly 100 to 140 ms. By duration, 70 to 200 ms is a sharp wave; under 70 ms is a spike. Looking pointed does not decide the name, because classification follows duration, which is why you measure before naming. 30 to 40 ms would be a spike and is the right answer for the other event on this page, not this one. 250 to 300 ms would be a slow wave. The technologist describes what is seen and its measured duration, and the physician interprets.

taskFlow.title: Brief event at right parietal
taskFlow.description: Now look at the right parietal channels (C4-P4 and P4-O2) near 4.4 s. The event is much narrower than the one at 2.2 s. The two channels that share P4 deflect in opposite directions.
taskFlow.question: What does the caliper read, and how is the event classed?
options: About 30 to 50 ms, a spike (20 to under 70 ms)
About 30 to 50 ms, electrode pop because it is so brief
About 90 ms, a sharp wave because it falls between 70 and 200 ms
About 30 to 50 ms, a sharp wave because it is a focal event
