taskFlow.explanation: The event is about 1 to 1.5 mm wide at 30 mm/s, which is 30 to 50 ms, in the spike range of 20 to under 70 ms. Focal location does not turn a spike into a sharp wave; duration decides. A reading near 90 ms would not match this page. An electrode pop is also brief and also shows in both channels that share the electrode, in opposite directions, so that alone does not tell them apart. The shape does: a pop jumps up abruptly and decays smoothly with no after-going wave, while this is a pointed wave with an after-going wave of opposite polarity and a little spread to neighboring channels. The technologist notes the measured duration and location without interpreting.

taskFlow.title: Frequency of the late burst
taskFlow.description: From about 6.4 s to near the end of the page (about 9.8 s) a repetitive spike-and-wave burst appears in every channel. Place the caliper from one spike to the next spike and compare with the 1-s grid lines.
taskFlow.question: What is the repetition rate of the burst?
options: About 6 Hz; one cycle is about 170 ms
About 30 Hz; one cycle is about 33 ms
About 3 Hz; one cycle is about 330 ms
About 1.5 Hz; one cycle is about 660 ms
taskFlow.explanation: Frequency in Hz = 1000 / period in ms. A spike-to-spike distance of about 330 ms (about 10 mm at 30 mm/s) gives 1000 / 330 = 3 Hz, and counting about 3 cycles inside each 1-s grid space agrees. 6 Hz would need cycles 170 ms apart, and 1.5 Hz would need 660 ms. 33 ms is the width of a single millimeter and would give 30 Hz, which would be an unreadable smear. The burst lasts roughly 3.4 s on this page; the technologist notes its onset, duration and any behavior change and does not diagnose.

taskFlow.title: A 5 s page changes the look
taskFlow.description: A colleague reloads the same recording at 5 s per page, so the same screen width now shows half the time. The 2.2 s sharp wave looks twice as wide, and a trainee says it must now be about 280 ms and therefore a slow wave.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct conclusion and note?
options: It really lasts about 250 ms on this view, so it is a slow wave
Its duration is unchanged, but the sharp-wave range stretches to 140 to 400 ms at a faster display
The caliper is only valid on 10 s pages, so the wave cannot be measured here
Duration is unchanged at about 100 to 140 ms and it is still a sharp wave; note the page length
taskFlow.explanation: Page length changes how wide a wave is drawn, not how long it lasts. The caliper reads time from the grid, so it still shows about 100 to 140 ms and the wave is still in the 70 to 200 ms sharp-wave range. The wave looks slower only because it is stretched, the same illusion that makes rhythms look slower at a faster paper speed. Class ranges are defined in ms and do not scale with the view. The caliper works at any page length because it reads time. Recording the page length (or paper speed) beside any measurement avoids confusion between viewers.

starterCases.title: Calibration Pulse: What Is the LFF?
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Quality check before a routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: Before a routine EEG, you record the calibration pulse at several LFF settings to see what each does. The pulse lasts 2.5 s so the decay of its top is easy to time with the caliper. You work from the pulse shape and then confirm against the header.

eegSummary.background: Normal waking background in a healthy adult; the calibration pulse is the subject

objectives: Time the pulse decay and convert time constant to LFF
Compare pulse decay on two pages to judge the LFF
Link LFF to slow-wave attenuation and HFF to rounded corners

taskFlow.title: Time the decay, find the LFF
taskFlow.description: Page 1 carries a 2.5 s pulse. Using the caliper, time how long the top of the pulse takes to fall from its peak to about 37% of its height (a bit under 20 uV on a 50 uV pulse). Work from the decay first, then check against the header.
taskFlow.question: What is the time constant and the LFF it implies?
options: About 0.5 s, so the LFF is near 0.3 Hz
About 0.5 s, so the LFF is near 3 Hz
About 1.6 s, so the LFF is near 0.1 Hz
About 0.16 s, so the LFF is near 1 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: The time constant is the time for the pulse top to fall to about 37% of its starting height, here roughly 0.5 s. LFF = 1 / (2 pi x TC) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 0.5) = 0.32 Hz, about 0.3 Hz. A TC of 0.16 s would mean an LFF near 1 Hz and a pulse that sags about three times faster than this one. Multiplying by 2 pi instead of dividing gives about 3 Hz. A TC of 1.6 s would mean an LFF near 0.1 Hz and a pulse that sags much more slowly than this one. The printed LFF on this page is 0.3 Hz, so the measurement agrees with the setting.

taskFlow.title: Compare two pages
taskFlow.description: Page 2 uses the same pulse, but its top falls to about 37% in roughly 0.1 s, about five times faster than on page 1. Both pages are going to be used to record a 1 Hz delta wave.
taskFlow.question: Which statement about the 1 Hz delta is correct?
options: Both pages reduce it equally, because 1 Hz lies above both of the cutoffs in use
Page 2 reduces it more, because the faster decay means a longer time constant and a lower LFF
Page 1 reduces it more, because its slower decay means a stronger low-frequency filter
Page 2 reduces it more, because faster decay means a shorter time constant and higher LFF
taskFlow.explanation: A short TC is a high LFF. TC of 0.1 s gives LFF = 1 / (2 pi x 0.1) = 1.6 Hz, which is above 1 Hz and cuts a 1 Hz wave to roughly half, while the 0.3 Hz filter on page 1 passes most of it. The slowly sagging pulse of page 1 reflects a weaker filter, so the claim that slower decay means stronger filtering is the reverse of the truth. The pages differ by a factor of five in cutoff, so they do not treat 1 Hz equally. A longer TC means a lower LFF, so the last claim has the relation backwards.

taskFlow.title: The extreme page
taskFlow.description: On page 3 the pulse collapses almost as soon as it rises; its top falls to about a third of its height in roughly 1 mm of paper (about 30 to 40 ms), and the pulse peak is lower than on pages 1 and 2. The header reads 5.3 Hz. You are comparing it with pages 1 and 2 (0.3 and 1.6 Hz).
taskFlow.question: How would a 1 Hz delta wave look on page 3 compared with pages 1 and 2?
options: It would shrink the most of the three, since a 30 ms time constant means the highest LFF
It would shrink about as much as on page 2, since both of those LFFs exceed 1 Hz
It would be unchanged, since an LFF only acts on activity above its setting in frequency
It would shrink the least of the three, since the fastest decay keeps slower waves intact
taskFlow.explanation: TC 0.03 s gives LFF = 1 / (2 pi x 0.03) = 5.3 Hz, the highest of the three, so a 1 Hz wave is cut to a small fraction of its size, much more than on page 2 (about half) or page 1 (almost none). Both pages 2 and 3 exceed 1 Hz, but they differ greatly in how much they cut. A fast decay reflects a strong high-pass filter, so the claim that it keeps slower waves is backwards. An LFF acts on frequencies below its cutoff, which is why 1 Hz is attenuated on this page. A page like this is for troubleshooting, not for recording slow activity.

taskFlow.title: The rounded corner
taskFlow.description: On page 4 the LFF is back to 1 Hz, but the leading edge of the pulse is slightly rounded and the pulse arrives more gradually than before. The header shows an HFF of 15 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What does the lowered HFF do here, and what would it do to brief spikes?
options: It makes the pulse top sag more, and it would also stretch slow waves on the page
It rounds the sharp corner with a slower rise, and would also round and shrink brief spikes
It raises the pulse above 50 uV, and it would also enlarge brief spikes on the page
It speeds the pulse decay, and it would also remove delta activity from the whole record
taskFlow.explanation: The HFF is a low-pass filter: it slows fast edges (a rounded, slower rise) and lowers brief fast events such as spikes and muscle. Its time constant, 1 / (2 pi x 15) = about 10 ms, is too short to time on a 10 s page, which is why this is judged from the shape of the corner and not from a measurement. Decay of the top is set by the LFF, and slow delta is mostly untouched by the HFF. No filter makes the pulse taller than its true 50 uV. If the corner looks rounded, check the HFF against protocol before accepting a smaller spike as real.

starterCases.title: Sweat Artifact or Delta? Choosing the LFF
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for episodes of confusion; patient warm and perspiring

history.eventDescription: A 40-year-old man arrives overheated after a long walk. The room is warm and he is sweating. Early in the recording an unusual slow movement appears on one side of the head, and later a short run of slow waves appears across many channels.

eegSummary.background: Awake background with a slow sway in right temporal channels and a short run of generalized slow activity late in the page
eegSummary.artifacts: Slow sway at T4 channels, near 0.3 Hz

objectives: Separate a single-electrode sweat sway from real slowing
Predict what LFF 0.1, 1 and 5.3 Hz do to both
Fix the technical cause first and document the setting used

taskFlow.title: A slow sway on one side
taskFlow.description: This page is at LFF 0.1 Hz. In F8-T4 and T4-T6 the pen swings slowly, about 3 s per cycle and about 45 mm tall, mostly in mirror image between the two channels. Other channels are comparatively quiet apart from a run of slow waves late in the page.
taskFlow.question: What does the sway in F8-T4 and T4-T6 represent?
options: Slow sweat or electrode artifact at T4, the one electrode shared by both channels
A fault of the low-frequency filter, which at 0.1 Hz passes drift from every electrode
Respiration artifact, since 0.3 Hz matches a normal breathing rate
Rhythmic 0.3 Hz delta in the right temporal lobe, to be reported as focal slowing
taskFlow.explanation: The sway appears only in the two channels that share T4 and is mirror-image between them (T4 is the second input of F8-T4 and the first input of T4-T6), which points to a single electrode. Its roughly 3 s period (about 0.3 Hz) and large size fit sweat, which changes the electrode-skin potential slowly. Cerebral delta would not be confined to one electrode or mirror itself across a shared input. Respiration artifact can also sit on one electrode, but it is locked to the patient's breathing movement, and here the cause points to the sweating (warm room, perspiring patient, very slow irregular sway at one electrode); check the chest or the electrode against breathing before naming it. An LFF of 0.1 Hz does let slow drift through, but only the channels that contain the sweaty electrode show it, so the filter is not the fault.

taskFlow.title: Raise the LFF: what remains
taskFlow.description: The LFF is now 1 Hz. The T4 sway is smaller but still visible (those two channels are still about twice as tall as their neighbors). From about 6 to 8.5 s a run of slower waves, roughly 1 to 2 cycles per second, appears in many channels, including the left and midline chains.
taskFlow.question: Which of the two slow events is more likely cerebral, and why?
options: Both, since any slow activity that survives a 1 Hz LFF must come from the brain
The T4 sway, because it is the largest and slowest event seen anywhere on the page
Neither, since slow events seen at this setting are all products of the filter itself
The 6 to 8.5 s run, since it spans many channels while the sway sits on one electrode
taskFlow.explanation: A wave that appears together in left, right and midline chains with a consistent time course has a field that spreads across the head, which fits cerebral activity. A wave that lives only in two channels sharing one electrode does not. Size is not the test, since artifacts from sweat are large. A slow wave at 1 Hz LFF can still be artifact, as the T4 sway shows. The run is also not a filter product: the LFF removes slow activity, it does not create it. The technologist describes what is seen and where and leaves interpretation to the physician.

taskFlow.title: A tempting quick fix
taskFlow.description: A colleague raises the LFF to 5.3 Hz to calm the T4 sway. On this page the sway is nearly gone, but the 6 to 8.5 s run is also much smaller than before, roughly a third of its height on the 1 Hz page.
taskFlow.question: Why is this a poor way to handle the sweat artifact?
options: It is acceptable as the routine setting, since an LFF near 5 Hz is standard for adult scalp EEG
It makes the sway larger on neighboring channels, because the filter spreads artifact around
It only attenuates activity below 0.5 Hz, so the slow run is not affected by the change
It shrinks the real slow run with the sway, so slowing could be hidden and the electrode stays faulty
taskFlow.explanation: An LFF of 5.3 Hz (time constant about 0.03 s) is a strong high-pass filter that attenuates everything below a few hertz, including genuine delta near 1 to 2 Hz. It removes the sway because the sway is very slow, but it removes much of the clinically relevant slowing too, and the sweaty electrode is still there. Routine adult EEG uses an LFF near 1 Hz or lower, not 5 Hz. Filters do not spread artifact across channels. The cutoff is not limited to sub-0.5 Hz activity: attenuation increases gradually, and it is already substantial at 1 to 2 Hz.

taskFlow.title: What to do and what to record
taskFlow.description: The page is back at LFF 1 Hz, with the sway still present in the T4 channels and the run still visible from 6 s. Recording continues and the patient is still warm and sweating.
taskFlow.question: What is the best response?
options: Leave the LFF at 0.1 Hz so no delta is lost and mention the artifact only if someone asks
Keep the LFF at 5.3 Hz for the rest of the study and label the T4 channels sweat artifact
Cool and dry the patient, re-prep T4, restore protocol LFF, annotate cause and fix
Delete the T4 segments afterward and report the 6 to 8.5 s run as slowing in your notes
taskFlow.explanation: The correct order is to fix the cause: cool the room or the patient, dry and clean the skin, re-prep and reapply the T4 electrode (check impedance), then record at the lab's protocol LFF, and annotate the artifact, the fix and any filter change. A high LFF hides the cause and the delta together. An unnecessarily low LFF leaves the sway large and unreadable, and not documenting leaves the reader guessing. Deleting data is not a technologist task, and describing the run as slowing is interpretation; the technologist describes the finding, with timing, and notifies the physician if the recording is affected.

starterCases.title: 60 Hz Interference: Fix First, Notch Last
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for suspected focal seizures; 60 Hz fuzz on part of the page

history.eventDescription: A 30-year-old woman is having a routine EEG after brief focal events. A fuzzy thickening of the trace appears in two channels on the left posterior chain. A spike-like event also appears in the left central channels around 6.5 s and you want it to stay visible.

eegSummary.background: Awake background with a thickened fuzzy trace in two left posterior channels
eegSummary.epileptiform: Brief sharp event over C3 near 6.5 s, to be described, not interpreted
eegSummary.artifacts: 60 Hz interference localized to T5-containing channels

objectives: Localize 60 Hz interference to a single electrode
Predict what HFF 15 Hz and the notch do to 60 Hz and to a spike
Fix attachment and impedance first and document any notch use

taskFlow.title: Where is the fuzz coming from?
taskFlow.description: Look at the fuzzy, thickened trace on this page. It is strong in T3-T5 and T5-O1 and barely visible in the other 16 channels.
taskFlow.question: Which input is the likely source of the interference?
options: Electrode T5, the one input shared by both noisy channels
Electrode T3, the first input of the earlier noisy channel
The ground electrode, since pickup in two channels signals a ground fault
Electrode O1, the last input in the second noisy channel
taskFlow.explanation: A technical artifact that appears in every channel containing one electrode and nowhere else points to that electrode. T5 is the only input shared by T3-T5 and T5-O1, so T5 (high impedance or poor attachment picking up 60 Hz) is the likely source. T3 appears only in the first noisy channel and also in F7-T3, which is clean. O1 appears in P3-O1, which is also clean. A ground problem would be expected to spread across many channels, not stay in two.

taskFlow.title: Lowering the HFF to 15 Hz
taskFlow.description: A colleague lowers the HFF to 15 Hz. On this page the fuzz is smaller but not gone in T3-T5 and T5-O1, and the spike over C3 near 6.5 s is lower and rounder than before.
taskFlow.question: What does a 15 Hz HFF do here?
options: It cuts the 60 Hz fuzz but does not remove it, and it also shrinks the C3 spike
It removes the 60 Hz fully, and it enlarges the C3 spike since noise no longer rides on it
It leaves the 60 Hz unchanged, since an HFF only acts on activity below its setting, but it blunts the spike
It removes the 60 Hz fully, because 60 Hz is above a 15 Hz cutoff, and leaves the C3 spike unchanged
taskFlow.explanation: A 15 Hz low-pass filter passes frequencies far above its cutoff with gradual roll-off, not an all-or-none cut, so 60 Hz is reduced to roughly a third of its height but remains visible. The same filter reduces fast components of the real spike (the spike here is roughly a quarter smaller and more rounded). Claiming it fully removes 60 Hz overlooks the gradual roll-off. Claiming it leaves the 60 Hz unchanged is wrong; the HFF attenuates activity above its setting. A filter never enlarges a spike. The cause is untouched, so this is a poor substitute for fixing the electrode.

taskFlow.title: First action on the real cause
taskFlow.description: The HFF is back at 70 Hz and the 60 Hz fuzz returns at full size in the same two channels. The patient is comfortable and not moving, and other electrodes show normal impedance.
taskFlow.question: What should you do first?
options: Lower the sensitivity to 15 uV/mm so the fuzz is smaller on the display screen
Switch on the 60 Hz notch right away, because the interference is exactly 60 Hz
Raise the LFF to 5.3 Hz to push the interference out of the signal on the page
Check T5 impedance and attachment, reseat or re-prep it, and inspect its cable
taskFlow.explanation: Fix the cause first: a high-impedance or loose T5 (dried gel, poor contact, a damaged lead or connector) lets mains interference in. Re-measure impedance, re-prep and reapply if needed, and check the cable path away from power cords. A notch hides the problem and can remove real 60 Hz content, so it is a last resort. Lowering the sensitivity shrinks the whole display and makes small cerebral waves harder to read while the interference stays. An LFF high-pass filter attenuates slow activity, not 60 Hz, so 5.3 Hz would blunt delta and leave the fuzz.

taskFlow.title: The notch as a last resort
taskFlow.description: You re-prepped T5 and checked cables, but a nearby piece of equipment cannot be unplugged and the fuzz returns. With the lab's approval you switch on the 60 Hz notch. On this page the fuzz is gone and the C3 spike looks as it did at 70 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What do you record?
options: Nothing further, since the notch removes only the interference and no real activity
That 60 Hz was seen at T5, with the notch left on for all of this patient's future EEGs
Only the time the notch was switched on; the cause is unnecessary now that the page looks clean
The notch is on and when, the T5 interference and steps tried, and the final impedance
taskFlow.explanation: The record should let a reader know the data were filtered and why: the notch is on from a stated time, the fuzz was at T5, what was tried (impedance, re-prep, cables), and where things ended. A notch also removes a little real 60 Hz content, so it is not free of cost, and silence about it hides a technical issue. A time alone leaves out the reason, the site and the attempts. Future recordings need fresh technical checks, so carrying a notch forward as a standing setting would mask a recurring problem. The page looks cleaner but the interference source was not eliminated.

starterCases.title: HFF, Muscle and Spikes: What It Costs
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Routine EEG for spells of altered awareness; tense during recording

history.eventDescription: A 35-year-old woman is anxious and clenching her jaw at times. A brief burst of fast fuzzy activity appears on the right side of the head, and sharp-looking waves appear in the left temporal channels at about 3.0, 6.2 and 8.4 s. The lab protocol allows temporary HFF changes.

eegSummary.background: Awake background with bursts of fast activity at right temporal sites and sharp events at the left temporal region
eegSummary.epileptiform: Left temporal sharp events at about 3.0, 6.2 and 8.4 s; described, not interpreted
eegSummary.artifacts: Right-sided muscle burst around 4.2 to 5.6 s

objectives: Recognize muscle fuzz and respond at the patient first
Compare HFF 70, 35 and 15 Hz on muscle and on a spike
Document a temporary HFF change and restore protocol

taskFlow.title: A fast burst on the right
taskFlow.description: This page is at HFF 70 Hz. From about 4.2 to 5.6 s there is a burst of dense fast activity in the right temporal channels (Fp2-F8, F8-T4, T4-T6). Nothing similar appears on the left, where the sharp events at 3.0, 6.2 and 8.4 s are seen. The patient is awake and tense during this page.
taskFlow.question: What is the burst, and what is your first response?
options: A possible seizure; stop the recording and call for emergency help at once for her
Muscle from the right temple or jaw; have her relax her jaw and forehead, adjust head support
A fault in the HFF setting; lower the HFF to 15 Hz right away to correct the page
Cerebral fast activity on the right side; describe it in the notes as a focal beta finding
taskFlow.explanation: Dense, fast, spiky fuzz limited to the right temporal chain that comes and goes over about a second and a half fits muscle (temporalis, jaw or forehead tension). The first response is to help the patient relax, adjust pillow and head support, and re-check electrode contact. Labeling it cerebral beta is an interpretation, outside scope. The HFF setting is not at fault, and lowering it is a trade-off rather than a first step. A short artifact burst with an awake, comfortable-looking patient is not an emergency; the technologist observes the patient, and escalation is for a clinical change.

taskFlow.title: HFF 35 Hz
taskFlow.description: The HFF is 35 Hz on this page. Compare the right temporal burst and the left temporal spike at 3.0 s with the 70 Hz page.
taskFlow.question: What changed on this page?
options: The muscle fuzz is completely gone and the left temporal spike is unchanged in height
Muscle fuzz is reduced but not gone, and the left temporal spike is only slightly smaller
The muscle fuzz is unchanged on the right and the left temporal spike is much smaller
The muscle fuzz is completely gone and the left temporal spike is cut roughly in half
taskFlow.explanation: Lowering the HFF to 35 Hz removes about a quarter of the muscle fuzz but leaves a clear remnant, while the spike height falls only a few percent (about 109 to 102 uV in T3-T5). The filter roll-off is gradual, so muscle is reduced, not eliminated. A claim that muscle is gone or that the spike is unchanged overstates the filter. A claim that muscle is unchanged while the spike collapses has the effects reversed. At 35 Hz the spike is still sharp, which is why this setting is often a reasonable temporary compromise within protocol.

taskFlow.title: HFF 15 Hz: the hidden cost
taskFlow.description: The HFF is 15 Hz on this page. The muscle burst is cut to about half its size (it is still visible). The left temporal spike at 3.0 s is lower and broader, about a quarter smaller than at 70 Hz.
taskFlow.question: Why is 15 Hz not a free fix for muscle?
options: It is fine to leave on for the whole study, since an HFF only removes activity above 70 Hz
It makes muscle look larger, because the filter amplifies slower waves in the same channels
It restores spike height if the sensitivity is also lowered to compensate for the filter
It also shrinks and rounds real spikes and fast activity, so findings can be hidden
taskFlow.explanation: A low-pass filter attenuates all fast activity, so at 15 Hz both muscle and the fast components of a cerebral spike are reduced; a spike that is shrunk and blunted can look like a slower wave and may be missed. It does not fix the cause, which is tension, so the patient and head support still need attention. Filters do not amplify slow waves meaningfully. An HFF of 15 Hz attenuates much below 70 Hz, not only above it. Changing the display sensitivity rescales the picture but cannot restore filtered detail.

taskFlow.title: Record the temporary change
taskFlow.description: After asking her to relax, repositioning her head, and re-checking contact, the muscle bursts become less frequent but still occur. You keep HFF 35 Hz on this page, and the page header reads 35 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What is the best way to handle and document the setting?
options: Leave 35 Hz for the rest of the recording without a note, since it is still a common setting
Record at 35 Hz silently and tell the reader afterward that spikes looked smaller than expected
Annotate the change from 70 to 35 Hz with time and reason, then restore 70 Hz once muscle settles
Use 15 Hz for the whole study and make it her standard setting for all of her future EEGs
taskFlow.explanation: A temporary HFF change within protocol should be annotated with the time and reason, and the protocol HFF restored when the cause (muscle) has settled, so the reader knows which pages were filtered more strongly and why spikes may be smaller. Leaving a changed setting without a note leaves later readers unsure. Making 15 Hz a standing setting for future studies would repeatedly blunt spikes. Telling a reader afterward that spikes look smaller hands them an avoidable surprise; the record should carry the setting information from the start.

learningLinks.label: Domain II: Filters, Sensitivity, Time Constants

starterCases.title: Slow Waves That Depend on the LFF
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Headaches over several months; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 52-year-old woman is referred for a routine EEG because of headaches. The amplifier was left at a higher LFF by the previous study. Your lab protocol calls for an LFF of 1 Hz or lower for routine recording and lets you adjust display settings, document each change and notify the reader.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult background with a posterior rhythm near 9.5 Hz; irregular slow waves limited to the left temporal channels, whose size depends on the LFF in use
eegSummary.focalFindings: Not interpreted by the technologist; documented as seen

objectives: Judge how an LFF of 1.6 Hz can shrink slow waves
Link a longer time constant to larger slow waves
Document each LFF change and tell the reader

taskFlow.title: A left temporal signal
taskFlow.description: The page was started at LFF 1.6 Hz (time constant 0.1 s), 7 uV/mm. Your protocol calls for 1 Hz or lower. In F7-T3 and T3-T5 irregular slow waves, roughly one per second, stand about 11 to 12 mm tall for the whole page. In F8-T4 and T4-T6 the background is only about 4 to 5 mm tall.
taskFlow.question: How should you describe this page, and what does the 1.6 Hz LFF mean for what you see?
options: Electrode drift at T3 only, which is best cleared by raising the LFF further and re-checking
Irregular slow waves confined to the left temporal chain, likely trimmed by this LFF, so a repeat is fair
Left temporal slow waves that are certainly an abnormality, to be reported to the reader as focal slowing
Slow waves of the same size on both sides, so the LFF has no bearing on how you describe them
taskFlow.explanation: The slow waves sit in F7-T3 and T3-T5 only (about 11 to 12 mm against 4 to 5 mm on the right), so they are lateralized, not symmetrical. A 1.6 Hz LFF is a first-order filter that passes only about 63% of a 1.3 Hz wave: gain = f / sqrt(f^2 + LFF^2) = 1.3 / sqrt(1.69 + 2.56) = 0.63. The true waves are therefore larger than they look, and your protocol allows a lower LFF, so a repeat is within scope. Calling the waves an abnormality or focal slowing is interpretation and belongs to the reader. Equal slow waves on both sides contradicts the page, and 1 to 2 Hz waves are well within the range an LFF of 1.6 Hz reduces. Drift at one electrode would not show as steady slow waves across the whole page, and raising the LFF would only cut the slow waves further.

taskFlow.title: The same page at 0.53 Hz
taskFlow.description: Per protocol you set the LFF to 0.53 Hz (time constant 0.3 s) and record the same stretch. F7-T3 and T3-T5 are now about 18 mm tall, against 11 to 12 mm at 1.6 Hz. The right temporal channels are still about 4 to 5 mm.
taskFlow.question: Why do the left temporal slow waves look larger at 0.53 Hz?
options: A longer time constant lets more of the 1 to 2 Hz activity through, so less of it is removed
A longer time constant raises the effective sensitivity of every channel on the page
A lower LFF adds gain at slow frequencies, so waves are amplified above their true size
A lower LFF removes faster activity, which makes the slow waves look larger by comparison
taskFlow.explanation: TC = 1 / (2 pi x LFF), so LFF 0.53 Hz is TC = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 0.53) = 0.3 s. A 1.3 Hz wave passes at 1.3 / sqrt(1.69 + 0.28) = 0.93 of its size, against 0.63 at 1.6 Hz, which is a gain of about 1.5 times, close to the 18 mm versus 11 to 12 mm on the page. A filter never adds gain; it only removes. Fast activity is not removed by a lower LFF, and the right-sided channels barely changed (4 to 5 mm), so it is not a relative effect. Sensitivity is a separate display control and stays at 7 uV/mm in the header.

taskFlow.title: A trial at 5.3 Hz
taskFlow.description: To see the effect, you try LFF 5.3 Hz (time constant 0.03 s) on the same stretch. F7-T3 and T3-T5 shrink to about 5 to 6 mm against about 3 to 4 mm on the right, so the left-right difference is much less obvious than at 0.53 Hz.
taskFlow.question: What does this setting do, and why is it not used for routine recording?
options: It removes only electrode drift, so the slow waves of cerebral origin pass through unchanged
It cuts much of the 1 to 2 Hz activity, so real slowing can hide; it is not a routine choice
It raises the left temporal slow waves above the alpha rhythm, which is why a protocol limits it
It leaves the waves smaller but visible, so it suits routine recording when drift is a concern
taskFlow.explanation: At 5.3 Hz a 1.3 Hz wave passes at 1.3 / sqrt(1.69 + 28.1) = 0.24, about a quarter of its size, which matches the drop to 5 to 6 mm. Real slow activity can then be missed, so your lab protocol keeps routine LFF at 1 Hz or lower, and a higher value is only a short, documented troubleshooting step. The filter does not raise slow waves relative to alpha; it lowers them. 'Smaller but visible' is the trap: a reader comparing sides may no longer notice a difference. An LFF removes any activity below its cutoff, cerebral or not, so it does not spare slow waves from the brain.

taskFlow.title: Restore and document
taskFlow.description: You return the amplifier to LFF 0.53 Hz for the rest of the study. The record now holds a segment at 1.6 Hz (start of study), a segment at 0.53 Hz, and a short test at 5.3 Hz. The left temporal slow waves are again about 18 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is the correct way to finish and document this?
options: Keep 0.53 Hz and write in your notes that the left temporal activity is focal slowing
Delete the 1.6 Hz and 5.3 Hz segments so the file shows only the final setting used
Keep 0.53 Hz and rely on the printed header, since the reader sees the LFF on every page
Keep 0.53 Hz, annotate which segment used which LFF, and tell the reader about the changes
taskFlow.explanation: Every setting change and where it was used should be documented and the reader told, because slow waves are different sizes in the three segments and a reader judging them needs to know which setting produced each page. Deleting segments hides the evidence of what the LFF did and is not appropriate. Calling the activity focal slowing is interpretation, outside technologist scope. Relying on the header alone is the subtle error: the value is printed but the reader is not warned that a short test or change took place and why, so an annotation and notification are expected.

starterCases.title: When Delta Hides the Spikes
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief arm jerks and staring spells; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 14-year-old boy has a routine EEG for brief arm jerks and staring spells. Early in the study, large slow waves fill most channels. Your lab protocol routinely uses an LFF of 1 Hz and lets you change display settings briefly, document each change and notify the reader.

eegSummary.background: Awake background with large widespread slow waves of about 1.4 Hz and a few brief sharp transients whose visibility depends on the LFF
eegSummary.pdrHz: Not clearly seen on this short page
eegSummary.artifacts: Later in the study a slow sway on one electrode

objectives: Explain why large slow waves can hide brief sharp events
State what a high LFF costs genuine slow activity
Refuse a high LFF as the fix for sweat artifact

taskFlow.title: Slow waves everywhere
taskFlow.description: This 5-second page is at 10 uV/mm with LFF 1 Hz and HFF 70 Hz. Broad slow waves, about 1.4 per second, stand about 10 to 20 mm tall in most channels (up to about 24 mm in Fp2-F4 and F4-C4). Brief sharp events of 13 to 16 mm sit in F3-C3, C3-P3, Fp2-F4 and F4-C4 near 1.5, 2.8 and 3.7 s, but they are hard to pick out.
taskFlow.question: What makes the brief sharp events hard to see on this page?
options: A 1 Hz LFF removes sharp events, so only a trace of each is left on the page
The sensitivity is too high, so the tops of the sharp events are clipped off the display
The slow waves are as tall as the sharp events and run into them, so they do not stand out
The 70 Hz HFF smooths brief sharp events into the surrounding background activity
taskFlow.explanation: The sharp events are about 13 to 16 mm and the slow waves 10 to 20 mm, so size alone does not make them stand out and slow waves add to or cancel them. Sensitivity does not clip events; the display scales every wave equally. A 1 Hz LFF removes content below about 1 Hz and passes a 50 ms event, which carries most energy well above 10 Hz. A 70 Hz HFF would reduce muscle and very fast activity but barely touches a 50 ms spike (about 20 Hz content).

taskFlow.title: The same page at LFF 10 Hz
taskFlow.description: You set the LFF to 10 Hz (time constant 0.016 s) for this same 5 seconds. The slow waves shrink to about 3 mm. Sharp events of about 9 mm appear in F3-C3 and C3-P3 near 1.5 s, and of about 10 mm in Fp2-F4 and F4-C4 near 2.8 and 3.7 s.
taskFlow.question: What did the higher LFF do to the page?
options: It added gain to brief events, which is why they now look sharper and larger than before
It raised the sensitivity, so every wave on the page is drawn larger
It removed muscle and eye artifact that had been covering the sharp events
It cut most of the 1.4 Hz slow waves, so the brief events stand out on a flat background
taskFlow.explanation: A 1.4 Hz wave passes at 1.4 / sqrt(1.96 + 100) = 0.14 of its size, so roughly 150 uV falls to about 20 to 30 uV (3 mm). A 50 ms spike has content near 20 Hz and passes at about 0.9, so it keeps most of its size (9 to 10 mm). Filters never add gain, which rules out added gain. Sensitivity is unchanged at 10 uV/mm, so a sensitivity change is wrong. There was no artifact on the first page to remove, only slow waves.

taskFlow.title: What was given up
taskFlow.description: The page is still at LFF 10 Hz. The slow waves are now about 3 mm and the background looks nearly flat. You are about to continue recording.
taskFlow.question: What does leaving the LFF at 10 Hz cost, and what do you do?
options: It costs nothing, since the slow waves seen at 1 Hz were artifact, so keep 10 Hz all study
It also cuts real slow activity, so use it briefly, document it and restore the routine LFF
It can be offset by raising the sensitivity to 5 uV/mm, which brings the slow waves back
It only removes drift, so cerebral waves are unchanged and nothing needs to be noted
taskFlow.explanation: An LFF removes any slow activity, genuine or not, so at 10 Hz the page cannot show how much slow activity the patient really has. It is therefore a short, documented change, followed by a return to the routine 1 Hz and a note to the reader. The slow waves were widespread and in the same form across the page, which is not how artifact looks, so assuming artifact is a mistake. The LFF is not limited to drift; it acts on every frequency below its cutoff. Raising sensitivity scales what remains but cannot restore filtered waves (about 14% passes), so it brings back nothing.

taskFlow.title: Sweat artifact, tempting fix
taskFlow.description: Later in the study the patient is warm and sweating. The page is at 10 uV/mm and back at LFF 1 Hz. F8-T4 and T4-T6 show a slow sway about 11 mm tall (about 3 to 7 mm in the other channels; the 50 uV calibration pulse near 0.5 s is not part of the sway), and from 6 to 8.5 s slower waves of about 5 to 10 mm appear in most channels. A colleague says to raise the LFF to 10 Hz again.
taskFlow.question: Is a high LFF the right response to the sway?
options: No; cool and dry the patient, reseat T4 and keep the routine LFF
Yes, raise it to 10 Hz as before, and note the change in the log
No; lower the HFF to 15 Hz, which smooths the slow sway while leaving slow waves alone
Yes, but only to about 5 Hz, which clears the sway with no effect on cerebral waves
taskFlow.explanation: The sway is on T4, the electrode shared by F8-T4 and T4-T6, so the cause is technical and should be fixed: cool and dry the patient, check T4 impedance, reseat or re-prepare it. A high LFF would also shrink the slow waves from 6 to 8.5 s: at 5.3 Hz a 1.5 Hz wave passes at 1.5 / sqrt(2.25 + 28.1) = 0.27, and at 10 Hz about 0.15. Choosing 5 Hz does not remove that cost, so cerebral waves are affected too. A lower HFF acts on fast activity and cannot change a slow sway, so it addresses the wrong end of the spectrum.

starterCases.title: Filters Move the Peaks
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Bench test of filters before a clinic day; no patient connected

history.eventDescription: Before the outpatient clinic starts you send a clean test sine wave through the amplifier at several filter settings, to see what each does to size and timing. Each row of the display is the same signal. Drag across the rows to place a time cursor; it reads the time in milliseconds.

eegSummary.background: Test signal only; no patient background

objectives: Relate time constant to size and timing of a 1 Hz wave
Compare the timing shift of an LFF with that of an HFF
Show that filters do not change the frequency

taskFlow.title: Which row is which
taskFlow.description: The display shows one 1 Hz test sine over 5 seconds, drawn four times with time constants 2.0 s, 0.3 s, 0.1 s and 0.03 s from top to bottom. The rows get smaller from top to bottom.
taskFlow.question: How are time constant, LFF and wave size related across these rows?
options: The longest time constant has the highest LFF and gives the smallest wave
A 1 Hz wave sits inside every passband, so all four rows should be the same size
The shortest time constant has the highest LFF and gives the largest wave
The shortest time constant has the highest LFF and gives the smallest wave
taskFlow.explanation: LFF = 1 / (2 pi x TC): TC 2.0 s gives 0.08 Hz, 0.3 s gives 0.53 Hz, 0.1 s gives 1.6 Hz and 0.03 s gives 5.3 Hz. The higher the LFF, the more of a 1 Hz wave it removes, which is why the rows shrink as the time constant shortens (about 100%, 88%, 53% and 18% of the top row). Reversing the relation (long TC equals high LFF) is the usual slip. A 1 Hz wave is not safe from the filter when the cutoff is at or above it: at 1.6 Hz and 5.3 Hz it is cut a great deal.

taskFlow.title: Read the peak times
taskFlow.description: Drag the cursor to the top of the first wave in each row and read the time.
taskFlow.question: How do the first peaks line up as the time constant shortens?
options: Every row peaks at about 250 ms, because a filter changes size but not timing
Each row peaks later than the one above it, because the filter adds a delay
Each row peaks earlier, but only by a few ms, too little to measure on this page
Each row peaks earlier than the one above it, to about 30 ms in the bottom row
taskFlow.explanation: A high-pass filter advances the wave: with a shorter time constant the peak moves earlier, from about 240 ms in the TC 2.0 s row to about 170 ms, 90 ms and 30 ms in the lower rows, a shift of more than 200 ms against the 250 ms peak an unfiltered 1 Hz wave would have (a quarter of its 1000 ms cycle). The shift is real and large for slow waves, not a few ms. 'Filters change only height' is the misconception this display is built to break, and a delay (later peaks) is the HFF behavior, not the LFF one.

taskFlow.title: Now the HFF
taskFlow.description: The display now shows a 20 Hz test sine over 0.4 seconds, drawn with no filter and with HFF 70, 35 and 15 Hz, top to bottom. The ticks are 50 ms apart; one 20 Hz cycle is 50 ms. Place the cursor on the first peak in each row. Compare where each row starts at 0 ms: the filtered rows begin lower, because they lag the unfiltered wave.
taskFlow.question: How does the effect of the HFF compare with the LFF rows you just read?
options: The rows get smaller as the HFF falls and the peaks move later, but only by a few ms
The rows get smaller and their peaks move earlier, as with the LFF
The rows stay the same size and only their peaks move later
The rows get smaller and their peaks move later by tens of ms, as much as with the LFF
taskFlow.explanation: An HFF is a low-pass filter: it reduces fast waves (the lowest HFF row is about half the unfiltered height) and delays them slightly, so the peaks move later, by roughly 4 to 8 ms in the HFF 15 Hz row against about 12 ms for the unfiltered peak. That is the opposite direction to the LFF shift, and far smaller than the 200 ms seen for the slow wave. Equal size with only a delay ignores the loss of height. 'Earlier' repeats the LFF pattern. Shifts of tens of milliseconds are not seen with a 20 Hz wave.

taskFlow.title: Does the frequency change
taskFlow.description: A colleague counts the complete cycles in each row of the 0.4 s page, from the unfiltered row to the HFF 15 Hz row, and asks whether the filter has changed the frequency of the test wave.
taskFlow.question: What does the count show, and what does it mean for reading real pages?
options: 8 cycles in every row; the filters change size and timing, not frequency
8 cycles in the unfiltered row and 6 in the HFF 15 Hz row, because a 15 Hz HFF passes only 15 Hz
8 cycles in the unfiltered row but fewer in the HFF 15 Hz row, because the filter removes some cycles
8 cycles in every row, which shows the filters do nothing, so the settings need not be recorded
taskFlow.explanation: A 20 Hz wave over 0.4 s has 20 x 0.4 = 8 cycles, and every row shows 8: a filter shrinks and shifts the wave but does not change how many cycles occur per second. So a steady wave keeps its frequency through the filters, and counting its cycles is reliable even though its height is not; real waveforms that are cut or smoothed can still look different, which is why the settings are recorded. A filter reduces the height of cycles rather than deleting them. The shrinking of the HFF rows shows the filters do act, and the settings must still be recorded because they change size and timing. An HFF does not make the amplifier pass only its cutoff frequency, which is a bandpass idea, not a low-pass one.

starterCases.title: Choosing the LFF for the Job
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Four outpatient routine EEGs in one clinic day, each needing an LFF decision

history.eventDescription: During a busy clinic day you meet four different recording problems, one per step; the age of each patient is printed on the page header. Your lab protocol sets a routine LFF of 1 Hz or lower, lets you change display settings briefly, and asks you to document every change and notify the reader.

eegSummary.background: Four awake outpatient recordings reviewed from earlier cases, each with a different filter question
eegSummary.artifacts: Slow sway on one electrode in the first recording

objectives: Pick the fix for a slow sway at one electrode
Choose the LFF that best shows focal slow waves
Document every setting change and restore the routine LFF

taskFlow.title: Sway on one side
taskFlow.description: A 40-year-old patient is warm and perspiring. At LFF 1 Hz, F8-T4 and T4-T6 show a slow sway about 15 mm tall, against about 5 to 8 mm in most other channels (the calibration pulse near 0.5 s is not part of the sway). The sway moves in opposite directions in the two channels, as expected at a shared electrode.
taskFlow.question: What is the best response?
options: Cool and dry the patient, reseat T4, keep the routine LFF and document what you did
Lower the sensitivity so the sway fits in the channel and the other channels look quieter
Mark the T4 channels as artifact and continue unchanged, leaving the cause as it is
Raise the LFF to 5.3 Hz for the rest of the study to flatten the sway, then note the change in the log
taskFlow.explanation: The sway appears only in the two channels that share T4 and is mirrored between them, so the cause is local, such as sweat or an unstable electrode. The technologist fixes the cause: cool and dry, check impedance, reseat or re-prepare T4. Raising the LFF to 5.3 Hz would also cut genuine slow waves (a 1.5 Hz wave would pass at about 27%). Lowering sensitivity only changes the drawing size, and marking the channels and carrying on leaves a continuing problem on the record.

taskFlow.title: Best setting for slow waves
taskFlow.description: A 52-year-old with headaches is recorded at LFF 0.53 Hz (time constant 0.3 s). Irregular slow waves in F7-T3 and T3-T5 stand about 18 mm tall. An earlier stretch at 1.6 Hz showed the same waves only 11 to 12 mm tall, and a trial at 5.3 Hz made them 5 to 6 mm.
taskFlow.question: Which LFF is best for the reader to see the left temporal slow waves, within protocol?
options: LFF 0.53 Hz (time constant 0.3 s), which keeps most of the 1 to 2 Hz activity
LFF 5.3 Hz (time constant 0.03 s), which quiets the background so the waves stand out
LFF 10 Hz (time constant 0.016 s), which gives the cleanest-looking background
LFF 1.6 Hz (time constant 0.1 s), which shows the waves and keeps drift down
taskFlow.explanation: Slow waves are shown best by the lowest LFF the recording can tolerate without drift. 0.53 Hz passes about 93% of a 1.3 Hz wave (18 mm), 1.6 Hz about 63% (11 to 12 mm), and 5.3 Hz about 24% (5 to 6 mm). A higher LFF makes the background look quieter, but only because it removes the slow activity the reader is trying to assess. 10 Hz is worse still.

taskFlow.title: Hunting for brief events
taskFlow.description: A 14-year-old is recorded at 10 uV/mm and LFF 1 Hz. Slow waves of 10 to 20 mm cover most channels, and brief sharp events near 1.5, 2.8 and 3.7 s are hard to tell from them. The reader asked you to look for brief sharp events.
taskFlow.question: Which approach suits this job?
options: Lower the LFF to 0.1 Hz so the brief events riding on the slow waves are drawn larger
Raise the sensitivity to 5 uV/mm so the brief events grow above the slow waves
Raise the LFF to 10 Hz briefly, record the time and change, then restore the routine LFF
Raise the LFF to 10 Hz and keep it there for the rest of the study so the brief events stay visible
taskFlow.explanation: For a short search for brief events, a higher LFF removes the 1.4 Hz slow waves (about 14% passes at 10 Hz) while a 50 ms spike keeps about 90% of its size, so the brief events become visible (about 9 to 10 mm over a 3 mm background). Because it also removes real slow activity, it is a brief, documented change followed by a return to routine. Lowering the LFF makes the slow waves bigger and hides the events more. Raising sensitivity scales slow waves and spikes alike. Keeping 10 Hz for the whole study throws away slow-wave information for the reader.

taskFlow.title: Write-up
taskFlow.description: The 14-year-old's page is at LFF 10 Hz: slow waves about 3 mm, sharp events about 9 to 10 mm in F3-C3, C3-P3, Fp2-F4 and F4-C4. You are about to restore the routine LFF and write your technologist notes.
taskFlow.question: What belongs in the notes?
options: The times of the sharp events, labeled as epileptiform discharges that a physician must review
LFF raised from 1 to 10 Hz for a stated stretch, restored after, with the reader told slow waves shrank
Only the final LFF setting, because the reader needs a single number to describe the whole study
Nothing, because the change lasted only seconds and the routine setting was restored afterwards
taskFlow.explanation: The reader must know which part of the page was recorded at LFF 10 Hz and that slow waves were reduced there, so they do not judge background slowing from it; the note should name the setting, the times, and what stayed the same (sensitivity, HFF), and the reader should be notified. Only the final LFF hides the change. Naming events as epileptiform is interpretation, outside scope. Even a brief change is documented, because the page looks different from the routine one.

starterCases.title: Ear Contamination: When A1 Carries the Discharge
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief episodes of lost time reported by family; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 27-year-old woman has a routine awake EEG. Your lab protocol lets you switch among the offered montages, requires that each change be documented, and asks you to notify the reader about reference problems. You do not interpret the findings.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult background with a posterior rhythm near 10 Hz
eegSummary.epileptiform: Repeated sharp negative discharge at T3 described by the technologist only by time and channel
eegSummary.artifacts: None significant; ear reference carries part of the T3 field

objectives: Explain why A1 channels deflect down with a T3 discharge
Estimate T3 amplitude by adding back the A1 share, and check it against All to A2
Document montage changes and notify the reader

taskFlow.title: Down in every left channel
taskFlow.description: A routine awake recording opens on the Ipsi ear tab (left electrodes to A1, right to A2) at 7 uV/mm. A sharp negative discharge repeats at 2.0, 5.1 and 8.2 s. T3-A1 deflects up about 9 mm. At the same instants F3-A1, C3-A1, P3-A1, O1-A1, F7-A1, T5-A1 and Fp1-A1 each deflect DOWN by roughly 4 to 9 mm, about equal in height from front to back. The right-sided channels stay small.
taskFlow.question: What best explains the downward deflections in the left channels that are not over the discharge?
options: A1 has poor contact and a high impedance, so it adds a downward artifact to every channel that shares it
The left-sided amplifiers are wired with opposite polarity to the right-sided ones, so left channels invert
The discharge spreads across the whole left hemisphere, so each left electrode is genuinely positive at that moment
A1 picks up part of the T3 discharge and turns negative, so every channel using it as input 2 swings positive (pen down)
taskFlow.explanation: Every channel is input 1 minus input 2, with negative up. T3 is strongly negative, so T3-A1 goes up. A1 sits close to the temporal field and also turns negative; F3 - (negative A1) is positive, so F3-A1 goes down, and the same happens in each left channel. The size is nearly equal from Fp1 to O1 (about 7 to 9 mm), which a real scalp field would not give, and the right channels use the clean ear A2, so they stay quiet. A spreading field would fall off with distance. A poor A1 contact would add noise all the time, not only at the three spike times. Opposite wiring would also flip T3-A1, which points up as expected.

taskFlow.title: How big is T3 really?
taskFlow.description: Same page, Ipsi ear tab, 7 uV/mm, first discharge at 2.0 s. T3-A1 is about 9 mm up (63 uV). F3-A1, C3-A1, P3-A1 and O1-A1 are each about 7 to 8 mm down (about 49 to 55 uV). Those electrodes are far from T3 and carry almost none of the discharge, so that deflection is mainly the A1 share. Add the A1 share to the T3-A1 height for a rough estimate of the T3 amplitude, then switch to All to A2 and read T3-A2 as a check.
taskFlow.question: What is the rough estimate of the T3 amplitude and height on this page?
options: About 63 uV, roughly 9 mm tall, because the ear adds nothing to the measurement
About 112 uV, roughly 16 mm tall once the A1 share is added back
About 14 uV, roughly 2 mm tall, because the ear share is subtracted from the measured 63 uV
About 49 uV, roughly 7 mm tall, taken from the F3-A1 deflection alone
taskFlow.explanation: T3-A1 = T3 - A1 = -63 uV (up). F3-A1 = F3 - A1 = +49 uV (down), and F3 is nearly silent, so A1 is about -49 uV. Adding the two readings gives (T3 - A1) + (A1 - F3) = T3 - F3, about -112 uV or 16 mm. This works only because the other electrodes record almost none of the discharge. In real recordings the field spreads, the ear is not the only source of the shared deflection, and no reference is truly zero, so treat the sum as an estimate and confirm it on All to A2, where T3-A2 reads about 16 mm. Subtracting 49 from 63 gives 14 uV, which reverses the sign of the ear share. Taking 63 uV at face value ignores the part of the discharge that A1 cancelled. Using 49 uV alone measures the ear, not T3.

taskFlow.title: Referring everything to A1
taskFlow.description: You open the All to A1 tab as a test. T3-A1 is still about 9 mm up, but the other 15 channels, right side included (Fp2, F4, C4, P4, O2, F8, T4, T6), all swing down about 5 to 8 mm at 2.0, 5.1 and 8.2 s. The page looks as if the whole head is involved.
taskFlow.question: What does this view show, and which change fixes it?
options: The downward deflections are a filter effect, so raising the LFF until they disappear gives comparable channels
The discharge has become generalized, so it should be described as generalized and the recording continued in this view
Every channel inherits A1's share of the T3 field; All to A2 uses the farther ear
A1 has failed, so the study should be stopped, both ears rewired and the whole recording restarted from the beginning
taskFlow.explanation: With A1 as input 2 everywhere, any potential on A1 appears in every channel as an inverted copy, so the right hemisphere seems to share the event. The cure is a different reference, here A2, which is far from the left temporal field. The technologist describes what is seen and does not call the discharge generalized, which would be interpretation. A1 is working (it records the discharge faithfully, which is the problem), so rewiring and restarting wastes time. An LFF change would alter the spike itself and does not remove a time-locked offset.

taskFlow.title: What goes in the notes
taskFlow.description: You switch to All to A2. T3-A2 is about 16 mm up at each discharge and every other channel stays under about 5 mm. Your lab asks that montage changes be documented and that the reader be told when a reference is not clean.
taskFlow.question: Which note is the most appropriate for your technologist worksheet?
options: Discharge originates in the left temporal lobe, as confirmed by the change to A2, and a repeat study is recommended
Only the final All to A2 view is recorded, so the page appears clean and the reader is not distracted by the earlier montage
Ipsi ear: T3-A1 about 9 mm, left A1 channels down. All to A2: T3-A2 about 16 mm. A1 shares the T3 field. Reader informed
A1 electrode replaced after the artifact appeared; no further comment is needed because the montage change is only a display choice
taskFlow.explanation: A useful note records what was seen in each montage, the measured heights, and that A1 shares the T3 field, so the reader knows why the Ipsi ear page understates T3 and sprays small down deflections into the left channels. Documenting only the clean view hides information the reader needs. Naming the lobe of origin or advising a repeat is interpretation, outside technologist scope. Replacing A1 is not indicated, since A1 is working; saying that a montage change needs no comment contradicts lab documentation practice.

starterCases.title: Choosing the Reference: Ear, Cz or Average
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Staring spells; routine outpatient EEG with a nap

history.eventDescription: A 27-year-old woman has a routine EEG that includes drowsiness and sleep. Your protocol lets you switch among the offered references, requires that each change be documented and asks you to inform the reader which reference was used. You choose and switch montages, you do not interpret them.

eegSummary.background: Awake alpha near 10 Hz, later stage N2 sleep with vertex waves and spindles
eegSummary.epileptiform: Repeated sharp negative discharge at T3 on the awake page, described by time and channel only
eegSummary.artifacts: Reference contamination depends on the montage used

objectives: Compare ear, Cz and average references on one page
Explain why Cz is unreliable in sleep
Pick a reference for left-right amplitude comparison

taskFlow.title: Which reference understates T3?
taskFlow.description: The reader wants the true height of a T3 discharge that repeats at 2.0, 5.1 and 8.2 s in an awake 27-year-old. The page opens on the Ipsi ear tab at 7 uV/mm, with T3-A1 near 9 mm. Step through the All to A2, Cz ref and Average tabs and compare the height of T3 and what happens in the other channels.
taskFlow.question: Which tab gives the least trustworthy amplitude for this discharge?
options: Average: because it includes T3 itself, T3-AV always reads exactly 50% of its true height
Ipsi ear: A1 shares the T3 field, so T3-A1 loses height and the other left channels deflect down
Cz ref: Cz sits nearer to T3 than A2 does, so it is the reference most likely to lose the T3 height
All to A2: the right ear always shares part of the left temporal field, so T3-A2 is too small
taskFlow.explanation: T3-A1 is about 9 mm, while T3-A2 is about 16 mm, T3-Cz about 17 mm and T3-AV about 15 mm. Only the Ipsi ear page also puts 4 to 9 mm downward deflections in the other left channels, because A1 is part of the discharge field. On this awake page Cz shows almost none of the discharge (T3-Cz about 17 mm, other channels under 4 mm), so it does not lose T3 height. A2 is far from the focus and the other left channels stay under about 3 mm. The average includes T3, so a slight loss and small deflections elsewhere occur, but the loss is far from 50%.

taskFlow.title: Vertex waves with a Cz reference
taskFlow.description: Later in the session the patient is asleep (stage N2, 10 uV/mm). The page opens on the Cz ref tab. At 2.4 and 6.6 s all 16 channels, frontal to occipital, deflect down together by about 5 to 10 mm. The same moments on the Ipsi ear tab show only 1 to 4.5 mm deflections.
taskFlow.question: What explains the simultaneous downward deflection in every channel?
options: A generalized discharge reaches every electrode in step, so all 16 channels truly become positive at that instant
The amplifier saturated on a large signal, so each channel dropped by the same fixed amount as it recovered
A vertex wave is negative at Cz, the reference, so subtracting it makes every channel go positive (pen down)
The patient moved, and movement artifact shifts every electrode together, which is why the pattern appears twice
taskFlow.explanation: Output = electrode minus Cz. Vertex waves are negative at the vertex, so each channel is E - (negative) = positive, and the pen goes down in all of them. The deflections are 5 to 10 mm everywhere, even at the temples and occiput. A generalized discharge would be interpretation and does not fit the Ipsi ear tab, which shows only small, central changes. Movement artifact would be irregular and show on the EKG or other channels as a shift in baseline. Amplifier saturation would flatten the traces, not give a smooth, brief pattern.

taskFlow.title: The same sleep page with ear references
taskFlow.description: You switch to the Ipsi ear tab. At 2.4 and 6.6 s the vertex waves now point up in the frontal, central and parietal channels (largest in C3-A1 and C4-A2, about 4 to 4.5 mm) and are only 1 to 2 mm, sometimes slightly down, in temporal and occipital channels.
taskFlow.question: What does this comparison show about the Cz reference during sleep?
options: The ear page is wrong, because ear references cannot show vertex waves and always reduce their height to near zero
The vertex wave is truly diffuse and equal everywhere, so the Cz page shows its real distribution and is the better view
The vertex wave is central-dominant; the Cz reference spread it into every channel, so Cz is a poor choice in drowsiness and sleep
Vertex waves appear in sleep only on ear-reference pages, so the Cz page is the one to trust for reporting sleep waves
taskFlow.explanation: With Cz as the reference, the vertex wave sits in input 2 of every channel and is copied (inverted) everywhere. The ear page keeps the central maximum. A truly diffuse wave would not shrink so much with a different reference. Vertex waves are not limited to ear pages, and ear references show them well (about 4 mm at the central electrodes). The ear page is not wrong; this is the reason to avoid Cz as a reference once the patient is drowsy or asleep.

taskFlow.title: A reference for left-right amplitude comparison
taskFlow.description: Back on the awake page, the T3 discharge is still present and A1 is the contaminated ear. The reader asks for a view that lets them compare the T3 height with the homologous T4 height. The page opens on the Cz ref tab: T3-Cz is about 17 mm and T4-Cz about 2 mm. There are no vertex waves or spindles on this awake page.
taskFlow.question: Which view is the best choice for comparing homologous amplitudes here?
options: Cz ref, since one reference serves both sides and this awake page has no vertex waves or spindles to leak into it
Ipsi ear, since each hemisphere uses its own ear and both sides can be compared on their own reference
Linked ears, since averaging A1 and A2 halves the contamination, so the two sides can be compared directly
Average, since the mean of all electrodes is zero at every instant, so no discharge can alter either side's height
taskFlow.explanation: Comparing sides needs the same reference on both. Cz, awake and with no vertex waves or spindles in the page, gives T3 about 17 mm and T4 about 2 mm without the A1 problem. On the Ipsi ear tab each side uses a different ear and A1 is contaminated, so the left side is understated and the left channels get spurious deflections. Linked ears only halves A1's share and spreads it into every channel. The average includes the large T3 discharge, so its mean moves with T3 and shifts every channel; it is not exactly zero.

starterCases.title: EKG at the Ears and the Linked-Ear Fix
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Memory complaints; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 58-year-old man has a routine awake EEG. The Ipsi ear page shows a regular artifact at the ears. Your protocol lets you switch among montages within protocol, document the choice and notify the reader. You do not read heart rhythms or interpret cerebral activity.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult background, posterior rhythm near 9.5 Hz
eegSummary.artifacts: Regular EKG artifact at both ear references, opposite polarity at A1 and A2, rate about 78 per minute

objectives: Recognise EKG at the ears by its opposite polarity
Explain why linked ears cancels it and what it does not fix
Document the montages used and the artifact

taskFlow.title: A beat that flips between sides
taskFlow.description: An awake recording opens on the Ipsi ear tab at 7 uV/mm. Sharp deflections occur about every 0.77 s (13 in the 10 s page) and line up with the QRS complexes on the EKG channel at the bottom. In the left channels (Fp1-A1 to T5-A1) they point DOWN about 2 to 4 mm. In the right channels (Fp2-A2 to T6-A2) they point UP about 4 mm.
taskFlow.question: What best explains this pattern?
options: Periodic discharges alternating between hemispheres, to be labelled as lateralized periodic discharges on the worksheet
Pulse artifact at the left ear, because a pulse wave follows each beat by a fraction of a second on one side only
EKG reaching the ear electrodes with opposite polarity at A1 and A2, so left and right ear-referenced channels flip
Mains interference at 60 Hz, because the regular shape and equal height in every channel point to line noise
taskFlow.explanation: The timing matches the QRS exactly and the polarity flips with the ear used as input 2, which is the EKG fingerprint at A1 and A2 on this page. The rate is 60 / 0.77 = about 78 per minute, equal to the EKG channel. Periodic discharges would not be locked to the EKG, and a technologist does not label them. Pulse artifact lags the QRS by a few hundred ms, is a slow wave and sits on one side. Mains interference is 60 Hz, which appears as a thick band, not a 1.3 Hz sequence.

taskFlow.title: Linking the ears
taskFlow.description: You switch to Linked ears (every channel to the average of A1 and A2). The same page now shows the QRS deflections at less than 2 mm in every channel; the EKG channel at the bottom still shows each beat.
taskFlow.question: Why did the QRS almost disappear from the scalp channels?
options: Linked ears adds a high-frequency filter to each channel, so the sharp QRS spike is removed from the page
A1 and A2 carry the QRS with opposite polarity, so their average reference holds almost none and nothing is left to subtract
The montage subtracts the EKG channel from every scalp channel, so the heart's signal is deleted from the page
The scalp electrodes record the QRS in the same polarity as each ear, so they cancel one another in every pair
taskFlow.explanation: Each channel is an electrode minus the (A1+A2)/2 average. If A1 has +x and A2 has -x at each QRS, the average is about 0, so input 2 no longer injects the EKG and the channels show roughly what the scalp itself picks up. No filter is added by choosing a montage, and the EKG channel is not subtracted; it is only displayed. The scalp electrodes do not cancel pairs in a referential montage; the scalp itself carries little EKG, which is why the longitudinal tab is also nearly free of it. Here the two ears carry equal and opposite QRS; in many recordings they do not, and linking the ears only reduces the EKG.

taskFlow.title: What the fix does not do
taskFlow.description: The Linked ears page is clean of QRS. The recording will continue for 20 more minutes. A colleague says to stay on Linked ears for everything because it solved the problem.
taskFlow.question: Which statement about this choice is correct?
options: It removes blink and muscle artifact as well, so no further artifact checks are needed once the ears are linked
It cancels the EKG only because the ears are opposite; if one ear picks up cerebral activity, linking spreads that into every channel
It turns the recording into an ordinary bipolar chain, so phase reversals can be read from it in the usual way
It permanently lowers the EKG at the ears, so the electrodes can stay as they are for the rest of the study
taskFlow.explanation: Linked ears works here because the two ears carry opposite EKG, which cancel in their average. The same average mixes anything else the ears pick up (for example a temporal discharge at one ear) and puts it in every channel. It does nothing to blink or muscle artifact, and it is not a bipolar chain, so phase-reversal logic does not apply to it. The EKG at the ears is still there; only its effect on the displayed channels is cancelled, so the technologist keeps checking the page and the electrode sites.

taskFlow.title: Documenting the EKG
taskFlow.description: You return to the Ipsi ear tab for the next part of the record. The heart rate on the EKG channel is about 78 per minute and regular. You make the worksheet entry for the reader.
taskFlow.question: Which entry is most appropriate?
options: Regular EKG artifact at A1 and A2 (opposite polarity), about 78/min. Ipsi ear and Linked ears used; QRS removed on Linked ears
Pulse artifact at A1, A1 electrode replaced, EKG artifact resolved and no mention of the Linked ears view
No entry needed, because the artifact is gone on the Linked ears page and the reader will review that page only
Cardiac arrhythmia suspected on the ear channels, with a cardiology review recommended before the study is read
taskFlow.explanation: The note describes what is seen, the montages used and what changed, and leaves the reading to the physician. A regular rate of 78 per minute is also no basis for any rhythm label, and recommending cardiology review is outside the technologist's scope. Saying nothing hides the fact that the Ipsi ear page carries EKG, which the reader may see on the saved pages. Calling it pulse artifact and replacing A1 misdescribes it, since the deflections are time-locked to the QRS, not delayed.

starterCases.title: Average Reference: A Peak at F4 and Blinks
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Single event with loss of awareness; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 19-year-old man has a routine awake EEG that includes some average-reference and Laplacian views. Your protocol lets you choose montages, requires that you document them and asks you to notify the reader. You describe what is displayed, you do not diagnose.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult background, posterior rhythm near 10 Hz
eegSummary.epileptiform: Repeated sharp negative discharge at F4 described by time and channel only

objectives: Read the average reference: peak and small distant opposite deflections
Explain why Fp1 and Fp2 are left out of the average
Use the Laplacian as a localising supplement

taskFlow.title: A peak at F4 and small deflections elsewhere
taskFlow.description: A 19-year-old is recorded awake at 7 uV/mm on the Average tab (all channels to the mean of the scalp electrodes). Sharp negative discharges repeat at 3.2 and 6.4 s. F4-AV deflects up about 14 mm. Most of the other 15 channels move only 1 to 3 mm, the majority pointing down.
taskFlow.question: What best explains the small downward deflections in the distant channels?
options: The average reference is switched to a Cz reference automatically whenever one channel is much larger than the rest
F4's negative potential is part of the average, so subtracting that negative mean gives a small positive (down) deflection elsewhere
The distant electrodes have a high impedance, so a small part of the discharge leaks to them from F4 through the skin
The discharge is spreading to every region and becoming positive at a distance, so it must be described as widespread
taskFlow.explanation: In the average montage each channel is E minus the mean of the scalp electrodes. A focal negative discharge at F4 pulls the mean slightly negative, and subtracting a negative gives a small positive value in each other channel (about 1 to 3 mm here, mixed with background). F4-AV, the peak, is 14 mm up, so the largest negativity is at F4. Calling the discharge widespread would be interpretation and does not fit one channel dominating. Impedance does not make signals leak over the scalp. The montage never changes reference by itself.

taskFlow.title: Blinks and the Fp electrodes
taskFlow.description: The same page shows large blinks at 1.2 and 8.3 s. Fp1-AV and Fp2-AV deflect down about 25 mm. The other 14 channels show only background-sized changes (about 1 to 4 mm, mixed up and down). The reader asks why the blinks do not show in every channel in this montage.
taskFlow.question: Which statement explains why the blink stays in the Fp channels?
options: Fp1 and Fp2 are left out of the average reference, so the blink never enters the mean that every channel subtracts
The blink is cancelled by the opposite eye movement on the other side, so only the two frontopolar channels remain
Blinks are too slow to enter an average, because only fast activity above 20 Hz is mixed into the reference mean
The LFF is high enough on this page to remove the slow blink wave from all channels except those closest to the eyes
taskFlow.explanation: The mean here is made from the scalp electrodes except Fp1 and Fp2 (the default of this page), so a blink, which is huge at Fp1 and Fp2, does not enter it. The Fp channels show the blink fully (about 25 mm down), while the others carry only background. There is no cancellation by an opposite eye movement; both Fp electrodes go positive together. An LFF would not select channels by location. Slow activity is part of any average, so the frequency of a blink is not the reason either.

taskFlow.title: The same recording with Fp1 and Fp2 included
taskFlow.description: You open the second page, the same recording where Fp1 and Fp2 are included in the average. At the blinks (1.2 and 8.3 s) Fp1-AV and Fp2-AV are still large and down at about 22 to 24 mm, but now most other channels (central, temporal, parietal, occipital) deflect UP by about 3 to 5 mm in step with the blink. On the first page the same channels moved only about 1 to 2.5 mm.
taskFlow.question: What does this comparison show?
options: The upward deflections show that the other electrodes are genuinely negative at the blink, so they are real frontal activity
A huge Fp potential adds to the mean and turns every other channel slightly negative, a false event; the Fp pair is left out
The blink has spread to the whole head because the patient was drowsy, so the page shows the true distribution
The larger average includes more electrodes and so reduces the noise, which makes this the preferred version of the page
taskFlow.explanation: With Fp1 and Fp2 inside the mean, the very large blink potential at those electrodes raises the average, and each of the other channels is E minus that average, so each gets a small inverted (upward) deflection that looks like a diffuse negative event. Leaving Fp1 and Fp2 out stops this and is the reason for the exclusion. The deflections are time-locked to the blink and do not reflect drowsiness or real cortical activity. Including more electrodes does not reduce this error; it adds a source of it.

taskFlow.title: Laplacian as a sharper look
taskFlow.description: You return to the first page and open the Laplacian tab (each electrode minus the mean of its four nearest neighbours, 19 channels with Fz, Cz and Pz). At 3.2 s F4-Lap is up about 13 mm. Neighbouring channels are small, mostly down by 1 to 4.5 mm; Fz-Lap is slightly up.
taskFlow.question: What is the best use of this view for your worksheet?
options: Replaces the need for any other montage, so the average and bipolar views no longer have to be saved for the reader
Shows the discharge is generalized, because every one of the 19 channels now has a visible deflection at 3.2 s
Proves the discharge is a right frontal lobe seizure focus, so the report can state the diagnosis and the lobe
Peak at F4 on the Laplacian at 3.2 and 6.4 s, with small opposite deflections nearby; record the montage names and times, no diagnosis
taskFlow.explanation: The Laplacian emphasizes a local peak and cancels broad fields, so it shows the peak at F4 with small opposite deflections around it. The technologist documents what is displayed, the montages used and the times (3.2 and 6.4 s) and leaves diagnosis to the reader. A tidy picture does not prove a seizure focus or a lobe of origin. The Laplacian is a supplement, not a replacement, and the reader still needs the standard views. The nearby channels are small, not equal to F4, so the discharge is not generalized.

starterCases.title: Reading Phase Reversals: Toward, Away and Flat
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Recurrent head-turning episodes reported by a relative; routine outpatient EEG

history.eventDescription: A 34-year-old woman has a routine awake EEG. Your protocol lets you switch between double banana and transverse montages, requires that you document what each page shows and asks you to notify the reader. You describe polarity and location, you do not diagnose.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult background, posterior rhythm near 10 Hz
eegSummary.epileptiform: Discharges at C3 and Cz described by polarity, time and channels only

objectives: Tell a negative from a positive phase reversal
Explain a flat channel between equal potentials
Confirm a finding in a second bipolar montage

taskFlow.title: Toward each other
taskFlow.description: A 34-year-old is recorded awake at 10 uV/mm in the double banana. At 3.0 and 6.6 s F3-C3 deflects DOWN about 12 mm and the channel below it, C3-P3, deflects UP about 12 mm. The other channels are small. (Switch to Transverse if you want a second look: T3-C3 is down and C3-Cz is up, about 11 mm each.)
taskFlow.question: How do you describe where this discharge is maximal?
options: No phase reversal, because one channel goes up and the other goes down, so the two cancel at C3
A positive phase reversal at C3: the two traces point toward each other, so C3 is the most positive electrode
A negative phase reversal at C3: the two traces point toward each other at the shared electrode, so C3 is the most negative
A negative phase reversal at F3 and P3, the outer electrodes, because those inputs have the largest deflections
taskFlow.explanation: F3-C3 = F3 - C3 goes down (positive), so C3 is more negative than F3. C3-P3 = C3 - P3 goes up (negative), so C3 is more negative than P3. Deflections that point toward each other at a shared electrode mark a negative phase reversal there. The outer electrodes F3 and P3 are the far inputs, not the maximum. A reversal is exactly one channel up and the neighbour down; it is not a cancellation. Positive reversals are the ones that point away from each other.

taskFlow.title: Away from each other
taskFlow.description: Later in the recording a second page, taken during a different run, shows at 3.0 and 6.6 s that F3-C3 deflects UP about 12 mm and C3-P3 deflects DOWN about 12 mm. The other channels are small.
taskFlow.question: What do you document about this page?
options: A flat channel at C3, because opposite deflections in neighbouring channels cancel and leave no maximum at the middle electrode
A negative phase reversal at C3: the traces point away from each other, so C3 is the electrode with the greatest negativity
A positive phase reversal at C3: the traces point away from each other, so C3 is maximally positive; check the polarity and note it
A negative phase reversal at F3 and P3, because the up and down deflections mean the maximum lies in the outer electrodes
taskFlow.explanation: F3-C3 up means F3 is more negative than C3 (C3 more positive); C3-P3 down means C3 is more positive than P3.
