Deflections pointing away from each other at the shared electrode make a positive phase reversal at C3. This is rarer than a negative one, so it is worth confirming that the electrode inputs and the polarity are right before notifying the reader, and describing it without interpretation. A flat channel needs two electrodes at equal potential, which would show as a small trace, not 12 mm. Negative reversals point toward each other.

taskFlow.title: A flat channel between two active ones
taskFlow.description: A third page (40 y, awake, 10 uV/mm) opens in Transverse. At 3.0 and 6.5 s T3-C3 deflects DOWN about 5 mm and Cz-C4 deflects UP about 5 mm, but C3-Cz between them is flat, under about 1 mm.
taskFlow.question: What is the most likely explanation for the flat C3-Cz channel?
options: There is no discharge at C3 or Cz, so the channel is correctly flat and the activity lies only at T3 and C4
C3 and Cz have equal potential, so input 1 minus input 2 is near zero between them, and the field is centred between those electrodes
C3-Cz is disconnected, so the channel is flat and the electrode inputs should be re-prepped before recording any further
The sensitivity of that channel is lower than the rest, so the same signal appears flat while the others show it
taskFlow.explanation: Two electrodes with the same potential cancel in the channel between them: C3 - Cz = 0. T3-C3 goes down (C3 more negative than T3) and Cz-C4 goes up (Cz more negative than C4), so both C3 and Cz are negative and equal, and the discharge field sits between them. A disconnected channel would be flat throughout the page, not only at the discharge time, and background activity would vanish too. Sensitivity is one setting for the whole page. Saying that no activity is at C3 or Cz contradicts the neighbouring channels.

taskFlow.title: Checking the flat channel in the other montage
taskFlow.description: You switch the same page to Longitudinal. At 3.0 s F3-C3 is down about 5 mm and C3-P3 is up about 5 mm; Fz-Cz is down about 4 mm and Cz-Pz is up about 6 mm.
taskFlow.question: What does this add to the Transverse page?
options: Two negative reversals, at C3 and at Cz, consistent with a field spanning both, so the flat channel was a cancellation and not an absence
No reversal at all, because chains that run front to back can never show a reversal for discharges at the midline
One reversal at the midpoint of C3 and Cz, so the Longitudinal page shows a single focus lying exactly halfway between
A positive reversal at C3 and at Cz, so the field has two positive peaks and the flat channel was a technical failure
taskFlow.explanation: In each parallel chain a down trace above and an up trace below, pointing toward each other, give a negative reversal: at C3 (F3-C3 down, C3-P3 up) and at Cz (Fz-Cz down, Cz-Pz up). Equal negativity at both explains why C3-Cz cancelled in the Transverse page. A positive reversal would point away. Reversals appear at electrodes, not at midpoints. Longitudinal chains show midline reversals well (as with vertex waves), so the last claim is false. Document both views and the times.

starterCases.title: Butterfly Pattern and the End of the Chain
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Staring and brief falls reported at school; routine outpatient EEG with sleep

history.eventDescription: A 12-year-old boy has a routine EEG, and a 46-year-old patient's sleep page is used for comparison. Your protocol lets you switch among bipolar montages, requires that you document what each shows and asks you to notify the reader. You describe polarity and location, you do not diagnose.

eegSummary.background: Age-appropriate awake background with a posterior rhythm near 9 Hz; stage N2 on the comparison page
eegSummary.epileptiform: Discharges at T3 and T4, and at O1, described by polarity, time and channels only

objectives: Read the butterfly pattern across two montages
Recognise a maximum at the end of a chain
Switch montage and document a missing reversal

taskFlow.title: The midline in the transverse chain
taskFlow.description: A 12-year-old is recorded awake at 10 uV/mm on the Transverse tab. At 3.0 and 6.5 s in the central row T3-C3 deflects UP about 9 mm, C3-Cz UP about 4 mm, Cz-C4 DOWN about 5 mm and C4-T4 DOWN about 8 mm. T3 and T4 are at the ends of this row.
taskFlow.question: What does the pair C3-Cz and Cz-C4 show at the midline electrode?
options: A positive phase reversal at Cz: the two traces point away from each other, so Cz is more positive than the electrodes on either side
No reversal at Cz, because the third and fourth channels have different heights, which prevents a phase reversal forming
A flat channel at Cz, because equal and opposite deflections in the two channels cancel and leave Cz at the baseline
A negative phase reversal at Cz: the two traces point toward each other, so Cz is the most negative electrode of the row
taskFlow.explanation: C3-Cz goes up (Cz more positive than C3) and Cz-C4 goes down (Cz more positive than C4). Traces pointing away from each other at the shared electrode make a positive phase reversal at Cz. This is the middle of a butterfly: two negative areas at T3 and T4 with a positive reversal between them. Toward each other would be negative. Reversals do not need equal heights (4 and 5 mm here). A flat channel needs near zero in the channel itself, whereas these two channels are 4 to 5 mm.

taskFlow.title: The same discharges in the double banana
taskFlow.description: You switch to the Longitudinal tab. At 3.0 s F7-T3 deflects down about 11 mm and T3-T5 up about 10 mm. F8-T4 is down about 11 mm and T4-T6 up about 10 mm. Both reversals occur at the same moments, 3.0 and 6.5 s.
taskFlow.question: What do you document from this view?
options: Negative phase reversals at T3 and T4 at the same times (3.0 and 6.5 s), matching the Transverse positive reversal at Cz; no interpretation
A generalized discharge, since both hemispheres are involved at once and the pattern is therefore not focal on this page
A single positive reversal at the midline because both temporal chains show the same pattern at the same time on the page
Reversals at F7 and F8, since the first channel of each chain has the largest downward deflection of the page at 3.0 s
taskFlow.explanation: F7-T3 down and T3-T5 up point toward each other at T3, a negative reversal; the same holds at T4. Together with the positive reversal at Cz in the Transverse chain this makes the butterfly. The technologist documents both reversals with times and montage names. A midline positive reversal belongs to the Transverse view, not to these two chains. F7 and F8 are outer inputs, not maxima. Calling the discharge generalized is interpretation, and the two negative foci with a positive reversal between them do not look like one diffuse pattern.

taskFlow.title: A maximum at the end of the chain
taskFlow.description: A 46-year-old is recorded in stage N2 at 10 uV/mm on the Longitudinal tab. At 2.5, 5.5 and 8.0 s T5-O1 and P3-O1 both deflect DOWN about 10 to 13 mm. No channel above or below them points clearly the other way (the others stay under about 3 mm). A vertex wave at 4.0 s is a separate event.
taskFlow.question: What do these two channels tell you, and what is your next move?
options: There is a negative phase reversal at O1, because both traces go down, so the maximum lies at O1 and nothing more is needed
O1 is the last electrode in both chains, so no reversal can form and the maximum may lie at O1 or beyond; switch to Transverse, where O1 is a middle electrode
There is a positive phase reversal at T5 and P3, so the maximum lies at those electrodes and the page can be used as it is
The pattern shows the discharge is widespread, because two channels move together, so the Longitudinal page should be left as is
taskFlow.explanation: O1 is input 2 in both T5-O1 and P3-O1. Both going down means O1 is more negative than T5 and P3, but with O1 at the end of each chain there is no channel beyond it to turn the opposite way, so no reversal can be seen and the maximum could lie at O1 or beyond it. Two chains moving the same way does not show spread. Switching to Transverse makes O1 a middle electrode, so a reversal can show if it is there.

taskFlow.title: Finding the reversal and documenting it
taskFlow.description: You switch to the Transverse tab for the same discharges. At 2.5, 5.5 and 8.0 s T5-O1 is down about 11 to 13 mm and O1-O2 is up about 10 to 13 mm; the neighbouring channels are small.
taskFlow.question: Which note is the best entry?
options: Longitudinal: negative reversal at O1. Transverse: negative reversal at O1. Both montages agree, so a single entry is enough
Longitudinal: positive reversal at T5 and P3 at 4.0 s together with the three discharges, since the vertex wave also looks like a reversal
Transverse: positive reversal at O2, because O1-O2 goes up and the up deflection marks the electrode with the greatest negativity
Longitudinal: no reversal, O1 at the end of both chains. Transverse: negative reversal at O1 at 2.5, 5.5 and 8.0 s. Reader informed
taskFlow.explanation: T5-O1 down and O1-O2 up point toward each other at O1, so the Transverse chain shows a negative reversal at O1 at the three times; the Longitudinal chain could not show one because O1 ends it. The entry should say so, name both montages and tell the reader. The Longitudinal page does not show a reversal at O1 (the claim of agreement is false). O1-O2 up means O1 is more negative than O2, not that O2 is the maximum. The vertex wave at 4.0 s is a separate sleep transient, shown at Cz.

starterCases.title: Reading the Background: Slow Rhythm or Extra Slow Waves
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Teaching review of four awake routine pages, each recorded from a different adult

history.eventDescription: Your lab runs a short teaching session on describing the background. You are shown four awake pages in turn, each from a different outpatient whose age is printed in the page header. Your job is to measure and describe with the caliper and ruler and to leave the interpretation to the reader.

eegSummary.background: Awake adult backgrounds with different posterior rhythm speeds and different amounts of theta and delta

objectives: Count the posterior rhythm with the caliper and report a number
Separate a slow background from extra slow waves on the page
State the usual association of each pattern without naming a cause

taskFlow.title: Count the posterior rhythm
taskFlow.description: The first page is an awake, eyes-closed stretch from a 52-year-old. The header reads LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz and 10 µV/mm. In T5-O1 and T6-O2 a regular rhythm runs through the whole page, about 8 mm tall, and the frontal channels carry low, fast activity only. Lay the time caliper across one second (one grid interval) in T5-O1 and count the waves.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the posterior rhythm matches what you count on this page?
options: About 5 Hz, a moderate slowing, with no extra theta or delta in the front
About 3 Hz, in the delta range, with slow waves dominating the whole page
About 7 Hz, just under 8 Hz, a mild slowing, with no extra theta or delta in the front
About 10 Hz, inside the usual adult range, so there is no slowing to describe
taskFlow.explanation: Counting about seven waves in each one-second interval gives about 7 Hz (a wave about 140 ms long on the caliper). In the teaching scale this description, a slow background with no excess theta or delta, is the lowest step, Grade IA. About 10 Hz would need ten waves per second and would not be slowed. About 5 Hz would show only five waves per second and is the moderate-slowing description. Delta at 3 Hz would show three waves per second and large slow waves in the frontal channels, which this page does not have. You report the number you measured; the reader decides what it means.

taskFlow.title: Measure three waves
taskFlow.description: A second page, from a 58-year-old, is recorded at 7 µV/mm with LFF 1 Hz and HFF 70 Hz. The posterior rhythm in T5-O1 and T6-O2 is clearly slower than on the first page, and the frontal channels stay low in amplitude, about 4 mm tall. Place the caliper across three consecutive waves in T5-O1 and read the time.
taskFlow.question: Which reading do you get, and how does it compare with the first page?
options: About 570 ms for three waves, near 5 Hz, slower than the first page
About 380 ms for three waves, near 8 Hz, the same rate as the first page
About 250 ms for three waves, near 12 Hz, faster than the first page
About 1.5 s for three waves, near 2 Hz, so delta has replaced the background
taskFlow.explanation: Three waves of a 5 Hz rhythm last 3 x 190 ms = 570 ms, so the rate is 3 / 0.57 s = 5.3 Hz. That is slower than the first page, where three waves took about 380 ms (3 / 0.38 s = 8 Hz). 250 ms for three waves would be 12 Hz and a faster rhythm than either page. 1.5 s for three waves would be 2 Hz, delta, with big frontal slow waves, which this page does not show. In the teaching scale a moderate slowing of the background alone, with no extra theta or delta, is Grade IB.

taskFlow.title: Slow rhythm or extra waves?
taskFlow.description: The third page, from a 47-year-old, is also recorded at 7 µV/mm. In the frontal and central channels irregular slow waves, some at about 5 to 6 per second and some at about 2 per second, are mixed into the tracing. In T5-O1 and P3-O1 a regular rhythm is still visible. Caliper the posterior rhythm over its clearest 2 seconds, then compare the front with the back.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits this page?
options: A posterior rhythm slowed to about 5 Hz, with no extra theta or delta anywhere
A posterior rhythm slowed to about 7 Hz, with no extra theta or delta anywhere
A near-normal posterior rhythm (about 9 to 10 Hz) with extra theta and some delta mixed in
A posterior rhythm near 12 Hz with excess beta in the front
taskFlow.explanation: Counting nine to ten waves per second in T5-O1 and P3-O1 gives a rhythm of about 9 to 10 Hz, so the background itself is close to normal. What is new is the extra slow activity, theta with some delta, in the front. That is the second pattern in the teaching scale: slow waves added to a near-normal background. A rhythm of 5 Hz or 7 Hz would be a slow background, which is a different pattern and does not match the counts. Excess beta near 12 Hz in the front would show fast, low waves, not slow ones.

taskFlow.title: Usual association of the pattern
taskFlow.description: The last page is from a 70-year-old, 7 µV/mm. Slow waves at about 1.7 Hz run through the frontal and central channels, often 10 to 12 mm tall, and behind them only slow activity of about 4 to 6 Hz remains; no 8 to 10 Hz rhythm appears in T5-O1 or T6-O2. The reader asks you how the pattern is usually described in the teaching scale. You may state an association but not a cause.
taskFlow.question: Which statement should you make?
options: Dominant delta with a slow background is usually linked to both cortex and white matter, not to a named cause
Delta dominates but the background is normal, so the usual association is cortical dysfunction alone
The background is slow and nothing else is added, so the usual association is white matter dysfunction alone
Dominant delta is the usual sign of one particular disease, and the technologist names it in the notes
taskFlow.explanation: In the teaching scale a slow background alone points to cortical dysfunction, extra theta or delta on a normal background points to white matter dysfunction, and both together point to cortex and white matter. This page has dominant delta and no 8 to 10 Hz rhythm, so both elements are present. The EEG is rarely specific for the cause, which is why the statement stops at the association. Calling the background normal is wrong for this page. Saying the background alone is slow ignores the large delta. Naming a disease is outside the technologist's scope and is not something the page can show.

starterCases.title: Theta, Delta and the Background: Grades II and III
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Teaching review of four awake pages with excess slow waves, each from a different adult

history.eventDescription: A senior technologist walks you through four awake pages that all show extra slow waves. Each comes from a different adult (age in the header). For every page you measure the posterior rhythm with the caliper and the slow waves with the caliper and ruler, and you say what separates each pair of pages. You do not name a cause or give the final grade.

eegSummary.background: Awake backgrounds with excess theta and delta on top of posterior rhythms of different speeds

objectives: Tell dominant theta from dominant delta using caliper readings
Separate a near-normal background from a slow one
Measure slow-wave height with the ruler at the page sensitivity

taskFlow.title: Theta on a good background
taskFlow.description: Page one is from a 47-year-old, awake, 7 µV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz. In the frontal and central channels runs of waves at roughly 5 to 6 per second dominate, with slower waves at about 2 per second between them. Place the caliper over the posterior rhythm in T5-O1 and P3-O1 and count the waves in one second.
taskFlow.question: Which description matches this page in the teaching scale?
options: A slow background near 5 Hz with theta and some delta added, so the background is slow
Dominant delta with the near-normal rhythm still present behind it
A normal rhythm with no added theta or delta, so only the background is described
A near-normal rhythm near 9 to 10 Hz with dominant theta and some delta added in front
taskFlow.explanation: Nine to ten waves per second behind the slow waves means the background is near normal. The extra activity is mostly theta (5 to 6 Hz) with some delta (about 2 Hz), so theta, not delta, dominates. That is the description of Grade IIA: dominant theta with some delta and a near-normal background. A background near 5 Hz would show five waves per second, which is the B subtype. The page is not free of extra slow waves, so the background-only description does not fit. Dominant delta would show large 1 to 2 Hz waves in every frontal channel, which is the next step up.

taskFlow.title: What separates A from B?
taskFlow.description: Page two is from a 64-year-old, awake, 7 µV/mm, same filters. The frontal and central channels again show waves at about 5 to 6 per second, most clearly in the frontal poles, with some slower ones, about as tall as on the first page (8 to 9 mm). Caliper the posterior rhythm in T5-O1 and T6-O2 and compare the back of the head with the first page.
taskFlow.question: What separates this page from the previous one, and what stays the same?
options: The page now shows only delta, with the theta gone from every channel
Dominant theta with some delta stays, but the posterior rhythm is now slow, near 5 to 6 Hz
The posterior rhythm has disappeared and nothing regular remains behind the front
Frontal slow waves are now about twice as tall as before, and that height separates A from B
taskFlow.explanation: Both pages have dominant theta with some delta in front. The B subtype is defined by the background: here the posterior rhythm has dropped from 9 to 10 Hz to about 5 to 6 Hz, so this is the dominant-theta page with a slow background (Grade IIB in the teaching scale). Height is not the dividing line, and the frontal waves are about the same size on both pages (8 to 9 mm at 7 µV/mm). Theta is still plentiful here. A rhythm is still present behind the front, just a slow one, so nothing has disappeared.

taskFlow.title: Delta with a near-normal rhythm
taskFlow.description: Page three is from a 55-year-old, awake, 7 µV/mm. In Fp1-F7 and Fz-Cz long slow waves dominate the frontal and central channels; behind them a faster rhythm persists in T5-O1 and P3-O1. Caliper one of the larger slow waves in Fp1-F7 from trough to trough and use the ruler to measure its height.
taskFlow.question: Which pair of readings fits this page?
options: About 1.1 s and 12 mm (0.9 Hz, about 84 µV), so the waves are slower than delta waves usually are
About 80 ms and 4 mm (12 Hz, about 28 µV), so the waves are fast activity
About 160 ms and 2 mm (6 Hz, about 14 µV), so the waves are theta
About 550 ms and 6 to 8 mm (1.8 Hz, about 40 to 55 µV), so the waves are delta
taskFlow.explanation: A wave of 550 ms has a rate of 1 / 0.55 = 1.8 Hz, which is in the delta range (below 4 Hz). At 7 µV/mm a height of 6 to 8 mm is 6 x 7 = 42 µV to 8 x 7 = 56 µV. The faster rhythm that persists behind the slow waves is about 9 Hz, so the background is near normal: the description of Grade IIIA. 160 ms is a 6 Hz theta wave and 14 µV is far too small for these waves. 1.1 s would be a very slow wave under 1 Hz and 12 mm is too tall. 80 ms at 12 Hz is alpha or faster activity, not the dominant frontal wave.

taskFlow.title: Delta with a slow background
taskFlow.description: Page four is from a 70-year-old, awake, also at 7 µV/mm. Slow waves at about 1.7 Hz again dominate the frontal and central channels, now reaching 10 to 12 mm in Fz-Cz and F3-C3. In T5-O1 and T6-O2 you find only slow activity of about 4 to 6 Hz. You compare it with the previous page.
taskFlow.question: Which single reading separates this B page from the A page before it?
options: The slow waves are about twice as tall as on the A page, and that height defines B
The delta waves are about 1 Hz faster than on the A page, near 3 Hz, which defines B
The 9 Hz rhythm of the A page is gone; only slow activity of about 4 to 6 Hz remains behind
The sensitivity setting differs on this page, which makes the slow waves look dominant
taskFlow.explanation: The A or B letter is set by the background. On the A page a rhythm near 9 Hz persisted behind the delta; here only slow activity near 4 to 6 Hz remains, which is the dominant-delta page with a slow background, Grade IIIB in the teaching scale. The delta rate is about the same on both pages (1.7 to 1.8 Hz). The waves are somewhat taller, but height does not define A or B. Both pages are at 7 µV/mm, so the display setting did not change and cannot explain the difference.

starterCases.title: Delta Without a Background: Amplitude Decides
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Stuporous inpatient on the ward; routine EEG requested, plus a teaching comparison page from another patient

history.eventDescription: A stuporous 66-year-old is recorded at the bedside on the ward. The page shows continuous slow waves and no posterior rhythm. Your protocol asks you to measure amplitudes with the ruler (mm x sensitivity), keep the sensitivity the lab starts with, document every change and notify the reader. You do not name a cause or give a final grade.

eegSummary.background: No posterior rhythm; continuous irregular delta of varying amplitude

objectives: Convert a ruler reading in mm to µV with the page sensitivity
Explain why the same record looks bigger or smaller at another setting
Write a log entry that records sensitivity changes and state

taskFlow.title: From millimetres to microvolts
taskFlow.description: The patient is stuporous, the header reads 66 y, stuporous, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz and 10 µV/mm. There is no rhythm in T5-O1 or T6-O2, and slow waves at about 1.5 to 2 per second run through every channel. Drag the amplitude ruler over a typical larger slow wave in F3-C3: it measures 13 mm.
taskFlow.question: What amplitude do you record for that wave?
options: About 1.3 µV, from 13 mm divided by 10 µV/mm
About 91 µV, using the 7 µV/mm of an earlier page
About 13 µV, taking the millimetres as microvolts
About 130 µV, from 13 mm x 10 µV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: Amplitude is height in millimetres multiplied by the sensitivity printed in the header: 13 mm x 10 µV/mm = 130 µV. Dividing by the sensitivity gives 1.3, which has no meaning in µV. Using the mm number directly ignores the setting. Taking 7 µV/mm from a different page gives 91 µV, a number that is wrong because it belongs to another recording. In the teaching scale delta above 50 µV with minimal or no background is the larger-amplitude description, Grade IVA. Your job is to report the 130 µV; the reader grades.

taskFlow.title: Smaller delta, other setting
taskFlow.description: The comparison page is a stuporous 73-year-old at 7 µV/mm. Again there is no posterior rhythm, and slow waves at about 1.5 per second run through the channels. A typical larger slow wave in F3-C3 measures 4 mm with the ruler.
taskFlow.question: Which reading and statement is correct for this page?
options: About 0.6 µV, from 4 mm divided by 7 µV/mm, so the page is too flat to describe
About 28 µV, from 4 mm x 7 µV/mm, under 50 µV, matching the lower-amplitude description
No amplitude can be given until the sensitivity matches the first page
About 40 µV, from 4 mm x 10 µV/mm, under 50 µV, matching the lower-amplitude description
taskFlow.explanation: 4 mm x 7 µV/mm = 28 µV, which is under 50 µV, so the page matches the lower-amplitude description (Grade IVB in the teaching scale). 40 µV reaches a similar conclusion, but it comes from the 10 µV/mm of the other page and would be an error in the log. Dividing by the sensitivity gives a meaningless 0.6 µV. Pages never need the same sensitivity to be measured: the ruler multiplies by whatever the header prints, so waiting is not needed.

taskFlow.title: Same record, other setting
taskFlow.description: You change the display to 20 µV/mm (less gain; the header now reads 20 µV/mm) on the same stuporous 73-year-old record to fit a cursor annotation. The slow waves you measured a moment ago at 4 mm now look like slight wobbles, the largest about 1.5 to 2 mm, and the page looks nearly flat. A colleague says the activity has dropped.
taskFlow.question: What is true about this page?
options: 20 µV/mm shows the true amplitude, because larger numbers show less noise and fewer errors
Nothing has changed: waves measure 4 mm at every sensitivity setting
The same waves now measure about 1.4 mm; only the display changed, and amplitude is mm x the header sensitivity
The waves have shrunk to about 14 µV, so the amplitude has fallen since the last page
taskFlow.explanation: The record is the same; only the display setting differs. The wave that was 4 mm at 7 µV/mm (28 µV) is 28 / 20 = 1.4 mm at 20 µV/mm. A larger number draws the same voltage smaller. Calling it 14 µV mixes up the mm reading with the voltage, and no number setting shows the true amplitude better than another. A fixed 4 mm at every setting is not possible, because height in mm changes inversely with the sensitivity. Whenever a page looks flat, read the header first, then measure.

taskFlow.title: What goes in the log
taskFlow.description: Back on the first patient, the reader asks for the same record at 7 µV/mm because the 10 µV/mm page leaves the waves small on screen. You change the sensitivity from 10 to 7 µV/mm and the larger slow waves now measure about 18 mm in F3-C3 and Fp1-F7. The patient remains stuporous on your protocol test, and the nursing sheet lists a sedating drug given earlier.
taskFlow.question: Which entry belongs in the technologist's log?
options: Slow-wave heights in mm only, since the reader converts them; drugs left to the nursing chart
Delta above 50 µV, so cortical damage; reader told the grade and the likely cause at once
Sensitivity is 7 µV/mm because the header prints it, so no entry is needed; delta described as large
Sensitivity changed from 10 to 7 µV/mm with the time; slow-wave heights in µV; stuporous; drug noted; reader told
taskFlow.explanation: A log entry records what you changed (10 to 7 µV/mm, with the time), the measurements you took (18 mm x 7 µV/mm = 126 µV, about 130), the state tested per protocol and the medication on the sheet, then you notify the reader. The header prints the setting, but the change itself is still documented. Giving a grade and a cause is outside your scope. Reporting millimetres without the sensitivity makes the number meaningless, and the drug note helps the reader even if the nursing chart also holds it.

starterCases.title: Burst Suppression: Time the Quiet Stretch
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Semicomatose ICU patient on continuous medication; bedside EEG ordered

history.eventDescription: A 61-year-old in the ICU is semicomatose. Your bedside recording shows bursts of activity separated by quiet stretches. The lab protocol asks for caliper timing of the quiet stretches, graded reactivity testing with each stimulus marked on the page, a record of every drug and sedative with times, and notification of the reader. You do not name a cause or give the final grade.

eegSummary.background: Bursts alternating with low-amplitude quiet stretches
eegSummary.epileptiform: Sharp transients inside the bursts, described only by timing

objectives: Caliper the quiet stretches and compare them with 5 s
Describe burst content and height with the ruler
Plan reactivity testing, drug notes and notification per protocol

taskFlow.title: First quiet stretch
taskFlow.description: The header reads 61 y, semicomatose, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz, 10 µV/mm. Three bursts of activity appear across all channels, about 13 to 17 mm tall, starting at about 0.4, 3.7 and 7.2 s. Between them the tracing is low, about 1 mm tall. Use the time caliper from the end of the first burst to the start of the second.
taskFlow.question: How long is the quiet stretch, and how does it compare with 5 s?
options: About 1.1 s, under 5 s, which matches the shorter-suppression description
About 3.7 s, under 5 s, which matches the shorter-suppression description
About 2 s, under 5 s, which matches the shorter-suppression description
About 6 s, over 5 s, which matches the longer-suppression description
taskFlow.explanation: The first burst ends at about 1.5 s and the second starts at about 3.7 s, so the quiet stretch lasts about 3.7 - 1.5 = 2.2 s, under 5 s. The second quiet stretch (about 4.9 to 7.1 s) is also about 2 s. In the teaching scale suppression periods under 5 s match Grade VA. 1.1 s is the length of the burst itself, not of the quiet stretch. 3.7 s is the time at which the second burst starts, a clock time, not a duration. About 6 s would make the quiet stretch longer than the whole interval between bursts and is not what the caliper shows.

taskFlow.title: A longer quiet stretch
taskFlow.description: On a second page from the same patient later in the shift (same header: 10 µV/mm, semicomatose) only two bursts appear, at about 0.3 and 8.3 s. They look much like the bursts on the first page, with the same height. Use the caliper from the end of the first burst to the start of the second.
taskFlow.question: Which statement matches this page?
options: The quiet stretch is about 8.3 s, measured from the start of the page to the second burst
The quiet stretch is about 2 s, as before, but the bursts are taller
The quiet stretch is about 1.2 s, because the caliper should span the bursts, not the quiet
The quiet stretch is about 6.5 s, longer than 5 s
taskFlow.explanation: The first burst ends at about 1.6 s and the second begins at about 8.2 s: 8.2 - 1.6 = 6.6 s, longer than 5 s. Only the quiet stretch has changed, while the bursts keep the same height and content. In the teaching scale suppression periods over 5 s match Grade VB. The 2 s figure belongs to the first page. 8.3 s is a clock time, and it also includes the start of the page. The caliper measures the quiet between bursts, not the 1.2 s burst.

taskFlow.title: What is inside a burst?
taskFlow.description: Go back to the first page (10 µV/mm). Study the burst that starts at about 3.7 s in several channels, one chain at a time, and compare its height with the quiet stretch next to it. The reader wants a description made only of what you can see and measure.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the bursts should you give?
options: A slow build-up of delta over 2 s in one hemisphere, fading gradually into the quiet
A rhythmic 3 per second spike-and-wave train in the frontal channels only, with clean quiet in between
Mixed delta, theta and faster activity with sharp transients, abrupt on and off, in all channels
Low fast activity about 1 mm tall with no slow waves, broken by brief muscle artifact
taskFlow.explanation: The bursts start and stop abruptly (within about 0.1 s) in every channel, contain a mix of slow waves, faster activity and sharp transients, and reach about 13 to 17 mm (130 to 170 µV at 10 µV/mm), against about 1 mm (10 µV) in the quiet stretch. The reader gets that description in numbers, with no cause attached. A 3 Hz spike-and-wave train in front only, a gradual build-up in one hemisphere and a flat low-amplitude page all describe patterns that are not on this page.

taskFlow.title: Tests, medications, notification
taskFlow.description: On the second page (quiet stretch about 6.5 s) the reader asks you to test reactivity. The patient is receiving sedating medication, and the nursing sheet lists doses and times. Your protocol lists the stimuli to use and the order to follow.
taskFlow.question: Which plan fits the protocol?
options: Start with the strongest stimulus on the list to be sure that a response is seen
Record drugs with times, give stimuli in protocol order, write responses, notify the reader
Record the grade and a cause, then skip stimulus testing since the pattern is obviously severe
Wait for the next medication list before writing about sedation and test reactivity only
taskFlow.explanation: Protocols grade stimuli from least to most intense, mark each one on the page with its time and describe the response (or its absence), and record drugs and sedatives with times so the reader can weigh them. The reader is told about the pattern, the quiet stretch length and the test results. Skipping stimulation, jumping to the strongest stimulus, or delaying the sedation note all break the protocol. A grade and a cause are the reader's work, not the technologist's.

starterCases.title: Low Voltage or Nothing? Check the Settings First
starterCases.chiefComplaint: ICU recordings that look nearly flat: a 73-year-old on two pages, then a 59-year-old on two pages; reader on call

history.eventDescription: You are recording in the ICU when a page looks almost flat. Your protocol says to check the display settings first, raise the gain (a smaller µV/mm number) as the protocol allows, check electrodes and cables, tell artifact from cerebral activity, document every change and notify the reader. You never call a record electrocerebral inactivity: that is a medical decision made under the protocol. The first two pages are from a 73-year-old; the last two are from a different 59-year-old.

eegSummary.background: Very low-amplitude slow activity on the first pages; a few microvolts on later pages
eegSummary.artifacts: EKG artifact on one chain on the last page

objectives: Check the header sensitivity before judging a flat page
Compare the same record at two sensitivities
Separate EKG artifact from cerebral activity at 2 µV/mm

taskFlow.title: Nearly flat page
taskFlow.description: The header of a stuporous 73-year-old reads LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz and 20 µV/mm. All channels look nearly flat: the largest wobbles are about 1.5 to 2 mm tall and nothing regular is visible. The nurse asks whether the brain is still active.
taskFlow.question: What do you do first?
options: Raise the HFF to 100 Hz so that more of the activity reaches the page, then note it
Read the header, raise the gain (a smaller µV/mm number, such as 7) and note the change
Re-prepare every electrode first, since flat channels always mean poor contact
Tell the reader the record shows no cerebral activity, since nothing exceeds 2 mm
taskFlow.explanation: At 20 µV/mm one millimetre is 20 µV, so a 2 mm wobble is only 40 µV and typical waves of 28 µV look like 1.4 mm. The cheapest and fastest check is the header: raise the gain (a smaller µV/mm number) as the protocol allows and document the change. Telling the reader there is no cerebral activity is a medical decision, not a conclusion from a display at the wrong setting. The HFF changes the fast end of the signal, not the height of slow activity. Re-preparing every electrode is a later check, and flat channels do not always mean poor contact.

taskFlow.title: Same record at 7 µV/mm
taskFlow.description: You change the sensitivity to 7 µV/mm (the header now reads 7 µV/mm). Slow waves at about 1.5 per second are now clear in every channel, the larger ones about 4 mm tall in F3-C3, and some activity in the front looks faster. You compare it with the 20 µV/mm page.
taskFlow.question: What does the comparison show?
options: The extra height is noise that the 20 µV/mm setting had filtered out
The same record: 1.4 mm at 20 µV/mm is about 4 mm at 7 µV/mm, both about 28 µV
The activity has grown since the last page, so you should tell the reader the patient is recovering
A different recording, because taller waves mean you must label the pages as two separate studies
taskFlow.explanation: A wave of 28 µV measures 28 / 20 = 1.4 mm at 20 µV/mm and 28 / 7 = 4 mm at 7 µV/mm; the ratio of heights is 20 / 7, about 2.9. Nothing in the record changed, only the display. Stating that the patient is recovering confuses the display with the signal and is also interpretation. The sensitivity is a display gain, so it does not turn one record into two. The sensitivity does not filter anything, so the extra height is the same slow activity, drawn larger.

taskFlow.title: A few microvolts left
taskFlow.description: Another ICU patient, a 59-year-old, is recorded (header: 59 y, semicomatose, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz, 2 µV/mm). The page shows low-amplitude slow waves in every channel, about 3 mm tall (about 6 µV), and the EKG channel at the bottom shows a steady 82 per minute. The reader on call asks for a check of the recording system before any decision.
taskFlow.question: Which sequence do you follow?
options: Report electrocerebral inactivity in your notes, since nothing taller than 4 mm remains at 2 µV/mm
Switch to 1 µV/mm without a note, since the header prints the sensitivity, and send the page on
Keep 2 µV/mm, check impedances and electrodes per protocol, describe the activity in µV, notify the reader
Replace the amplifier at once, since a record this small can only mean an equipment failure
taskFlow.explanation: A flat-looking record is first a technical question. At 2 µV/mm you keep the sensitivity the protocol names, check impedances and cables, test that the system responds (for example by a documented integrity or touch test per protocol), describe what is seen in numbers (about 6 µV of slow activity, 3 mm tall) and tell the reader. Calling the record electrocerebral inactivity is a medical decision under the protocol. Changing the sensitivity without a note breaks the documentation rule. Replacing the amplifier before any check assumes a fault without evidence.

taskFlow.title: Small deflections that repeat
taskFlow.description: A final page (header: 59 y, semicomatose, 2 µV/mm) shows almost nothing in most channels, about 1 mm or less. In T5-O1 a small upward deflection about 1.5 mm tall repeats about every 0.7 s, with a smaller downward one, about 1 mm, in F7-T3. Use the caliper to compare their spacing with the R waves in the EKG channel. The reader asks what you would write about them.
taskFlow.question: Which statement belongs in your notes?
options: EKG artifact: the deflections repeat about every 0.7 s with the R waves in the EKG channel; documented and the reader notified
Electrode pop at T5 and T3; the technologist re-applies both at once and stops the recording
Low-voltage fast activity of cerebral origin in T5-O1 and F7-T3, so the technologist calls it a low-voltage record
Breathing artifact; the technologist lowers the LFF to 0.1 Hz to remove it and does not log the change
taskFlow.explanation: The deflections occur at the heart-rate interval (60 / 82 = 0.73 s) and line up with the R waves in the EKG channel, so they are described as EKG artifact in the T5 and T3 channels. Cerebral activity does not follow the heartbeat, and a pop is a single abrupt jump, not a regular repeat. Changing the LFF to remove an artifact without a log entry breaks the rule that every setting change is documented. Describe it, document it and notify the reader; calling the record electrocerebral inactivity is not the technologist's decision.

starterCases.title: One Patient Over Three Days: Documenting Change
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Repeated bedside EEGs on a 66-year-old whose alertness is falling

history.eventDescription: You record the same 66-year-old at the bedside on day 1, day 2, and the afternoon and night of day 3. Alertness is falling, and the ICU flow sheet gives the GCS and drug changes. For each page you compare it with the last one using numbers, record state and settings, document every change and tell the reader. You do not name a cause or give a final grade.

eegSummary.background: Worsening sequence: slow background with theta, then dominant delta, then delta without a background, then bursts with quiet stretches
eegSummary.epileptiform: Sharp transients inside the bursts on the last page

objectives: Compare successive pages by background, slow waves and amplitude
Convert amplitudes with each page's header sensitivity
Record GCS, drug changes and times, and notify the reader

taskFlow.title: Day 1 baseline
taskFlow.description: On day 1 the patient has the eyes open and speaks clearly; the flow sheet lists GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). The page is awake, 7 µV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz. In T5-O1 and T6-O2 you count a rhythm of about 5 to 6 per second, and the frontal and central channels carry theta with some slower waves, about 6 to 8 mm tall.
taskFlow.question: What should the day-1 entry hold as the baseline for later comparison?
options: The label Grade IIB with no measurements, although the page shows about 5 to 6 Hz at 7 µV/mm
Only the header settings (7 µV/mm, LFF 1 Hz, HFF 70 Hz), since the reader will describe the waves from the page
A cause for the slowing, the posterior rhythm of about 5 to 6 Hz and the 7 µV/mm sensitivity, as a baseline
Posterior rhythm about 5 to 6 Hz by caliper, theta with some delta in front, awake, GCS 15, drugs, 7 µV/mm
taskFlow.explanation: A baseline is useful only if it holds numbers that a later page can be compared with: the rhythm speed from the caliper, a description of the slow waves with heights and the sensitivity, the state and GCS, and the drugs. A cause is not something the technologist can state. Settings alone leave the reader with nothing to compare. A grade label with no numbers cannot be checked against the page. Describing the page this way matches the description of Grade IIB in the teaching scale, but you record the measurements.

taskFlow.title: Day 2
taskFlow.description: On day 2 the flow sheet lists GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6) and a new evening drug with its time. The page is awake, 7 µV/mm, the same header as day 1. In the frontal and central channels slow waves of about 1.7 per second now dominate and reach about 9 to 12 mm, and in the back only slow activity of about 4 to 6 Hz can be counted.
taskFlow.question: Which statement about day 2 is accurate?
options: The slow waves are taller only because the sensitivity setting changed since day 1
Frontal waves are taller (9 to 12 mm, not 6 to 8) and delta leads; drug recorded; reader told
Nothing differs from day 1 apart from the GCS, so the day-1 entry is simply copied forward
The new drug explains the slow waves, so no notification is needed and the day-1 entry stands unchanged
taskFlow.explanation: Both pages are at 7 µV/mm, so millimetres compare directly: the frontal slow waves have grown from 6 to 8 mm (42 to 56 µV) to 9 to 12 mm (63 to 84 µV), and delta now leads over theta. That is a change from day 1, so the reader is told, and the drug and its time are recorded as information for the reader. A technologist does not decide that a drug explains a change. The sensitivity did not change. Copying the day-1 entry forward would hide the difference.

taskFlow.title: Day 3 afternoon
taskFlow.description: On the afternoon of day 3 the patient opens the eyes only to pain and says single inappropriate words; the flow sheet lists GCS 9 (E2 V3 M4), and you note stupor on your protocol test. The header now reads 10 µV/mm, not 7. No rhythm can be counted in T5-O1 or T6-O2, and slow waves at about 1.5 per second run through every channel; the larger waves in F3-C3 measure about 13 mm.
taskFlow.question: Which statement about the change from day 2 is correct?
options: Sensitivity is the same as on day 2, so the larger waves are a real increase and need no conversion
Sensitivity went from 7 to 10 µV/mm, so 13 mm is about 130 µV, and no rhythm remains
A higher sensitivity number magnifies the waves, so the new height is only a display effect
A rhythm has returned near 4 Hz, so the background is better than on day 2
taskFlow.explanation: The header changed, so the mm must be converted: 13 mm x 10 µV/mm = 130 µV. The same voltage would look 10 / 7 = 1.4 times taller on day 2's setting, so these waves are clearly bigger than the day-2 waves (about 70 to 85 µV). A larger µV/mm number draws the same wave smaller, so the height is not just a display effect. No regular rhythm can be counted in the back, so the background has not recovered. Documenting the new setting and its time is part of the entry, and the reader is told about the loss of the background.

taskFlow.title: Day 3 night
taskFlow.description: At night the patient does not open the eyes to pain and the flow sheet lists GCS 6 (E1 V2 M3). A nursing note says a sedative dose was raised two hours ago. The page is at 10 µV/mm, header semicomatose: bursts about 1.1 s long, 13 to 17 mm tall, in every channel, separated by quiet stretches of about 2 s that are about 1 mm tall.
taskFlow.question: What do you record and do?
options: The drug change explains the bursts, so a routine entry is enough and the reader is told in the morning round
The patient has improved, since the bursts are taller than the day-3 delta and the quiet stretches are short ones
Bursts about 1.1 s long with quiet stretches of about 2 s now replace delta; GCS and drug change recorded; reader told now
The record is labelled burst suppression, drug-induced, so that the reader can skip a full review
taskFlow.explanation: Compared with the afternoon, continuous delta has been replaced by bursts with quiet stretches of about 2 s (under 5 s, the shorter-suppression description in the teaching scale). You record the numbers, the GCS, the drug change and its time, and tell the reader at once because the pattern has changed. The reader weighs the drug; the technologist does not conclude it explains the pattern or delay a notification. Tall bursts do not mean improvement, and attaching a cause to the label is outside the technologist's role.

starterCases.title: Which lobe? Matching the deficit to the delta
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Four stroke-unit patients, each with a different focal deficit, have routine awake EEGs

history.eventDescription: A stroke unit sends four adults, each with a different deficit after a recent stroke. You record a routine awake EEG for each and compare left with right chains. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis. The questions below ask which region, territory or mechanism a picture is typical of, as exam practice.

eegSummary.background: Posterior rhythm about 9.5 Hz in each patient
eegSummary.focalFindings: One region of irregular slow waves per patient, with a normal opposite side

objectives: Match a focal deficit to the lobe and the chains with slow waves
Explain focal delta as deafferentation of cortex
Link a visual-field deficit to its arterial territory

taskFlow.title: Patient 1: halting speech and a weak leg
taskFlow.description: Patient 1 is 54 years old. Since the stroke his speech is effortful and halting in short phrases, he understands what is said, and his right leg is weak. The page is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. Compare the left chains (Fp1-F3, F3-C3, F7-T3) with the right chains (Fp2-F4, F4-C4, F8-T4) using the amplitude ruler.
taskFlow.question: Which chains carry the focal slow waves, and which lobe is this picture typical of?
options: Fp2-F4 and F4-C4 on the right: right frontal lobe, since the weak leg is on the right side of the body
Fp1-F3 and F3-C3 on the left: left frontal lobe, with the dominant speech area and the leg motor strip
F7-T3 and T3-T5 on the left: left temporal lobe, since any speech problem points to the temporal region
C3-P3 and P3-O1 on the left: left parietal lobe, since a weak limb points to sensory cortex
taskFlow.explanation: Fp1-F3 and F3-C3 show irregular slow waves of about 12 to 13 mm peak to peak (roughly 85 to 90 uV at 7 uV/mm), while Fp2-F4 and F4-C4 stay near 5 mm. Effortful speech with preserved comprehension is typical of the dominant inferior frontal region (Broca area), and leg weakness fits the frontal motor strip, so this is typical of a left frontal lesion. The right chains are the quiet side, so the right-sided option has the crossed-side error: the deficit is on the right because the left hemisphere controls it. Receptive (fluent, poorly understood) speech is the temporal pattern, and Fp1-F7 and F7-T3 stay lower (about 6 and 9 mm) because the maximum is at F3. A parietal lesion gives sensory loss or neglect rather than halting speech.

taskFlow.title: Patient 2: a weak right hand
taskFlow.description: Patient 2 is 63. After the stroke the right hand is weak and clumsy; speech and vision are normal. The page is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. Measure the slow waves in F3-C3 and C3-P3 and in F4-C4 and C4-P4, and look for an arch-shaped 9 Hz rhythm in the central chains.
taskFlow.question: Which statement correctly links this page to the deficit?
options: Slow waves of about 13 mm in left F3-C3 and C3-P3, against about 8 mm on the right; the left central cortex serves the right hand
Slow waves in left C3-P3 and P3-O1 mean a left parietal lesion, which is the usual source of hand weakness
The left and right central chains carry the same slow activity, so this page cannot be matched to either side
Slow waves of about 13 mm in left F3-C3 and C3-P3; the right central cortex is damaged, because the weak hand is on the right
taskFlow.explanation: F3-C3 and C3-P3 measure about 13 mm peak to peak against about 8 mm in F4-C4, and the right central chain also shows an arch-shaped 9 Hz mu rhythm that the left chain lacks (a destructive lesion removes mu). Motor control of the hand sits in the opposite precentral gyrus, so a right-hand deficit is typical of a left central lesion. Choosing the right cortex is the crossed-side error: the lesion is on the side opposite the weakness. Saying the sides are equal ignores the measured difference. Weakness is motor, which is precentral; parietal lesions produce sensory loss and neglect, and P3-O1 is not the abnormal chain here. The difference is real but modest, so describe it with numbers and leave the lobe to the reader.

taskFlow.title: Patient 3: fluent speech that makes no sense
taskFlow.description: Patient 3 is 57. Speech is fluent but filled with wrong words, and he does not follow spoken instructions. The page is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. The left anterior temporal chains Fp1-F7 and F7-T3 show irregular slow waves of about 10 to 15 mm peak to peak, against about 5 mm on the right. A trainee asks why a lesion produces slow waves instead of faster activity.
taskFlow.question: Which explanation of the slow waves is accurate?
options: The scalp electrodes record the slowed action potentials of damaged neurons, which is why the waves are slow
Dying cortical neurons fire more slowly on their own, so the cortex alone produces the delta waves
Cortex that loses its thalamic and white-matter input is deafferented and falls into slow, irregular activity
The lesion raises impedance under the nearest electrodes, so only the lowest frequencies pass to the amplifier
taskFlow.explanation: Delta is produced when cortex is deafferented from the thalamus or ascending systems, or when white matter is damaged, so a focal white-matter lesion gives focal polymorphic delta. The scalp records summed postsynaptic potentials, not action potentials, so the first distractor misdescribes the signal. The idea that cortex makes delta by itself is the common mistake that ignores the loss of input. Impedance changes add noise or attenuation across all frequencies and would not give a regular side-to-side difference limited to one region. Fluent, poorly understood speech is typical of a dominant temporal lesion; the technologist records the side and amplitude and leaves the localization to the reader. Wernicke area lies in the posterior superior temporal gyrus; this page's focus is anterior temporal, so only the lobe is being matched.

taskFlow.title: Patient 4: half the visual field is gone
taskFlow.description: Patient 4 is 66. He suddenly lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes, while the central field is preserved. The page is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. T6-O2 shows the largest slow waves (about 11 to 16 mm peak to peak in a one-second stretch) and P4-O2 about 8 to 9 mm; on the left, T5-O1 and P3-O1 show a clearer 9 to 10 Hz rhythm of about 6 to 12 mm among smaller slow waves, while the right-sided rhythm is reduced.
taskFlow.question: Which arterial territory is this picture typical of?
options: Posterior cerebral artery
Vertebrobasilar reticular system
Anterior cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery, lateral surface
taskFlow.explanation: A left homonymous hemianopia comes from the right occipital lobe or its radiation, and sparing of central vision (macular sparing) is typical of a posterior cerebral artery lesion because the occipital pole has dual supply. The right occipital chains T6-O2 and P4-O2 carry the slow waves, which fits. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex and gives leg weakness and abulia. The middle cerebral artery gives face and arm weakness, aphasia or neglect. A vertebrobasilar lesion in the reticular system causes impaired arousal or coma. The technologist reports the chains, side and amplitude; naming a vessel is for the clinician.

learningLinks.label: Physiology: Where the EEG comes from
Domain I: Neuroanatomy and EEG localization

starterCases.title: The 3 Hz absence: a thalamocortical loop
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Staring spells many times a day at school; routine EEG with hyperventilation

history.eventDescription: A 9-year-old girl is referred for brief staring spells that begin and end abruptly. You record a routine awake EEG with hyperventilation (HV) at 10 uV/mm, LFF 0.5 Hz. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Normal awake background with a posterior rhythm near 9 Hz

objectives: Measure a spike-and-wave rate with the caliper
Describe a generalized, synchronous burst by amplitude and timing
Test and document responsiveness during a burst

taskFlow.title: Caliper the spike-and-wave
taskFlow.description: The page is awake, longitudinal, 10 uV/mm. A normal posterior rhythm runs until 2.6 s, where a regular burst begins at a marker and continues to 8.4 s. Place the caliper on one spike and drag to the next spike in the stretch after 6 s.
taskFlow.question: What interval and rate do you read?
options: About 330 ms between spikes, so roughly 3 Hz
About 500 ms between spikes, so roughly 2 Hz
About 170 ms between spikes, so roughly 6 Hz
About 100 ms between spikes, so roughly 10 Hz
taskFlow.explanation: Rate = 1 / interval = 1 / 0.33 s = 3 Hz. Early in the burst the complexes are slightly faster (about 3.4 Hz, near 290 ms), so the rate settles toward 3 Hz, which fits the typical range of 2.5 to 4 Hz. An interval of 170 ms would be reached only by counting the spike and the slow wave as two separate cycles. 500 ms would be 2 Hz, the rate of slower syndromes. 100 ms is 10 Hz, the rate of the posterior rhythm before the burst. Always measure from spike to spike.

taskFlow.title: Where does it start, and how big is it?
taskFlow.description: Switch to the Ipsi ear tab (left electrodes to A1, right to A2). Use the amplitude ruler on F3-A1, F4-A2, C3-A1, C4-A2, O1-A1 and O2-A2, and note when each channel first shows the burst.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the distribution is accurate?
options: Two independent bursts, one on each side, that happen to overlap in time
A focal left frontal onset that spreads slowly to the right over several seconds
Generalized and bilaterally synchronous, largest frontally, with similar size on both sides
A right-sided discharge that reaches the left through the A1 reference
taskFlow.explanation: Every channel begins together at about 2.6 s. F3-A1 and F4-A2 each swing about 32 mm peak to peak (320 uV at 10 uV/mm), C3-A1 and C4-A2 about 23 mm, and O1-A1 and O2-A2 about 13 to 14 mm, so left and right match and the frontal maximum is clear in the referential view. A focal onset would show one side first and a time lag. Independent bursts would differ in rate and timing between sides. Ear contamination would add equal downward deflections to channels sharing the ear, not matching spike-and-wave in both hemispheres. This generalized, symmetric picture is typical of an absence pattern, but the technologist describes it and leaves the interpretation to the reader.

taskFlow.title: Why 3 Hz?
taskFlow.description: After the study, the child's parent asks what the regular rhythm is thought to be. You review the mechanism for your own preparation.
taskFlow.question: Which mechanism is the 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave associated with?
options: Reduced sodium current in inhibitory neurons from a sodium channel gene variant
An abnormal thalamocortical loop driven by low-threshold T-type calcium channels and GABA-B signalling
Cortex deafferented by white-matter damage, which produces slow rhythmic waves
A single irritable cortical focus in the dominant hemisphere that fires about three times a second
taskFlow.explanation: Absence seizures arise when the thalamocortical loop oscillates abnormally: low-threshold T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and GABA-B-mediated inhibition of the relay neurons by the reticular nucleus drive a regular 3 Hz cycle with abrupt onset and offset. A single cortical focus would give focal, not generalized, discharges. Loss of sodium current in inhibitory neurons is the mechanism associated with a different syndrome, Dravet. Deafferentation explains focal delta, not a rhythmic generalized spike-and-wave. Mechanism is background knowledge; at the bedside the technologist describes and tests.

taskFlow.title: During the burst
taskFlow.description: On the same page, the burst runs from 2.6 s to 8.4 s while the girl is overbreathing. She is staring and her counting has stopped. You must test responsiveness and document the event within protocol.
taskFlow.question: What do you do and record?
options: Give a short phrase to repeat, note whether and when she responds, and log the start and stop times of the burst
Mark the page as an absence seizure at 2.6 s so the reader knows which seizure type it was
Wait until the burst ends, then ask her to describe what she felt and write down her account
Call for emergency help as in status epilepticus, and wait for a break in the burst
taskFlow.explanation: During a burst you test responsiveness with a short phrase or task, note the words used, whether she responded and when, and mark the burst start and stop; the burst on this page lasts 8.4 - 2.6 = 5.8 s. Calling an emergency for a short burst is an overreaction; continue HV for its full protocol time only if she can cooperate and the seizure is not prolonged; follow your lab protocol and the reader's instructions. Asking afterwards loses the time-locked information because she cannot report what she missed. Writing a seizure type is a diagnosis and outside technologist scope. Describe what you see and hear and let the reader classify it.

starterCases.title: Infant with spasms: three ages, three patterns
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Clusters of brief jerks on waking in a 6-month-old, after a stormy neonatal course

history.eventDescription: Over a day you record two infants whose EEGs show very different patterns that both sit in the spectrum of early epileptic encephalopathies: a 1-month-old, then a 6-month-old, recorded again during a spasm. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: No organized background; high-amplitude disorganized activity
eegSummary.epileptiform: Burst suppression in the youngest infant; hypsarrhythmia and an electrodecrement in the older one

objectives: Tell burst suppression from hypsarrhythmia by measuring
Calculate amplitude from sensitivity
Document spasms and state accurately

taskFlow.title: The 1-month-old
taskFlow.description: A 1-month-old with tonic spasms is recorded at 20 uV/mm. High-amplitude activity with spikes appears from about 0.6 to 2.2 s and from 7.1 to 8.7 s. Use the caliper to measure the stretch between those bursts, and use the ruler to compare burst height with that stretch.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits the page?
options: Hypsarrhythmia: continuous chaotic high-amplitude slow waves with multifocal spikes across the whole page
Burst suppression: bursts of about 1.6 s, then a nearly flat stretch of about 4.7 s
Periodic complexes: stereotyped discharges repeating about every 6.5 s on a slowed background
Electrodecrement: one sudden attenuation of about 2 s that follows a single large slow wave
taskFlow.explanation: Bursts of 11 to 17 mm (220 to 340 uV at 20 uV/mm) alternate with a nearly flat stretch under 1 mm from about 2.3 to 7.0 s (about 4.7 s), and the bursts come back at 7.1 s. That is burst suppression, which is typical of the earliest infantile encephalopathies and persists in waking and sleep. Hypsarrhythmia has continuous activity between its spikes; it does not alternate with a nearly flat stretch. The burst-to-burst interval (6.5 s) looks periodic, but periodic complexes are stereotyped single events, not bursts of mixed spikes with a flat gap. An electrodecrement is a one-time drop after a spasm, not a repeating cycle.

taskFlow.title: The 6-month-old: how big?
taskFlow.description: A 6-month-old has clusters of brief flexor jerks on waking. The page is awake at 20 uV/mm. Chaotic slow waves with multifocal spikes run through all channels, and the largest slow waves measure about 30 mm peak to peak with the amplitude ruler.
taskFlow.question: What amplitude is that, and how does it compare with the usual hypsarrhythmia range?
options: About 600 uV (30 mm x 20 uV/mm), well above the 200 uV that hypsarrhythmia often exceeds
About 1.5 uV (30 mm / 20 uV/mm), far too small to matter
About 210 uV (30 mm x 7 uV/mm), using the sensitivity of an adult page
About 300 uV (30 mm x 10 uV/mm), using the usual default sensitivity
taskFlow.explanation: Amplitude = height x sensitivity = 30 mm x 20 uV/mm = 600 uV peak to peak, which is higher than the 200 uV that hypsarrhythmia is often described as exceeding. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 1.5, an arithmetic error. Using 10 or 7 uV/mm assumes a different setting; always read the sensitivity in the header, and note that infants are often recorded at 20 uV/mm because their activity is large. Hypsarrhythmia is a pattern, not a diagnosis, and many causes produce it; the technologist reports the measured amplitude and the setting.

taskFlow.title: The marked spasm
taskFlow.description: Later the same infant has a spasm marked at 5.0 s. A large slow wave appears at about 4.8 s, and the channels Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8 show brief muscle activity from about 5.0 to 5.2 s. Look at all channels from 5 to 8 s.
taskFlow.question: What is the best description of the change after the marker?
options: An electrodecrement: all channels drop to low amplitude from about 5.1 to 7.2 s, after which the chaotic activity returns
Muscle artifact that hides the cerebral activity in every channel until the movement stops
The suppression phase of burst suppression, so the infant's pattern has changed to the neonatal type
Electrode disconnection: all channels go flat because the common reference lead has come loose
taskFlow.explanation: An electrodecrement is a generalized attenuation after a slow wave that accompanies the spasm. Here activity drops from about 15 to 30 mm to about 2 to 3 mm in all channels from about 5.1 to 7.2 s, then the chaotic pattern returns. A loose reference would not recover by itself and would give noise, not clean low-amplitude traces. The suppression of burst suppression recurs in cycles on a different background and does not follow a marked spasm. The muscle artifact is limited to four frontal electrodes and is visible only around 5.0 to 5.2 s, so it cannot explain the drop in the posterior channels. Mark the time of the spasm precisely, because muscle can mimic or hide the change.

taskFlow.title: What goes in the notes
taskFlow.description: The page is now shown in the Ipsi ear montage. Spasms keep clustering over the next minutes. The parent says they usually occur on waking. You are writing the technologist notes.
taskFlow.question: Which documentation is best?
options: A line saying the infant has West syndrome with hypsarrhythmia, so the reader does not need to search
Time of each spasm, awake or asleep state, medications with times, and any muscle over the change
Only the time of the first spasm, since the later spasms in the cluster show the same finding
The medication list only, because the spasms are visible on the page and so need no separate log
taskFlow.explanation: Mark every spasm with its time, record state (awake or asleep, because hypsarrhythmia changes in sleep), list medications and times, and note when muscle artifact might hide the electrodecrement. Naming the syndrome is diagnosis and belongs to the reader. Logging only the first spasm loses the cluster count the reader needs. Leaving out the log assumes the page alone is enough, but the paper record and event marker must match, and the medications are needed to read the background. Describing the findings with times is the technologist's contribution.

starterCases.title: Rolandic and occipital spikes in the child
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Facial twitching and speech arrest from sleep in an 8-year-old; second child with eye-closure spikes

history.eventDescription: You record an 8-year-old boy who has had facial twitching and trouble speaking after falling asleep, then a 7-year-old girl referred for a different pattern. For both you use the montage tabs to show polarity and location. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Normal sleep background with a spindle near 4.2 s

objectives: Find the phase reversal and its polarity
Read the frontal positive pole of a horizontal dipole
Describe eye-state dependence of occipital spikes

taskFlow.title: Where does it reverse?
taskFlow.description: The boy is in N2 sleep at 10 uV/mm, longitudinal montage. High-amplitude spikes recur at about 1.2, 2.3, 3.4, 5.1, 6.4, 8.2 and 9.2 s on the right. Look at the right parasagittal chain Fp2-F4, F4-C4, C4-P4 and P4-O2.
taskFlow.question: Where is the phase reversal and what is its polarity?
options: No reversal, because C4 is in the middle of the chain and only one channel moves
At F4, negative, because Fp2-F4 is the first channel in the chain that deflects
At C4, positive: the two channels point away from each other at that electrode
At C4, negative: F4-C4 points down and C4-P4 points up, toward each other
taskFlow.explanation: At each spike F4-C4 deflects down about 16 mm and C4-P4 deflects up about 12 mm. Their deflections point toward each other at C4, which marks a negative phase reversal (maximum negativity at C4). Pointing away from each other would be a positive reversal. Fp2-F4 stays small (under 3 mm), so F4 is not the maximum. A reversal needs two adjacent channels sharing an electrode, and here both move, so the one-channel reading is wrong. A centrotemporal location is typical of a rolandic pattern, but the technologist reports the electrode and polarity.

taskFlow.title: The frontal downward deflections
taskFlow.description: Switch to the Ipsi ear tab (left to A1, right to A2). At each spike C4-A2 goes up about 13 mm. At the same instants Fp2-A2 goes down about 5 mm and F4-A2 down about 4 mm, while T4-A2, P4-A2 and O2-A2 stay within about 2 mm of baseline.
taskFlow.question: What best explains the small downward deflections at Fp2-A2 and F4-A2?
options: A2 has picked up the discharge, so every right-sided channel using it swings down by the same amount
The positive pole of a horizontal dipole: negative at C4 and positive over the frontal region
Amplifier saturation in the channels beside the largest deflection
Blink potentials that happen to coincide with each spike, seen through the frontopolar channel
taskFlow.explanation: In the rolandic pattern the spike has a tangential, horizontal dipole with a negative pole centrally and a positive pole frontally, so Fp2 and F4 go positive (down) while C4 goes negative (up). If A2 were contaminated, T4, P4 and O2 would also swing down by a similar amount, but they do not. Blinks do not repeat in step with each spike, and they would show on both frontopolar channels. Saturation clips the largest channel and does not create a small opposite deflection elsewhere. Sleep activates these spikes and they can shift sides, so describe the side, time and polarity.

taskFlow.title: Eyes closed, eyes open
taskFlow.description: The girl is 7 and awake at 10 uV/mm. The page has markers: Eyes open at 3.4 s and Eyes closed at 7.2 s. Spikes with a slow wave appear in the occipital chains (T5-O1, T6-O2) and in P3-O1 and P4-O2. Compare the stretch from 3.6 to 7.0 s with the rest of the page.
taskFlow.question: What does the page show about the spikes and eye state?
options: Spikes continue unchanged through eye opening, so eye state has no bearing on them at all on this page
Spikes appear with eyes closed (0.7 to 2.7 s, 7.8 to 9.2 s) and not with eyes open, as in fixation-off sensitivity
Spikes are caused by the eye opening itself, so they are eye-movement artifact over the occipital chains
Spikes occur only once after eye closure at 7.2 s, so the page shows a single occipital burst only
taskFlow.explanation: Spikes of about 8 to 12 mm in T5-O1 and T6-O2 fall at 0.7, 1.4, 2.1 and 2.7 s and again at 7.8, 8.5 and 9.2 s; between 3.4 s (Eyes open) and 7.2 s (Eyes closed) the channels are quiet. This eye-state dependence (fixation-off sensitivity) is typical of the occipital spikes of self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (Panayiotopoulos syndrome). Unchanged spikes would not fit the quiet stretch. Eye-movement artifact appears in frontopolar channels, not as occipital spikes with a slow wave. A single burst after 7.2 s ignores the earlier burst before 3.4 s. Mark each eye-state change so the reader can see the link.

taskFlow.title: What you can say about course
taskFlow.description: The page is now shown referentially. Occipital spikes reach about 10 to 14 mm in O1-A1 and O2-A2. The referring team asks what is usually expected for children with these patterns; the questions below treat this as exam knowledge.
taskFlow.question: As exam knowledge, which statement about the usual course is most accurate?
options: Occipital seizures in Panayiotopoulos-type epilepsy are typically generalized convulsions with no autonomic features at all
Both syndromes continue unchanged into adult life, so lifelong follow-up and treatment are certain
Both are childhood syndromes that usually remit with age; sleep activates centrotemporal spikes and eye closure occipital ones
Rolandic spikes never change side, and occipital spikes are always present with the eyes open throughout
taskFlow.explanation: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes typically occurs from about 3 to 14 years and resolves in adolescence; self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (Panayiotopoulos) occurs from about 1 to 14 years (peak 3 to 6) and usually remits with age. Rolandic spikes can shift sides, so never is wrong; occipital spikes appear with eye closure and may vanish with the eyes open, the opposite of always present. Lifelong persistence is not the usual course. Occipital seizures in this syndrome typically include autonomic features such as vomiting and eye deviation. In the notes, describe the EEG and document sleep and eye state; prognosis is for the clinician.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Focal and generalized patterns

starterCases.title: Temporal lobe epilepsy: from the sharp wave to the seizure
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Rising stomach sensation, then staring and lip-smacking, for two years

history.eventDescription: A 34-year-old woman has episodes that begin with a rising epigastric feeling and fear, followed by staring and lip-smacking. You record a routine EEG that includes drowsiness. Later in the study she has a spell on the monitor. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Alpha slows to about 8.5 Hz in drowsiness
eegSummary.epileptiform: Left anterior temporal sharp waves; later a rhythmic theta seizure pattern

objectives: Describe a temporal sharp wave by channel, time and polarity
Explain why a transverse chain shows no reversal at F7
Document responsiveness and behavior during a seizure

taskFlow.title: Describe, do not diagnose
taskFlow.description: The woman is drowsy, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. Sharp waves with an after-going slow wave occur at 2.2, 5.9 and 8.4 s. Fp1-F7 deflects down about 16 mm and F7-T3 up about 13 to 16 mm each time, and left temporal slowing runs from about 3.5 to 7.5 s. The reader asks for your description of the page.
taskFlow.question: Which note describes it the way a technologist should?
options: Typical left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, with benign wicket spikes of drowsiness ruled out on the shape of the waves alone
Drowsy. Sharp waves at 2.2, 5.9, 8.4 s, about 16 mm, reversal at F7 (Fp1-F7 down, F7-T3 up), then a slow wave; left temporal slowing 3.5 to 7.5 s
Benign variant of drowsiness: wicket spikes, so no further action or comment is needed in the report notes at all
Left frontal artifact from the eye muscles, with a reversal at F7 caused by eye movement during the drowsy state
taskFlow.explanation: Describe with numbers: times, amplitude (about 16 mm x 7 uV/mm = 110 uV), polarity, the electrode of reversal and the state. A negative reversal at F7 means Fp1-F7 and F7-T3 point toward each other there. The after-going slow wave and the focal slowing are features the reader weighs against benign drowsy variants such as wicket spikes, which are arciform runs without a following slow wave; describing the features lets the reader decide. Naming the syndrome or declaring a variant benign is interpretation. Eye muscle artifact shows as muscle or eye-movement potentials, not repeated sharp waves with a slow wave and a localized reversal.

taskFlow.title: The transverse chain
taskFlow.description: Switch to the Transverse tab. At 2.2 s F7-Fp1 goes up about 16 mm and F7-F3 goes up about 15 mm. The other channels are within about 3 mm of baseline.
taskFlow.question: What does the same-direction deflection in these two channels mean?
options: Equal potentials at F7 and F3 that cancel in the channel between them, so the maximum lies at F3
A negative reversal at F3, because F7-F3 and F3-Fz point toward each other, so the maximum is at F3 and not at F7
No reversal: F7 is the first input of both channels, so they move together; the reversal shows in the longitudinal chain
A positive reversal at Fp1, the electrode shared by F7-Fp1 and Fp1-Fp2, so the maximum is frontopolar
taskFlow.explanation: F7-Fp1 and F7-F3 both have F7 as input 1, so a negative peak at F7 moves both channels up. With the maximum at the first input of the first channels, this is an end-of-chain situation and gives no phase reversal; the reversal is seen in the longitudinal chain where F7 lies between Fp1-F7 and F7-T3. Fp1-Fp2 stays small (about 2 to 4 mm), so there is no positive reversal at Fp1. Equal potentials would give a flat channel; F7-F3 is 15 mm tall. F3-Fz is also small, so F7-F3 and F3-Fz do not point toward each other. Reporting where the maximum lies and which montage shows the reversal is accurate and in scope.

taskFlow.title: The spell on the monitor
taskFlow.description: The woman is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. A marker reads Onset at 2.4 s. Over the next seconds a rhythmic pattern appears in the left temporal chains Fp1-F7 and T3-T5. Count the waves in a 1 s stretch near 3 s and again near 9 s, and compare the heights; also compare left central and frontal channels with the right.
taskFlow.question: Which description of the evolution is accurate?
options: Fast activity near 20 Hz that fades within a second and stays on the right side only, with no spread
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave that starts at the marker and stops abruptly after a few seconds
Left temporal theta slowing from about 6 toward 5 Hz while growing, with left central and frontal channels joining later
Rhythmic theta that speeds up from 5 to 6.5 Hz while shrinking, and stays at the onset site
taskFlow.explanation: Near 3 s you count about 6 waves per second (about 165 ms apart); near 9 s about 5 per second (about 190 ms), so the rhythm slows from about 6.5 to 5 Hz. T3-T5 grows from about 2 mm rms to about 4 to 5 mm rms, and left C3-P3 and Fp1-F3 rise to about 2.8 and 1.8 mm rms while the right F4-C4 and F8-T4 stay near 0.8 mm. Rhythmic theta that grows, slows and spreads is typical of an ictal temporal pattern. A fast fading burst, 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave and a speeding, shrinking rhythm each contradict the page. Describe the numbers; the reader decides the seizure type.

taskFlow.title: During the event
taskFlow.description: The page is now shown in the Ipsi ear montage and the pattern is still running. The woman stares, her lips move, and her left hand picks at the sheet. You are at the bedside.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Describe the event afterwards from memory, since speaking aloud would disturb the recording
Tell the family this is a temporal lobe seizure so they can plan, then log the page afterwards
Stop recording to protect the equipment and wait until she stops moving before restarting the study
Keep recording, call to her and test responsiveness, describe what you see, mark the time, and notify the reader
taskFlow.explanation: Keep recording; test responsiveness with a name and a short phrase, describe what you see (staring, lip movements, hand picking), mark the onset time and the response, keep her safe, and notify the reader. Stopping the recording loses the ictal data. Describing from memory loses the time-locked timing and responsiveness. Telling the family a diagnosis is interpretation and outside scope. Document the actions and the time so the clinical signs can be matched to the EEG.

learningLinks.label: Domain III: Ictal EEG seizure patterns

starterCases.title: Frontal lobe and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
