starterCases.chiefComplaint: Brief nocturnal seizures in a 22-year-old; next, a 15-year-old with morning jerks

history.eventDescription: A 22-year-old man has brief, frequent nocturnal seizures with thrashing and little confusion afterwards. Afterwards you record a 15-year-old who has jerks of the arms soon after waking. For both, a sleep or waking record has been requested. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Normal for state
eegSummary.pdrHz: Not applicable in N2; 10 Hz awake
eegSummary.epileptiform: Left frontal spikes with a short bilateral burst; later generalized polyspike-wave bursts

objectives: Find the F3 reversal in the longitudinal chain
Explain a bilateral burst that follows a focal spike
Document jerks and plan photic stimulation safely

taskFlow.title: Where is the reversal?
taskFlow.description: The 22-year-old is in N2 sleep at 10 uV/mm, longitudinal. Spikes recur at 1.6, 3.9 and 7.4 s. At 3.9 s Fp1-F3 deflects down about 14 mm and F3-C3 up about 15 mm; F4-C4, Fp2-F4 and the temporal chains stay under 3 mm.
taskFlow.question: Where is the phase reversal, and what does it mean?
options: At Fp1: Fp1-F3 is the first channel that moves, so the maximum is frontopolar
At F3: Fp1-F3 and F3-C3 point toward each other, a negative reversal
At C3: F3-C3 points up, so the maximum lies at the second electrode
There is no reversal, because a bilateral discharge cannot have a focal maximum
taskFlow.explanation: Deflections that point toward each other at an electrode mark a negative reversal there, so the maximum is at F3. In referential view F3-A1 is also the tallest channel (about 13 to 15 mm). Fp1 and C3 are the outer ends of the two channels, not the shared electrode. Spikes at F3 alone on this page are unilateral; they do not make the discharge bilateral. Interictal spikes can be scarce in frontal lobe epilepsy because much of the frontal cortex is deep, medial or inferior, so a record can look normal; describe the spikes you do see.

taskFlow.title: The burst at 5.3 s
taskFlow.description: On the same page a rhythmic burst runs from 5.3 to 6.5 s. Fz-Cz, F3-C3 and F4-C4 each measure about 16 to 19 mm peak to peak, with the same size on both sides, at roughly 3 complexes per second. P3-O1, T5-O1 and T6-O2 stay near 4 to 5 mm.
taskFlow.question: Which explanation of a short, symmetric burst on a recording whose repeated spikes are only at F3 is the most plausible?
options: A second, independent right frontal focus that happens to fire at the same moment as the left focus
Rapid spread to both frontal regions (secondary bilateral synchrony), as across the corpus callosum
Jaw muscle artifact, because the burst is largest over the frontal and central chains of the montage
Reference contamination, because the burst appears in both hemispheres at the same time on the page
taskFlow.explanation: The burst is about 1.2 s long, is bilateral and symmetric, and has a smooth, rhythmic spike-and-wave shape at about 2.9 Hz, which is consistent with fast bilateral spread of a frontal discharge across the corpus callosum. Two independent foci would not lock together in time with identical rhythm. In a bipolar longitudinal montage no shared reference can be contaminated, so the second explanation is wrong. Muscle artifact is irregular, fast and high frequency, not a smooth 3 Hz rhythm. Describe the burst as bilateral and 1.2 s long, and give the F3 spike times separately. The page shows no focal lead-in, so describe the burst only as bilateral and symmetric with its times; the reader decides whether it is secondary bilateral synchrony or a separate generalized discharge.

taskFlow.title: A burst with no jerk marked
taskFlow.description: The next patient is 15 and awake, 10 uV/mm. Short bursts of irregular spikes and slow waves appear generalized at 2.2, 4.8 and 7.6 s. Markers read Jerk at 2.2 and 7.6 s only; you saw no jerk at 4.8 s.
taskFlow.question: How do you document the burst at 4.8 s?
options: Record it as a subclinical seizure, since the discharge occurred without a jerk
Leave it out, because a burst with no marker has no clinical importance
List it with the others as a generalized burst at 4.8 s; note no jerk was marked
Treat it as artifact, because a real discharge would have produced a jerk
taskFlow.explanation: Document every burst by time (2.2, 4.8, 7.6 s) and note which ones have a marked jerk; the burst at 4.8 s has no marker. Omitting it hides information the reader needs. Calling it subclinical is a clinical classification outside scope. A generalized polyspike-and-slow-wave complex of this size (about 6 to 10 mm in the longitudinal chains) is cerebral and is not excluded by the absence of a jerk; artifact does not repeat as the same complex. Typically, brief generalized polyspike-and-slow-wave complexes (here each lasts about 0.5 s) occur singly or in runs of 1 to 3 s, often soon after waking.

taskFlow.title: Planning the rest of the study
taskFlow.description: The page is now shown in the Transverse montage. Bursts are symmetric (F7-F3 and F4-F8 each about 11 to 13 mm). The order asks for a waking or sleep-deprived record, and photic stimulation is part of the lab protocol.
taskFlow.question: Which plan is best?
options: Hold the study until the neurologist confirms the diagnosis so the correct protocol can be chosen first by that physician
Skip photic stimulation because the page already shows bursts without any flashing lights being used at all
Run every flash frequency to the end of the protocol, even after a burst, so that the set is complete for the reader
Record after waking or sleep deprivation as ordered, run photic per protocol, and stop at a generalized photoparoxysmal discharge
taskFlow.explanation: Bursts are often activated by sleep deprivation and awakening, and photic stimulation can provoke a photoparoxysmal response, so you run it per protocol while observing the patient and the tracing and stop at the first generalized discharge or clinical event. Skipping photic stimulation removes a protocol step. Continuing through a burst risks a seizure and is not protocol. Waiting for a diagnosis delays the study and is not required; the technologist follows the written order and documents what is recorded.

starterCases.title: Slow spike-wave, fast bursts and sleep-activated spike-wave
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Several seizure types and developmental delay in a 6-year-old; three comparison children

history.eventDescription: A 6-year-old boy has several seizure types, slow development and drop attacks. Your lab day also includes a 9-year-old with staring spells, an 8-year-old recorded in sleep, and a 7-year-old with language regression. You compare rate, state dependence and sleep content. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Slow background in the 6-year-old; normal in the 9-year-old
eegSummary.pdrHz: About 6.5 Hz in the 6-year-old, 9 Hz in the 9-year-old
eegSummary.epileptiform: Slow spike-and-wave, 3 Hz spike-and-wave, generalized fast bursts and near-continuous sleep spike-wave

objectives: Measure the rate of generalized spike-and-wave
Tell fast bursts from a sleep spindle by measurement
Know what to record for sleep-activated spike-wave

taskFlow.title: Caliper the slow spike-wave
taskFlow.description: The 6-year-old is awake at 10 uV/mm. The background posterior rhythm is slow, about 6.5 Hz. From 1.6 s to 7.6 s a regular generalized spike-and-wave burst runs. Place the caliper from one spike to the next in the middle of the burst.
taskFlow.question: What interval and rate do you read?
options: About 270 ms, so about 3.7 Hz
About 540 ms, so about 1.8 Hz
About 800 ms, so about 1.25 Hz
About 330 ms, so about 3 Hz, the rate of classic absence
taskFlow.explanation: Rate = 1 / 0.54 s = 1.85 Hz. Bursts of generalized spike-and-wave slower than 2.5 Hz (often 1.5 to 2.5 Hz) in a slow background are described with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. 330 ms would be 3 Hz, a different rate, and 270 ms (3.7 Hz) is still in the faster absence range. 800 ms would be 1.25 Hz, slower than what you measure. The burst lasts about 6 s, with about 11 complexes. The technologist reports the measured rate and background and leaves the syndrome to the reader.

taskFlow.title: Contrast with a 9-year-old
taskFlow.description: The next child is 9 and awake at 10 uV/mm. A normal posterior rhythm runs until 2.6 s, then a regular generalized burst runs to 8.4 s. Measure the rate with the caliper and compare the background before the burst with the previous page.
taskFlow.question: Which statement about this page is accurate compared with the previous one?
options: The rate is about 1.8 Hz, the same as before, but the bursts are shorter
The burst is focal on the left at a rate near 6 Hz, on a normal background
The rate is about 3 Hz, with a normal 9 Hz posterior rhythm before the burst
The rate is about 3 Hz, but the background is as slow as on the previous page
taskFlow.explanation: Spike-to-spike intervals near 330 ms give about 3 Hz in the second half of the burst, and the posterior rhythm before 2.6 s is about 9 Hz, a normal background. The previous page had 1.8 Hz and a slow background of about 6.5 Hz. The burst here lasts 5.8 s, not shorter, and it begins in all channels together, so it is generalized, not focal. Rate and background are two of the features that separate a typical absence pattern from the slow spike-wave of a diffuse encephalopathy.

taskFlow.title: Fast bursts in sleep
taskFlow.description: An 8-year-old is in N2 sleep at 10 uV/mm. Two generalized bursts marked Fast burst begin at 2.4 s and 6.6 s and last about 1.4 s each; a sleep spindle sits at 4.6 s. Count the waves in 1 s inside a burst and compare heights in C3-P3.
taskFlow.question: Which description is best?
options: Muscle artifact, because activity this fast in sleep cannot be cerebral in origin at all
Alpha rhythm returning after an arousal, because it is rhythmic and generalized across the head
Sleep spindles, because anything near 12 Hz in N2 is a spindle and needs no description in the notes
Generalized bursts of about 12 Hz and 1.4 s in non-REM sleep, taller than the similar-frequency spindle at 4.6 s
taskFlow.explanation: You count about 11 to 12 waves per second (about 85 ms apart). C3-P3 reaches about 8 mm in the bursts against about 5 mm at the spindle, so the bursts are larger, abrupt and generalized, with onset and offset. Frequency alone cannot separate them, so describe amplitude, onset and offset. Generalized paroxysmal fast activity (10 to 20 Hz) in non-REM sleep is described with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and may be a tonic seizure. Muscle is irregular and brief, not a regular 12 Hz rhythm with an even envelope. An arousal would be recorded with a state change, and the patient is asleep throughout. Mark the bursts and the state and notify the reader if there is a clinical event.

taskFlow.title: A page that is almost all spike-wave
taskFlow.description: A 7-year-old with regression of language is in N2 sleep at 10 uV/mm. Generalized spike-and-wave at about 2.2 Hz runs through the whole page. In the awake part of the record there was far less.
taskFlow.question: What do you do?
options: Record sleep through its cycle, mark state changes, and describe near-continuous 2.2 Hz activity, leaving proportion to the reader
Wake the child to see whether the activity stops, then report the exact percentage of the record
Stop after 20 s because epileptiform activity is already proven and more sleep would add nothing new
Write a spike-wave index of 85 percent on the page so the reader does not have to calculate it
taskFlow.explanation: In this pattern the discharges take up most of non-REM sleep and are much less abundant awake, so a sleep recording is essential and you do not stop early. The caliper gives about 450 ms between complexes (2.2 Hz). Describe the rate and distribution and mark state changes; the amount of spike-wave in sleep is measured by the reader. Waking the child to test the activity is not protocol and would remove the state of interest. Writing a percentage is a measurement of the reader, outside the technologist role.

learningLinks.label: Syndromes: Slow spike-wave and sleep activation

starterCases.title: Periodic patterns and coma
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Fever and confusion; later a rapidly progressive dementia, a child with jerks, and a comatose patient

history.eventDescription: During one ICU shift you record a 58-year-old with fever and confusion, a 64-year-old with rapidly progressive dementia, an 11-year-old with myoclonic jerks, and a 41-year-old who is comatose. For each you describe the pattern with numbers and never name a cause. Your role is to describe with numbers, mark events, record state and medications, and notify the reader; you do not name a diagnosis.

eegSummary.background: Slowed backgrounds with repeating complexes in three patients
eegSummary.focalFindings: Lateralized in one patient, generalized in two

objectives: Measure complex intervals with the caliper
Separate lateralized from generalized periodic patterns
Test and document reactivity in a comatose patient

taskFlow.title: Fever and confusion
taskFlow.description: The 58-year-old is awake, longitudinal, 7 uV/mm. Sharp-and-slow complexes repeat across the page, starting near 0.5 s. Use the caliper from one complex to the next and compare Fp1-F7, F7-T3, T3-T5 and C3-P3 on the left with F8-T4 and T4-T6 on the right.
taskFlow.question: What interval and distribution do you describe?
options: About 5 s apart over the left temporal channels, with the right side quiet
About 1.1 s apart over the left temporal channels, with the right side quiet
About 0.5 s apart over the left temporal channels, with the right side quiet
About 1.1 s apart, generalized and symmetric over both hemispheres
taskFlow.explanation: Complexes fall at about 0.5, 1.6, 2.7, 3.8, 4.9, 6.0, 7.1, 8.2 and 9.3 s, so the interval is 1.1 s. Left channels reach about 20 mm peak to peak (T3-T5 and Fp1-F7 about 22 mm; 150 uV at 7 uV/mm), while right chains stay at about 8 mm, over a slowed left temporal background. Periodic lateralized discharges in a destructive focal illness, such as an acute infection of one temporal lobe, show this pattern, but you never name the cause. The generalized option ignores the quiet right side. 0.5 s halves the true interval, and 5 s is the pattern of a different disease with long intervals.

taskFlow.title: Rapidly progressive dementia
taskFlow.description: The 64-year-old is awake, 7 uV/mm. Stereotyped complexes repeat across the page, with the first near 0.45 s. Measure the interval with the caliper and compare left and right chains such as F3-C3 and F4-C4, T5-O1 and T6-O2.
taskFlow.question: Which statement is accurate compared with the first page?
options: Complexes recur about every 2 s in both hemispheres, with a jerk marked on each
Complexes recur about every 0.95 s in both hemispheres (F3-C3 and F4-C4 similar in height), on a slowed background
Complexes recur about every 5 s in both hemispheres, with a jerk marked on each
Complexes recur about every 0.95 s but are confined to the left temporal channels, as before
taskFlow.explanation: Complexes fall at about 0.45, 1.35, 2.3, 3.3, 4.2, 5.2, 6.1, 7.05, 8.0, 9.0 and 9.9 s, which is about 0.95 s apart, and F3-C3 (about 8 mm) and F4-C4 (about 7.5 mm) match closely, while T5-O1 (about 10 mm) and T6-O2 (about 13 mm) are similar; some other chains differ by two-fold or more, which is why the pattern can look asymmetric early. Generalized, fairly symmetric periodic complexes about once per second on a slowed background are described with a rapidly progressive dementia, but the pattern can be asymmetric early. No jerks are marked on this page, and the 2 s and 5 s intervals do not match the measurements. Stimulus responses and sedation can change complexes, so record both and name no cause.

taskFlow.title: A child with jerks
taskFlow.description: The 11-year-old is awake at 20 uV/mm. Large stereotyped complexes appear at 1.4 s and 6.6 s with a marker at each. Place the caliper from the first complex to the second.
taskFlow.question: What do you read, and what do the markers show?
options: About 0.5 s between complexes, with a Jerk marked at only one
About 10 s between complexes, so only one complex is on the page
About 5.2 s between complexes, with a Jerk marked at each
About 1 s between complexes, with a Jerk marked at each
taskFlow.explanation: The interval is 6.6 - 1.4 = 5.2 s, with a marker reading Jerk at each complex. The longer interval is typical of the complexes of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (usually 4 to 10 s) and is why a long page or time base helps: on a short page you could see only one. The 20 uV/mm setting is used because the complexes are large (about 10 to 14 mm in several chains, 200 to 280 uV). Intervals of 0.5 to 1 s belong to the other periodic patterns. Mark each jerk with its time and describe the interval; name no cause.

taskFlow.title: A comatose patient
taskFlow.description: The 41-year-old is comatose, 7 uV/mm. A low-amplitude rhythm of about 9 Hz is present in all channels, taller in Fp1-F7, F3-C3, Fz-Cz and Cz-Pz (about 5 to 6 mm) than in P3-O1, T5-O1 and P4-O2 (about 3.5 mm). The rhythm is regular and does not change across the page.
taskFlow.question: What is the best next step for the record?
options: Give one loud sound, and if the tracing looks the same, note that no reactivity test was needed
Apply each protocol stimulus in turn, mark each time, and describe any change; record state and medications
Report a normal alpha rhythm, because the frequency is about 9 Hz and the page is regular
Call it alpha coma and name anoxic injury as the cause so the team can act quickly
taskFlow.explanation: A frontally predominant 9 Hz rhythm in a comatose patient that does not respond is the pattern described as alpha coma, which is unlike a normal posterior alpha that blocks with eye opening. Document reactivity by giving each protocol stimulus (for example voice, touch, then painful per protocol), mark each time and describe any change; also record state, medications and temperature if known. A normal posterior rhythm would be maximal posteriorly and block. Naming a cause is outside scope. A single stimulus is not the protocol, so a lack of change after one sound is not a complete reactivity test. Drug-induced beta is faster, about 13 to 30 Hz, and leaves a posterior rhythm intact, which is how you separate it.

starterCases.title: Tuberous sclerosis: spasms and tubers
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Clusters of head-drops and arm extensions; white skin patches noticed at birth

history.eventDescription: A 6-month-old has clusters of sudden head-drops and arm extensions on waking, and several pale (hypomelanotic) skin patches. A heart tumour was seen on a scan. Four years later she is seen again for staring and focal seizures. You record both studies. Your role is to describe, mark and compare the two sides; you never name the genetic cause.

eegSummary.background: Chaotic and slow in infancy; slow with focal spikes later

objectives: Describe hypsarrhythmia without naming a cause
Mark a spasm and the attenuation that follows
Describe a focal spike field with its times

taskFlow.title: The infant's awake record
taskFlow.description: The 6-month-old is awake, longitudinal, 20 uV/mm. The background is made of high-amplitude slow waves of irregular shape with spikes that change place and side from one moment to the next. No organized rhythm is present.
taskFlow.question: Which description should go in the report?
options: Chaotic high-amplitude slow activity with multifocal spikes and no organized background
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave over a normal background rhythm for age
Repeated bursts of activity separated by long flat stretches of suppression
A normal alpha rhythm of about 8 Hz that blocks when the eyes are opened
taskFlow.explanation: The page shows disorganized slow activity with multifocal spikes, which is hypsarrhythmia. Activity is present between spikes, so it is not burst suppression, and it is not 3 Hz spike-and-wave. An 8 Hz alpha rhythm is not expected at 6 months, and the infant is not following eye commands. Tuberous sclerosis is one cause of this pattern, but you describe only what you see.

taskFlow.title: A cluster of spasms
taskFlow.description: The infant has a spasm at 5.0 s. The chaotic activity flattens in all channels for about two seconds, with muscle artifact in the frontopolar channels, and then the chaotic pattern returns.
taskFlow.question: How should the spasm be documented?
options: Remove the section from the record because muscle artifact makes it unreadable
Mark 5.0 s, describe the attenuation and the muscle artifact, and note the clinical movement
State in the notes that the flattening proves infantile spasms and nothing else
Wake the infant and restart the recording so that the attenuation is not recorded
taskFlow.explanation: Infantile spasms are accompanied by a sudden attenuation of the background (an electrodecrement), often with muscle artifact, so you mark the time and describe both the EEG change and the movement you saw. Removing the section loses the event, naming the diagnosis is the reader's role, and restarting loses the information the study was made to capture.

taskFlow.title: Four years later
taskFlow.description: The child is now 5 years old and awake, longitudinal, 10 uV/mm. Sharp transients repeat at T6 at about 1.5, 3.2, 5.8 and 8.4 s, each with a slow wave, over a background of focal delta near T6. Two smaller spikes appear at F3 at about 4.4 and 7.1 s.
taskFlow.question: Which description is best?
options: Right posterior temporal spikes with focal slowing, plus left frontal spikes at 4.4 and 7.1 s
Left temporal spikes only, with a phase reversal at F7 in the longitudinal chain
Bilateral symmetric 3 Hz spike-and-wave with abrupt onset and abrupt offset
Generalized hypsarrhythmia, as at 6 months, repeating across both hemispheres
taskFlow.explanation: The page shows two separate foci: a right posterior temporal focus with focal delta (T5-O1 and T6-O2 in the longitudinal chain) and a smaller left frontal focus at F3. Tubers can lie in any lobe, so multifocal discharges are common. Hypsarrhythmia and 3 Hz spike-and-wave are different patterns, and the larger focus is on the right, not the left.

taskFlow.title: Planning the next study
taskFlow.description: The reader asks for a comparison with the earlier study and for sleep.
taskFlow.question: What is the best recording plan?
options: Use a higher sensitivity on the right than on the left so that the right-sided focus is clearer
Stop the study as soon as the first spike appears so the report is not complicated
Record wakefulness and sleep at the same sensitivity on both sides, and mark each spike location
Record only the first ten minutes awake, since the earlier study already showed the findings
taskFlow.explanation: Sleep activates spikes, equal sensitivity on both sides keeps asymmetry honest, and marking each location lets the reader compare studies. A short awake study will miss sleep findings, different sensitivities distort the comparison, and stopping early loses the data.

starterCases.title: Sturge-Weber, Angelman and NF2 in the lab
starterCases.chiefComplaint: A toddler with a port-wine stain, a child with frequent laughter and ataxia, and a teenager with hearing loss

history.eventDescription: In one clinic day you record a 2-year-old with a port-wine stain on the right forehead and a first seizure, a 5-year-old with ataxia, no speech and frequent laughing, and a 16-year-old with bilateral hearing loss and a family history of neurofibromatosis. You never name the cause; you describe, compare sides and adapt the test.

eegSummary.background: Asymmetric in one; rhythmic delta in one; normal in one

objectives: Compare amplitude on the two sides at one sensitivity
Describe a frontal rhythmic delta with numbers
Adapt a responsiveness test to hearing loss

taskFlow.title: A toddler with a port-wine stain
taskFlow.description: The 2-year-old is awake, longitudinal, 10 uV/mm. Rhythmic activity of about 7 Hz is clearly visible in the left channels (Fp1-F3, F3-C3, C3-P3, T5-O1). The right channels (Fp2-F4, F4-C4, T4-T6, T6-O2) show much lower activity.
taskFlow.question: Which description should you give?
options: Increased amplitude over the right hemisphere, with a normal left hemisphere
A generalized slowing with the same amplitude over both hemispheres at all times
Reduced amplitude and less rhythmic activity over the right hemisphere than the left, at the same sensitivity
Symmetric activity over both hemispheres, with the right side only slightly lower
taskFlow.explanation: The right side shows much less amplitude than the left on the same page and at the same sensitivity, which is attenuation on the side of the stain. Higher amplitude on the right is the opposite of what is seen, and the sides are clearly not symmetric. The same finding can be caused by other conditions, so you describe it and do not name the cause.

taskFlow.title: Electrodes on a skin lesion
taskFlow.description: The port-wine stain extends under the planned position of Fp2 and F8.
taskFlow.question: What is the best action?
options: Move the electrode to a position on the left that has clean skin
Abrade the skin firmly so that the impedance is as low as possible
Leave out the electrode and say nothing, so the montage is not changed
Prepare the skin gently, place the electrode, and note the lesion in the report
taskFlow.explanation: Skin over a vascular lesion needs gentle preparation to avoid injury or bleeding, and the report should say why the setup differs. Firm abrasion can cause harm, silent omission removes data without a record, and moving to the left breaks the 10-20 positions and the comparison between sides.

taskFlow.title: A child who laughs
taskFlow.description: The 5-year-old is awake, longitudinal, 10 uV/mm. A large rhythmic delta repeats across the whole page, about 5 waves each two seconds, largest in the frontal channels (Fp1-F3, Fp2-F4, Fp1-F7, Fp2-F8). Sharp transients are mixed with it at about 1.9, 4.4 and 7.3 s.
taskFlow.question: Which description fits the record?
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave with abrupt onset and offset at 4.4 s
Frontal-predominant rhythmic delta of about 2.5 Hz with sharp transients at 1.9, 4.4 and 7.3 s
Occipital rhythmic delta at 3 Hz that stops when the child opens the eyes
A 10 Hz posterior rhythm that blocks with eye opening and returns on eye closure
taskFlow.explanation: About 5 waves in 2 seconds is about 2.5 Hz, with frontal emphasis and sharp transients mixed in. This is the kind of record described in Angelman syndrome, but you only describe it and mark movement and laughing. Spike-and-wave at 3 Hz is a different pattern, and the rhythm does not stop with eye opening or look like alpha.

taskFlow.title: A teenager with hearing loss
taskFlow.description: The 16-year-old is awake, with a normal posterior rhythm. He has profound hearing loss from bilateral vestibular schwannomas, and the protocol includes a responsiveness test.
taskFlow.question: How do you test responsiveness?
options: Use only a louder voice, because responsiveness must be tested by sound
Use photic stimulation as the responsiveness test, since it is a visual stimulus
Omit the test, because a patient with hearing loss cannot take part
Use touch and visual stimuli as well as voice, and describe the response
taskFlow.explanation: Hearing loss can hide a response to voice, so you add touch and visual stimuli and describe what happened. A louder voice may still fail, omitting the test loses information, and photic stimulation is an activation procedure, not a test of responsiveness.

starterCases.title: Rett, lissencephaly and GLUT1 deficiency
starterCases.chiefComplaint: Regression with hand-wringing; a one-year-old with spasms; an infant with seizures and a small head

history.eventDescription: You record a 5-year-old girl who lost words and hand skills after 14 months and wrings her hands, a 1-year-old with spasms and severe delay, and an infant with a small head and morning seizures. You note the movements and the last meal, and you describe the findings without naming a gene.

eegSummary.background: Slowed, high-amplitude fast, and generalized spike-wave
eegSummary.epileptiform: Centrocentral spikes in sleep; generalized spike-wave

objectives: Describe centrocentral spikes in sleep
Separate stereotypy artifact from a seizure
Describe a high-amplitude fast rhythm in an infant
Record the time of the last meal

taskFlow.title: The girl in stage N2
taskFlow.description: The 5-year-old is in stage N2 sleep, longitudinal, 10 uV/mm. The background is slow. Sharp transients with a slow wave appear in the right central channels (F4-C4, C4-P4) at about 1.8, 4.9 and 8.0 s, and smaller ones in the left central channels at about 3.3 and 6.5 s.
taskFlow.question: Which description is best?
options: A normal sleep background with isolated vertex waves at 1.8, 4.9 and 8.0 s on both sides
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave bursts lasting several seconds at each marked time
Right temporal spikes with a phase reversal at F8 and no spikes in the left hemisphere
A slowed background with right central spikes at 1.8, 4.9 and 8.0 s and left central spikes at 3.3 and 6.5 s
taskFlow.explanation: Sharp transients with a slow wave over the central regions, on both sides, are spikes. The vertex waves of sleep are symmetric and appear at Cz, and there is no 3 Hz burst here. The spikes are central, not temporal, and they occur on both sides. This pattern, a slow background with central spikes in sleep, is described in Rett syndrome, but you describe it and leave the diagnosis to the reader.

taskFlow.title: Hand-wringing
taskFlow.description: Between sleep stages she is awake and wrings her hands. The reader later asks how a technologist keeps rhythmic hand movement from being mistaken for a seizure.
taskFlow.question: How should the hand movements be documented?
options: State in the notes that the child has Rett syndrome because of the hand movements
Mark the time, describe the movement and its rate, and note whether the rhythm follows it
Remove it from the record, because anything caused by movement has no value to the reader
Mark it as a generalized seizure, since rhythmic activity in many channels is ictal
taskFlow.explanation: Rhythmic hand stereotypies can produce rhythmic artifact that resembles a seizure. Marking the time and describing the movement lets the reader see whether the rhythm follows it. Calling every rhythm a seizure ignores that clue, removing it hides the information, and naming the syndrome is not your role.

taskFlow.title: The infant with spasms
taskFlow.description: The 1-year-old is awake, 20 uV/mm. A fast rhythm of about 14 Hz at a very large amplitude is present across the page. It is largest in the parasagittal chains (Fp1-F3, F3-C3, C3-P3, P3-O1) and much smaller in the temporal chains.
taskFlow.question: What should be reported?
options: Generalized high-amplitude fast activity of about 14 Hz, with its distribution and the medication history
Muscle artifact, since high-frequency activity in an infant is always muscle
Normal beta activity, since 14 Hz is a normal frequency for a one-year-old
A generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern at a high amplitude
taskFlow.explanation: A fast rhythm of this size in an infant is not normal beta, which is much smaller. It is regular and spread widely, so it does not look like muscle, and it is not 3 Hz spike-and-wave. This pattern appears in lissencephaly, but the technologist describes the frequency, amplitude and distribution and records the drug history.

taskFlow.title: The infant with a small head
taskFlow.description: An infant with a small head and morning seizures shows bursts of generalized spike-and-wave at about 3 Hz in this recording. His parents say the bursts and the seizures seem worse before the first feed.
taskFlow.question: What should you record in the report?
options: A statement that the spike-wave proves a glucose transport disorder
The time of the last feed and the times of the bursts, so the reader can compare
A note to withhold the next feed until the bursts stop
Nothing about feeding, since a feed cannot change the EEG
taskFlow.explanation: In GLUT1 deficiency, discharges can increase when fasting and decrease after a meal, so the time of the last feed helps the reader. A feed can change the EEG in this condition, you do not withhold feeding without an order, and naming a diagnosis is not your role.
